News.title: American Idol pastor Caleb Flynn cries in court as he is found GUILTY in murder of wife shot dead while she slept
News.content:
Next

FORMER American Idol contestant Caleb Flynn has been found guilty of murdering his wife.

Prosecutors said Flynn, 40, killed his wife Ashley while she was asleep on February 16, stressing that he shot her twice in the back of the head before attempting to make the death look like the result of a home invasion.



Flynn consistently denied murdering Ashley, who was a school teacher and volleyball coach.

But on Tuesday, Flynn was led out of the courtroom in handcuffs after jurors returned guilty verdicts on all nine counts – including aggravated murder – following just over two hours of deliberation.



The verdict appeared to overwhelm him emotionally, as he cried and repeatedly wiped his pained face.

A sentence of life behind bars without the possibility of parole awaits him.

Read more on Caleb Flynn GUN HORROR American Idol star holds back tears after 'killing wife & staging home invasion'

During closing arguments, Matthew C. Joseph, an assistant prosecutor with the Miami County Prosecuting Attorney’s Office in Troy, Ohio, argued that the evidence showed Flynn’s version of events was entirely fabricated.

Damning texts messages between Flynn and his ex-mistress, Alleigha Botner, shocked the courtroom.

In a slew of text messages, Flynn told Botner that he had stayed awake until 4am thinking about “ways to kill her and not go to jail.”

Botner responded that she did not want Ashley killed.



“I’m not asking that you take her life,” she wrote, according to the evidence, while adding that making the divorce happen would “change everything.”

Flynn answered: “I’ll work on getting rid of her. Until then, I love you.”

According to Flynn’s account to police, he was sleeping in a separate room with the couple’s daughters when he heard a gunshot.

He said he later found Ashley dead.

The texts were presented as evidence of Flynn’s state of mind and his relationship with his wife.



Flynn’s defense team has disputed the prosecution’s case, arguing that investigators zeroed in on him early in the investigation.

They also maintained that his affair with Botner drew disproportionate attention and influenced how authorities viewed the evidence against him.

Flynn appeared on Season 12 of American Idol in 2013. He performed during the televised auditions in Chicago but did not advance to the main competition.



Flynn’s story began to unravel after his wife, Ashley, was found fatally shot inside their Ohio home.

He had called police early that morning, claiming an intruder had entered the house and shot her. Flynn told investigators he was in his daughters’ bedroom when he heard a gunshot.

He also said he later discovered a door leading toward the garage standing open.

But investigators found no evidence that anyone had fled the property. They also determined that damage around the garage-side door did not appear consistent with a typical forced entry, according to CNN.

Inside Flynn’s truck, officers noticed that the center console was open—the same location where Flynn said he kept his handgun.



As investigators continued questioning him, Flynn insisted that there had been no serious problems in his marriage “whatsoever.”

That account became more complicated when authorities uncovered his relationship with Alleigha Botner.

According to testimony, Flynn and Botner had been involved in an affair for approximately 18 months. Their relationship generated an enormous digital trail: jurors were told the pair exchanged more than 100,000 messages.

Those communications would later become a major part of the prosecution’s case.

In one message from September 2025, Flynn described everything he was willing to risk to stay with Botner, including his daughters, his quarter-million-dollar salary, his home, his position at a church, and the possibility of public humiliation.



Botner said she met Flynn at 21 while interning at Christian Life Center in Dayton, where he served as a music pastor.

She later became a worship leader at the church.

Botner, meanwhile, repeatedly pushed Flynn to leave Ashley.

“Until she’s gone, I’m gone,” she wrote in one exchange, according to evidence presented at trial.

Botner testified that she met Flynn in 2022 at Christian Life Center in Dayton.



She was 20 and working as an intern at the time, while Flynn was in his mid-30s. Their relationship eventually became romantic in early 2024.

Prosecutors have focused particular attention on their conversations immediately before Ashley’s death.

The night before the shooting, Botner sent Flynn information concerning divorce, child custody, deleting messages and ways Ashley could potentially prove he was unfaithful.

Then, shortly before midnight, Flynn messaged her:

“Good night, tomorrow’s a big day. I’ve got to get to bed. I choose you, I’m about to be free.”



Hours later, Ashley was dead.

Botner testified that the shooting immediately raised questions for her. She said she initially messaged Flynn asking whether he had been involved, but deleted the message because she feared investigators might search his phone and discover their affair.

During closing arguments, Flynn’s lawyer, Patrick Mulligan, argued that infidelity should not be interpreted as evidence of murder.

Mulligan also told jurors the prosecution had failed to present concrete evidence, saying that “connecting a couple of meaningless dots doesn’t solve the case.”

The alleged home invasion also made her suspicious because of its timing.



Botner told the jury that she could not shake the coincidence: “In my mind, it just seemed like too much of a coincidence that, the day he’s divorcing her, she’s just dead all of a sudden.”

News.title: Grieving mum fears early release of 700 inmates will cost more lives after her son was stabbed to death by a robber
News.content:
Next

A MOTHER whose son was stabbed to death by a robber released on licence fears more families will lose loved ones because of the Government’s early release scheme.

Donna Thompson’s son Shane, 32, was murdered by Robert Goodwin, who had left jail two weeks earlier.



About 700 inmates will be freed tomorrow, many on tags despite the probation watchdog warning the devices give a false sense of assurance.

Donna, 56, co-founded Voice (Victims Oversight In Criminal Enforcement) and is in touch with 25 families whose loved ones were killed by monitored lags.



She said: “They’re letting people out too early with not the right resources.

“When they come out, there’s no drug rehabilitation, probation isn’t knocking on the door for surprise visits.

“If they are on tag, if it’s tampered with, the police should be round.”

Builder Shane was found with 17 stab wounds in Birmingham in 2021.

He had given Goodwin a job as a helping hand.

Goodwin had previously cut off his ankle tag and skipped a probation appointment.



Despite PM Andy Burnham barring killers and rapists from early release, Donna fears anyone with a history of violence could be a risk.

As Manchester mayor last year, Mr Burnham promised to back her group “all the way”.

Donna is now calling for him to stay true to his word.



She added: “When you have that police officer knock on the door, that is the end of your life. I don’t want that to happen to any other families. So the Government needs to sort this out. It doesn’t matter how much money they’re going to put into it.

“It’s people’s lives, this is actual life and death.”

The Ministry of Justice said: “This was a horrific crime and our thoughts remain with Shane’s loved ones.

“The offender is now rightly back behind bars. This Government is investing a record £700million in the probation service with the toughest-ever controls on offenders.”

News.title: Slippery Andy Burnham would rather flog us ‘hope’ than tackle UK’s real problems – we’ve heard it all before
News.content:
Next

PM Andy Burnham has a Club biscuit approach to politics.

He nibbles the sweet stuff around the edges that pleases the party faithful, but has yet to bite into the hard centre ground of politics where true leaders dare to go.



Tackling the ruinous welfare bill and NHS waste, lowering spending, stopping the small boats, growth incentives for business . . . the tricky stuff that requires a PM to make decisions that might actually upset people — including his own side.

Instead, his speech was full of socialist crowd-pleasers and did little for economic growth.

There’s no denying his words were well delivered, came from the heart and had a noble keynote promise — an NHS-style National Care Service.



But he’s not the PM of Cloud Cuckoo Land, he’s running UK PLC and the detail on how it’s all going to be paid for was lacking.

“A galaxy of progressive cliches with no substance or detail” said one caller to LBC radio, while another likened it to a scientology convention.

It felt like a wasted opportunity for him to show substance rather than just the style we’ve become accustomed to since he got the top job.

The word-salad guff about “growth in every postcode” (no sign yet) and “hope in every heart” — a sugary phrase that belongs on an embroidered ­cushion in TK Maxx, not in the serious business of politics.

He also goes jogging a lot, presumably to demonstrate the energy behind that other lame political cliché: “Getting things done”.



And now, as large swathes of the country fret about paying their mortgages and the looming prospect of winter fuel bills, we have the ­Labour Party conference slogan of “hope again”.

Or should that be “hope again” followed by a collective deep sigh from the electorate.

We’ve been here before, haven’t we?

Make Britain Great Again (Con, 1950), You Know Labour Government Works (1966), New Labour, New Life For Britain (1996), Get Brexit Done (Con, 2019), and, God help us, Not Flash, Just Gordon (Lab 2007).

Now, yawn, Burnham is flogging “hope” just two years after Sir Keir Starmer sold us “change”.



You can’t run a country on the hope of what might happen in 2030. We need someone to seize the gearstick and start driving change now, or much worse is to come.

British hedge-fund billionaire Chris Rokos paid a reported £330million in tax in a single year before moving abroad — presumably because he’s sick of being the lemon that constantly gets squeezed.

This week, Peter Hargreaves, a billionaire investor who started his business from his Bristol bedroom in 1981, said we can’t afford to keep losing our “big taxpayers”.



He told the FT: “This country is never, ever coming back. It’s ­finished.

“There are so many people on the public purse that it would be very difficult for any government to change that.”

Indeed. You can’t fund an ever-expanding state with the taxes of people who no longer live here, and fixing that means making difficult decisions on tax, welfare and spending.

It takes bottle to upset Labour MPs, unions and activists, and one suspects Burnham is paralysed by his need to be Mr Nice Guy.

But being PM isn’t a customer relations job.



You can shake every hand from Manchester to Margate, but if your policies don’t make those people better off, what’s the point?

The “No.10” North scenario doesn’t help either, because he and his team spend a lot of time in transit and are hard to pin down.

As for Chequers, the palatial country retreat that Prime Ministers since Lloyd George have enjoyed the use of, he doesn’t seem to be using it.

A government source said: “He is barely ever there because he likes to spend weekends at home in Manchester. But he’s thinking of holding a New Year’s Eve party there.”

Great. We’ll look forward to it.



In the meantime, unless he gets his teeth into the hard stuff, voters may have a rather less uplifting two-word slogan for him by the next party conference.

Jog on.

GRIEF HAS NO LIMIT TWO years on from the death of her husband Dave Myers – aka one of the Hairy Bikers – his wife Liliana has been subjected to comments suggesting she should “get on with her life” and “stop crying all over Facebook”. How callous. Grief doesn’t come with a time limit, and nor should it. It can hit you on birthdays, Christmas, other special events, or sometimes just a moment in a day that reminds you of a loved one lost. Liliana says her posts are “for people living through loss . . . and, for those people I will keep on writing”. Quite right too. And if you’re one of those bothered by her emotional posts, there’s a simple solution. Don’t watch.

Mum’s the word on Diana? Let Harry know

PRINCE William has reportedly rejected the offer to make a film to mark the 30th anniversary of his mother’s death next year.

Ten years ago, he and his brother Harry collaborated on two documentaries about Princess Diana, and friends of William have said he considers them to be a “final catharsis” he does not wish to revisit, preferring to mark it privately.



At a screening for one of the 20th anniversary documentaries, William told guests that he and Harry considered it to be their last word on Diana and “we won’t speak as openly about her again”.

Hmmm, something tells me his estranged brother hasn’t got that memo.

PILATES PUFFED THE Duchess of Sussex has reportedly signed up for reformer Pilates classes at swanky members’ club Soho Farmhouse in the Cotswolds. A source said it was a great way for her to meet new friends in the area. Seriously? I have attended just two reformer Pilates sessions of late and, on both occasions, if anyone had tried to talk to me afterwards they’d have had to wait at least an hour before I could summon the breath to utter a single word.

CODES TO END SPYING

TEN employees have been suspended by an NHS Trust after they accessed the medical records of Noah Woods without permission.

Noah, three, from Brantham in Suffolk, drowned in a nearby pond after running away from a relative who had taken him to a local playground.



This latest scandal follows that of 11 members of NHS staff being fired for looking at the records of Barnaby Webber and Grace O’Malley-Kumar who were killed by Valdo Calocane in Nottingham, and up to 40 staff “inappropriately” looked at the confidential medical details of the child seriously injured after being pushed into the crocodile pit at a zoo in Cambridgeshire earlier this year.

If I have to sign an important document online, it’s commonplace for it to be protected by an access code given only to me or anyone else who needs to know.

So it beggars belief that people’s medical records aren’t kept safe under the same system.

TAX NOT SO FAB A VOLUNTARY £1 levy on the cost of tickets for large concerts and festivals was designed to help Britain’s struggling grassroots music venues. But guess who’s been the “single biggest beneficiary” of the scheme?

HMRC has taken more than £1million in tax. Altogether now, courtesy of The Beatles, who once played the small venues before they hit the big time . . . “If you try to sit, I’ll tax your seat, if you get too cold, I’ll tax the heat, if you take a walk, I’ll tax your feet.”

A NEW study says that if you greet someone you don’t know with a hug, they will like you better and be more inclined to look at your holiday photos.

Niche, but I digress.



I’ve never been a fan of hugging people I don’t know and now, knowing that if I did they might show me their holiday photos, I never will.

News.title: Huge TikTok celebrity & wannabe pop star who lived life of luxury arrested alongside mother in money laundering probe
News.content:
Next

A HUGE TikTok celebrity and wannabe pop star who flaunted a life of cash and luxury has been arrested alongside her mum in a £19.5million money-laundering probe.

Michelle Jamileth Macías Peñarrieta, 23, known to her army of followers as Queen Michelle, was dramatically detained in Colombia on Sunday.



The influencer is the daughter of notorious gang boss José Adolfo Macías Villamar – better known as Fito – the feared leader of Ecuadorian crime group Los Choneros.

Michelle was seized alongside her mum, Inda Mariela Peñarrieta Tuárez, at a ranch in Sabana de Torres, Santander.



The pair were wanted by Ecuadorian authorities under Interpol Red Notices over the sprawling “Blanqueo Fito” money-laundering investigation.

Authorities are probing more than $25.8million (£19.5million) in financial movements allegedly linked to Fito’s criminal empire.



Michelle had meanwhile carved out a glitzy online persona as Queen Michelle, amassing a staggering 65million-plus TikTok followers with singing, dancing and viral videos.

She also launched a music career and released tracks linked to her infamous father.



In 2023, Michelle appeared in El Corrido del León, a song dedicated to Fito.

That same year she released F La Leyenda, a corrido tumbado accompanied by a flashy music video showing her on a ranch surrounded by horses and luxury vehicles.

Other posts associated with her accounts have shown eye-watering stacks of cash, expensive vehicles and luxury goods.

One clip which resurfaced following her arrest appears to show a huge haul of banknotes.

But behind the glamorous social-media image, Ecuadorian investigators allege Michelle and her mother were involved in laundering dirty money through a web of companies.



A judge indicted 17 people in the case in March, with investigators scrutinising at least four firms allegedly used to give illicit funds a veneer of legitimacy.

The probe is examining money movements, assets and businesses allegedly connected to Fito and his associates.

Authorities also allege Michelle and her mum attempted to forge alliances with Colombian criminal organisations for activities linked to arms trafficking, drug trafficking and money laundering.



The pair had reportedly been holed up at the Sabana de Torres ranch for around four months after previously spending time in Bucaramanga and Medellín.

A surveillance operation eventually tracked them down before Colombian forces swooped.

The huge cross-border operation involved Colombia’s Military Gaula, the DIJIN criminal investigation directorate and prosecutors, alongside the FBI and Ecuadorian police.

Ecuadorian President Daniel Noboa hailed the arrests, writing: “This is how it’s done, Abelardo: working together and delivering results. We arrested them in Colombia, and they will face justice in Ecuador.”

He claimed the women were facing trial over money laundering for Los Choneros and alleged the cash was used to “buy weapons, pay hitmen and fund extortion”.



Michelle’s father Fito rose to become the notorious leader of Los Choneros, one of Ecuador’s most powerful criminal organisations.

He was extradited to the United States last year to face drug-trafficking charges.

It is not the first time his daughter’s name has been thrust into the headlines.



Michelle was kidnapped in the Ecuadorian city of Manta in November 2021 when she was just 19.

She and another young woman were reportedly snatched as they left a cosmetology salon, sparking a frantic four-day hunt.

Michelle was eventually freed by Ecuador’s then Anti-Kidnapping and Extortion Unit on November 21.

Five years later, the influencer is now herself at the centre of a major international criminal investigation.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Michelle and her mother are expected to be returned to Ecuador.



Officials have said they will be held at La Roca, the notorious maximum-security prison in Guayaquil, as the mammoth money-laundering case continues.

News.title: TikTok boat migrant who called for ‘death to Jews’ living in taxpayer funded 3-bed as Home Office bids to boot him out
News.content:
Next

A HAMAS fanatic who called for “the slaughter of Jews” on TikTok is living in a taxpayer-funded three-bed UK semi, boasting: “I want to stay here.”

Abu Wadee livestreamed his arrival on a small boat and has posted antisemitic threats online as well as pictures posing with AK-47s.



But his life in Britain could soon come to an end after Home Office officials confirmed they are working to remove him from the country.

Wadee, also known as Abu Wadei and by his full name Mosab Abdulkarim al-Gassas, arrived on the Kent coast in March 2025 after paying £1,300 for a dinghy crossing.



The Palestinian had previously unsuccessfully applied for asylum in Greece, Germany and Belgium before reaching Britain.

He was jailed for nine months for immigration offences that May but was later released on an ankle tag after serving around 40 per cent of his sentence under the Government’s early release scheme.



Wadee, 34, now shares a £157,000 house in Corby, Northamptonshire, with three other migrants.

He was said to have been a member of Gaza’s “Tyre-Burning Unit”, a militant group known for hurling firebombs at Israeli forces.

But Wadee now insists he has abandoned his pro-Hamas views and says he has a “very nice” Jewish friend.

He told the Northamptonshire Telegraph he “loved” Corby and had no desire to leave now he was no longer “under Hamas rule”.



A taxi arrived to collect Wadee from the property following the revelations, but the driver was turned away by a housing officer.

One neighbour, who did not want to be named, said she was “appalled” he was living on the street.

She said: “A lovely family lived there a few years ago. I still speak to them.



“They were asked to move out and it became a house in multiple occupation.

“The other people staying have been very nice. I believe that we should help people from war-torn countries and welcome them here.

“But to say death to Jewish people? I am appalled.

“That is not welcome here. Not in this country, or this street.”

Another resident said learning Wadee lived on her street was “scary” and she feared he could influence her son or other youngsters.



Wadee has also been accused of earning money from videos he posts online.

In May, he is believed to have uploaded a clip showing his ankle tag while chanting the Arabic phrase: “A strange world, full of injustice after injustice.”

The video racked up more than one million views.



Last month, he is believed to have posted footage of himself riding a bike which helped identify his whereabouts.

Other TikTok clips have shown him encouraging youngsters to shout “Free Palestine”.

His online activity was investigated by the Campaign Against Antisemitism last year.

The group said it found that in 2024 he had posted calls for Allah to “kill all Jews” and “destroy them, scatter them completely”.

It said Wadee had been identified using facial recognition technology before his details were passed to the Home Office.



A spokesperson said: “Hiding behind undisclosed ethnic friends to deflect accusations of racism or extremism is ridiculous at the best of times, and even more so for someone with Abu Wadee’s record.

“After we threatened to privately prosecute him he was charged with illegally entering the UK.

“We thought the authorities might be trusted to take it from there, but when we wrote to the CPS calling for Wadee to be charged with terrorism offences they refused.

“So now he’s here earning money online. Companies like TikTok have a responsibility to monitor accounts run by individuals who breach their policies.”



The group has previously argued that Wadee’s ability to continue posting online despite previous bans makes a “mockery” of Home Office policies.

It also questioned why he remained in Britain following his immigration conviction.

Local Labour MP Lee Barron said he was “appalled” by Wadee’s presence in Corby and vowed to contact the Home Secretary seeking his immediate deportation.

He said: “We have done this before in Corby and we’ll do it again.”



Home Office officials confirmed they are actively working to remove Wadee from the country.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

A Government spokesman said: “Any foreign national who receives a prison sentence in the UK is referred for deportation at the earliest opportunity and will be barred from ever returning.

“Over 11,000 foreign criminals have been returned or deported since the election.”

News.title: Man dies after explosion on residential street – as locals describe hearing ‘massive bang’ from miles away
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

DEATH PROBE Man dies after explosion on residential street – as locals describe hearing ‘massive bang’ from miles away







Next

A MAN has been killed in an explosion on a residential street, after locals reported hearing a “massive bang” from the area.

Emergency services were called to the row of terraces on Clifton Mount in Rotherham, South Yorkshire, at 1.20pm today.

A man was sadly pronounced dead at the scene and an investigation has been launched into the cause of the explosion.

Cops temporarily cordoned off the area before confirming there was no further risk to the public and reopening the street.





One local said: “I was walking through Clifton Park, sounded like a bomb had gone off”.

Another reported hearing a “massive bang” from over a kilometre away at the McDonald’s in Rotherham.

One resident said he heard a loud noise thinking it was a “shooting”.

He told the BBC: “I’m just shocked, bemused.”

“I can’t believe what’s happened.”

A Tactical Support Group van was spotted at the site, alongside eight police cars.

South Yorkshire Police told the Rotherham Advertiser: “At 1.18pm today we were alerted by the fire service of reports of an explosion on Clifton Mount, in Rotherham.

“Emergency services attended and a man was sadly found deceased.



“In collaboration with South Yorkshire Fire and Rescue Services, enquiries are ongoing to confirm the cause of the explosion.

“Initial enquiries indicate that there is no risk to the wider community. Clifton Mount was closed but has since been reopened.”

Cadent Gas told the BBC that its role has been to “support emergency services” on site following the “tragic” loss of life.

It added that the explosion was “not related” to their gas network.

News.title: Mystery as £16million of cocaine vanishes from court after it’s swapped for FLOUR in long-running drug trial
News.content:
Next

COCAINE worth £16 million has been stolen from the evidence room of a Fiji court house – and replaced with flour.

Seven out of 39 bars vanished from the High Court in Suva, the capital of the Pacific island nation, while the rest were filled with powder for baked goods.

Local media warned this is yet another apparent example of the internal corruption that has plagued Fiji’s authorities.

Justice Minister Siromi Turaga vowed that those responsible for the theft would face the full ⁠force of the law.





“It’s shocking … no one will be spared,” he told news outlet Fiji One, adding it was not the first such instance.

Fiji Police issued a statement on Tuesday afternoon confirming “forensic tests” of the drugs had come back negative.

“The exhibits were all tampered with, and the investigation is focused on those directly charged with the management of the exhibits at the High Court Registry,” the statement said.

“A person of interest allegedly involved is currently overseas and will be questioned.”

The drugs were seized from Fiji-Canadian national Joshua Aziz Rahman in 2019 and stored ‌at the court as evidence.

He was charged with possession of 39.5 kg of cocaine, which were found at his Caubati home, and sentenced to 23 years in prison

But Rahman later appealed the verdict and walked free in February 2026.

Fiji Police Assistant Commissioner Mesake Waqa told ABC earlier this year that the force was “not a corrupt institution”.



He added: “We have officers who have crossed the line, and we have been transparent about it.

“In every case that is reported to us, we will investigate it.”

Around £2 billion worth of drugs were seized in the country between 2022 and 2025, according to data from the People’s Alliance Party.

Cases involving ‌drugs such as methamphetamine and ⁠cocaine have surged in Fiji since 2018.

Drug trafficking in other countries of the Pacific region has also been observed, but at considerably lower levels than.iji.

News.title: Burnham vows to end existing pension triple lock in 2030 to help fund care
News.content:
Before turning to the pension triple lock changes, Burnham accepted he may "pay a political price" by trying to make the reforms but argued "someone has to go through the pain barrier and rip the plaster off".

The triple lock was introduced in 2010 by the coalition government and designed to ensure the value of the state pension was not overtaken by the increase in the cost of living or the incomes of working people.

It means the state pension rates rise every April by either inflation, earnings growth or 2.5% - whichever is the highest.

Burnham said this will stay in place until 2030, at which point he would like to "adjust it".

He said: "The state pension will continue to rise every year at least by prices or 2.5%. And it will hold its value relative to earnings over time so that pensioners will always share in the rising prosperity of the nation.

"But this change will generate significant savings which we will use to build up our national care service.

"Some may not realise it but older people with nothing more than the state pension, or only a little more, can find themselves paying care changes today from that small income. Under my plan, this will no longer happen."

Officials have suggested the change could save Â£15bn a year by 2040.

Jonathan Cribb, deputy director at the Institute for Fiscal Studies, said savings "are likely to be relatively small in the first few years, but rise substantially over time".

He also said "we should not expect this reform to save enough that it could fund universal social care in the next parliament".

Sharon Graham, general secretary of the Unite union, told the BBC she believed the government should have "pulled another lever", such as a wealth tax, rather than making changes to the triple lock.

The political backlash was immediate.

Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch said "more tax rises are inevitable" under Labour's plan, while Reform UK's Nigel Farage accused the PM of "launching an offensive against our elderly".

Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said families "cannot wait until after another election and it can't be funded from the pockets of our poorest pensioners".

News.title: Chris Mason: Burnham delivers deeply political speech with a personal core
News.content:
What stood out in this speech was its breadth. His pitch could, very broadly, be divided into the short term - what he hopes to achieve before a general election; and the long term - the prospectus he is beginning to assemble to put to the country when polling day comes around inside the next three years.

The biggest ideas have the longest timeframe and, perhaps, the greatest need for a lengthy debate in their gestation.

Take the headline grabber: revamping social care in England. Previous attempts to do so, by both Labour and the Conservatives, haven't survived the intensity of a general election campaign, having been announced close to an election.

The aim of Burnham's plan is to seed a conversation now about what a new system might look like â the idea being that the argument is won in advance.

Let's see. The debate is only just beginning.

The plan to fund this by making increases in the state pension from 2030 less generous than they are now was more detailed than some expected at this stage.

The triple lock means the state pension currently increases annually in line with inflation, average wage growth or 2.5%, whichever is highest.

But from April 2030, if Labour win the next election, the annual earnings link will be dropped. It would, Labour figures say, be increased further if needed, to ensure that it stays above 30% of the full time average wage.

Knowing they would face blunt criticism about binning the existing triple lock â note the reaction of the Unite union and Labour's political rivals â it would appear the prime minister was keen to offer as much of what he hopes will be reassuring detail to many.

Also going into the next Labour manifesto, he said, a change in the Westminster voting system and â after a review to come â the idea of a closer relationship with the European Union.

How much closer, with what trade offs and prompting what reaction, we don't yet know.

And from the longer term stuff to the here and now â including housing reform in England, more public control of the water industry and the electricity grid.

There was an energy and sense of urgency to Burnham's pitch and without question he has created a battalion of dividing lines with Labour's political opponents which are likely to dominate the debate ahead.

His cabinet and many in his party are relishing the battle of ideas the prime minister has set up and is enthusiastically leaning into.

It was noteworthy that beyond a broad reference to Labour's opponents on the Right, the party's rivals didn't get a mention in a speech lasting more than an hour.

The question is: does he and his government have the capacity to deliver?

And do they have the capacity to convince you, the voter, they have a vision you regard as coherent, appealing and affordable?

You hardly need reminding of the backdrop that contributed to thwarting many of his recent, many predecessors: a persistently sclerotic economy and a persistently turbulent international picture, for starters.

Neither will make turning all of this into a reality straightforward.

News.title: Man City guilty of 'sham' contracts and misleading accounts
News.content:
Manchester City arranged "sham contracts" with a number of its commercial partners as part of a scheme to disguise secret funding of more than Â£830m, the Premier League says.

The League confirmed that City have been found guilty of all charges related to breaches of Premier League financial rules between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons.

An independent commission found that, during that time period, the club arranged the "sham contracts" as well as "relying on sham agreements to artificially inflate the club's revenues and reduce its costs".

The club continues to deny any wrongdoing and have until 2 October to submit an appeal.

News broke last week that City had been found guilty of breaking the majority of the 115 financial rules they were accused of breaching, but on Tuesday the Premier League published a redacted version of the commission's report.

The commission's report said the charges "concerned well over 100 alleged individual breaches of Premier League Rules across four broad charge categories".

It also found the club guilty of all charges except one relating to non-cooperation with the Premier League investigation and said that "a number of important Club witnesses gave false evidence in key respects and that some knowingly gave untrue and dishonest evidence".

The sham commercial deals were described as being part of a "disguised funding scheme" to the scale of Â£830.69m.

City recorded Â£360m in sponsor fees in the three seasons they won the Premier League - 2011-12, 2013-14, and 2017-18. Only Â£43m of it was legitimate - the rest came from their owners and was disguised.

"The relevant sponsorship agreements were found to be shams, or at minimum did not reflect their economic substance," the commission said.

It also describes "deliberate or reckless conduct intended to circumvent the Premier League rules" and that the "sham" scheme devised by City allowed the club "to avoid recording what would otherwise have been the largest single-season loss in Premier League history in 2009-10".

The commission highlighted the scale of evidence it had to consider by pointing out that the index alone ran to more than 750 pages, while the core bundle of documents "ran to many tens of thousands of pages".

City are owned by the Abu Dhabi United Group, who took over the club in 2008 and are referred to as "ADUG" in the commission's report.

News.title: 'Quantity of petrol' but no explosives found in three vehicles near RAF Fairford
News.content:
A quantity of petrol but no explosive devices were found during searches of the three vans near RAF Fairford in the west of England, counter-terror police have said.

Five men were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences and later terrorism offences after the vehicles were spotted in the early hours of Sunday, sparking a major security incident around the base which is operated by the US military.

They were released on bail the following day in what police described as an "investigative decision" which was "grounded in experience and strategy".

It comes after US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said it was clear a "foreign actor" had been involved, without providing evidence.

Police were alerted to "three suspicious vehicles" in Whelford, a village which lies directly east of the base, by a member of the public in the early hours of Sunday morning.

The woman who called 999 told the BBC it was "pure luck" she had spotted them, having arrived home to find the road blocked and a "large group of hooded and masked men".

"I believe that my 999 call foiled whatever plans they had," she said.

A bomb disposal team arrived on scene shortly afterwards and a 400m (1,312ft) cordon was put in place.

But Laurence Taylor, head of Counter Terrorism Policing, told reporters on Tuesday that the police response that morning was due to "a range of information".

Police cordons near the base are expected to be completely lifted on Wednesday, while residents from the 85 homes evacuated on Sunday have been allowed to return to their properties.

The five men are all UK nationals aged between 23 and 25. Four of them live in Westminster and one in Camden, and searches of their homes are now complete.

Assistant Commissioner Taylor previously said their bail was "subject to stringent conditions on their movement and contact with others" as they remained under investigation.

"The safety of the public is at the forefront of our investigative decision-making, and this was certainly the case yesterday," he said on Tuesday.

"I understand why this development was surprising to some, but I would like to reiterate that this is an investigative decision and one which is grounded in experience and strategy."

It comes a day after US President Donald Trump said he would not have let the five men out on bail and that he was "surprised" they had been released.

News.title: How did the RAF Fairford incident go from 'suspected bomb plot' to police bail?
News.content:
On Sunday morning, the world was watching as drama unfolded in the village of Whelford.

Before sunrise, residents were called from their beds and told to evacuate as a huge police operation unfolded in the village, which is next door to RAF Fairford, a base used by the US Air Force.

One villager managed to take a picture of five men sitting on the ground, stripped to the waist, handcuffed and under armed guard.

They were arrested for offences under the Explosives Act. But now counter-terrorism detectives say no explosives were found in their three vans, only an "accelerant" - petrol.

What some newspapers called a "suspected bomb plot" ended in the suspects being bailed. So what was going on?

The US President Donald Trump asserted that the men had been trying to do "big damage" to the base. "We had them under view for a long time, and we got them," he declared.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said: "What could have happened in the UK over the weekend is a very serious situation. It's one that clearly involved the hands of a foreign actor."

But in a veiled criticism of that, the head Counter Terrorism Policing in the UK Laurence Taylor said that the worry that a lot of people had been experiencing had been "heightened by the international commentary".

He also defended his detectives' decision to give the suspects police bail with "very strict conditions". This had been criticised by President Trump.

Taylor said it was an "investigative decision and one which is grounded in experience and strategy".

This suggests there were good tactical reasons for releasing the men on bail, perhaps to encourage their cooperation.

News.title: Three teenagers die after car enters River Wear
News.content:
Three teenagers have died after a car entered the River Wear.

Northumbria Police said just before 13:30 BST a black Audi A3 came off the road at Panns Bank near Wearmouth Bridge, in Sunderland, and entered the water.

Four people were in the car at the time and a 17-year-old boy managed to reach safety. He is currently in hospital with non-serious injuries, and has subsequently been arrested in connection with the incident, the force said.

The bodies of two teenage boys and a teenage girl have been recovered from the water.

No other vehicles are believed to have been involved.

Ch Supt Scott Cowie, area commander for Sunderland, said it was "a truly tragic incident".

"Our thoughts are with their families, friends and all those impacted by what has happened," he said.

He added the investigation was at an early stage and the force was working to establish the circumstances.

News.title: Watch: US journalist Evan Gershkovich describes being detained by Russian agents
News.content:
US journalist Evan Gershkovich has told the BBC's Today programme about the 16 months when he was detained in Russia.

In his first UK broadcast interview, the Wall Street Journal correspondent said he realised he had been "lured into a trap" when masked men surrounded him at a restaurant in March 2023, and arrested him.

He was later sentenced to 16 years on espionage charges, but released in 2024 as part of a high-profile prisoner exchange.

He and his employer have always maintained that the charges were false, and following his arrest, then-US President Joe Biden said he had "no higher priority" than bringing Gershkovich home.

Read more on this story.

News.title: Prince William and Catherine's surprise visit to Kevin Sinfield's charity run
News.content:
The Prince and Princess of Wales made a surprise visit to support rugby league star Sir Kevin Sinfield, on the third day of his endurance challenge to raise funds for Motor Neurone Disease (MND) charities.

"What you're doing is so inspiring â the unity that you're building," Catherine told Sir Kevin.

Prince William and Catherine caught up with Sir Kevin in Wakefield, West Yorkshire, as he carries out what he says will be his final fundraising challenge.

Sir Kevin is aiming to complete seven ultra marathons in seven days, running between Hull and Manchester, in a challenge inspired by his former teammate Rob Burrow, who died from MND in 2024.

News.title: Burnham to fight next election on pledge to change voting system
News.content:
Andy Burnham has promised that Labour will fight the next general election on a pledge to change the UK's voting system.

In his first party conference speech as prime minister, he announced plans for a national commission to explore options for electoral reform.

He invited other parties to work with the commission to ensure "everyone's vote counts, and everyone's voice is heard".

He has previously supported moves towards a proportional representation (PR) model, telling last year's conference that "PR's time has come".

Westminster's first-past-the-post system, under which candidates with the most votes in each seat are elected, has been called into question as the UK political landscape has fragmented in recent years.

Debate over the system has intensified since Labour amassed a huge parliamentary majority with a 34% vote share in 2024.

Around 100 Labour MPs recently supported a parliamentary amendment in favour of setting up a commission to examine alternative options, a move Burnham himself supported last year when mayor of Greater Manchester.

In his speech Burnham told delegates: "We will all have failed in our public duties if we carry on as we are and open the door of No 10 to a divisive government on less 30% of the vote or less."

He added: "We can't succeed in the eyes of the world if we continue with the levels of political turbulence we have seen in recent times."

News.title: No 'deliberate' contact to stop car in A66 crash
News.content:
No evidence of "tactical contact" or the use of a stinger has been found before the A66 crash which killed five young men and two police officers, an initial investigation has revealed.

The crash between a Volkswagen Passat and a marked Cleveland Police vehicle happened at South Bank, near Middlesbrough, on 22 August and followed a police pursuit which was abandoned.

The initial investigation by the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said there was no evidence police had initiated contact with the Passat.

However, director of engagement, Emily Barry, said it will take the IOPC months to conclude its full investigation due to the amount of information to review.

PC Matthew Blades, 37, and PC Tom Clough, 38, who had not been following the Passat, were killed.

The five people in the Passat were Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Jakub Matusiak, 23, Makai Saddington, 18, and 17-year-olds Theo Rae and Cole Robert Worthy.

News.title: Soho House venue under investigation for food safety
News.content:
A venue of private members club Soho House is being investigated by the local council after a former member of staff raised concerns about rats and out-of-date food allegedly being served.

The former staff member told BBC News he was pressured replace labels on prepared food if it was not sold at the end of the day and said he regularly saw rats at the venue.

His contract was terminated two months after he first raised concerns, but Soho House said this was unrelated to his complaints.

It added that the food incident was isolated and re-labelling unsold food was not company policy, but it did not comment on the rats claim.

Hackney Council has confirmed it is investigating food safety and hygiene at Soho House's Shoreditch location.

Soho House is a popular haunt for A-list celebrities. Prince Harry and Meghan Markle reportedly had their first date at one of its London venues.

The former staff member at Shoreditch House, Kamran Khan, first raised concerns informally about the alleged re-labelling practice before formally filing a complaint with Soho House.

Khan was on probation at the venue when he raised the concerns in July, and his employment was terminated earlier in September.

Following his formal complaint, the company investigated and told Khan on 24 August there was evidence to support his claim and steps were being taken to address the matter.

Khan claimed the practice continued despite the assurances he was allegedly offered, leading him to complain to Hackney Council instead.

A spokesperson for the council said: "We have received a report about food safety and hygiene at Shoreditch House and have opened an investigation."

Speaking to BBC News, Khan said he was told in a probation meeting to continue the practice.

The 30-year-old, who told BBC News he has had several jobs in catering and hospitality said he was told "if I don't change labels on my own initiative, [they] would take that as a performance concern".

He said he felt compelled to raise the issue because he saw a lot of children and pregnant women at the restaurant.

"I told them that I don't want to be held personally liable for anyone that gets injured," he said.

Food served in a restaurant must legally be labelled with information including the best-before or use-by date.

Khan also said there had been rats at the venue for a long time and that cleaners were told to check daily for rat droppings.

A spokesperson for Soho House apologised for the incident, saying: "This is not how we expect our houses to operate and it is not company policy."

They said an external, independent investigation and audit was conducted.

"Delivering the highest level of food safety for our members and guests is incredibly important to us," they added.

"For clarity, the former employee's contract was terminated for reasons entirely unrelated to food labelling."

Soho House membership starts from Â£291.67 monthly or Â£204.17 for under-27s.

The group opened its first club in London in 1995, and now has 46 Soho Houses in Europe, North America and Asia, as well a string of other up-market hospitality businesses.

The company listed on the New York Stock Exchange in 2021, but its share price dropped sharply in the following years as it struggled to make a profit and fought accusations it was losing its exclusivity.

It was bought by a consortium of investors last year, with actor Ashton Kutcher joining the company's board.

News.title: Sir Ranulph Fiennes' relatives tell BBC it's 'very painful' not being able to visit him
News.content:
Relatives of the British explorer Sir Ranulph Fiennes have said it is "very painful" he appears to have been hidden away from them.

Speaking to BBC Newsnight, his former sister-in-law told the BBC that she did not know where he was, and nobody had been able to see him.

It has been alleged that Sir Ranulph, 82, has been admitted to a number of care homes under assumed names, after a family rift involving his second wife, Louise Millington-Cotes.

Louise Millington-Cotes did not immediately respond to the allegations, or the BBC's request for comment.

Cheshire Police have said they are aware of the concerns regarding Sir Ranulph, and are satisfied he is living in an appropriate setting with suitable care.

They said there were "no immediate safeguarding concerns".

Sir Ranulph has not been seen in public for nearly two years, just months after opening up about a diagnosis of Parkinson's disease, a progressive disorder affecting the brain, nervous system, and muscle control.

He was the first person to visit both north and south poles by surface means in the early 1980s and has been described by Guinness World Records as "the world's greatest living explorer".

Spending his childhood between the UK and South Africa, he joined the British Army after leaving school, going on to serve in the SAS.

Sir Ranulph's stepson, Alex Millington-Cotes, told BBC Newsnight he wanted to see the power of attorney "removed from my own mother" and placed in the hands of people who "have fully his best interests in mind".

"He's not an isolated type of person, and so to see him isolated now is very painful," he said.

Last week, he launched a crowdfunding campaign for legal fees to "locate and safeguard" the explorer, and so far it has raised almost Â£26,000.

He wrote that the fundraiser had been created as "a result of our concern and desperation" after trying "multiple avenues" to locate his stepfather.

Questions about Sir Ranulph's whereabouts grew in prominence after a report in the Telegraph earlier this month, external in which "members of his inner circle" raised concerns about his whereabouts.

The paper also reported concerns about Sir Ranulph have been raised with the Office of the Public Guardian (OPG), the government agency which helps people to stay in control of decisions about their health and finances.

In a statement to the BBC, an OPG spokesperson said: "We have a strict duty of confidentiality to all individuals who have made a lasting power of attorney, and it would be deeply inappropriate to comment on a specific case.

"We take all safeguarding concerns seriously and investigate thoroughly where there is the evidence and legal basis to do so."

News.title: Body of newborn baby found on shoreline in Wales as police search for mother
News.content:
The force has not revealed any information about the baby's gender or age.

Giraud said they "have real concerns for the health of the mother".

"We recognise that she is likely to be extremely vulnerable. She may be fearful of seeking the support she needs through fear of identifying herself.

"You may feel you have nowhere to turn, or that you cannot speak to anyone about what has happened. Please do not feel that you have to face this alone.

"We don't yet know all the circumstances surrounding your baby's death but what is important right now is that we find you, make sure you are safe, and ensure you receive any medical attention and support you may need.

"I am asking you personally, to please get in touch with us. You can speak to a healthcare professional, approach a police officer or attend a police station.

"If you are watching or listening to this appeal, please know that we want to hear from you. Please take the first step and contact us. There are people to help you."

Det Sgt Kelly Wynne said they were concerned the mother "may not be in a position to reach out for support", and appealed to the baby's father and the mother's family, friends, neighbours or colleagues who may have information.

"If you have any information regarding a woman or girl you think may have been pregnant or whose behaviour has been unusual or out of character over the past few months including withdrawing from friends, family or social ties, please contact us.

"We appreciate coming forward is difficult, but inaction is not an option."

News.title: Daniel Thomas refused bail over alleged boat damage
News.content:
Anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas has been refused bail during a crown court hearing over the alleged slashing of a dinghy in the English Channel.

Thomas, known to his supporters as Danny Tommo, appeared via videolink at Portsmouth Crown Court accused of criminal damage after a video appeared to show him slashing at the boat with a knife.

The 37-year-old, whose address was withheld by the court at a previous hearing, is also charged with failing to disclose the PIN to his phone.

He has been remanded in custody, with a provisional trial date set for 1 March.

The defendant, wearing a grey t-shirt and holding a copy of the Bible, did not enter a plea during the hearing but previously pleaded not guilty to both charges at Basingstoke Magistrates' Court on Friday.

News.title: Snooker champion Graeme Dott jailed for seven years for child sex abuse
News.content:
Former world snooker champion Graeme Dott has been jailed for seven years after being convicted of child sexual abuse.

Judge Lord Harrower said Dott robbed his victims of "a significant part of their childhood" and said his behaviour bore the hallmarks of grooming.

Dott had denied two charges of lewd and libidinous behaviour towards a girl and a boy between 1993 and 2010 but was found guilty following a trial at the High Court in Glasgow.

The 49-year-old Scot, who won the world snooker title in 2006, showed no emotion as he was sentenced, only nodding to someone in the public gallery as he was led away.

News.title: Nowak killer given leave to appeal against sentence
News.content:
The man who murdered student Henry Nowak is being allowed to appeal against the length of his sentence.

Vickrum Digwa stabbed 18-year-old Henry Nowak to death in Southampton in December 2025. In June, he was jailed for life with a minimum term of 21 years.

He has now been given permission to challenge the length of that sentence at the Court of Appeal on 5 November.

The court will also decide on a referral by the Attorney General's office, which argued the sentence was too lenient.

Digwa has also applied to appeal against his conviction for murder, which will be decided separately.

The 23-year-old was also sentenced for possessing a knife in public, despite claiming in court that the 21cm (8in) blade was being carried as part of his Sikh faith.

News.title: Homeland Security tapped $20 million in taxpayer funds for pro-Trump ads
News.content:

The Department of Homeland Security has allocated $20 million toward campaign-style s praising President Donald Trump, drawing widespread backlash from both Republicans and Democrats who argue the move misuses taxpayer funds and likely violates anti-propaganda laws.

In a letter sent Tuesday to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, two top Democratic senators stated that the money was drawn from Trump's "One Big Beautiful Bill" and was originally designated for U.S. Customs and Border Protection.

"We should not have to remind you that using government funding to create or air political ads like the ones that have been running over the last few days is illegal and a shockingly corrupt misuse of taxpayer dollars," wrote Sen. Patty Murray of Washington, the top Democrat on the Senate Appropriations Committee, and Sen. Chris Murphy of Connecticut, the ranking Democrat on the subcommittee overseeing Homeland Security funding.

Writing to Mullin, the senators demanded responses within the next 48 hours detailing "how this president is literally stealing their tax dollars to air campaign ads celebrating himself."

They asked the secretary whether the department plans to spend additional federal resources on airing these broadcasts or creating new ones, while requesting that contracting information be shared with Congress. The lawmakers also asked Mullin if he had spoken directly with Trump regarding the use of public funds for the s.

The White House has defended the spots, which explicitly disclose that they are financed by the U.S. government, classifying them as public service announcements ( Getty Images )

The political fallout surrounding the flattering spots, which began airing last week during high-profile college and National Football League telecasts, shows no sign of waning as critics across the spectrum voice concern over public spending so close to the midterm elections.

The White House has defended the spots, which explicitly disclose that they are financed by the U.S. government, classifying them as public service announcements.

Ad spend is up to $2.5m as criticism and legal scrutiny grow

The unusual commercials, which echo the GOP's midterm election slogans, against imagery of Trump's tenure in office — one with a “Love me, Love me” song refrain in the background — appear to violate a law against congressionally appropriated funds being used for propaganda. Experts also have said the ads, which are airing on network and cable TV and streaming, differ from other administrations’ PSAs because they aren’t designed to help Americans access any specific program.

Over the weekend, a new ad promoting the president resembles a black-and-white video from his own 2024 campaign that shows Trump walking down a hallway as his voice can be heard warning of a “final battle” against “globalists” and “warmongers.” It ends with Trump staring straight into the camera lens with the “Paid for by the U.S. Government” message printed.

Sen. Thom Tillis, a Republican from North Carolina, compared Trump's ads to those used by authoritarian former leader Viktor Orban of Hungary. Senate Majority Leader John Thune, a Republican from South Dakota, said it “shouldn’t be paid for with taxpayer dollars.”

Data from the outside firm AdImpact shows more than $2.5 million was spent on the three ads over the past seven days. The actual amount spent could be significantly more, depending on whether networks classified the ads as political.

The senators said that DHS has committed $20 million to the campaign.

A person who was unauthorized to discuss the situation and granted anonymity confirmed the findings, which were first reported by the Wall Street Journal.

Trump's ads use taxpayer dollars, likely skirting the law

The unusual ad campaign comes as Republicans face an increasingly volatile midterm election season with their control of the House and Senate — and Trump's future agenda — all at risk.

Voters say they are struggling with high prices of gas and groceries, and are concerned about the lengthy U.S. war against Iran, now in its seventh month. Democrats are gearing up for vast oversight of Trump and his administration if they seize power, and impeachment is not off the table.

House Democrats said Trump's director of the Office of Management and Budget, Russ Vought, moved the money from Homeland Security to the ad campaign on Sept. 19.

The Homeland Security funds are part of a whopping $175 billion Congress gave the department in the “Big, Beautiful, Bill” as part of his immigration enforcement and deportation agenda. Democrats voted against that package, which Trump signed into law last summer, in part because of its steep cuts to Medicaid and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, known as SNAP.

Rep. Rosa DeLauro of Connecticut, the top Democrat on the House Appropriations Committee, and Rep. Henry Cuellar of Texas, the ranking Democrat on the Homeland Security subcommittee, said that after gutting $1 trillion from Medicaid and social services and “more than quadrupling funding for mass deportations, it turns out the Trump administration used Republicans’ One Big Beautiful Bill to pay for President Trump’s political ads.”

They said when Democrats regain control, they "will work to uncover and reverse misuses of taxpayer money like this and hold those who abused their power accountable.”

What's also striking about the administration's use of taxpayer dollars for the ads is that Trump's own political campaign committee MAGA Inc. is sitting on hundreds of millions of dollars of funding that could be used during the midterm season. Groups aligned with MAGA Inc. have started shelling out funds for the House and Senate races.

The administration has defended the use of the taxpayer dollars for the ads and shown no signs of changing course.

Six Flags Magic Mountain has permanently closed its X2 roller coaster after a series of lawsuits alleged that riders suffered severe brain injuries on the California attraction.

The Valencia theme park announced Tuesday that it had decided to retire the ride after nearly 20 years.

The ride, which Six Flags once called “a rite of passage for the ultimate daredevil,” reached 76 mph and 200 feet, with 3,610 feet of track, but has been closed since July 12 after two riders suffered life-threatening brain injuries less than a week apart.

“While X2 consistently passed a multitude of safety tests, we have decided to close the ride because we believe it’s the right thing to do,” Magic Mountain President Brian Oerding said in a statement posted to the park’s website.

“Ride safety is a cornerstone of our business, and when we see guest confidence affected, we take it seriously,” he added.

open image in gallery X2 at Six Flags Magic Mountain in Valencia, California, has permanently closed following reports of more than 100 alleged brain injuries and two deaths, the park announced Tuesday ( AP )

The coaster opened as X in 2002 and was redesigned with lighter trains before reopening as X2 in 2008. Its seats rotate 360 degrees as riders navigate drops, twists and inversions. Over 16 million people have ridden X2 since its 2008 reopening, Six Flags said.

However, more than 100 people allege that the two-minute, 34-second ride caused lasting brain injuries, according to a CNN investigation published last week.

Six Flags faces multiple lawsuits over the alleged injuries. CNN identified more than a dozen reports of serious injuries and hospitalizations associated with X2 over nearly two decades, including two deaths. Two riders suffered brain hemorrhages after riding the coaster in July, CNN reported.

Among the three most recent cases is Pamela Guillen, who visited Magic Mountain with her family in July to celebrate her daughter's 16th birthday. Guillen said she became confused and disoriented after riding X2 and later woke up in a hospital, where she learned she had suffered a traumatic brain injury and undergone emergency surgery.

“Everything went blank. My next memory is waking up in the hospital about two weeks later,” Guillen told ABC7 Los Angeles.

"I had suffered a traumatic brain injury and needed emergency brain surgery to stop the bleeding and had to be intubated. I was in a coma. I spent almost a month at the hospital," Guillen said.

Six days later, Naomi Greer-Wilkinson, 25, rode X2 and lost consciousness shortly afterward, according to her family's attorneys. She was taken to a hospital and underwent emergency brain surgery. Her family said she remained hospitalized and was unable to breathe on her own as of ABC7 Los Angeles’ report last week.

A third recent plaintiff, Michael Wick, also alleges he suffered a brain injury after riding X2. His attorney said Wick underwent two brain surgeries and is now unable to practice law because of a disability.

open image in gallery Magic Mountain President Brian Oerding said Tuesday that X2 ‘consistently passed a multitude of safety tests’ but the park decided to close the ride ‘because we believe it’s the right thing to do’ ( Jeremy Thompson/Wiki Commons )

The recent lawsuits follow the 2022 death of Christopher Hawley, 22, who lost consciousness shortly after getting off X2 and died the following day after suffering severe brain bleeding, according to his family's lawsuit.

His parents sued Six Flags, Magic Mountain and S&S Worldwide, the company associated with the ride's trains. The family reached a settlement in August, according to KTLA.

Hilda Farias, 28, also died after riding X2 in 2010, according to court records cited by the Los Angeles Times. She developed a brain bleed that led to her death.

Six Flags has declined multiple outlets’ requests for comment, citing pending litigation.

The Independent has contacted Six Flags for comment.

The X2 closure comes as Magic Mountain prepares to open Thrill Glider in 2027. Six Flags describes it as the world’s first suspended, multi-launch Thrill Glider coaster, featuring bike-like seats, five inversions, multiple launches and speeds of up to 50 mph.

News.title: Czech Republic v England LIVE: Anthony Gordon and Harry Kane goals sink 10-men hosts in Nations League
News.content:

Tuchel rues mistakes after England fails to land 'decisive punch' in defeat to Spain

England travel to the Czech Republic this evening for their second group A3 match of their Nations League campaign looking to bounce back after being beaten 3-2 by Spain at Wembley last Saturday.

The Three Lions were behind in just the second minute but showed mental resiliance and fortitude to make a comeback in the match before the world champions clinched victory in the second half. Thomas Tuchel praised the performance but will want to build on the positives and make sure his team cut out the errors that blighted their display against Spain.

The Three Lions will be confident about getting points on the board this evening with their outing against the Czech Republic as they have only lost once in five competitive meetings with the Central European side.

For their part, Czech Republic competed against fellow group opponents Croatia in their opening Nations League fixture with Adam Karabec cancelling out Luka Modric’s opener before Marco Pasalic’s second half goal inflicted a loss on them. Like England, they will be hoping to bounce back from that result and secure some points tonight.

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul on Tuesday called for an investigation into Cornell University's response to a 2024 gang rape allegation in which a woman says she was sexually assaulted by seven students after being plied with alcohol and drugs.

The woman filed a lawsuit this month saying she was sexually assaulted at the Chi Phi fraternity house on Cornell's campus in October 2024. Her suit says the assault occurred after she was pressured into snorting ketamine, smoking marijuana and drinking alcohol, to the point where she was incapable of consenting to sex.

The woman reported the incident to Cornell's campus police department, but the local district attorney's office opted not to prosecute anyone at the time. It reopened the criminal investigation Monday as public outrage built over the woman's allegations.

Hochul, a Democrat, said she supported Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten’s decision to reopen his investigation, but said bigger questions remain about Cornell’s reporting, response, and prevention systems, as well as its campus culture. The governor called for an outside law firm to be hired to independently investigate the university’s response.

“The allegations in this case are nothing short of horrifying," Hochul said in a statement. “For any student to come forward after an experience like this takes extraordinary courage. No student should ever be left wondering whether the institutions meant to protect them will listen and act.”

An email seeking comment was sent to Cornell on Tuesday.

Van Houten defended his office's actions Tuesday in several media interviews, arguing that while the male students involved did things that were “morally wrong,” the woman's initial account of the incident to police didn't include allegations that she was drugged, incapacitated beyond the ability to consent, or forced into sex.

“She went to the police because she knew it wasn’t right,” Van Houten told CNN.

Van Houten has not released the victim's sworn statement to police, but instead released a summary with some of her direct quotes included. He also defended his office's decision not to do additional investigation after the woman, who was identified in court filings by the pseudonym Jane Doe, initially spoke to police.

“There were no question marks. There was no additional need to find information because we had all of the information that the police collected from Jane Doe through her very detailed, very comprehensive statement that she provided," Van Houten said.

Van Houten's office did not talk directly to the victim, but the district attorney had told the police that he would sit down with her to explain the law.

Shortly after the woman first made her allegations in 2024, Cornell publicly disclosed that it was investigating “serious and deeply disturbing allegations of drug abuse and sexual violence at the Chi Phi fraternity house.” It also announced that the fraternity and several students had been suspended, and that parallel police and school investigations were underway.

On Monday, the university said in a statement that it supported the decision to reopen the criminal investigation, adding that its own investigation had led to some students being disciplined or expelled. The Chi Phi chapter remains barred from campus. Cornell has declined to release more information on discipline for individual students, citing privacy rules.

The woman’s complaint accuses the university of not preventing the alleged assaults and of failing to properly address sexual violence on campus. It includes a photo that it says shows a group chat between frat members discussing the night’s events.

Van Houten called the photo a “red herring," saying that it had no bearing on the legal analysis of the case.

“We received it, but it was not relevant to the assessment of whether Jane Doe consented or whether there was any evidence of lack of consent on her part as defined by the penal law,” he said.

The Trump administration has withdrawn the United States from a top European anti-corruption watchdog as it forges ahead with plans to disengage from international and multilateral organizations that it accuses of exceeding their mandates, being inefficient or not adapting to U.S. policies.

The Council of Europe said Tuesday that the U.S. formally notified it that it would leave the Group of States against Corruption, or GRECO. Only two other countries have left GRECO before — Russia and Belarus.

A U.S. official confirmed the withdrawal and said it had been submitted on Monday. The official spoke on condition of anonymity to confirm the move ahead of a public announcement from the State Department.

“The United States has participated in GRECO since 2000 and has been a valuable contributor to its work and to the exchange of experience and good practice in preventing and combating corruption,” the Strasbourg-based Council of Europe said in a statement. “GRECO remains open to resuming cooperation with the United States in the future in support of shared efforts to prevent corruption, strengthen integrity and uphold the rule of law.”

The decision was announced a week after the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe said the U.S. had declined to invite its members to observe November’s congressional midterm elections, a sharp break from past practice.

The U.S. has already withdrawn from a number of European-based U.N. and multilateral agencies, including the World Health Organization and the U.N. Human Rights Council, and is weighing further such steps.

The U.S. withdrew in January from another Council of Europe panel — the Venice Commission, which is an advisory body on constitutional law.

GRECO was created in 1999 by the Council of Europe to monitor compliance with the organization’s anti-corruption standards. Membership is not limited to European Union members, and the United States joined a year after its founding.

After the most hard-hitting language possible, the Premier League’s independent commission has set up the most hard-hitting sanctions. There is surely little choice but to expel Manchester City from the competition. The conclusions are so profoundly damning that it even raises the question of whether opposition clubs could or would want to play with them.

Worse, the new Independent Football Regulator has an even bigger decision than to whether to expel. The question will be now whether to exercise their statutory power to force a sale.

The new body made considerable noise about their ability to remove “rogue owners” around the difficulties of Sheffield Wednesday and Morecambe.

open image in gallery Manchester City are set to appeal after being found guilty on almost every charge ( Getty )

The details in the Premier League’s decision of the eight-year City case, published on Tuesday afternoon, go way beyond such a description.

The word “sham” was used eight times over 40 pages, in reference to sponsorship, image rights and other arrangements that inflated revenue and reduced costs by more than £900m.

One conclusion was “that certain of those factual witnesses had given evidence at the hearing that they knew to be untrue and so had been dishonest”. The Premier League itself went on to say “the club filed mis-stated accounts and concealed the true state of its finances from its auditors and football regulators”, with City accused of being “significantly in breach of both the Premier League’s and Uefa’s spending limits”.

Although the decision doesn’t use the words, the details mirror Uefa’s previous description of “a sophisticated, thoughtful and fundamental attempt to circumvent or violate” the rules.

The actual words used were still far more damning than even some of City’s most vocal critics – as well as sources that worked on previous cases – expected.

open image in gallery The Premier League’s statement was strong ( Getty )

As one source with knowledge of that previous Uefa case says, “it exposes them for exactly who they are and what they did”.

Consequently, it now looks worse than what had been one of football’s biggest corruption scandals, Italy’s Calciopoli. This isn’t about interpretation of phone calls. It is hard figures on pages.

It amounts to the biggest scandal in club football history – a complete revisionism of the most dominant champions the Premier League has ever seen, the blackening of the name of a club, while also going to geopolitical levels. The observations on the course of the proceedings detail that both parties relied on evidence from experts in the fields of “Abu Dhabi politics and governance”.

Even the Premier League statement accompanying the decision, seemed to betray an attitude that they were finally fed up with this.

open image in gallery The Premier League appears fed up with the case ( PA Archive )

Executives at rival clubs had strong suspicions that City were “cheating” long before the football leaks of 2018. Here it was all is written down.

Except, the only language more strident was that in the club’s own statement.

City re-iterated their innocence and again referred to “a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence”.

“The club will therefore be relentless, and where necessary proactive, in any and all appropriate regulatory legal forums”.

It went on that City “will now pursue the appeal avenues open to it, on the basis that the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe”.

Previous statements were meanwhile elaborated on, as there was a reference to how they “diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League Board and Executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence”.

open image in gallery Manchester City Chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak, former manager Pep Guardiola, CEO Ferran Soriano, and Director of Football, Txiki Begiristain ( PA )

It’s clear to read between the lines there. They intend on turning this legal cold war into open conflict.

Chief executive Ferran Soriano, whose own role at the club is surely at risk pending the outcome, delivered a three-minute video to staff stating that “the whole Premier League case against us is based on a single false accusation” and that “every other false charge that has been thrown at us comes from that simple, central and completely false accusation.

Soriano also described the “Premier League’s conspiracy theory”.

This is where we are.

It’s why it’s actually hard to see how games can even be played in anything like a proper football atmosphere. Opposition fans up and down the country are just going to have banners declaring “sham”.

open image in gallery How can the Premier League go on unchanged? ( PA Archive )

Many will be furious at the amount they invested, for a competition that was made - yes - a mockery of. Perhaps even a “sham”, given City’s success.

That is why points deductions don’t feel sufficient. The scale of the impact in the other direction has been far too great. Expulsion would require a special shareholder vote, and a vote of 15, but feeling is currently running that high.

As regards their potential success in an appeals process, that is open to question. The scope under the remit of the rules is limited.

The widespread belief in football is that they will attack the process, as with the strategy against Uefa. One big difference is that this is described as a “rock solid” process.

They may go to the High Court. But that delay would be even more damaging for the context of their games. It could become a diplomatic incident.

As one geopolitical expert says: “The one thing that Gulf autocracies like Abu Dhabi won’t accept is embarrassment or shame. But will they use up political capital to preserve City when so much else is at stake?

“They already lean heavily on the UK to ensure they evade accountability in Sudan.”

This is the level we’re talking about.

And yet this decision went to levels that no one expected.

It is football’s worst ever scandal. It warrants a punishment to fit.
