The Lionesses face Greece in the first leg at the Pankritio Stadium in Heraklion, Crete on Friday 9 ­October before the return at Leicester’s King Power ­Stadium the following ­Tuesday, needing victory to reach the second decisive round of the ­playoffs in December.

England are having to contest the playoffs despite winning five of six matches in their qualifying group, having missed out on top spot to the world champions, Spain, based on the head-to-head record from their meetings in April and June, in repeats of the 2023 World Cup final. England will be heavily fancied to progress to next summer’s finals in Brazil.

That tournament could be ­Wiegman’s last with England because her contract expires after the World Cup. She gave little away when asked about any contract discussions.

“We have regular conversa­tions together, and we talk about the future at moments, but at this point I’m just focusing on Greece. We want to get through and qualify for the World Cup. Of course I talk to Mark [­Bullingham], every two weeks, and we speak about what’s ­happening now, what’s in the future, but there’s nothing new.”

Sports.title: Aston Villa sack manager Natalia Arroyo with club second-bottom of WSL
Sports.content:
Aston Villa have sacked Natalia Arroyo as their women’s manager, with the side winless and second-bottom of the Women’s Super League.

Arroyo was let go on Monday night, after Villa endured a 4-0 defeat at Tottenham on Sunday. It was a second loss in their opening four games of the season, with a 4-1 defeat by Manchester City sandwiched between 1-1 draws with Chelsea and Brighton, with performances largely poor.

Arroyo was appointed in January 2025, signing a three-and-a-half-year contract with the club. The former Barcelona and Espanyol player, who spent time as a journalist before focusing on her coaching career, joined Villa following four impressive years in charge at Real Sociedad where she guided the club to a second-place finish in the 2021-22 season and a Copa de la Reina final in her final campaign.

The 40-year-old replaced Shaun Goater, who took temporary charge following Robert de Pauw’s departure amid allegations over remarks he had made to players. Villa had only two wins from their first 12 WSL games when Arroyo took charge. Five consecutive league defeats followed as the team adapted to the new manager and they won their remaining five games to finish sixth.

Villa finished ninth in Arroyo’s first full campaign, with 20 points from 22 games, but a poor run of form and four successive defeats blighted the end of the season. “Everyone at Aston Villa would like to thank Natalia for her efforts and wish her all the best in her future endeavours,” the club said in a statement.

Villa have confirmed that Brian Sørensen, the women’s technical adviser, will take temporary charge of the team, including for their Subway Players Cup tie against Newcastle on Wednesday. Sørensen joined Villa as technical adviser in March, following his exit from Everton in February after four years with the Merseyside club.

Sports.title: How important is a fast start for teams chasing the Premier League title?
Sports.content:
The first international window gives us time to take stock and make sense of what has happened in the early weeks of the Premier League season. Manchester City are the only team to have won all five of their matches. They have started life after Pep Guardiola in the best way possible on the pitch, opening a three-point gap over champions Arsenal, but how important is a fast start?

Of course, we do not yet know the punishment they may face for breaking the Premier League’s financial fair play rules so, for the purposes of this article, we will put that matter to the side.

Enzo Maresca’s side became the 15th different team to win their opening five games of a Premier League season, and it’s the fourth occasion City have managed it. They have only won the title in one of the three previous seasons, though. They won the league in 2023-24, but failed to capitalise on their five early wins in 2015-16 and 2016-17.

That follows a wider trend across the league. Only four of the 14 teams that have won their first five matches of the season have gone on to win the title (29%): Manchester City in 2023-24, Liverpool in 2019-20, and Chelsea in 2009-10 and 2005-06.

Perhaps most importantly, all four teams went on to add to their winning streak to start those seasons. Chelsea in 2009-10 and Manchester City in 2023-24 extended their run by another game (six wins); Liverpool started with eight wins in 2019-20; and Chelsea (nine wins in 2005-06) went on the longest winning run to start a Premier League season.

Tottenham hold the record for the most consecutive wins to start a top-flight league season. They won their first 11 games in 1960-61 and, unsurprisingly, won the title that campaign. But a winning start does not guarantee success, as Manchester United found in 1985-86. Despite winning their first 10 games that season (and remaining unbeaten in their first 15) under Ron Atkinson, they collapsed and ended the season in fourth place.

It must be said, City have benefited from having an easy run of fixtures. According to the Opta Power Rankings, City had the second-easiest start this season, with their opponents having an average rating of 91.2. Only Liverpool (91.1) were handed a simpler start to the season by the Premier League fixture computer.

Another statistic that will give City fans reason for pause is that none of the previous seven clubs to start a Premier League season with exactly five wins have gone on to win the title in that campaign.

The most recent of those was Liverpool last season. The reigning champions won games against Bournemouth, Newcastle, Arsenal, Burnley and Everton to open the 2025-26 campaign before losing four in a row. The fact Liverpool won four of their first five games with goals scored after the 83rd minute pointed to their run being unsustainable, and so it proved.

Question marks about City’s defensive qualities this season suggest this may be another unsustainable winning run. Their credentials will be tested when the Premier League returns and they visit Anfield to face Liverpool, who are still unbeaten under new boss Andoni Iraola.

View image in fullscreen Illustration: Opta

The lowest position a team has finished after winning their first five games of a season is sixth (Newcastle United in 1994-95), although that did come in a 42-game campaign. Looking back at all English top-flight history, City’s current streak is the 40th different occasion of a team winning their first five games in a season. Just 14 of the previous 39 have gone on to win the league title (36%).

The average points won by Premier League champions from the first five games across the previous 34 Premier League campaigns is 11.3, which is above the total secured by Arsenal last season. They won 10 points from their first five games, dropping points by losing at Liverpool and drawing against Manchester City at home. Mikel Arteta’s side have started this season better this time around, winning 12 points from a possible 15, with their only blemish the shock 3-0 loss at Brighton.

The fewest points eventual Premier League champions have won from their first five games was in the inaugural season in 1992-93. Manchester United won only seven points from their first five matches (two wins, one draw and two defeats), but Alex Ferguson’s side recovered and finished 10 points clear of runners up Aston Villa after the 42-game season.

No team has won a Premier League title in a 38-game season after winning fewer than eight points from their first five matches. United have won the league four times after winning exactly eight points from their opening five games (in 1998-99, 2002-03, 2007-08 and 2008-09), with City replicating that feat in 2020-21. What we’re trying to say is, Hull City and Newcastle fans, it’s still possible.

The most astonishing turnaround by title winners has to be Sunderland’s effort in 1912-13, though. They failed to win any of their first seven games, drawing two and losing the other five, but they went on to win the First Division title. With just two points for a win back then, it was easier for teams to recover from a run of poor results; a monumental comeback nevertheless.

This is an article by Opta Analyst

Sports.title: Football Daily | Oh Jürgen! Mixed fortunes for the Nations League’s fab four
Sports.content:
GREECE LIGHTNIN’

This time last week, Football Daily romanticised a continental renaissance of sorts. The arrival of Jürgen Klopp, Zinedine Zidane and Xavi Hernández on the international management scene piqued our interest. We were also impressed by the clanging brass stones of Roberto Mancini, who returned to the Italy ejector-seat three years after abruptly pulling the lever and abandoning his country in order to take the Saudi riyal. Two games in and it’s time to appraise the respective early efforts of this glitzy A-list quartet of trophy-hoarding aristocrats, one of whom has had a somewhat chastening introduction to life in the international lane. Oh Jürgen!

Having begun his reign as Germany head coach by warning the national press not to intrude on his family’s privacy, Klopp was forced instead to contend with their coverage of him picking a 44-man squad in order to speed up “the process of opening the door for many new faces” as part of his plan to revolutionise the German squad. “There’s still plenty of room for improvement,” he honked after his side drew his first match in charge against Xavi’s Netherlands, before failing to show any in a historic first-ever defeat by Greece. “The lineup, the formation, the many changes – that is all 100% down to me,” he sighed. “Football, that’s how it is. I don’t think we deserved that, but here we are.” Here we are, being in third place in their Nations League group and already facing a must(ish)-win match against Serbia to avoid possible relegation.

Xavi, meanwhile, chalked up his first Netherlands win in Belgrade against Serbia. The Barcelona legend had late callup Mexx Meerdink to thank at the final whistle after the AZ striker scored both goals in a 2-1 win. Next comes Thursday’s match against the group-leading Greeks. Responding to suggestions that there were many moments when the Dutch needed to attack the spaces but didn’t do it, a contrite Xavi confessed, “there were many moments when we needed to attack the spaces, but we didn’t do it”. In danger of losing their global status as dark horses to Greece, Turkey rolled over to give Mancini the first win of his second spell in charge of Italy, who lost to Belgium last week. After being reappointed, the Italian apologised for doing the dirty on the Azzurri first time around in order to take up a lucrative contract with Saudi Arabia. He has since had to face down questions about another of his former nation state paymasters. After referring to claims he had a “double contract” during his time at Manchester City, Mancini described the current scandal surrounding his former club as “not a problem that concerns me”.

On a night when Michael Kayode marked the occasion of becoming the first Brentford player in history to represent Italy by scoring a goal, Mancini said the 22-year-old “will improve even more after another year in the Premier League”. Given his lack of popularity among many Italy fans, whether he’ll still be around to see Kayode blossom remains to be seen. Their next appointment is in Paris on Friday against France, whose manager Zidane is the only one of our four heroes to get off to a perfect start in his new gig. After back-to-back 1-0 wins in Turkey and Belgium, the latter won by a sensational Michael Olise solo effort late-doors, Zidane was asked about his meme-worthy touchline celebration that involved a sprint, a little dance and leathering a spare ball off a cone. “I saw the ball,” he giggled. “I was forced to shoot it, be a bit ridiculous but it doesn’t matter.” Never mind the tactical revolutions of Jürgen, Xavi and Roberto, when the chips are down just go full Zizou and get it launched.

LIVE ON BIG WEBSITE

Join Rob Smyth at 7.45pm BST for Czechia 1-3 England, while Taha Hashim will bring you goal updates on the rest of the night’s action with his Nations League clockwatch at the same time.

QUOTE OF THE DAY

“I was just a kid and no one was there for me. I’m angry with Everton for not looking after me. Listen, I’m no angel. I’ve played my part, but there are other people who played their part in the demise of Billy Kenny. So I’m still bitter and frustrated today, at the age of 53. It was an absolute waste of talent” – Billy Kenny explains the drinking culture that enveloped him as a teenager, his time in jail, struggles with depression and how he got clean, in this must-read interview with Donald McRae.

View image in fullscreen Billy Kenny there. Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian

RECOMMENDED LOOKING

It’s your man David Squires on … the Manchester City verdict and Nations League tensions.

Football Daily’s lawyers are never this fast. Illustration: David Squires/The Guardian

double quotation mark It’s December 2009 and, after my morning shower, I go up the M6 from my home in Nuneaton to Eastlands to watch Manchester City beat Sunderland 4-3. With light snow falling, Mark Hughes comes on the pitch at the end to acknowledge the crowd. I haven’t a clue who Roberto Mancini or Manuel Pellegrini are, I’m vaguely aware of Pep Guardiola. I go back down the M6 in the snow and think about the big sign over one of the stands in Salford saying ‘34 years’. Good job I took that shower! Otherwise everyone in the ground, except Hughes, would have known that he’d already been sacked and we were about to enter a 17-year dream. Until I took that shower in December 2009. Yours, sadly” – Paul Cashian.

double quotation mark Reading Rob Draper’s excellent article on Arsène Wenger’s 30-year anniversary (yesterday’s Still Want More, full email edition) and I spotted Gunnersaurus in the accompanying picture – the only member of Arsenal’s Invincibles who is still there. He really is evergreen (sorry)” – Paul Farey.

If you have any, please send letters to the.boss@theguardian.com. Today’s prizeless letter o’ the day goes to … Paul Cashian. Terms and conditions for our competitions, when we run them, are here.

Sports.title: Man City found guilty of HUGE financial 'sham' as Premier League confirm verdict in blistering statement: Club cooked their books by £900m - and now could be RELEGATED
Sports.content:
Man City found guilty of HUGE financial 'sham' as Premier League confirm verdict in blistering statement: Club cooked their books by £900m - and now could be RELEGATED

Manchester City cooked the books to the tune of £900m in a nine-year period peppered with ‘sham’ deals during which they became the major force in English football, a commission has found.

In a damning 40-page verdict City, who won eight trophies during the spell involved, artificially inflated sponsorship agreements and pumped money into the club from its Abu Dhabi owners via disguised payments in a bid to swerve Premier League spending rules.

The eight-times champions were found guilty of ‘all charges related to serious breaches’ of the regulations and the majority of those in relation to its failure to co-operate with the competition’s probe.

City witnesses were also accused of lying in front of the three-person panel, in an explosive verdict that will further send shockwaves through football after news of the club’s guilt first leaked on Friday.

All punishments, including expulsion, transfer bans and points deductions are open to the Premier League and a sanction hearing will take place in due course.

However, City quickly confirmed that it would be launching an appeal ahead of Friday’s deadline and - amid extraordinary scenes - accused the Premier League of creating a ‘conspiracy theory’.

The Premier League has confirmed that Manchester City have been found guilty of 'all charges related to serious breaches' of the league's financial regulations

City's chief executive Ferran Soriano (centre) later circulated a video sent to club staff stressing that the allegations were false

A fiery club statement branded the verdict ‘opinion’ and tellingly labelled the independent panel a ‘Premier League commission’. In a video sent to 1,000 staff and seen by Daily Mail Sport, infuriated chief executive Ferran Soriano said the allegations were ‘just not true’ and repeated the claim that they had provided ‘irrefutable evidence’.

‘Very soon we will look back at this as another time in our history when we dealt with adversity and overcame it together,’ he added.

The bombshell statement was released late on Tuesday afternoon. In it, the Premier League said the panel found City arranged ‘sham contracts (which misrepresented the true agreement between the parties) with a number of its commercial partners, as well as relying on ‘sham’ agreements with others, to artificially inflate the club’s revenues and reduce its costs’.

It added that the panel, whose hearing concluded in December 2024, had found that the club had falsely altered the financial picture at the Etihad to the tune of £900m.

The Premier League said that City was actually ‘significantly in breach of both the Premier League’s and UEFA’s spending limits’ during the time period in question - 2009-2018 - when it won eight major trophies.

Deals with a number of sponsors were part of ‘a disguised funding scheme, whereby those companies were only required to pay a portion of the relevant sponsorship fees’, the statement added, saying that ‘the remainder was funded by Abu Dhabi United Group Investment & Development Ltd (ADUG), which owned the club’.

The panel also found further ‘sham’ arrangements, funded by ADUG, which allowed City to record lower operating expenses that it incurred, along with a ‘”sham” circular arrangement with Fordham, an entity that purchased the club’s players’ image rights, that was funded by ADUG’.

The result was that the club had ‘filed misstated accounts and concealed the true state of its finances from its auditors and football regulators’.

Premier League CEO Richard Masters claimed that the commission's verdict had 'vindicated' the league's decision to pursue the charges

Had City reported accurately ‘it would have been in breach of both the League’s and UEFA’s spending limits by a very substantial amount’.

The panel also found that City committed multiple breaches of its duties of co-operation and good faith in that it failed to assist the Premier League’s four-year investigation, triggered by the emergence of club emails obtained by a hacker. Indeed, City had ‘made concerted efforts to stop and frustrate the Premier League investigation’.

The report noted that issues ‘were fiercely contested between the parties’. It added that proceedings lasted for 42 days and acknowledged that it had ‘taken us much longer than we would have wished’ to reach a conclusion, which ‘was regrettable’. Transcripts of evidence given ran to more than 7,000 pages.

The lop-sided verdict also rounded on ‘a number of important factual witnesses’ who gave evidence on behalf of the club, saying such evidence was ‘false’ and stating that some gave evidence ‘they knew to be untrue and so had been dishonest’.

From 2009 to 2018 it found City claimed commercial income of £949.94m when only £119.25m had come from sponsors – which was the figure which should have appeared in the accounts.

The statement added that City’s core defence was ‘untrue’, describing it as an explanation ‘concocted well after the event in an attempt to obscure and conceal the realities of the Disguised Funding Scheme’.

Richard Masters, Premier League chief executive, said the competition had been ‘vindicated’ and that the club had ‘systematically broken Premier League rules for nearly a decade’.

‘It is a key responsibility of the Premier League to ensure that the Rules, approved by the clubs themselves, are upheld to protect the integrity of the competition,’ he said. ‘It is paramount that the League remains competitive and fair for all clubs and for the fans. We take that role extremely seriously.

‘This disciplinary case, and this decision, are the most significant in Premier League history. There are elements of the case that remain to be decided, including, importantly, what sanction must follow for these breaches. Now we have the Commission’s decision, we are committed to moving swiftly through the remainder of the process, to provide certainty for the League, our clubs and fans.’

Premier League rules state that after City lodges its appeal the chair of the panel should appoint a three-person appeal board ‘as soon as reasonably practicable’. Any objections to the subsequent appointments should then be lodged within two working days. The whole process should be concluded within 12 weeks. Whether that will be the case remains to be seen. It is unclear whether a sanction will be handed down before an appeal takes place.

In a statement released shortly after the Premier League, City said it was ‘both disappointed and surprised by the opinion of the Premier League Commission’.

It added: ‘The club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case. The club will therefore be relentless, and where necessary proactive, in any and all appropriate regulatory and legal forums.

‘The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements uncompleted. Manchester City will now pursue the appeal avenues open to it, on the basis that the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe.’

Soriano added: ‘The whole Premier League case against us is based on a single false accusation – that the owner’s personal money was somehow and secretly put into the club via some sponsors from Abu Dhabi. This is just not true. Irrefutable evidence has been provided that shows it could not happen and that it did not happen. This includes bank statements, money transfers, witnesses and everything necessary to categorically demonstrate the money did not come from the owner.

‘Surprisingly for us and our lawyers after nearly two years the Premier League’s commission has issued an opinion that supports the Premier League’s conspiracy theory.’

Sports.title: Police share major update on PAC's shocking death at age 40 after AEW wrestler was found 'slumped' in car
Sports.content:
Police share major update on PAC's shocking death at age 40 after AEW wrestler was found 'slumped' in car

The sudden death of AEW star PAC is not being considered suspicious, police have told TMZ.

Benjamin Satterley, who performed as PAC, was found 'passed out' in a vehicle in a CAVA parking lot near Chicago O'Hare International Airport on Sunday. He was later pronounced dead at age 40.

Now, police have told TMZ that no signs of foul play were discovered at the scene.

As for the cause and manner of death, that information is still pending further examination by the Cook County Medical Examiner. That office has conducted an autopsy, but further testing remains that could take up to several weeks to complete.

Medics responded to the Des Plaines location of the Mediterranean-themed restaurant around 4:00pm on Sunday, according to dispatch audio reviewed by the outlet.

'This is going to be a slumper,' authorities said in the audio. 'We can't confirm breathing at this time.'

More details have been revealed after the death of AEW wrestler Benjamin Satterley

'This is going to be a slumper in a car. We cannot confirm breathing yet. At this point, we're still on the phone getting further,' they later added.

Later in the audio, an official could be heard saying that Satterley, who is British, was found dead on arrival.

A witness told the outlet that some customers at the restaurant saw Satterley 'passed out' in his vehicle and called 911.

They also tried to find any medical equipment inside the restaurant to attempt to help the wrestler before emergency personnel arrived.

'There was an ambulance, police and a fire truck, all outside,' the witness said.

According to the Cook County Medical Examiner's office, Satterley was pronounced dead at 4:08pm.

No cause of death has been revealed as results from an autopsy are still pending.

Satterley, who previously competed in the WWE as Adrian Neville, had wrestled for AEW the night before in Chicago, taking on Andrade at the NOW Arena.

While he lost his All Out pay-per-view contest, he would make another appearance later during a main event matchup between Jon Moxley and Will Ospreay.

Then performing in WWE as Adrian Neville, the wrestling icon is seen at Wrestlemania in 2017

The wrestling star died just hours after performing on AEW's latest PPV event in Chicago.

The wrestling promotion announced his passing in a post shortly after 6:00pm on Sunday.

'A native of Newcastle upon Tyne, England, Satterley began his wrestling career in 2004 and went on to perform for wrestling organizations all over the world, captivating fans with innovative high-flying moves and incredible in-ring ability,' AEW said in the statement.

'Pac signed with All Elite Wrestling in 2019 and held multiple AEW Championships and competed in some of the most memorable matches in AEW history.

'Our condolences go out to Satterley's family, friends and fans.'

Sports.title: IAN HERBERT: I exposed Man City's cheating and sham deals eight years ago - their threatening response was the most shocking experience of my 30-year career... but today I feel vindicated
Sports.content:
It is an episode which illustrates the struggle there has been in extracting transparency and truth about Manchester City, whose relentless, bullying corporate machine has looked to shut down investigation and inquiry through years of deceit.

Eight years ago, I wrote a story, published by The Independent, whom I worked for at the time, about an obscure and puzzling company called Fordham Sports Image Rights, to which City had supposedly sold the club’s future image rights for £24.5million – a sum they needed to avoid breaching financial sustainability rules in the 2012-13 season.

City had made no secret of earning this figure. They stated it in their annual accounts. Yet Fordham’s directors, detailed in their Companies House listing, were City’s very own legal officer Simon Cliff and non-executive director John MacBeath – a qualified chartered accountant.

Fordham clearly had a very distinct link to the club. And when I made more inquiries about City selling off those image rights to such a firm, there were blank looks. Several sources confirmed to me that, contrary to this notion, City were still raking in millions from those deals.

The sources were significant people. A Spanish financier Esteve Calzada, chief executive of Saudi club Al Hilal these days, who as an adviser to City at that time had negotiated image rights deals for Kevin De Bruyne and others, said he was working for the club itself.

Calzada, a good friend of City chief executive Ferran Soriano, told me: ‘I’ve always been working on a commercial arrangement with the club. We help the club bring in deals.’

My sources on the Fordham story included an adviser to City chief executive Ferran Soriano (right, pictured with chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak)

Those controlling City’s information are not the only ones you go up against when challenging the notion of Sheikh Mansour (centre) as a beneficent altruist

The detail might seem arcane and dry. The small financial details get crushed these days in the stampede for the next soundbite or headline. But it was fundamental to City's attempts to comply with the rules set out for any teams wishing to compete in the Champions League, at a time when UEFA were investigating the club.

We published the article. ‘Manchester City earning millions from image rights after telling UEFA investigators they had sold them,’ our headline stated.

The full force of Manchester City’s lawyers came down on us in a way which I have not experienced in more than 30 years in this business. There was an immediate threat to sue. A demand from the specialist internet law firm City employed that the digital piece be removed. That an apology for it be published. And that I personally tweet out that apology. It would have been an unprecedented level of 'contrition'.

Ours was not a big operation. As I recall, the managing editor who fielded this, Will Gore, was juggling 1001 tasks and did not have a sea of lawyers in the next office. But we were not cowed. A detailed, 1,500-word defence of the story was sent in return. We waited. And we waited. And we heard no more from Manchester City or their specialist internet lawyers.

In November 2018, a cache of documents extracted by hacker Rui Pinto, and subsequently published, suggested that we actually only had half of the story.

City's owners, Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG) were in fact financing Fordham, according to the leaks – effectively paying part of the players' wages through the shell company which had paid City the £24.5m for the ‘image rights’. Not only were City boosting their income against the rules but reducing their headline wage bill as they did so.

Of course, those controlling City’s information are not the only ones you go up against when challenging the fluffy PR notion of Sheikh Mansour as a beneficent altruist. Many's the time that their weaponised supporters have dispensed filth on social media. They still will.

Last Friday’s revelation that City had been found guilty on all but one relatively inconsequential charge was justification for all who have seen through City’s deceit and questioned the absurd notion that they are the victims of some Manchester United and Liverpool led ‘red cartel’.

And, let it be said, justification for the staff of the Premier League, for whom this experience has not been easy. The Premier League, more than any, have refused to be intimidated.

Staff at the Premier League, including CEO Richard Masters, have remained steadfast in their pursuing of the City case despite outside pressure

But when the League’s explosive and utterly damning statement was published late on Tuesday afternoon, there, in the relatively brief summary of how the club had artificially reduced its costs by £900million over nine seasons, was the name: ‘Fordham.’

It was detailed as one of the ‘sham arrangements’, entered into to enable City to ‘record lower operating expenses than it actually incurred.’ Yes, the statement related, there had been ‘a “sham” circular arrangement with Fordham.'

This was a rather more succinct and emphatic way of putting it than we accomplished in November 2018 for an article that was never removed and is still very much there. We were right all along and despite the mess, waste and ugliness of this interminable case, there is a sweet kind of vindication about that.

Sports.title: How JAMIE CHADWICK made Formula One history: Daily Mail Sport meets the first female star to drive an F1 car in over 10 years
Sports.content:
How JAMIE CHADWICK made Formula One history: Daily Mail Sport meets the first female star to drive an F1 car in over 10 years

There are moments in a racing driver's career that are measured in victories, championships and podiums.

Then there are the moments that transcend the results sheet.

For Jamie Chadwick, this was one of them.

Daily Mail Sport was in Portugal as the 28-year-old climbed into the Williams FW47 at Portimao and became the first woman to drive a modern Williams Formula One car since Susie Wolff in 2015.

Seven years after first joining the Williams Driver Academy, Chadwick finally got the opportunity she had once thought might never become reality.

And, speaking exclusively to Daily Mail Sport after completing 32 laps of the Autodromo Internacional do Algarve, she admitted the experience could ultimately sit at the very top of a career which already includes three consecutive W Series titles, victories in Indy NXT and the European Le Mans Series.

Jamie Chadwick climbed into the Williams FW47 at Portimao and became the first woman to drive a modern Williams Formula One car since Susie Wolff in 2015

Seven years after first joining the Williams Driver Academy, Chadwick finally got the opportunity she had once thought might never become reality

'I haven't done my list of achievements yet, but once I've done it, I would imagine it will be right up there as number one,' Chadwick said. 'It's not like I'm racing, so obviously, racing and winning is another feeling altogether.

'But so few people get the chance. It's the pinnacle of our sport. It's such an extreme level in terms of the level of the sport at the moment. So yeah, it's going to be pretty surreal and it's certainly top until the next step.'

The scale of the opportunity had not been lost on her before she even reached the circuit. Chadwick revealed she had deliberately tried not to get too excited after the prospect of the test had been discussed for some time.

'It was spoken a bit about not that long ago, and then it kind of went down to the chances of 50-50,' she said. 'I try to manage expectations even now until I've actually driven. I'm not going to believe that it's actually happening.

'So yeah, I try to manage my expectations, but also enjoy it. It's pretty surreal and it's a dream come true for sure.'

Then came the reality.

After simulator running, neck training and a seat fit at Williams' Grove headquarters, Chadwick arrived at Portimao and was finally faced with the FW47.

'The first time I got into the car for the seat fit, it was pretty surreal,' she said. 'I think when you see the steering wheel, you see the vision that you have when you play a computer game. That first feeling was unbelievable.'

But nothing compared with the moment the car left the garage.

'The first drive out of the garage and the first lap, that was something else, just the sheer acceleration,' she recalled. 'Even the feeling in the pit lane felt crazy enough.'

Chadwick has driven some formidable machinery during her career, including IndyCar and a Hypercar.

View this post on Instagram

Speaking to Daily Mail Sport after completing 32 laps of the Autodromo Internacional do Algarve, she admitted the experience could ultimately sit at the very top of a career

The Williams, however, was operating in another world.

'I think the F1 car sits where I expected it to, and that it is fully in a league of its own,' she said. 'I've been lucky enough to drive a few different amazing cars, IndyCar, Hypercar, but nothing really compares to what this car does and what it's able to do on a lap like Portimao.

'Just in terms of the sheer downforce, the grip, the straight-line speed. It's phenomenal.'

There was another, more personal, detail that followed Chadwick around on the day.

For years, she has written the word 'confidence' on the inside of her racing gloves - a reminder to back herself whenever doubts creep in behind the wheel. It started during her W Series days.

'I did it for my last W Series race in Austin in I think 2022, maybe 2021,' she explained. 'I always lacked a bit of confidence in the car, and for me, a lot of performance comes from confidence in a race car.

'So I wrote confidence to remind myself to be confident to do what I needed to do every time I looked down.'

She did not have the word written on her gloves for this particular test though. Perhaps she no longer needed it.

'Maybe today I should have had it,' Chadwick laughed. 'But yeah, I think it's seeped into my skin now. It's ingrained in me now.

'I'm just confident. I know what I am capable of. I don't need that reminder.'

That confidence has been built over years of experience - much of it alongside Williams.

Chadwick joined the team's Driver Academy in 2019 and has since progressed through different roles, while continuing to compete at the highest levels of motorsport.

She is now an ambassador and F1 Academy Adviser for the team, giving her a unique perspective on what it takes to reach the very top.

View this post on Instagram

Chadwick used to write 'confidence' on her racing gloves to inspire her while driving

The 28-year-old's CV already includes three consecutive W Series titles, victories in Indy NXT and the European Le Mans Series

'I think the level Formula One teams operate at is such a high level. You learn a huge amount,' she said. 'The infrastructure of a Formula One team, the inner workings. It's not just about one individual. There's multiple departments, multiple people, all kind of follow suit.

'I think how that operates, the level at which it operates, the technicality of a Formula One car in itself, everything, and then you throw that into a sporting setting is incredible.

'So I've been very lucky to be a part of it, and I've learned a huge amount over the years.'

Her test was also significant because of what it represented beyond Chadwick herself.

She became the first woman to drive a modern Williams F1 car since Wolff's 2015 test, underlining the progress made in creating pathways for female drivers while also highlighting just how difficult the final step remains.

Chadwick believes one of the biggest obstacles is simply the size of the talent pool.

'I think the reason we've not seen a woman in over 50 years is a few reasons,' she said. 'One is the talent pool is just so small. This is changing, but still, I think when you start in the sport, there's so few women, and so naturally to filter through to the pinnacle, there's only 22 seats in Formula One.

'It's such a small amount that it takes a lot more, I think, to be getting into the sport.'

But she believes that is changing. F1 Academy, grassroots karting initiatives and the growing involvement of Formula One teams are helping identify and develop female talent at an earlier age.

'Hopefully, eventually we're going to see some women racing in Formula One,' Chadwick said.

And perhaps that is why the significance of her day at Portimao goes beyond the 32 laps she completed.

She can now take the experience of actually driving a modern F1 car directly to the young women hoping to follow her.

'I now think my feeling of the sport at the top level is that much greater,' she said.

'I better understand what it takes to be a Formula 1 driver, and that's what a lot of these young drivers have aspirations of, and now I can feel a little bit closer to that.'

For Chadwick herself, though, the little girl who first climbed into a kart could never have imagined where it would lead.

She has previously spoken about getting into karting after going to a party with her brother Ollie - initially driven by the very simple desire to beat him.

Years later, she is a three-time champion, an Indy NXT and Le Mans race winner, a Williams ambassador and now a woman who has driven a Formula One car.

And yet there is still one driving-related problem she has apparently failed to solve.

'Still struggle with parking,' she admitted with a laugh.

'I wouldn't want to show you the state of the rims on my car. It's not even the rims. I've done even worse than that.

'I think I've done a few corners as well. So yeah, it's just parking, reversing. I mean, it's the stereotype, isn't it? But yeah, it's not good. It's bad.'

Parallel parking? Bay parking?

View this post on Instagram

'Honestly, all of it,' she said. 'Trying just not to hit anything. So then I think I panic so much about hitting other cars as well. And yeah, it's like when I get into those situations, I'm either fine and I nail it, or it's terrible.'

The irony is hard to miss.

A woman capable of controlling a Formula One car around one of Europe's most demanding circuits at extraordinary speeds, but still liable to panic when asked to reverse into a parking space.

Yet perhaps that is what makes the significance of the day all the greater.

Because beneath the history, the technology and the Williams badge was simply a driver living out a dream she once never expected to come true.

'Big Jamie's pretty overwhelmed,' she said when asked what the younger version of herself would make of it. 'It's insane. It's a dream come true more than anything else, and very surreal.

'I mean, to anyone that's not driven a Formula One car, it's hard to put into words just what that feeling is like.

'It's phenomenal. It's something so few people get the chance to do, and yeah, it's unbelievable.'

And for the next generation of girls watching her do it, Chadwick has one simple message.

'Don't let anything put you off,' she stressed. 'If there's a tiny bit of today's feeling that you can feel in the future, then it's absolutely worth it.

'Days like today are unbelievable, and yeah, I think it's possible.

'I cannot wait for the day that we see a young female driver line up on the Formula One grid.'

Sports.title: OLIVER HOLT: Man City have been exposed as the most famous cheats in English sporting history. The gory details revealed by the Premier League leave no doubt - nothing less than relegation will suffice for this sinister, dishonest club
Sports.content:
The Premier League shoved the owners of Manchester City into a beam of light on a dark stage on Tuesday evening. And the club that has dominated English football for much of the last 20 years stood there, defrocked and unmasked. Guilty of all charges, the League said. But that was not all it said.

In fact, it was the tone of the League’s statement that was the most startling thing about it. They are often circumspect and dull, these offerings. Not this time. This time, it was angry and it was vengeful.

It gloried in the gory details of the industrial-scale cheating it said City had indulged in for year after year as it duped the rest of football with a ‘disguised funding scheme’.

The anger was in the vocabulary, too. ‘Sham contracts,’ the Premier League statement hissed as it outlined the tactics of the Abu Dhabi United Group Investment & Development Ltd (ADUG), which owned the club.

‘Sham commercial deals,' it added later. Sham, sham, sham. Some had been expecting a conciliatory move from the League in the wake of its victory but this was anything but that.

To read that statement was to see the Premier League dancing on the grave of the club that had come to embody its excellence and its appeal. All the exasperation and all the frustration of years of obstruction and intransigence from City’s Abu Dhabi owners as they fought the 115 charges ranged against them came spilling out on that page.

This was an end to patience. This was an end to keeping one’s counsel. This was an end to diplomacy.

After the accusation, this was the confrontation. The most eye-catching part of it was the revelation of the extent of City’s wrongdoing. This was the juiciest steak the Premier League had to offer and they tossed it out into the public domain with uncommon relish.

‘The purpose of these schemes,’ its statement said, ‘was found to have been to artificially inflate the club’s revenues, and reduce its costs, by more than £900million during the affected period, to appear to comply with financial rules.’

The Premier League have accused Manchester City of 'artificially (inflating) the club’s revenues, and (reducing) its costs, by more than £900million'

To read that statement was to see the Premier League dancing on the grave of the club that had come to embody its excellence and its appeal under (from left) Khaldoon Al Mubarak, Txiki Begiristain and Ferran Soriano

This is English football’s civil war in all its ugliness and its violence and its ferocity. The League’s statement hinted at what is to come. City have until Friday to launch an appeal, which they will almost certainly do but when that is done, it appears the League will press for severe sanctions to quell the inferno of City’s misdemeanours.

The level of City’s duplicity, outlined by the Premier League, laid bare the extent of the advantage that they had gained over the period involved. The punishment will have to fit that. It is harder to see City escaping relegation than it was on Tuesday morning. Anything lesser than that, the League will surely believe, will not be enough to deal with the crimes uncovered.

In the hours that followed the release of the statement, television screens showed reruns of City’s moments of triumph – Phil Foden holding aloft the Premier League trophy on one of the club’s many open-top bus rides, Pep Guardiola and City’s chairman, Khaldoon Al Mubarak, standing together on the pitch at the Etihad Stadium, holding up six fingers to signify the number of leagues Guardiola won.

The footage did not speak of triumphs any more, though. It spoke of subterfuge and shame. Those scenes of jubilation, it now appears, were dishonestly earned. Those trophies were dishonestly won. The club had cheated and cheated and cheated to get to a position where it was held up as the exemplar of all that was good in the game.

The more we know, the worse this feels. The more we know, the more stupid we seem that we were duped, that we believed.

This is moving into Lance Armstrong territory now. This is Chicago Black Sox territory. City, a team once famous for hitting new heights of dominance, are now the most famous cheats in English sporting history.

Their owners are still sticking to their story, even in the face of the findings of the independent commission and the details now provided by the Premier League. Their response has not been humility or contrition. Their response has been, actually, the sinister language of threat and reprisal.

City’s owners are serious people. Al Mubarak, many say, is the equivalent of the prime minister of the UAE. Others equate his role to cabinet secretary. He wields much power and he is the guardian of much wealth. No one takes him on like this and now that someone has, he is fighting to the end.

For now, City are sticking to Al Mubarak’s insistence that they have ‘irrefutable evidence’ that proves their innocence.

It is a curious defence. If the evidence is irrefutable, why has it not been presented already? Why has it been hidden away? Were these men not so powerful and astute, it would be tempting to say that their stance is becoming faintly comical.

The more we know, the more stupid we seem that we were duped, that we believed. Some would say this whole affair is moving into Lance Armstrong territory now

City are sticking to Al Mubarak’s insistence that they have ‘irrefutable evidence’ that proves their innocence. If the evidence is irrefutable, where is it?

‘Manchester City FC is both disappointed and surprised by the opinion of the Premier League Commission,’ a City statement said. ‘The club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case.

'The club will therefore be relentless, and where necessary proactive, in any and all appropriate regulatory and legal forums.’

Relentless? That is redolent of Al Mubarak’s notorious assertion more than a decade ago, when City were fighting UEFA, that he would rather spend £30m on the best 50 lawyers in the world and sue UEFA for the next 10 years than lose the Financial Fair Play case in which they were adversaries.

I wonder if some of those who have lionised Al Mubarak for his statements will reconsider now. They said they would when it came to a point when City’s guilt was outlined for all to see. Well, it is out there now. It is there in all its sad and ugly detail. Perhaps some of City’s fans will start to realise now that they, too, have been deceived.

City’s owners, though, will not back down. It is not their style. After months and years of shadow-boxing, the gloves are off. And City stand alone in the ring.

Sports.title: Martin Keown reveals his dementia fears as Arsenal legend walks 100 laps of Lord's for Alzheimer's Society after witnessing mother's ordeal
Sports.content:
Martin Keown reveals his dementia fears as Arsenal legend walks 100 laps of Lord's for Alzheimer's Society after witnessing mother's ordeal

Under the watchful gaze of Old Father Time, Martin Keown takes another step around the famous Lord’s turf as he reflects on how much we can lose as the clock ticks away.

Daily Mail Sport joined the former Arsenal and England defender as they and nearly 100 others walked a century of laps around the outfield – the equivalent of more than 31 miles – to bring up their own century at Lord’s and raise money for Alzheimer’s Society.

Keown’s mother Angela has lived with Alzheimer’s for more than 20 years, and now resides in a care home. Before then, he passed up the chance to work with Arsene Wenger after his playing career to help his dad care for her.

The former Arsenal and England defender also talks as we walk, his wife Nicola alongside him, about how a career playing the sport he loves has likely robbed him of precious time with his loved ones later in life, so close is the link between dementia and heading the ball.

Keown has admitted in the past his worries about a 21-year career heading a football. Towards the end of his playing days, he got dizziness and double vision when heading one travelling at speed.

‘The game you love has kind of taken away vital time ahead of me to spend with my loved ones,’ he says. ‘It’s like a paradox, isn’t it? But I made those choices. I didn’t know the outcome that playing football would be so problematic. But I don’t regret it.’

Martin Keown, whose mother Angela has lived with Alzheimer’s for more than 20 years, has helped to raise money for Alzheimer’s Society by completing laps around Lord's

Keown has admitted to having his own fears that heading a football during a 21-year career has likely robbed him of precious time with his loved ones later in life

Only, as Keown is keen to point out, it is far from just footballers who are at serious risk. That is not the reason he’s here, walking lap after lap. One in three of us born in the UK will develop dementia in our lifetime and yet one in three people living with the condition do so without being diagnosed.

‘We need to create an awareness of what’s happening with dementia and Alzheimer’s,’ says Keown. ‘How poorly it’s funded and how, if you have a loved one in this terrible plight, how you get some help on this journey. Because it's a very difficult journey.’

Alzheimer’s disease and dementia remain the biggest killers in the UK, accounting for nearly 77,000 deaths a year. There remains no cure.

’It’s not just something you get when you’re old, let’s be clear about that,’ he adds. ‘When I go to visit my mum, I see quite young people. I wonder is it a carer or a patient and, invariably, it’s a patient.’

As always with dementia, it’s as much about the toll it takes on those close to the sufferer. ‘Who is caring for the carer? My father said “Look, we supported you for 22 years as a player”. I had a real dilemma but I needed to commit to my family. The most amount of care is coming from a loved one and you cannot put a price on that.

‘My dad said it was the biggest fight of his life to keep my mum at home. It really was. He learned to cook. He learned to sew. This was a guy that was in management and he just completely retrained himself. It was unbelievable.

‘My mum, believe it or not, could still iron. She was one of the quickest ironers. She could still remember. She didn’t want that taken away but then she’d leave the iron on and would burn herself. It was becoming dangerous but she could still remember. You hear of people with dementia still being able to play piano.’

‘When you’ve got a loved one, you just get drowned in it all. It becomes so solemn and you wonder what’s life for, what you’re battling for. You see someone work their whole life for their retirement and the minute they get there, they’re just looking out of the window like a mannequin.

It can demotivate you but we need to make sure that doesn’t happen to other people. That’s where the motivation has to be, doesn’t it? All of this walking takes us a step closer to finding a cure.’

Sports.title: Ian Wright urges Premier League to hit Man City with 'unprecedented' punishment for £900m financial sham after being found guilty of 'cheating on an industrial scale' - and warns of impact on current season
Sports.content:
Ian Wright urges Premier League to hit Man City with 'unprecedented' punishment for £900m financial sham after being found guilty of 'cheating on an industrial scale' - and warns of impact on current season

Manchester City should be hit with an 'unprecedented punishment' by the Premier League for their financial sham, says Ian Wright.

Wright blasted City for cheating 'on an industrial scale' and fears for the 'messy' ongoing fallout, with City set to appeal despite being found guilty of all the major charges against them.

The Premier League condemned City for making 'sham' agreements to articifically inflate their revenue and reduce their operating costs over a nine-season period which saw them win eight trophies.

Speaking before England's match against Czechia, Wright told ITV Sport: 'It's cheating on an industrial scale. It's quite surreal seeing it written down like that.

'The amount of stick I've taken off that. Unprecedented punishment is required here. It's a massive day for the Premier League. They've taken on a whole country, massive.

'Very messy. It's a problem for them to be going to Liverpool (in their next fixture). In their real time, Liverpool were the team chasing them down. Look at what Jurgen Klopp went through to break them - it probably broke him.

The Premier League have confirmed that Manchester City are guilty of the most serious financial rule breaches

Ian Wright said Man City deserved the punishment but that it is 'not good for the league'

'It's so sad. It's probably going to get very litigious.'

Roy Keane added: 'It's very damaging for the league, the brand is huge all over the world, but for them to be caught cheating, they deserve that punishment.

'It's bittersweet. You deserve to be punishment but it's not good for the league. What about the players who have been part of the problem, new players, what happens now going forward?'

On Friday, Daily Mail Sport reported how City had been found guilty of a series of breaches over a nine-year, glittering period in its history, in a verdict which sent shockwaves through football and opened the door to huge penalties including possible expulsion.

However, there had been no official comment from the Premier League on the findings of an independent panel who oversaw a hearing that concluded in December 2024.

That has now dramatically changed. In a lengthy statement, the Premier League say City arranged 'sham contracts (which misrepresented the true agreement between the parties) with a number of its commercial partners, as well as relying on "sham" agreements with others, to artificially inflate the club's revenues and reduce its costs'.

It also says the club falsely altered the financial picture at the Etihad to the tune of £900m. The club had agreed exorbitant sponsorship deals with a number of companies, but those sponsors only paid part of the fee.

The rest was propped up by the Abu Dhabi United Group Investment & Development Ltd (ADUG), which owned the club.

Premier League CEO Richard Masters claimed that the commission's verdict had 'vindicated' the league's decision to pursue the charges

As the Premier League note, this allowed the City to 'artificially inflate the club’s revenues' and therefore spend more under Premier League rules. The higher the revenue a club records, the more they are permitted to spend.

Moreover, further 'sham' deals, funded by ADUG, allowed the club to 'record lower operating expenses than it actually incurred'.

The Premier League say that revenues were inflated and costs reduced to the tune of £900m in an attempt to comply with spending rules. The result was that the club 'filed misstated accounts and concealed the true state of its finances from its auditors and football regulators'.

It added that the club was 'significantly in breach of both the Premier League's and UEFA's spending limits' during the time period in question, 2009-2018 when it won eight major trophies.

Had City reported accurately 'it would have been in breach of both the League's and UEFA's spending limits by a very substantial amount'.

The panel also found that City committed multiple breaches of its duties of co-operation and good faith in that it failed to assist the Premier League's four-year investigation, triggered by the emergence of club emails obtained by a hacker.

Indeed, City had 'made concerted efforts to stop and frustrate the PL investigation'.

Richard Masters, Chief Executive of the Premier League, said: 'The core decision establishes the facts of what happened at Manchester City during this period. It details how the club systematically broke Premier League Rules for nearly a decade.

'It also vindicates the Premier League's decision to pursue this case against Manchester City. While the process to date has been both long and difficult, the League has remained determined that the facts be established independently.

'It is a key responsibility of the Premier League to ensure that the Rules, approved by the clubs themselves, are upheld to protect the integrity of the competition. It is paramount that the League remains competitive and fair for all clubs and for the fans. We take that role extremely seriously.

'This disciplinary case, and this decision, are the most significant in Premier League history. There are elements of the case that remain to be decided, including, importantly, what sanction must follow for these breaches. Now we have the Commission's decision, we are committed to moving swiftly through the remainder of the process, to provide certainty for the League, our clubs and fans.'

Manchester City have insisted on their innocence throughout the saga (Pep Guardiola pictured with chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak)

In a statement released a short time later, City said it was ‘disappointed and surprised’ and referred to the ‘opinion of the Premier League Commission’.

It added: ‘The club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case. The club will therefore be relentless, and where necessary proactive, in any and all appropriate regulatory and legal forums.

‘The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements uncompleted. Manchester City will now pursue the appeal avenues open to it, on the basis that the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe.

‘The club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League Board and Executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence.

‘The club is obviously restricted in what it can say further until all future proceedings are complete.’

City have until Friday to appeal.

Man City were first charged with the 115 breaches in February 2023. While that totemic number stuck, the figure – as they subsequently corrected – was actually 130.

Of those, 54 were charges of ‘failure to provide accurate and up-to-date financial information’ while there were 14 charges of ‘failure to provide accurate financial reports for player and manager compensation’.

Both sets related to alleged offences between 2009 and 2018 (2009-2018), an eight-year period which saw the club win four Premier League titles, the FA Cup, and three League Cup competitions.

There were also five charges of ‘failure to comply with UEFA’s regulations, including Financial Fair Play Regulations’ and seven charges of breaching the Premier League’s profit and sustainability regulations (PSR) between 2015 and 2018.

There were also 35 counts of failure to co-operate with Premier League investigations between 2018 and 2023.

The hearing into the 130 breaches began last September at London’s International Dispute Resolution Centre, with the Premier League sparing no expense and enlisting KCs Adam Lewis and Andrew Hunter to take its case.

There are elements of the case that remain to be decided, including, importantly, what sanction must follow for these breaches. Now we have the Commission’s decision, we are committed to moving swiftly through the remainder of the process, to provide certainty for the League, our clubs and fans."

Article continues below

City have the right to appeal the verdict that has been reached by the independent commission, with the deadline set for this Friday (October 2).

Sports.title: Premier League chief breaks silence on Man City's 'systematic' and 'decade-long' rule breaking
Sports.content:
Premier League chief breaks silence on Man City's 'systematic' and 'decade-long' rule breaking

The Premier League have released a statement confirming Manchester City's guilty verdict with the top-flight club responding

View 2 Images Richard Masters, CEO of the Premier League, has released a statement on Manchester City's rule breaches. (Image: PA Wire)

Premier League chief executive Richard Masters has broken his silence on Manchester City's 'systematic' breaching of rules over a nine-year spell. The top-flight released a statement today (Tuesday) revealing the outcome of the investigation into their alleged 115 charges, relating to financial regulations and failure to co-operate with the League’s investigation.

‌



City were found guilty of 'all charges related to serious breaches of the Premier League’s financial rules over a nine-season period, and the majority of charges in relation to its failure to co-operate with the League’s investigation.' The club still maintain their innocence.

‌



In a statement, Masters said: "The core decision establishes the facts of what happened at Manchester City during this period. It details how the club systematically broke Premier League Rules for nearly a decade.

‌



"It also vindicates the Premier League’s decision to pursue this case against Manchester City. While the process to date has been both long and difficult, the League has remained determined that the facts be established independently.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

"It is a key responsibility of the Premier League to ensure that the Rules, approved by the clubs themselves, are upheld to protect the integrity of the competition. It is paramount that the League remains competitive and fair for all clubs and for the fans. We take that role extremely seriously.

‌



"This disciplinary case, and this decision, are the most significant in Premier League history. There are elements of the case that remain to be decided, including, importantly, what sanction must follow for these breaches.

"Now we have the Commission’s decision, we are committed to moving swiftly through the remainder of the process, to provide certainty for the League, our clubs and fans."

View 2 Images Manchester City have been found guilty of 114 charges of breaching Premier League financial regulations (Image: Michael Regan, Getty Images)

‌



City have, in turn, responded to the statement and said: "Manchester City FC is both disappointed and surprised by the opinion of the Premier League Commission, which has been published today.

"The Club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case.

"The Club will therefore be relentless, and where necessary proactive, in any and all appropriate regulatory and legal forums.

‌



"The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements uncompleted. Manchester City FC will now pursue the appeal avenues open to it, on the basis that the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe.

"The Club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League Board and Executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence.

"The Club is obviously restricted in what it can say further until all future proceedings are complete."

Sports.title: Premier League drop damning Man City 115 charges verdict as 'sham' contracts called out
Sports.content:
The Premier League have confirmed that Manchester City have been found guilty of breaches of financial rules, calling it the most significant disciplinary case in the division's history in a scathing statement.

A three-person independent panel has upheld the charges brought by the Premier League to City in February 2023, over a year after the hearing ended. It has been confirmed that City were found guilty of 'all charges related to serious breaches of the Premier League’s financial rules over a nine-season period, and the majority of charges in relation to its failure to co-operate with the League’s investigation'.

City's transgressions include 'sham deals' that helped to artificially inflate the club’s revenues by more than £900 million. City strongly deny the charges, and are expected to lodge an appeal against the verdict. They have until October 2nd to do so.

The division has released a statement outlining where the club fell foul. Predominantly four areas:

‌



Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

- Manchester City arranged ‘sham’ contracts (which misrepresented the true agreement between the parties) with a number of its commercial partners, as well as relying on ‘sham’ agreements with others, to artificially inflate the club’s revenues and reduce its costs

- The club filed misstated accounts and concealed the true state of its finances from its auditors and football regulators - Manchester City was significantly in breach of both the Premier League’s and UEFA’s spending limits - During the Premier League’s investigation, Manchester City committed multiple breaches of its duties of co-operation and utmost good faith towards the League (three of the four alleged breaches were upheld)

The Premier League's statement added: "The independent Commission found that Manchester City arranged ‘sham’ commercial deals with a number of its sponsors during the period, which were part of a disguised funding scheme, whereby those companies were only required to pay a portion of the relevant sponsorship fees. The remainder was funded by Abu Dhabi United Group Investment & Development Ltd (ADUG), which owned the club. As part of the scheme, further ‘sham’ arrangements, funded by ADUG, were entered into to enable the club to record lower operating expenses than it actually incurred, as well as a ‘sham’ circular arrangement with Fordham, an entity that purchased the club’s players’ image rights, that was funded by ADUG.

‌



"The purpose of these schemes was found to have been to artificially inflate the club’s revenues, and reduce its costs, by more than £900 million during the affected period, to appear to comply with financial rules. The consequence of this, as the Commission found, was that the club filed misstated accounts and concealed the true state of its finances from its auditors and football regulators. The Commission concluded that ‘by its conduct the club clearly intended to circumvent the PL Rules‘.

"As a result, Manchester City failed to accurately report its income and expenditure for the purposes of the Premier League’s Profitability and Sustainability Rules and UEFA’s Club Licensing and Financial Fair Play Rules. The Commission found that, had all of the relevant agreements been reported accurately in the club’s accounts, it would have been in breach of both the League’s and UEFA’s spending limits by a very substantial amount.

"In addition, during the course of the four-year investigation conducted by the Premier League, the club committed multiple breaches of its duties of co-operation and utmost good faith towards the League. The Commission concluded that the club had ‘made concerted efforts to stop and frustrate the PL investigation’."

‌



Richard Masters, Chief Executive of the Premier League, said: “The core decision establishes the facts of what happened at Manchester City during this period. It details how the club systematically broke Premier League Rules for nearly a decade.

“It also vindicates the Premier League’s decision to pursue this case against Manchester City. While the process to date has been both long and difficult, the League has remained determined that the facts be established independently.

“It is a key responsibility of the Premier League to ensure that the Rules, approved by the clubs themselves, are upheld to protect the integrity of the competition. It is paramount that the League remains competitive and fair for all clubs and for the fans. We take that role extremely seriously.

“This disciplinary case, and this decision, are the most significant in Premier League history. There are elements of the case that remain to be decided, including, importantly, what sanction must follow for these breaches. Now we have the Commission’s decision, we are committed to moving swiftly through the remainder of the process, to provide certainty for the League, our clubs and fans.”

‌



JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

Manchester City maintain their innocence and have expressed their shock at the independent panel's decision. They claim to have irrefutable evidence.

"Manchester City FC is both disappointed and surprised by the opinion of the Premier League Commission, that has been published today," they said.

"The Club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case. The Club will therefore be relentless, and where necessary proactive, in any and all appropriate regulatory and legal forums.

‌



"The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements uncompleted. Manchester City FC will now pursue the appeal avenues open to it, on the basis that the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe.

"The Club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League Board and Executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence.

"The Club is obviously restricted in what it can say further until all future proceedings are complete."

The statements follow reports of the guilty verdict on 114 of the 115 charges surfaced on September 25. At that time, City released a statement via a spokesperson.

‌



“The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements to be completed, and subject to strict confidentiality," it read. "As such Manchester City FC’s position remains consistent with the club’s statement of February 2023.

“The club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis the Premier League board and executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair minded regulator, free from partisan influence.”

Around 24 hours later, City chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak published an open letter to fans. "I have been part of this Club for 18 years," it read.

"I have had the privilege to stand with you in the Etihad, at Wembley, and in Istanbul. This Club matters to me, and you have shown and told me – time and time again - how much Manchester City matters to you. This is why I am writing to you today.

‌



"Following Friday’s media reporting, many of you will have spent your evening answering questions and responding to messages from friends, family and colleagues. So have I. Here’s what I said to my family: The Premier League process still has a long way to run, and our confidence and intent in proving the Club’s innocence is just as strong as when this began.

"There are so many things that I would like to be able to share with you to help you understand why we feel so confident in our position. But the strict confidentiality of the legal process and our determination to respect it means I cannot do that at the moment. Even this letter underwent several legal checks to make sure it complies.

View Image Man City Chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak released an open letter to fans following the reports. (Image: Martin Rickett/PA Wire)

"I ask you to please carefully read the statement below, which we gave on Friday, and the statement we issued in February 2023. Every word matters and holds true.

‌



"While some people have been quick to reach their own conclusions, and there is so much noise swirling around us, nothing has changed. We have faced challenges together before and have prevailed. There remain many who want to undermine the momentum of our Club. We will not give them that opportunity.

"We have some exciting moments to look forward to after this international break. We travel to Anfield in a fortnight, and then host Paris St Germain in the Champions League back at Etihad Stadium - moments that give us an opportunity to celebrate the strength of the Manchester City family.

"Thank you, as always, for your constant support."

The aforementioned statement released by City in 2023, when the charges were first brought to them, said: "Manchester City FC is surprised by the issuing of these alleged breaches of the Premier League Rules, particularly given the extensive engagement and vast amount of detailed materials that the EPL has been provided with.

‌



"The Club welcomes the review of this matter by an independent Commission, to impartially consider the comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence that exists in support of its position. As such we look forward to this matter being put to rest once and for all."

Sports.title: Why Man City stars signed in £700m rebuild did not insist on relegation clauses - despite 115 charges
Sports.content:
When Erling Haaland signed a record nine-and-a-half year deal in January 2025 to keep him at Manchester City until his 34th birthday, the obvious first question was about the 115 charges.

Haaland was asked if his new deal had an escape clause should City be found guilty, the Norway striker replied: “No.”

City have locked down their biggest asset - arguably the most lethal striker in the world - for nearly a decade and the best years of his career. He is still only 26.

Every major club in the world is now watching what happens next with Haaland and be ready to pounce if he suddenly becomes available. But that also goes for the rest of City’s huge list of superstars who have helped them enjoy so much success for the past few years.

‌



However, it is not just Haaland who does not have an escape clause should the worst happen and City are found guilty and kicked out of the Premier League as by way of punishment.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

Other huge names signed in the last three transfer windows - City’s net spend has been in excess of £300m between July 2025 and September 2026 - do not have escape clauses either.

‌



But it does beg the question: how did Manchester City negotiate deals for players with everyone knowing that the day of reckoning was coming?

The charges for breaching Premier League financial rules were lodged in February 2023 but that has not stopped the club’s success or attracting the best players in the meantime.

Rayan Cherki, Gianlugi Donnarumma, Antooine Semenyo, Marc Guehi all joined in 2025-2026, before the huge £450m outlay on an entirely new midfield this summer, including Enzo Fernandez, Elliott Anderson, Ayyoub Bouaddi, plus Iliman Ndiaye.

Argentina midfielder Fernandez had his heart set on Manchester City. Not only did he tell Chelsea he wanted to leave - but he also made it clear he wanted to go to City.

‌



England international Anderson had a straight choice between City and Manchester United - and chose City. It was the same for other players. Guehi could have had the pick of his clubs in the summer if he had waited to be a free agent - and yet chose City in January. Semenyo probably knew Arsenal would revisit a possible deal if he had bided his time.

View 3 Images Erling Haaland signed a nine-and-a-half year deal with City in 2025 (Image: Offside via Getty Images)

And if you look at the overhaul, City have completely changed their squad. From keeper (Ederson replaced by Donnarumma), a new-look defence and midfield with the likes of Kevin De Bruyne and Bernardo Silva moving on and Anderson, Fernandez and so on coming in.

Surely this is beyond a squad rebuild. There must have been some contingency planning in there in case they do get found guilty and not only face relegation but also get a transfer ban. But City do not see it like that. Either way, the squad is now incredibly well stocked.

‌



But the key factors in persuading those players to sign was not relegation clauses but a promise to honour any bonuses, add-ons and payments based on success. Bonuses which would ordinarily be easily achievable. They will honour those contracts. The contracts will be water tight legally and that is down to a good agent to ensure his client is protected.

The other thing that people overlook is the power of City’s belief that, as a club, they will ultimately prove their innocence.

Inside the club, there has always been a genuine belief that they have enough evidence to answer the accusations and over the accusations. It is unshakeable - no matter what we think from the outside. There has never been any doubt in the words, hearts and minds of City executives when talking to players, agents and families. That is pretty persuasive.

View 3 Images Enzo Fernandez joined City for a British record transfer fee (Image: Richard Sellers/Allstar, Getty Images)

‌



Ultimately, players probably do not need relegation escape clauses. If the ultimate punishment comes, the club will not be able to keep that wage bill in the Championship let alone League One, no matter who owns the club.

The likes of Haaland and Co have a genuine feeling for this club. And that should not be underestimated. That will be the same for others. But it would be naive to suggest that players will not want to leave to play Champions League football and fight for the biggest trophies. City’s hand will probably be forced. That is how football works.

But the storm which has been brewing for years, never remotely affected City’s ability to attract and sign the best players to stay at the top no matter what.
