World.title: Breaking: NNPC’s Profit Up 33% to N7.2tn as Revenue Hits N34.5tn
World.content:
Emmanuel Addeh in Abuja

The Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited (NNPC) on Tuesday afternoon released its 2025 Audited Financial Statement (AFS), reporting a 33 per cent surge in Profit After Tax (PAT) to N7.2 trillion, up from N5.4 trillion recorded in 2024.

The announcement was made during a press briefing at the NNPC headquarters in Abuja by the Group Chief Executive Officer (GCEO), Mr. Bayo Ojulari.

Besides, the state-owned energy company generated a total revenue of N34.5 trillion for the year, while delivering an earnings per share of N35.9.

Notably, remittances to the federal government in the form of taxes, royalties, and other statutory payments climbed by 39 per cent to reach N22.3 trillion.

Explaining the operational dynamics, Ojulari noted that total revenue declined year-on-year due to lower global crude oil prices and reduced white product volumes following market deregulation.

However, he stated that profit grew significantly as a result of improved operational efficiency and sustained financial discipline across the business.

On the operational front, he revealed that crude oil and condensate production reached a five-year peak of 1.77 million barrels per day (bpd).

In the same vein, natural gas supply hit a three-year high of 7.2 billion standard cubic feet per day, driven by targeted investments in key assets and infrastructure.

Details later…

World.title: Tosin Bee Returns to Big Stage With Heavenly Praise Affair
World.content:
​Lagos stood still on Sunday, September 20, 2026, as Regal Hall in Oregun, Ikeja, transformed into a sanctuary of divine encounters for Praise Affair with Tosin Bee: The Thanksgiving.

Draped in rich royal purple and gold aesthetics, the night delivered a seamless fusion of refined worship, cutting-edge production, and infectious high praise.

​For the celebrated Afro-gospel and highlife minister, songwriter, and music director, the evening was more than a performance it was a triumphant return to headline billing.

Tosin Bee’s last major concert was Switch with Tosin Bee at the MUSON Centre in September 2019.

Though he kept audiences global through live recordings, single releases, and international tours, Lagos was hungry for his homecoming.

​”This night was simply our way of saying thank you to God,” Tosin Bee stated.

“The Thanksgiving was not a concert; it was an altar, and the Beezle People came ready to worship.”

​Backed by his Beezle Nation team, Tosin Bee guided the audience through dynamic worship sessions in English and Yoruba, smoothly shifting from quiet adoration to electric praise.

​Clergy, VIPs, Gospel Powerhouses Unite At Regal Hall

​The event drew prominent church leaders and notable figures from across the state.

Chairman of the Lagos State Pentecostal Fellowship of Nigeria (PFN), Pastor Yemi Davids, offered a memorable address to the packed auditorium, reminding attendees that “when we are praising God, we are exalting His abilities,” before offering prayers for Tosin Bee, his team, and the congregation.

​Adding to the glory of the night was an exceptional roster of guest ministers, including: Beejay Sax, Kaestrings, Adeyinka Alaseyori, Laolu Gbenjo, Eniola Olusoga, Steve Hills, Elijah Daniel, SMJ and Lillian Nneji.

​By the end of the night, attendees were already buzzing about Praise Affair 2027—a clear indication that Tosin Bee has firmly reclaimed his spotlight on the gospel music scene.

World.title: Man City CEO Defiant over Premier League Charges
World.content:
Manchester City Chief Executive, Ferran Soriano, has issued a defiant message to the executives of other teams about the club being found guilty of a majority of Premier League charges, BBC Sport has been told.

He was speaking at a board meeting of European Football Clubs (formerly the ECA) in Copenhagen before its general assembly on Tuesday.

Soriano was said to have vowed to fight the charges and the process had a long way to run, reiterating what the club’s Chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak said in a letter to fans.

The Press Association reported Soriano told the executives “it’s taken eight years to get here and it’s going to take a lot more time”, referring to the start of the Premier League’s investigation in 2018.

He then left the meeting without answering any questions from the media.

The report added Manchester United’s Chief of International Football Relations, Jean-Claude Blanc, and Everton owner Dan Friedkin – there in his capacity as owner of Roma – were among those to attend.

City were accused of a wide range of rule breaches, centering around claims they inflated sponsorship revenue from connected companies and made other “off the books” payments to circumvent financial regulations.

On Friday, it emerged they had been found guilty of the vast majority of the 115 charges brought against them.

World.title: Peak Celebrates Super Eagles’ Madagascar Victory with Breakfast in Uyo
World.content:
Peak Milk, the Official Milk of the Super Eagles, treated players and officials of Nigeria’s senior national football team to a special Peak Breakfast on Saturday, celebrating their 2-1 victory over Madagascar and rallying the team ahead of today’s crucial AFCON 2027 qualifier against Guinea-Bissau.

The breakfast activation, held at the team’s Four Points by Sheraton camp in Ikot Ekpene, brought together the 24 players invited by Head Coach Eric Chelle and members of the technical crew for a morning of nourishment, celebration and camaraderie following Friday’s hard-fought win.

The players enjoyed a range of Peak dairy products as the brand continued its long-standing tradition of nourishing and supporting the Super Eagles through some of the team’s biggest moments.

Super Eagles Captain Wilfred Ndidi expressed the team’s appreciation for Peak’s enduring support.

“I always cherish these moments with Peak Milk. I have been part of Peak Breakfast with the Super Eagles on several occasions, and it always gives me joy,” Ndidi said.

“On behalf of the entire team, I thank Peak for this gesture. The support means a lot to us, and we hope to keep giving Nigerian fans the victories they deserve whenever we step onto the pitch.”

Head Coach Eric Chelle described the activation as another timely boost as Nigeria seeks to build momentum in the AFCON qualifying campaign.

“This gives us additional encouragement as we prepare for the next challenge,” Chelle said. “We appreciate Peak for putting this together and for continuing to stand behind the team.”

Speaking at the event, Omolara Banjoko, Marketing Manager, Peak FrieslandCampina WAMCO, said Peak Breakfast was designed to nourish the players while reinforcing the positive atmosphere in camp following the opening victory.

Peter James, Category Brand Manager, Peak, said the activation was deliberately designed to create a connection with the players beyond the football pitch. As the Official Milk of the Super Eagles, Peak has consistently stood behind Nigeria’s number one football team.

“This breakfast is another expression of that commitment—nourishing the players, celebrating their victory and encouraging them as they continue their AFCON qualification journey.”

“As the Official Milk of the Super Eagles, Peak is proud to be part of their journey and to continue nourishing their passion.”

Peak’s relationship with Nigerian football dates back to 1998, when the brand supported the Super Eagles on their journey to the global football finals in France. The brand was also part of the Eagles’ memorable 2013 Africa Cup of Nations triumph in South Africa and has remained closely associated with the national team through successive generations.

Friday’s victory provided even more reason for celebration at the breakfast.

Debutants George Ilenikhena and Moses Usor were on target as Nigeria overcame a determined Madagascar side 2-1 to open their AFCON 2027 qualifying campaign with three valuable points.

The occasion was particularly memorable for Moses Simon, who marked his 100th appearance for Nigeria—a milestone that provided another fitting reason for celebration during Saturday’s Peak Breakfast.

Attention now turns to Tuesday, when the Super Eagles face Guinea-Bissau in a top-of-the-table encounter at the 24 de Setembro Stadium in Bissau, while Madagascar host Tanzania.

For Peak, the mission remains unchanged: nourishing the Super Eagles as they pursue another successful journey on the African football stage.

World.title: ‘The nation is angry’: Ramaphosa names slain women and girls
World.content:
In his national address, President Cyril Ramaphosa named victims, spoke of women still lying unidentified in mortuaries and admitted government had not done enough to stop the violence. Images: Facebook/Nabeelah Shaik, SAPS, SABC and X/SA Government.

President Cyril Ramaphosa has named several of the women and girls killed across South Africa in recent weeks as he confronted the country’s deepening gender-based violence crisis.

During his address to the nation on Tuesday night, 29 September, Ramaphosa said the number of women’s bodies found in Ekurhuleni since July had risen to 11, before naming victims from Gauteng and other parts of the country.

He said the names represented only some of the women and girls whose lives had been taken.



“These are only some of the women and girls whose lives have been taken away from us in recent weeks,” Ramaphosa said.

“Theirs are the names we know. There are others whose names we do not know yet.”

Ramaphosa also spoke of unidentified women still lying in government mortuaries, waiting for families to claim them and take them home for burial.

“There are women lying tonight in government mortuaries waiting to be identified, waiting for someone to claim them, waiting to be taken home and laid to rest,” he said.

The address came after weeks of killings in Ekurhuleni that have triggered a national-level police investigation and intensified scrutiny of South Africa’s response to gender-based violence and femicide.

Ramaphosa names Ekurhuleni victims

Ramaphosa named several women whose deaths have formed part of the wave of killings under investigation in Ekurhuleni.



They included Busisiwe Mahlangu, Itumeleng Kekana, Nomfesane Mjobo, Gracious Nkomo, Elizabeth Moselakgomo, Dineo Motapane, Jabulile Ntimba and Ntombifuthi Nxumalo.

Another woman’s body found in Springs on Sunday pushed the number of women found dead in Ekurhuleni since July to 11.

Police have made arrests in some cases and identified persons of interest in others.

Investigators have also collected DNA, blood samples, clothing, cellphones and cellphone records as they try to establish whether any of the cases are linked.

The Council for Scientific and Industrial Research is assisting with digital forensic work.

‘There are others whose names we do not know’

Ramaphosa then widened his address beyond Ekurhuleni and named women and girls killed elsewhere in South Africa.

He referred to victims from communities including Delft, Orlando East, Komani, Richmond, Limpopo and Port Alfred.

Among those he mentioned were 10-year-old Octavia Swartz, Nomakwezi Zeta, Josephine Tshabalala, Siyavuya Mlunguza, Mariette Mouton, Christina Nyalungu, Sibongile Mthali, 15-year-old Amokhela Mutswaiedi, Pinky Shalembe, Nombizane Mbanjwa and Amanda Gosani.

He said those names still did not capture the full scale of the violence.

“Behind each of these terrible deaths was a human being, a daughter, a mother, a sister, a friend, an aunt, a grandmother, whose life had value, whose future mattered and whose absence has left a family and a community grieving,” Ramaphosa said.

‘The nation is angry’

Ramaphosa opened his address by acknowledging the anger and grief surrounding the killings.

“The nation is angry. The women of South Africa are angry. Their anger is justified. I too share that anger,” he said.

He described violence against women as a source of “profound pain and national shame”.

Ramaphosa said women across South Africa were living with the fear that they could be next.

“No woman should have to live with that fear.”

Ramaphosa admits government has not done enough

The President also made a direct admission about government’s response to gender-based violence.

“What we have done has not been enough,” he said.

“It has not been enough to prevent women from being killed.”

Ramaphosa recalled addressing South Africans about the same crisis seven years ago.

“What weighs on me most is that seven years ago, in this same month, I stood before the nation to speak about the same crisis,” he said.

“Yet here we are, once more having to confront the terrible reality of violence against women in our country.”

He said the identities of the victims had changed, but the violence had not.

“The names of the victims are new, but the crime is not.”

Ramaphosa said government had also failed to make women safe in their homes, on the streets, on public transport, at work and in places of learning.

“As President of the Republic, I acknowledge this. As government, we must do better.”

Ekurhuleni killings probe elevated nationally

Ramaphosa confirmed that authorities had elevated the investigation into the Ekurhuleni killings to national level.

The Deputy National Commissioner for Detective Services is coordinating the specialised multidisciplinary investigation.

The team includes detectives, Crime Intelligence, forensic specialists, investigative psychologists, digital investigators and other specialist capabilities.

Police have already made arrests in some of the cases.

A suspect was arrested in connection with the killing of Ntombifuthi Nxumalo, whose body was found at Mooifontein Cemetery in Thembisa.

Two suspects have also appeared in court in connection with Jabulile Ntimba’s killing, while another suspect remains in custody in connection with Busisiwe Mahlangu’s murder.

In other cases, police have identified persons of interest and continue to analyse forensic evidence.

No evidence yet of a single killer

Ramaphosa also addressed fears that one person could be responsible for several of the deaths.

“At present, the police have not found evidence establishing that these killings were committed by a single perpetrator,” he said.

However, investigators have not ruled out other possibilities.

“All possibilities remain under investigation.”

The clustering of several cases in and around Ekurhuleni has fuelled public concern and placed increasing pressure on police to determine whether any of the killings are connected.

Only two victims had been reported missing

Ramaphosa also revealed that only two of the women found dead in Ekurhuleni had been reported missing.

He stressed that families do not need to wait 24 hours before reporting someone missing.

“There is no requirement to wait 24 hours before reporting a person missing,” he said.

The President urged South Africans with information about the cases to approach police.

“If you know something, say something.”

‘These cases will not be allowed to go cold’

Ramaphosa promised the families of the women killed in Ekurhuleni that authorities would continue pursuing those responsible.

“To the families of the women who have been brutally killed, I say that these cases will not be allowed to go cold,” he said.

“The state is bringing together its available capabilities to establish what happened and to identify those responsible.”

He said government would continue providing updates without compromising ongoing investigations.

Ramaphosa says women should not live in fear

The President said South African women should not have to constantly calculate whether an everyday decision could put them in danger.

He said women should not have to think about where they could walk, what time they could travel, what they could wear, whom they could trust or whether rejecting someone could place their lives at risk.

Ramaphosa also rejected any attempt to blame victims for the violence committed against them.

“Responsibility for violence always belongs to the person who commits it, never the victim,” he said.

“No woman causes herself to be abused. No item of clothing causes rape. No argument justifies assault.”

He added that no relationship gave one person ownership over another.

“No rejection should justify violence. And no man has the right to take the life of a woman because she chooses to leave him.”

‘No President should have to say this again’

Ramaphosa ended his address by looking ahead seven years.

“Seven years from now, no President of the Republic should have to stand before this nation and say the same words again,” he said.

He called on South Africans not only to mourn or condemn violence against women, but to act.

“Let us honour the women whose lives have been taken not only through our words but through what we do from this day forward.”

For families who have spent recent weeks identifying bodies, attending court appearances and burying loved ones, those words now come with an expectation that government turns them into action.

World.title: End of the Green ID book: What happens if you still have one after the deadline?
World.content:
Home Affairs says the green ID book will eventually stop being recognised. Image: file / canva

Millions of South Africans are still using the old green barcoded ID book, but Home Affairs is preparing to bring an end to its use.

The department has been steadily moving towards a Smart ID-only system, with around 16 million green ID books still in use. Home Affairs says the old document is vulnerable to fraud because its physical photograph can be manipulated or replaced.

But as the deadline approaches, an important question remains: what actually happens to your green ID book once it is no longer recognised?



Home Affairs has confirmed that the green ID book will eventually stop being recognised as a valid form of identification.

President Cyril Ramaphosa said in June that the department would progressively discontinue the green ID books and would set a date after which they would no longer be recognised.

And Home Affairs Deputy Director-General for Operations Thulani Mavuso has subsequently said that people with green ID books have roughly two years left to make the switch.

That points to 2028, but it is important not to treat 2028 as a confirmed final date yet.

Home Affairs has not announced an exact day on which the green book will become invalid.

That distinction matters because the department’s current position is that it will set the formal date.



Your green book won’t simply disappear

The planned change is about whether the document will continue to be recognised as an official form of identification.

It does not mean that people will physically hand over their green books and suddenly have no identity document.

Instead, Home Affairs wants people to replace the old book with a Smart ID card.

What could you be unable to do with an expired green ID?

This is where the exact consequences of the final cut-off date will matter.

Once the green book is no longer recognised as a valid form of identification, organisations that require valid identification would be expected to rely on the replacement Smart ID or other accepted identification documents.

The green book could therefore become problematic for things such as banking, applying for certain government services, employment-related identification and other transactions where proof of identity is required.

Home Affairs itself has highlighted the importance of moving away from the old document because it wants the Smart ID to become the secure official identity document.

However, the department has not yet published a final list of every transaction that will be affected after the cut-off date.

That means it would be premature to say, for example, that a particular bank account or benefit will automatically be frozen simply because someone still has a green book.

The practical consequences should become clearer when Home Affairs formally announces the discontinuation date and the rules surrounding it.

What if you simply don’t replace your green book?

At this stage, Home Affairs has not said that people could be fined simply for still possessing a green ID book when the transition takes effect.

The issue is instead that the document will eventually cease to be recognised as a valid form of identification.

In other words, the bigger risk is not necessarily having the old book in your possession; it’s relying on it after the government has stopped recognising it.

The department is therefore encouraging people not to wait until the final deadline.

And the move away from green books is not even starting from scratch.

Home Affairs says it issued a record four million Smart ID cards during the 2025/26 financial year, more than 1.3 million above its previous annual average.

The department’s banking partnership has also significantly increased access to Smart ID services.

In July, Home Affairs said that its partnership had expanded to 327 participating bank branches, in addition to 214 modernised Home Affairs offices.

World.title: Ramaphosa unveils four-point GBV plan after 11 Ekurhuleni killings
World.content:
President Cyril Ramaphosa announced a four-point plan to tackle gender-based violence and femicide during his address to the nation on Tuesday, 29 September 2026. The measures include a national review of stalled cases, action on forensic backlogs and safety audits in municipalities. Image: X/SA Government

President Cyril Ramaphosa has unveiled a four-point gender-based violence (GBV) plan with strict 60- and 90-day deadlines, ordering urgent action on unresolved murder and rape cases, forensic backlogs and unsafe public spaces across South Africa.

This forms part of government’s latest response to gender-based violence and femicide as police investigate the deaths of 11 women found in Ekurhuleni since July.

Addressing the nation on Tuesday night, 29 September, Ramaphosa ordered police, justice officials, forensic authorities and municipalities to account for stalled cases and failures that could leave women at risk.



The measures include a national case recovery operation for unresolved murders, attempted murders, rapes and serious sexual offences involving women and children, as well as safety audits in every municipality.

Ramaphosa also acknowledged that government’s existing response had failed to stop the violence.

“What we have done has not been enough,” he said.

“It has not been enough to prevent women from being killed. It has not been enough to make women safe in their homes, in our streets, on public transport, in workplaces and places of learning.”

The announcement comes seven years after Ramaphosa previously announced emergency measures to strengthen South Africa’s response to gender-based violence, including action on poorly investigated cases, forensic delays and DNA backlogs.

Here are the four immediate measures in Ramaphosa’s GBV plan and the deadlines government must now meet.



1. National operation to recover stalled GBV cases

Ramaphosa ordered the Police and Justice and Constitutional Development ministers, working with SAPS and the National Prosecuting Authority, to launch a national case recovery operation.

The operation will focus on unresolved:

murders;

attempted murders;

rapes; and

serious sexual offences involving women and children.

Within 60 days, authorities must determine how many unresolved cases remain and how long they have been outstanding.

They must also identify cases waiting for forensic evidence, cases where suspects have been identified but not arrested, and investigations or prosecutions that have faced unreasonable delays.

Within 90 days, officials must draw up individual recovery plans for priority cases and cases that have stalled.

Each plan must identify what action remains outstanding, which official is responsible and the deadline for moving the case forward.

“A case must not collapse because a docket has been lost, an investigation has been poorly conducted, or a survivor has been treated without dignity,” Ramaphosa said.

“Where the state fails women, we must hold ourselves accountable and correct those failures.”

2. Forensic backlogs face 60-day deadline

Ramaphosa’s second directive targets delays in forensic evidence.

He ordered the Police Minister, national police commissioner and relevant forensic authorities to present a funded plan within 60 days to reduce forensic backlogs.

The plan must set out the size and age of the backlog, shortages of staff and equipment, the resources required and deadlines for reducing outstanding work.

Authorities must ring-fence priority forensic samples linked to the rape or murder of women and children for urgent processing.

“A forensic sample must not sit unprocessed while a perpetrator remains free,” Ramaphosa said.

Government must also publish progress against forensic turnaround targets every quarter.

The forensic issue has featured prominently in the Ekurhuleni murder investigation.

Police previously revealed that forensic evidence had linked persons of interest to some of the identified victims.

3. Every municipality ordered to conduct women’s safety audit

Ramaphosa’s third measure places responsibility on municipalities to identify physical conditions that could place women at risk.

Every municipality must begin a women’s safety audit without delay, working with provincial governments and police.

Within 60 days, authorities must identify hazards including:

broken streetlights;

overgrown public spaces;

abandoned buildings;

unsafe transport routes and facilities;

poorly secured parks; and

cemeteries and other high-risk spaces.

Ramaphosa specifically referred to cemeteries after Ntombifuthi Nxumalo was found dead at Mooifontein Cemetery in Thembisa.

Within 90 days of completing the audits, municipalities must fix the most urgent hazards or place them into funded implementation plans with firm completion dates.

The results must also be made public.

“Women should not have to live in fear because government has failed to repair a light, clear a public space, process evidence, or enforce a law,” Ramaphosa said.

4. Ramaphosa targets alcohol-related violence

Ramaphosa’s fourth directive targets harmful alcohol use and enforcement around liquor outlets.

Provincial and municipal authorities must intensify enforcement of liquor laws and bylaws, particularly against unlicensed outlets and establishments operating outside the hours allowed under their licences.

The President also ordered the Minister of Trade, Industry and Competition to work with the ministers of Health, Social Development, Police and Cooperative Governance on a coordinated legislative and enforcement package.

They have 60 days to submit the package to Cabinet.

Ramaphosa stressed that alcohol could never excuse violence against women.

“Alcohol does not cause gender-based violence and it can never excuse it. Responsibility always lies with the perpetrator,” he said.

However, he said harmful alcohol use remained a significant aggravating factor in interpersonal violence and had to form part of prevention efforts.

Ekurhuleni murder probe elevated nationally

Ramaphosa also gave an update on the investigation into the women found dead across Ekurhuleni.

A specialised multidisciplinary investigation has been elevated to national level under the Deputy National Commissioner for Detective Services.

The team brings together detectives, Crime Intelligence, forensic specialists, investigative psychologists, digital investigators and other specialist capabilities.

The Council for Scientific and Industrial Research is assisting with digital forensic investigations.

Police have also collected evidence including DNA, blood samples, clothing, cellphones and cellphone records.

No evidence yet of a single killer

The discovery of several women’s bodies across Ekurhuleni has sparked fears that one killer could be responsible.

Ramaphosa addressed those concerns directly.

“At present, the police have not found evidence establishing that these killings were committed by a single perpetrator,” he said.

However, investigators have not ruled out other possibilities.

“All possibilities remain under investigation.”

Arrests already made

Ramaphosa confirmed arrests in some of the cases.

Police arrested a suspect following the killing of Ntombifuthi Nxumalo, whose body was found at Mooifontein Cemetery in Thembisa.

Two suspects have also been arrested and appeared in court in connection with the killing of Jabulile Ntimba.

Another suspect remains in custody in connection with the murder of Busisiwe Mahlangu.

In other cases, investigators have identified persons of interest and collected forensic and digital evidence.

“To the families of the women who have been brutally killed, I say that these cases will not be allowed to go cold,” Ramaphosa said.

First progress report due within 90 days

Ramaphosa also placed reporting requirements on government.

The Interministerial Committee on Gender-Based Violence and Femicide and the National Council on Gender-Based Violence and Femicide must monitor the measures.

Government must issue its first consolidated public progress report within 90 days.

Reports must then follow every quarter.

“These directives are not just a statement of good intentions,” Ramaphosa said.

“They establish responsibilities, deadlines and a duty to submit reports on a regular basis to the nation.”

Seven years after Ramaphosa addressed South Africa over the same crisis, he acknowledged that the country had reached another grim moment.

“The names of the victims are new, but the crime is not.”

This time, government’s response comes with deadlines attached.

World.title: Bad news for Durban property owners
World.content:
EThekwini Municipality says around 10 000 objections to the 2026 property valuation roll were lodged. Image: canva

Thousands of Durban property owners are still waiting for the outcome of objections to the city’s new property valuations, with eThekwini Municipality saying the process could take up to 12 months.

The municipality’s Property Valuations and Management Directorate has received approximately 10 000 objections to the 2026 General Valuation Roll (GV2026), along with a large number of enquiries from property owners wanting to know the status of their objections.

So far, only around 2 000 objection outcomes have been processed.



The municipality says its valuation team is continuing to work through the remaining submissions as a priority.

Durban property owners wait for valuation objection outcomes

The large number of objections is one reason for the lengthy process, but the municipality says each objection also requires a detailed investigation.

Depending on the objection, a municipal valuer may need to examine supporting documents, compare the property with recent sales in the area, check property details or physically inspect the property.



Officials may also process objections in groups where properties are located in the same neighbourhood, sectional title development, gated complex or estate.

This means objections are not necessarily dealt with strictly in the order they were submitted.

The municipality says grouping properties allows valuers to assess comparable properties and conduct several inspections in the same area at once, helping to speed up the overall process.



What happens to your property value?

The new GV2026 property values came into effect on 1 July 2026, along with the applicable tariffs for the new financial year.

However, if an objection results in a property receiving a lower valuation, the municipality says the adjustment will be applied retrospectively from 1 July 2026.

This means property owners who successfully challenge their valuation will have the adjustment backdated to the start of the new financial year.



The new valuation can be important because a property’s municipal valuation is used in calculating property rates. A change in the valuation can therefore affect the amount a property owner is charged.

How long will the process take exactly?

EThekwini has planned for the objection process to take approximately 10 to 12 months, taking into account the number of objections received and the investigations required.

The municipality says officials first had to register and capture all the documentation received. Where submissions were incomplete, officials also had to contact property owners before the reviews could begin.



Property owners who successfully lodged their objections also do not need to submit them again.

World.title: Zimbabwe’s massive payout to former farmers: What the latest figures show
World.content:
Zimbabwe has issued US$508.8 million (about R8.36 billion) in Treasury bonds to former commercial farmers as the Government continues its long-running compensation programme.

The latest figures were reported by The Herald following an update by the country’s Finance, Economic Development and Investment Promotion Deputy Minister Kudakwashe Mnangagwa in Parliament.

According to Mnangagwa, 623 claimants have received upfront cash payments, while Treasury bonds worth US$508.8 (about R8.36 billion) million have been issued to beneficiaries under the first two batches.



The first batch comprised 378 claimants who received US$3.19 million (about R52.5 million) in cash and Treasury bonds worth US$305.47 million (about R5.02 billion).

The second batch involved 245 claimants, who received US$2.09 million (about R34.4 million) in cash and bonds valued at US$203.29 million (about R3.34 billion).

A third batch of 258 claimants has received US$2.15 million (about R35.4 million) in upfront cash payments, but Treasury bonds for this group have not yet been issued.



Zimbabwe’s US$3.5 billion compensation deal

The payments are part of the Global Compensation Deed signed by the Government and representatives of former commercial farmers in 2020.

The agreement commits Zimbabwe to paying about US$3.5 billion (R57.6 billion.) to approximately 3 500 former farm owners for improvements made on compulsorily acquired land during the fast-track Land Reform Programme.

The compensation for these farmers covers improvements rather than the value of the land itself.



Meanwhile, farmers whose properties were protected under qualifying Bilateral Investment Promotion and Protection Agreements are entitled to compensation for both land and improvements.

What the Treasury bonds offer

The Treasury bonds issued to former farmers carry a fixed annual coupon rate of 2% and have a 10-year maturity period.

According to The Herald, payments associated with the bonds, including annual coupon payments, are exempt from taxation.



The Government also intends to engage the Victoria Falls Stock Exchange to list the bonds, potentially allowing beneficiaries to sell them before maturity if they require access to cash.

The bonds have also been classified as liquid assets and granted prescribed asset status, potentially making them attractive to institutional investors such as pension funds.

The latest compensation payments form part of broader Government efforts to address its outstanding obligations and support Zimbabwe’s arrears clearance and debt resolution programme.

World.title: From broken streetlights to stalled cases: Ramaphosa outlines four GBV immediate measures
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - For families still waiting for answers about their loved one who's gone missing, women who fear to walk home after dark, and survivors whose cases have stalled, President Cyril Ramaphosa has put government departments on the clock.

During a national address on Tuesday night, Ramaphosa announced four immediate measures to deal with gender-based violence and femicide (GBVF) in the country.

Deadlines in these measures ranged from 60 days to 90 days.

The first intervention outlined was a national case recovery operation into unresolved murders, attempted murders, rapes and serious sexual offences involving women and children.

READ | Ekurhuleni Murders | 'It's a shame on the men of SA' - Ramaphosa on discovery of

He directed this measure to the Minister of Police and the Minister of Justice and Constitutional Development, working with the South African Police Service and the National Prosecuting Authority.

Ramaphosa said within 60 days they must establish the number and age of unresolved cases, cases awaiting forensic evidence, cases in which suspects have been identified but not arrested, and cases in which investigative or prosecutorial action has been unreasonably delayed.

And within 90 days, he said they are to outline what he called an individual recovery plan for priority cases and cases that have been stalled.

READ | The fight against GBV must start at school - GBV survivor

The second intervention targeted one of the biggest obstacles to criminal investigation: Forensic backlogs.

Ramaphosa, as such, instructed the Minister of Police, the National Commissioner of Police and the relevant forensic authorities to present “a funded plan to reduce forensic backlogs and establish clear turnaround standards for priority gender-based violence and femicide cases" within 60 days.

Additionally, he said priority forensic samples in cases involving the rape or murder of women and children must be ring-fenced for urgent processing.

READ | Chapter 9 institutions team up for national inquiry into the state's response to GBVF

Ramaphosa’s measures of fighting GBV went beyond courtrooms and police stations.

He also put municipalities to the task of ensuring women’s safety through audits

“High-risk areas must be identified, working with provincial governments and the police. Within sixty days, these audits must identify broken streetlights, overgrown public spaces, abandoned buildings, unsafe transport routes and facilities, poorly secured parks and other conditions that place women at risk,”

Municipalities are expected to draw up a funded implementation plan with clear completion dates after completing audits, Ramaphosa added.

And finally, the President turned his attention to alcohol-related violence.

“Alcohol does not cause gender-based violence, and it can never excuse it. Responsibility always lies with the perpetrator. But harmful alcohol use is a significant aggravating factor in interpersonal violence, and it must be addressed as part of our wider prevention effort."

As such, Ramaphosa directed the Minister of Trade, Industry and Competition, working with the Ministers of Health, Social Development, Police and Cooperative Governance, to submit to Cabinet within 60 days a coordinated legislative and enforcement package to reduce alcohol-related violence.

World.title: 'People need help right now' - NGOs unimpressed with Ramaphosa's GBVF measures
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - President Cyril Ramaphosa’s national address on the government’s plans to tackle gender-based violence has left some non-profit organisations unimpressed.

Celest Louw from the Tears Foundation said Ramaphosa’s speech was nothing but a repeat of plans that have been in place for seven years but have not been addressed.

Ramaphosa announced four immediate measures to deal with gender-based violence and femicide (GBVF) in the country. Deadlines in these measures ranged from 60 days to 90 days.

READ | WATCH | Ramaphosa addresses the nation on government's GBVF response

These included a national case recovery operation into unresolved GBVF cases involving women and children, dealing with forensic backlog, ensuring women’s safety through audits, as well as intensifying enforcement of existing liquor laws and by-laws.

But Louw viewed the President as one who is disconnected from the real problems.

“Government is completely divorced from what's going on the ground. Because we can talk about these deaths and we're talking about a list of names, but that list of names isn't anywhere near the actual list of people that are dying every day.”

Louw said NGO’s working with victims of GBVF face a funding issue, but nothing is being done to address this in the same breath; victims still deal with officials who refuse to assist them in opening cases.
