World.title: 𝗗𝗿. 𝗖𝗮𝗿𝗼𝗹𝘆𝗻 𝗕𝗮𝗶𝗻𝗱𝘂 𝗠𝗼𝗼𝗿𝗲: 𝗔 𝗟𝗶𝗯𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗮𝗻 𝗦𝘁𝗼𝗿𝘆 𝗪𝗼𝗿𝘁𝗵 𝗖𝗲𝗹𝗲𝗯𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴
World.content:
𝘍𝘳𝘰𝘮 𝘔𝘢𝘬𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘏𝘪𝘴𝘵𝘰𝘳𝘺 𝘐𝘯 𝘙𝘰𝘣𝘰𝘵𝘪𝘤 𝘚𝘶𝘳𝘨𝘦𝘳𝘺 𝘛𝘰 𝘈𝘥𝘷𝘢𝘯𝘤𝘦𝘥 𝘊𝘢𝘳𝘥𝘪𝘰𝘵𝘩𝘰𝘳𝘢𝘤𝘪𝘤 𝘛𝘳𝘢𝘪𝘯𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘈𝘯𝘥 𝘈 𝘔𝘪𝘴𝘴𝘪𝘰𝘯 𝘛𝘰 𝘚𝘵𝘳𝘦𝘯𝘨𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘯 𝘏𝘦𝘢𝘭𝘵𝘩𝘤𝘢𝘳𝘦 𝘐𝘯 𝘓𝘪𝘣𝘦𝘳𝘪𝘢

𝗕𝘆 𝗗𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗸 𝗠. 𝗠𝗼𝗼𝗿𝗲

There are Liberians doing extraordinary things around the world whose stories many of us simply do not know. One of them is my cousin, 𝗗𝗿. 𝗖𝗮𝗿𝗼𝗹𝘆𝗻 𝗕𝗮𝗶𝗻𝗱𝘂 𝗠𝗼𝗼𝗿𝗲, daughter of Janet Moore-Dalmeida and Alphonsus Dalmeida.



Carolyn is a 𝗯𝗼𝗮𝗿𝗱-𝗰𝗲𝗿𝘁𝗶𝗳𝗶𝗲𝗱 𝘁𝗵𝗼𝗿𝗮𝗰𝗶𝗰 𝘀𝘂𝗿𝗴𝗲𝗼𝗻 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗮𝗱𝘃𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲𝗱 𝗳𝗲𝗹𝗹𝗼𝘄𝘀𝗵𝗶𝗽 𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗶𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗶𝗻 𝗰𝗮𝗿𝗱𝗶𝗼𝘁𝗵𝗼𝗿𝗮𝗰𝗶𝗰 𝘀𝘂𝗿𝗴𝗲𝗿𝘆 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗿𝗼𝗯𝗼𝘁𝗶𝗰 𝘀𝘂𝗿𝗴𝗲𝗿𝘆. Her journey has taken her through some of the most demanding levels of medical and surgical training in the United States.

She earned her medical degree from the 𝗨𝗻𝗶𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗼𝗳 𝗣𝗶𝘁𝘁𝘀𝗯𝘂𝗿𝗴𝗵 𝗦𝗰𝗵𝗼𝗼𝗹 𝗼𝗳 𝗠𝗲𝗱𝗶𝗰𝗶𝗻𝗲, completed her general surgery residency at 𝗠𝗼𝗿𝗲𝗵𝗼𝘂𝘀𝗲 𝗦𝗰𝗵𝗼𝗼𝗹 𝗼𝗳 𝗠𝗲𝗱𝗶𝗰𝗶𝗻𝗲, and continued into highly specialized training at 𝗕𝗿𝗶𝗴𝗵𝗮𝗺 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗪𝗼𝗺𝗲𝗻’𝘀 𝗛𝗼𝘀𝗽𝗶𝘁𝗮𝗹 and the 𝗨𝗻𝗶𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗼𝗳 𝗞𝗮𝗻𝘀𝗮𝘀 𝗠𝗲𝗱𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹 𝗖𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿. Today, she practices with Penn Highlands Cardiovascular and Thoracic Surgery in Pennsylvania.

𝗠𝗮𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗛𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗿𝘆 𝗔𝘁 𝗠𝗼𝗿𝗲𝗵𝗼𝘂𝘀𝗲

One achievement in Carolyn’s journey deserves special recognition. In 𝟮𝟬𝟭𝟴, 𝘀𝗵𝗲 𝗯𝗲𝗰𝗮𝗺𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗳𝗶𝗿𝘀𝘁 𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗶𝗱𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗶𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗵𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗿𝘆 𝗼𝗳 𝗠𝗼𝗿𝗲𝗵𝗼𝘂𝘀𝗲 𝗦𝗰𝗵𝗼𝗼𝗹 𝗼𝗳 𝗠𝗲𝗱𝗶𝗰𝗶𝗻𝗲 𝘁𝗼 𝗯𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗲 𝗰𝗲𝗿𝘁𝗶𝗳𝗶𝗲𝗱 𝗶𝗻 𝗿𝗼𝗯𝗼𝘁𝗶𝗰 𝘀𝘂𝗿𝗴𝗲𝗿𝘆.

Robotic surgery is one of the major advances in modern minimally invasive medicine. The surgeon remains fully in control while using highly sophisticated instruments that can allow certain complex procedures to be performed through much smaller incisions than traditional open surgery. For appropriate patients, that can mean smaller wounds, less postoperative pain and faster recovery.

For Carolyn, however, robotic surgery was only one part of a much larger professional journey.

She later completed advanced fellowship training in thoracic surgery at 𝗕𝗿𝗶𝗴𝗵𝗮𝗺 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗪𝗼𝗺𝗲𝗻’𝘀 𝗛𝗼𝘀𝗽𝗶𝘁𝗮𝗹 𝗶𝗻 𝗕𝗼𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗻, one of Harvard Medical School’s major teaching hospitals, where she also served as a 𝗛𝗮𝗿𝘃𝗮𝗿𝗱 𝗖𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹 𝗙𝗲𝗹𝗹𝗼𝘄 𝗶𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗼𝗿𝗮𝗰𝗶𝗰 𝘀𝘂𝗿𝗴𝗲𝗿𝘆. She then completed additional fellowship training in 𝗰𝗮𝗿𝗱𝗶𝗼𝘁𝗵𝗼𝗿𝗮𝗰𝗶𝗰 𝘀𝘂𝗿𝗴𝗲𝗿𝘆 𝗮𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗨𝗻𝗶𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗼𝗳 𝗞𝗮𝗻𝘀𝗮𝘀 𝗠𝗲𝗱𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹 𝗖𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿.

Cardiothoracic and thoracic surgeons work in some of the most delicate areas of the human body, treating complex conditions involving the 𝗵𝗲𝗮𝗿𝘁, 𝗹𝘂𝗻𝗴𝘀, 𝗲𝘀𝗼𝗽𝗵𝗮𝗴𝘂𝘀, 𝗰𝗵𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝘄𝗮𝗹𝗹 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗼𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝘀𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲𝘀 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗰𝗵𝗲𝘀𝘁. Carolyn’s current practice focuses on thoracic surgery and includes complex procedures such as lung resections, chest-wall surgery and other specialized operations.

Her accomplishments have also earned her another important professional distinction.

Carolyn was 𝗶𝗻𝗱𝘂𝗰𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝗮𝘀 𝗮 𝗙𝗲𝗹𝗹𝗼𝘄 𝗼𝗳 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗔𝗺𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗻 𝗖𝗼𝗹𝗹𝗲𝗴𝗲 𝗼𝗳 𝗦𝘂𝗿𝗴𝗲𝗼𝗻𝘀 — 𝗙𝗔𝗖𝗦. For those who may not be familiar with the designation, Fellowship in the American College of Surgeons is awarded to surgeons who meet rigorous professional standards involving surgical training, competence, ethical practice and commitment to high-quality patient care.

It is recognition that carries considerable weight within the surgical profession.

𝗟𝗶𝗯𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗮 𝗢𝗻 𝗛𝗲𝗿 𝗠𝗶𝗻𝗱

As Carolyn’s medical career developed, one question continued to follow her:

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗰𝗮𝗻 𝗜 𝗱𝗼 𝘁𝗼 𝗵𝗲𝗹𝗽 𝗺𝘆 𝗰𝗼𝘂𝗻𝘁𝗿𝘆?

That question eventually led her to establish the 𝗟𝗶𝗯𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗮 𝗚𝗹𝗼𝗯𝗮𝗹 𝗛𝗲𝗮𝗹𝘁𝗵 & 𝗦𝘂𝗿𝗴𝗲𝗿𝘆 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘀𝗼𝗿𝘁𝗶𝘂𝗺 — 𝗟𝗚𝗛𝗦𝗖, an organization designed to bring together healthcare professionals, educators, researchers, institutions, members of the Liberian diaspora and international partners around the goal of strengthening healthcare in Liberia.

What I particularly admire about Carolyn’s vision is that it goes beyond bringing doctors into Liberia for a few days, treating patients and returning home. Those missions have value and can save lives, but Carolyn is looking at the longer-term question: 𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝗱𝗼 𝘄𝗲 𝗵𝗲𝗹𝗽 𝗟𝗶𝗯𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗮 𝗯𝘂𝗶𝗹𝗱 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗲𝗼𝗽𝗹𝗲, 𝘀𝗸𝗶𝗹𝗹𝘀, 𝗲𝗾𝘂𝗶𝗽𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘀𝘆𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗺𝘀 𝗻𝗲𝗰𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗮𝗿𝘆 𝘁𝗼 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘃𝗶𝗱𝗲 𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗼𝗳 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗰𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗶𝘁𝘀𝗲𝗹𝗳?

Her approach emphasizes training Liberian healthcare professionals, strengthening diagnostic services, improving surgical systems, sharing medical knowledge and developing long-term institutional partnerships.

Liberia needs doctors and equipment, but a functioning surgical system also needs trained nurses, anesthesia professionals, laboratories, diagnostic services, biomedical technicians, reliable equipment and continuing professional education.

That is the larger challenge LGHSC is attempting to address.

𝗠𝗼𝘃𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗙𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝗩𝗶𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗧𝗼 𝗔𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻

And this is not simply an idea on paper.

In 𝗝𝗮𝗻𝘂𝗮𝗿𝘆 𝟮𝟬𝟮𝟲, Liberia’s Ministry of Health entered into a formal partnership with the Liberia Global Health & Surgery Consortium focused on strengthening surgical and diagnostic care, training, technical assistance and health-system capacity.

The work has also begun attracting support from established medical institutions. Through Duke University’s REMEDY program, medical and surgical supplies and protective equipment have been donated to LGHSC for use in Liberia.

The Consortium is also preparing for expanded activities in Liberia, including clinical training, surgical missions and partnerships involving Liberian healthcare institutions and professionals.

That shows that Carolyn is doing more than talking about change. She is helping build the relationships, resources and infrastructure needed to make that change possible.

𝗦𝘂𝗰𝗰𝗲𝘀𝘀 𝗧𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗥𝗲𝗮𝗰𝗵𝗲𝘀 𝗕𝗮𝗰𝗸 𝗛𝗼𝗺𝗲

There is something especially meaningful about a Liberian professional reaching this level in her field and then asking how that knowledge and opportunity can benefit Liberia.

Carolyn could have concentrated entirely on her medical career in the United States. Instead, she is using the experience, professional relationships and knowledge she has acquired to help create something larger.

Her achievement at Morehouse demonstrated what she could accomplish individually. Her surgical career demonstrates what years of training and discipline can produce. But the 𝗟𝗶𝗯𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗮 𝗚𝗹𝗼𝗯𝗮𝗹 𝗛𝗲𝗮𝗹𝘁𝗵 & 𝗦𝘂𝗿𝗴𝗲𝗿𝘆 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘀𝗼𝗿𝘁𝗶𝘂𝗺 represents something different: an effort to multiply the impact of that success.

If Liberian doctors and nurses receive additional training, if hospitals improve their diagnostic capabilities, if surgical teams obtain needed equipment, and if international medical institutions establish lasting partnerships with their Liberian counterparts, Carolyn’s impact can eventually reach patients she may never personally meet.

That, to me, is where her story becomes even more powerful.

𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝗪𝗲 𝗖𝗮𝗻 𝗦𝘂𝗽𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁 𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗦𝗵𝗲 𝗜𝘀 𝗕𝘂𝗶𝗹𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴

The Liberia Global Health & Surgery Consortium is actively seeking support for efforts designed to strengthen surgical and diagnostic care in Liberia.

Its priorities include providing surgical instruments, improving diagnostic laboratory capacity and supporting advanced clinical training for healthcare professionals.

Support does not have to come only from physicians or large donors. Hospitals and healthcare institutions can develop partnerships. Medical professionals can contribute expertise. Companies can assist with equipment and technical support. Organizations can help with grants, and members of the Liberian diaspora can connect LGHSC with institutions and individuals who may be able to help.

Those interested in learning more, volunteering, partnering or contributing can reach the 𝗟𝗶𝗯𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗮 𝗚𝗹𝗼𝗯𝗮𝗹 𝗛𝗲𝗮𝗹𝘁𝗵 & 𝗦𝘂𝗿𝗴𝗲𝗿𝘆 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘀𝗼𝗿𝘁𝗶𝘂𝗺 through its official website:

𝘄𝘄𝘄.𝗹𝗶𝗯𝗴𝗵𝘀𝗰.𝗼𝗿𝗴

The organization also lists its Liberia office at 𝗦𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗱 𝗙𝗹𝗼𝗼𝗿, 𝗔𝘁𝗹𝗮𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗰 𝗛𝗼𝘂𝘀𝗲, 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝗴𝗼 𝗧𝗼𝘄𝗻, 𝗠𝗼𝗻𝗿𝗼𝘃𝗶𝗮, and can be contacted at: 𝗟𝗴𝗵𝘀𝗰𝗶𝗻𝗰@𝗴𝗺𝗮𝗶𝗹.𝗰𝗼𝗺

Financial contributions can be made through the official donation links provided on the LGHSC website.

𝗔 𝗟𝗶𝗯𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗮𝗻 𝗦𝘁𝗼𝗿𝘆 𝗪𝗼𝗿𝘁𝗵 𝗞𝗻𝗼𝘄𝗶𝗻𝗴

This is one of the reasons I believe we need to do a better job of telling the stories of Liberians who are accomplishing extraordinary things around the world.

Dr. Carolyn Baindu Moore became the 𝗳𝗶𝗿𝘀𝘁 𝗠𝗼𝗿𝗲𝗵𝗼𝘂𝘀𝗲 𝗦𝗰𝗵𝗼𝗼𝗹 𝗼𝗳 𝗠𝗲𝗱𝗶𝗰𝗶𝗻𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗶𝗱𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗰𝗲𝗿𝘁𝗶𝗳𝗶𝗲𝗱 𝗶𝗻 𝗿𝗼𝗯𝗼𝘁𝗶𝗰 𝘀𝘂𝗿𝗴𝗲𝗿𝘆. She continued through advanced thoracic and cardiothoracic training, became a 𝗙𝗲𝗹𝗹𝗼𝘄 𝗼𝗳 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗔𝗺𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗻 𝗖𝗼𝗹𝗹𝗲𝗴𝗲 𝗼𝗳 𝗦𝘂𝗿𝗴𝗲𝗼𝗻𝘀, and built a career treating patients with complex surgical conditions.

Now she is using what she has learned, and the professional network she has developed, to help strengthen surgical and diagnostic care in Liberia.

There are young Liberians who need to see people like Carolyn and understand what is possible. There are Liberian professionals around the world who may learn about what she is building and decide that they, too, have something they can contribute. And there are many of us who may never enter an operating room but can still support those working to make Liberia stronger.

𝗛𝗲𝗿 𝗮𝗰𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗶𝘀𝗵𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀 𝗱𝗲𝘀𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗲 𝘁𝗼 𝗯𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗴𝗻𝗶𝘇𝗲𝗱 𝗯𝘆 𝗟𝗶𝗯𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗮𝗻𝘀 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆𝘄𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲. 𝗦𝗵𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝗽𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗱 𝗼𝗳 𝗲𝘅𝗰𝗲𝗹𝗹𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲, 𝗱𝗶𝘀𝗰𝗶𝗽𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗲 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗺𝗶𝘁𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝘁𝗼 𝗰𝗼𝘂𝗻𝘁𝗿𝘆 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘄𝗲 𝘀𝗵𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱 𝗰𝗲𝗹𝗲𝗯𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲, 𝗲𝘀𝗽𝗲𝗰𝗶𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝘄𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘀𝘂𝗰𝗰𝗲𝘀𝘀 𝗶𝘀 𝗯𝗲𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘂𝘀𝗲𝗱 𝘁𝗼 𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗴𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝗟𝗶𝗯𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗮.

She has already made history in her profession, and she is now working to ensure that some of what she has achieved reaches back home.

𝗧𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗶𝘀 𝗮 𝗟𝗶𝗯𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗮𝗻 𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗿𝘆 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝘁𝗵 𝗰𝗲𝗹𝗲𝗯𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴.

World.title: Liberia: Opposition Puts Issues First in Bid to Break Its Losing Habit; Can Five Parties Do What the CPP Couldn’t?
World.content:
MONROVIA – For most of the last two decades, Liberia’s opposition has had a habit of losing to itself. Parties meet, pledge unity, sign documents, then split over who leads before the ruling party breaks a sweat. So when George Manneh Weah and four other political leaders (Alexander Cummings, Dee-Maxwell Saah Kemayah, Simeon Freeman and Jonathan Mason) put their names to an eight-page communiqué on Sunday, the question was not whether they could agree on grievances. That part is easy. The question is whether they have found a way to stay together long enough to matter in 2029.

By Rodney D. Sieh

What the Communiqué Actually Is



Read closely, the document is two things at once. The first is a charge sheet: Foya and the Guinea border, the US$10 million Foya project, the US$8 million SIB transfer, the drug busts, the Supreme Court, the Cybercrime Act, evictions, the EU ambassador, the US deportee deal. It is the most comprehensive attack on the Boakai-Koung government to come from the opposition since the 2023 transition.

The second is a governance arrangement, and that is the more interesting part. The parties have not merged, have not named a leader, and have not touched the 2029 ticket. Instead, they have created a Joint Technical Committee, two members per party, to write policy positions and build county-level outreach. They say outright that they will not try “to manufacture opposition political unity by declaration.”

That line is aimed squarely at the ghost of the Collaborating Political Parties.

What Is Different This Time

The CPP brought together the ANC, Liberty Party, Unity Party and All Liberian Party with a framework that demanded a single standard bearer. It won the 2020 Montserrado senatorial seat, then tore itself apart over the framework document and the question of who would carry the flag. By 2023, its members were running against each other and Boakai rebuilt the Unity Party on his own terms. The lesson most opposition figures drew is that the ticket question, asked too early, destroys everything else.

This arrangement is built differently in at least four ways.

It has an anchor. The CPP was a gathering of roughly equal, mid-sized parties with no dominant base. This effort is organized around a former president who lost the 2023 runoff by about 20,000 votes and can still fill the road from RIA to Monrovia. That changes the arithmetic. The smaller parties bring policy credibility, regional contacts and technocratic names; the CDC brings the votes.

It puts the ticket last. By design, the parties have agreed on issues before structure, and structure before candidates. Cummings has spoken openly about drawing lessons from the CPP collapse, and the sequencing reflects that.

It is spreading ownership. The first roundtable was at Weah’s Jamaica Resort; the second was hosted by Freeman at the Sinkor Palace. Small as it sounds, rotating the host chips away at the charge, made loudly by Musa Bility before the first meeting, that this is a CDC project with a pre-appointed leadership.

It is issue-driven, not personality-driven. The communiqué reads like an opposition policy platform in draft. If the technical committee produces real positions on the economy, the courts, the NEC and the drug war, the group will have something the CPP never had: a reason to exist beyond beating the incumbent.

The Fault Lines

None of that guarantees survival, and the cracks are already visible.

The Citizens Movement for Change walked out three days before the signing, saying it would not endorse the draft and wanted cooperation tied to a clearly defined national reform agenda, including changes to the system of government. Bility’s objection, that hosting a meeting does not confer leadership over the opposition, has not gone away. It has simply left the room with him, and it may return from the others once the ticket question comes due.

Then there is the CDC’s own record. A communiqué that indicts selective justice, opaque procurement and pressure on the courts invites the obvious reply: what about 2018 to 2024? The Unity Party will point to missing money, the sanctions on CDC-era officials and the way the Weah government treated critics. The opposition’s claims will be judged partly on whether its lead party can answer that history.

The absences also matter. The Liberty Party is not at the table. The National Patriotic Party is divided, with its executive suspending partisans who endorsed the roundtable while its political leader, former Vice President Jewel Howard-Taylor, faces drug-related charges she denies. Senator Samuel Kogar attended the first round but is not a signatory.

And the hardest question has only been postponed. Weah remains constitutionally eligible for another term. Cummings has run twice and is unlikely to stand aside quietly. Kemayah signs as his party’s “Standard Bearer.” A structure that defers the ticket can hold only if it also agrees, sooner rather than later, on how the ticket will be chosen: a primary, a polling formula, a negotiated power-sharing deal. Without that, 2029 becomes 2023 again.

Can It Become a Viable Opposition?

It can, if it does three things over the next 18 months.

First, turn the charge sheet into policy. Liberians have heard grievances before. What they have rarely heard from an opposition is a costed answer to squatter settlements, health worker pay or border diplomacy. The technical committee is the vehicle for that, and its output will show whether this is a movement or a press release.

Second, go where the votes were decided. The 2023 runoff was lost in the northwest and the southeast swing counties, not in Montserrado. County-level structures, which the communiqué promises, matter more than Monrovia roundtables.

Third, settle the selection rule early, even if the name comes late. The CPP died over process, not personalities. A signed, public mechanism for choosing a standard bearer would be the clearest signal that this effort has learned something.

What the Unity Party Should Do

The ruling party’s first instinct has been dismissal. Secretary General Amos Tweh, launching the Boakai 2029 Reelection Movement, said the opposition gathering posed no serious threat. That may be good for morale at party headquarters, but it is weak strategy. The communiqué is not really asking voters to love Weah; it is asking them to doubt the government. Dismissing the messenger does nothing about the message.

The more durable response is to take the sharpest charges off the table:

• Publish the Foya file. Funding sources, contracts and the MRU question. A US$10 million project in the President’s hometown will be a campaign issue for three years unless it is fully explained now.

• Let the drug investigation breathe. The opposition’s proposal for a commission including the Bar, the Press Union, churches and mosques is not radical. Accepting some version of it would take the “selective justice” line away from the opposition.

• Stop fighting the courts and the critics. Compliance with Supreme Court opinions and restraint in using the Cybercrime Act cost the government little and deny the opposition its “police state” narrative.

• Explain the deportee arrangement and the EU rift. Both are foreign-policy stories that are becoming domestic ones.

• Show delivery. The communiqué itself concedes the US$1 billion revenue milestone. The Unity Party’s best argument is to make that number visible in salaries, clinics and resettlement for displaced families.

There is also an internal question the UP will eventually have to face. President Boakai would be 84 in 2029. A reelection movement launched this early suggests the party intends to run him again, but voters will ask about continuity, and an opposition built around renewal will make the most of it.

The Bottom Line

Sunday’s communiqué does not mean Liberia’s opposition is united. It means five parties have agreed on what they are against and have built a slower, looser structure designed to survive the fights that killed the CPP. That is a genuine change in approach. Whether it becomes a change in outcome depends on two things no document can settle: whether the lead party can carry its own past, and whether the leaders can agree on a way to choose one of themselves before 2029 chooses for them.

For the Unity Party, the warning is simpler. The margin in 2023 was barely 20,000 votes. An opposition that stops beating itself does not need to win many hearts to reverse that.

World.title: Liberia: ‘Jaw Dropping’ El Niño” Could Test Liberia’s Weak Weather Warning System and Put Thousands of Lives at Risk, Experts Warn
World.content:
The sea continues to wash away at homes in the West Point township, in Monrovia. Credit: Allison Hunter for New Narratives

Summary

Scientists warn that a historically severe El Niño – a climate pattern that disrupts weather around the world – could bring erratic rainfall, and severe flooding, extreme heat, fishing and agricultural disruption to Liberia in coming months.

Experts say the government needs to invest in preparedness strategies now to protect people from to extreme heat and weather in coming months with extreme heat alone predicted to kill 450,000 people globally by February.

Liberia lacks adequate weather stations and relies heavily on global models, limiting its ability to issue accurate, community-specific warnings and meaning millions of Liberians will be left vulnerable.

By Nemenlah Cyrus Harmon, climate and environment reporter with New Narratives

The sea off Liberia turns a deceptive shade of calm every year around this time as the rains give way to the dry season – warm, glassy, inviting.



But Nathaniel Blama, Liberia’s former chief environmental regulator, has learned to read that as a warning rather than an invitation.

“When you see the water very warm during that period, it’s time to be afraid because having storm surge, the movement of the current is completely different than normal,” he said. “A lot of people, children, go on the beach. They don’t come back.” Houses and livelihoods are also swept away.

But this year is shaping up to be much worse. New data by climate researchers shows the world is experiencing an exceptionally powerful weather pattern called El Niño—likely the strongest in at least 1,000 years—layered on top of human-caused climate change from burning fossil fuels. This combination means 2027 is expected to be the hottest year ever recorded by scientists.

The climate crisis is already making extreme weather more intense and deadly. Rising heat is now killing one person every minute globally. The El Niño will make this worse, intensifying heatwaves, droughts, and floods across the planet, including Africa. Newly released data from the U.S. based Climate Impact Lab estimates that more than 450,000 people are projected to die globally from the additional heat brought by the super El Niño by February, more than 30,000 in Nigeria alone.

“So, in many places around the world we will see never-before-experienced heat extremes, with all their consequences on health, food security and water stress,” Prof. Friederike Otto of Imperial College London told The Guardian .

In West Africa, where millions rely on rain-fed agriculture, those shifts can be especially damaging. For Liberia, changes in the timing and intensity of rainfall could threaten crops, worsen flooding and increase pressure on already vulnerable communities.

“Farmers could face unreliable rainfall, while hotter, drier conditions threaten crops, water supplies, hydropower and increase the risk of bushfires in places like Wologizi and Foya,” said Isaac Nyaneyon Kannah Teah, a Liberian climate expert.

El Niño is a natural climate pattern that occurs when waters in the Pacific Ocean become unusually warm, disrupting weather patterns across the world. It can shift rainfall, intensify heat and bring drought to some regions while causing heavy rains and flooding in others.

Some experts are calling this a “monster” weather event. Temperatures in the Pacific at the heart of El Niño reached a record 3.05C in September. Forecasts project the warming could peak at about 4 C in November and December. A rise above 2C is classified as a very strong, or “super,” El Niño.

Teah said the full impact of the developing El Niño on the country’s current rainy season, ending this month, remains uncertain, but changes in weather conditions in coming months appear certain.

“El Niño may contribute to a hotter and drier January-to-March dry season, placing pressure on water supplies, agriculture, forests and electricity generation,” Teah said. It could also make the beginning of the farming season less predictable, including false rainfall starts followed by prolonged dry spells that damage newly planted crops.

Farmer Oretha Weatoe of James Town, River Cess, looks on as her crops struggle to grow. Photo Eric Opa Doue/New Narratives.

Nearly seven out of 10 Liberians depend on farming for what they eat, so disrupted rainfall could threaten both food and income. Four in every five Liberians is already facing food insecurity. Just 1.6 percent is irrigated, leaving farmers heavily dependent on the rains.

At Liberia’s Meteorological Service, forecasters are already watching the signal build, but they are severely limited by a lack of sophisticated equipment. “We are not even having a marine weather station to give us the actual sea surface temperature,” said Albert Momolu Sherman, director of Liberia’s Meteorological Service, which operates under the Ministry of Transport. “We normally rely on global models.”

Those global models are consistent enough to worry him. He described how an intensifying El Niño fools farmers into planting too early.

“Farmers think that, ‘Okay, the rainy season has started,’ not knowing that this is just a false start,” Sherman said. Then, once the West African monsoon reasserts itself, the rain that finally does come arrives harder and more suddenly than usual, raising the risk of seedlings being waterlogged and communities swamped by flash flooding in a country whose drainage systems were never built for it.

Unlike other countries in the region, the Liberian government does not have a mechanism for warning Liberians about coming heatwaves and heavy rains. The Meteorological Service publishes a ten-day agricultural bulletin meant to guide farmers’ planting decisions. But reaching the people who need it most – in communities without reliable radio, internet or electricity – depends on partnerships with the Liberia Telecommunications Authority, the National Disaster Management Agency and the Red Cross that have yet to fully materialize.

It should not have been like this. International donors made a fund of $10 million available to establish a warning system six years ago. FrontPage Africa/New Narratives documented the suspected corruption and lack of capacity under the Weah administration that led to four-year delays in the project. The Boakai administration reports that it has got the project moving but it has also faced delays.

Teah said it is still too early to determine its effect on Liberia’s entire 2027 season but even if the farmers are spared, they’ll be hit by impacts elsewhere. Because Liberians depend on imports for 80 percent of their food , they could also face higher food prices as El Nino reduces agricultural production in countries from which we import rice and other foods.

Excessive heat will add another dimension. In addition to impacting farming, heat makes it harder for people to work—farmers, fishermen, and construction workers will tire faster in extreme temperatures, earning less money to buy food. Water sources dry up or become contaminated, spreading waterborne diseases that weaken children’s bodies and make malnutrition even more deadly.

A satellite weather-monitoring system used to forecast weather at Roberts International Airport. Photo credit: Liberia Meteorological Service.

For the millions of Liberians who are already food insecure, already eating less nutritious food because they cannot afford better, an intense heat wave could push families from precarious to catastrophic: crops will fail, prices will spike, work will become impossible, and children will face acute hunger. The rural communities hit hardest by heat—with no air conditioning, limited access to clean water, and no cushion of savings—will be the most vulnerable.

The knock-on effects reach further than the farm gate. St. Paul River which supplies the Mount Coffee Hydropower plant near Monrovia can run low as evaporation increases, threatening the electricity supply. It has already reduced electricity generation in recent years as dry-season water levels in the river fell, contributing to widespread power cuts across Liberia. This coming dry season could be worse.

Fishermen monitor the weather as their canoes sit offshore at West Point. Photo by Nemenlah Cyrus Harmon.

Offshore, artisanal fishers face a quieter but no less consequential disruption: warming waters altering fish stocks and pushing dangerous sea conditions closer to shore, threatening both catches and the fishers themselves.

Rising heat brings its own toll for humans: heat stress and other health complications for a population with limited access to cooling or medical care. It will be dangerous for the elderly, infants and those weakened by illness.

Experts said the government has a role to play in helping communities prepare for possible weather-related challenges.

“Closely monitor forecasts from the Liberia Meteorological Service and strengthen preparedness for heat, water shortages, bushfires, agricultural losses and possible flooding,” says Sherman.

The government can also put in measures to save lives including including cooling centers where people can shelter, increased staffing for medical facilities at the hottest times and protections for outdoor workers.

President Joseph Boakai will be immersed in discussion of climate change and the super El Nino during his time at this month’s UN General Assembly. The issue has been a central topic of the meeting with world leaders approving a new declaration to tackle sea level rise with 770 million people live in coastal areas affected by sea level rise. 230,000 Liberians will lose their homes by the end of the century, according to UN models.

Experts said they hope the president comes home from the assembly with a renewed vigor and new ideas to protect Liberians in coming months.

World.title: “The People Did a Fantastic Job” — Mary Broh Defends Defendants in Saudi Rice Trial
World.content:
Monrovia-Former General Services Agency Director General Mary T. Broh, delivered one of the defense’s strongest accounts Monday, September 28, in Liberia’s ongoing Saudi-donated rice trial, telling Criminal Court “C” that the government officials involved in handling the controversial donation “did a fantastic job” and questioning how they could be accused of stealing rice that, according to her testimony, was subsequently distributed to communities and government institutions.

By: Willie N. Tokpah

Broh, appearing as a Subpoenaed witness on Monday, September 28, maintained that the movement of the Saudi-donated rice to the GSA was carried out through an inter-agency arrangement involving the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the National Disaster Management Agency, NDMA, the Ministry of Internal Affairs and the GSA.



Her testimony provided a detailed account of how the GSA came to warehouse thousands of bags of the donation and sought to distance the accused officials from any suggestion that the movement of the rice was undertaken for personal benefit.

And as she walked out of the courtroom after her testimony, Broh was reportedly heard making an even more direct statement about the accused, “The people are innocent, the people didn’t do anything.”

The remark was made outside the witness stand and was therefore not evidence given under oath. But it underscored the position Broh had advanced during her testimony, that the officials involved were performing government duties and that the movement of the rice should not automatically be interpreted as theft.

“The People Did a Fantastic Job,”

Broh’s most striking testimony came when she addressed the allegation that the Saudi rice had been stolen or improperly diverted.

She questioned what happened to the rice that was actually distributed to communities and government institutions.

According to her testimony, “the people did a fantastic job.”

Broh challenged the suggestion that the movement of rice from one government institution to another, or its distribution to institutions and communities, in itself established that the officials had stolen the donation.

Her testimony presented a different picture from the prosecution’s case, one in which govand ernment officials were attempting to move, warehouse and distribute a large humanitarian donation through several state institutions.

She raised a concern, in substance, whether the officials had stolen the rice, what became of the rice that ultimately reached communities and institutions.

That question is central to the defense’s effort to distinguish between accounting discrepancies, administrative decisions and proof of criminal appropriation.

‘The People Are Innocent’

Broh’s statement after leaving the courtroom added an unusually personal dimension to her testimony.

As she reportedly walked away from the proceedings, she was heard saying, “The people are innocent, the people didn’t do anything.”

The statement appeared to refer to the officials whose handling of the Saudi rice has become the subject of criminal proceedings.

Broh did not make that statement while testifying under oath, and it therefore carries a different evidentiary status from her testimony before the judge and jury.

But it closely reflected the position she presented while on the witness stand, that the officials were acting pursuant to government instructions and an inter-agency mandate.

‘When He Called, We Must Work for Him’

Broh told the court that she became involved after receiving a call from then Foreign Affairs Minister Dee-Maxwell Saah Kemayah.

“When I got the call from Ambassador Kemayah, he said he needed my assistance in term of warehousing the Saudi Donated rice at the GSA,” Broh testified.

She maintained, that Kemayah was a government colleague and that when he called for assistance, she agreed.

A meeting was subsequently held at the GSA involving the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Ministry of Internal Affairs, NDMA and GSA.

According to Broh, Kemayah chaired the meeting, but she emphasized that the resulting mandate came from the meeting involving the institutions and not from Kemayah acting alone.

That distinction is important to the defense because the prosecution has alleged that Kemayah and former Deputy Foreign Minister Thelma D. Sawyer became improperly involved in the handling and distribution of rice that had been donated for disaster victims.

Broh’s account, however, was that the process involved several government agencies.

25,000 Bags Came

Through GSA

Broh confirmed that 11,200 bags of the Saudi-donated rice were stored at GSA.

She further testified that 13,895 additional bags were moved from NDMA to GSA.

According to her account, the rice came into GSA custody through two deliveries, with the total quantity estimated at approximately 25,195 bags.

Broh also challenged the use of figures contained in the indictment when compared with the actual movement records.

She told the court that the indictment cited one quantity, but that the gate passes showed a higher figure.

For that reason, she suggested that the quantities should have been calculated from the gate passes and other actual movement records.

Distribution Was Never Halted

Broh further testified that she did not know of any decision halting the distribution of the Saudi rice.

“The general distribution was never halted under GSA,” she told the court.

She acknowledged that portions of the rice were distributed to institutions including the Liberia National Police, Ministry of Justice and Ministry of National Defense, although the original donation was intended for disaster-affected persons.

But Broh offered an explanation for such institutional distributions.

She said that when she received a mandate to move rice to another location or institution, she could not simply reject the instruction when government officials had provided reasons for doing so.

She pointed particularly to prisons, saying a shortage of food in correctional facilities could create serious problems and even lead to scuffles.

In her view, preventing such a situation could itself be considered a disaster-related concern.

‘We Were Following Instructions’

Broh also told the court that she was never provided a concept note explaining the broader project.

Instead, she said, she was following instructions arising from the inter-agency meeting.

She said Kemayah did not tell her why he wanted the rice moved from NDMA.

His instruction, according to Broh, was that the rice should be moved as soon as possible.

She said GSA had the capacity to warehouse and implement the relevant part of the op eration.

Broh further explained, that Madan Thelma Duncan Sawyer became involved in a particular aspect of the implementation but was not involved in every stage of the process.

No Knowledge, ,of Sale

Broh den,i,ed having knowledge of the donated rice.

She also said she was unaware of any investigative committee allegedly established by Kemayah to examine the rice issue.

Madam Broh at the same time m, maintained that the meeting she attended concerned the movement of rice from NDMA to GSA.

Her testimony therefore sought to draw a line between the administrative movement of the rice and the allegations of subsequent misuse or sale.

Bonner Testimony Adds to Defense Challenge

Broh’s testimony followed that of defense witness Kpakolo Bonner, who testified last week about the distribution of rice to Norvling Town Community in Paynesville.

Bonner, a resident of the community and an employee of the Forestry Development Authority, testified that rice distributed to the community was intended for people affected by flooding.

He said the rice was distributed openly to affected residents, including people whose homes had been destroyed or damaged by floodwaters.

Bonner said he signed for rice as acting youth chairman and participated in verification and distribution.

However, when shown a waybill in court, he disputed the signature appearing on the document, saying it was not his.

His testimony has given the defense another basis for questioning whether every discrepancy in the documentary record can automatically be attributed to the defendants.

A Case Turning on Where the Rice Went

The prosecution has presented evidence alleging that substantial quantities of the Saudi donation were improperly handled or diverted.

The defense, however, has increasingly focused on the question of where the rice actually went and whether the documentary evidence can establish criminal responsibility beyond a reasonable doubt.

Broh’s testimony was particularly significant because she occupied a senior position at the GSA, one of the institutions that physically handled a substantial quantity of the rice.

Rather than denying that the rice was moved, she acknowledged the transfers and distributions but described them as actions taken within an inter-agency framework.

Her testimony therefore gives the defense an argument that the existence of transfers, gate passes or institutional distributions should not by itself establish criminal intent.

The Saudi Donation

The Saudi government donated 29,412 bags of 25-kilogram rice to Liberia as humanitarian assistance.

The prosecution has alleged that thousands of bags were subsequently misapplied, diverted or stolen.

The defendants have denied the allegations and have maintained that the rice was handled as part of government efforts to respond to vulnerable and disaster-affected populations.

As the defense case continues, Broh’s testimony places emphasis on the distinction between the movement of the rice and the alleged criminal taking of the rice.

And her two statements, one from the witness stand that “the people did a fantastic job” and the other reportedly made as she left the courtroom that “the people are innocent, the people didn’t do anything”, have become the clearest expression yet of her view of the officials whose actions are now being examined by the court.

World.title: Liberia: Bon Jallah Seeks Acquittal As DNA Evidence Links Him to Four Exhibits, Defense Points to Crime-Scene Dispute
World.content:
Prosecution Given Until Tuesday to Resist Motion as Criminal Court “E” Suspends Trial; Rwandan Forensic Expert Says DNA Match Cannot Establish When or How Biological Material Was Deposited

MONROVIA — Lawyers representing Peter Bon Jallah have asked Criminal Court “E” to acquit their client, arguing that inconsistencies surrounding the alleged crime scenes and the circumstances of DNA evidence presented at trial raise reasonable doubt.

By Willie N. Tokpah



The motion was filed Monday, September 28, during the 42nd day of jury sitting at the Temple of Justice, following testimony from a Rwandan forensic expert that Bon Jallah’s DNA profile matched biological material found on four exhibits.

Judge Wesseh Alphonsus Wesseh, Sr. gave the prosecution until noon Tuesday, September 29, to file a written resistance and suspended the trial pending a ruling on the motion.

The defense does not dispute the DNA match. Instead, it challenges what the scientific evidence establishes about the alleged offenses.

DNA Match Does Not Establish When or How Material Was Deposited

Pascal Bavugirije, Acting Division Manager of the Biology Division at Rwanda’s Forensic Institute, testified that DNA profiles obtained from a white T-shirt, black T-shirt, shorts and boxer matched Bon Jallah’s reference DNA profile.

A forensic report dated January 22 concluded that Bon Jallah could not be excluded as a contributor to the DNA profiles obtained from the four exhibits.

However, Bavugirije told the court that the laboratory could not determine when the biological material was deposited, how it was deposited, or the circumstances under which it came to be present on the clothing.

The laboratory’s role, he explained, was to examine materials submitted by Liberian investigators and compare the resulting DNA profiles with reference samples. It was not tasked with reconstructing the alleged events.

The forensic evidence also included a mixed DNA profile obtained from tissue or toilet paper reportedly collected from a crime scene. According to the report, that profile did not match the reference samples of either Bon Jallah or the alleged victim.

Bavugirije said the unidentified profile could potentially be compared with samples from other individuals if such persons were identified and reference samples obtained.

Defense Challenges Camp Johnson Road Crime Scene

The defense has also challenged the prosecution’s evidence concerning the alleged Camp Johnson Road location.

Two locations had been scheduled for a judicial inspection on September 24: a residence associated with Bon Jallah and the Camp Johnson Road location where the alleged victim testified that one of the incidents occurred.

The Camp Johnson Road site was not visited.

The defense cited testimony from Linsay Gould, identified during the trial as chief investigator of the Women and Children Protection Services, that investigators took the alleged victim to Camp Johnson Road on two occasions but that she was unable to identify the precise location.

Defense lawyers argue that the inability to identify the alleged crime scene undermines that portion of the testimony and contributes to reasonable doubt.

Dispute Over Inspection of Bon Jallah’s Residence

The inspection of Bon Jallah’s residence in the Airfield-Matadi area also became part of the defense’s argument.

According to the court record, representatives of both sides and their lawyers visited the residence on September 24. One room was opened while another remained closed after the family identified one room as the master bedroom and declined to open the other.

Defense counsel Cllr. Wilfred Sayeh argued that testimony before the court had identified the master bedroom as one of the locations where an alleged incident occurred, while the defense maintains that the inspection did not resolve discrepancies concerning the residence.

The defense has further pointed to an alleged difference between the police charge sheet and the alleged victim’s testimony regarding which room was involved.

The prosecution is expected to address those issues in its resistance.

Defense Invokes Criminal Procedure Law

In seeking an acquittal before Bon Jallah presents a defense, lawyers relied principally on Sections 2.1 and 20.10 of Liberia’s Criminal Procedure Law.

Section 2.1 provides for the presumption of innocence and requires acquittal where reasonable doubt remains as to whether guilt has been established.

Section 20.10 provides for judgment of acquittal where the evidence is insufficient to sustain a conviction.

Defense lawyers argued that the prosecution’s evidence has exposed inconsistencies sufficient to justify ending the case at this stage.

Prosecutors requested additional time to respond, saying the defense had raised several issues requiring a detailed answer. Judge Wesseh granted the request but ordered the written resistance filed by noon Tuesday.

Court to Decide Whether Case Continues

The filing of the motion does not constitute a ruling that the prosecution’s evidence is insufficient. The court must now determine whether the evidence presented by the Republic is legally sufficient for the trial to continue.

If the motion is denied, Bon Jallah will retain his right to present evidence in his defense.

If the motion is granted, he would receive a judgment of acquittal. Liberia’s Criminal Procedure Law provides the Republic a right to appeal an order granting a motion for judgment of acquittal.

For now, the immediate issue before Judge Wesseh is whether the prosecution’s evidence—including the DNA match on four exhibits and testimony surrounding the alleged crime scenes—is sufficient to allow the case to proceed.

The court’s ruling following Tuesday’s resistance will determine the next stage of the proceedings.

World.title: Chiluba’s seized assets still undisposed-ACC
World.content:
Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC) Director General Daphne Chabu says the lack of a legal framework governing the management of seized assets has delayed the disposal of property seized from late former President Frederick Chiluba.

Ms Chabu said the property, which includes shoes and other items, remains in the custody of the State.

Speaking at an ongoing stakeholders’ consultative meeting on the Draft Criminal Asset Management Bill in Kabwe, Ms Chabu said the absence of a comprehensive legal framework has adversely affected the management of seized and restricted assets after cases are concluded in court.

“We have a big challenge of managing seized properties, including some of the property that was seized from former President Chiluba. The shoes and other properties are yet to be disposed of,” Ms Chabu said.

She said the government has since proposed the Draft Criminal Asset Management Bill, which seeks to establish a Criminal Assets Management Agency responsible for the disposal of seized assets in the country.

Ms Chabu said the establishment of the agency would enhance transparency and professionalism in the management of seized assets.

She said asset management is a critical component in the fight against corruption.

“There is a need for stakeholders to actively participate in the enactment of the proposed law by making the necessary submissions towards the process,” she emphasised.

Ms Chabu said the ACC is currently conducting consultation meetings in all 10 provincial centres to strengthen and refine the Draft Criminal Asset Management Bill.

She said Zambia needs a dedicated institution to handle seized and restricted assets in order to build public confidence in the fight against corruption.

Ms Chabu further emphasised that the Commission remains committed to delivering on its mandate of spearheading the fight against corruption in the country.

World.title: Lumezi South UPND’ candidate seeks nullification of election or vote recount
World.content:
Losing Lumezi South Member of Parliament, Lufeyo Ngoma has asked the Chipata High Court to nullify the parliamentary election results or, alternatively, order a recount of the votes.

Mr Ngoma, who contested the election on the United Party for National Development (UPND) ticket, has challenged the results, alleging that the polls were marred by vote buying, intimidation, violence and other electoral malpractices.

He has also alleged discrepancies in election figures, alteration of figures and other irregularities during the electoral process.

Testifying before Chipata High Court Judge-in-Charge Justice Charles Kafunda, Mr Ngoma alleged that National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP) candidate Oliver Mwale who won the seat, engaged in electoral malpractices, including vote buying, violence and political intimidation.

Mr Ngoma alleged that on August 12, 2026, Mr Mwale, in the company of NRPUP polling agents, was seen distributing salt, soya pieces, ballpoint pens and K20 notes to electorates in Chibande Ward.

The court heard that Mr Ngoma subsequently decided to tour all six polling stations in the ward, but was unable to hold successful meetings because some people allegedly demanded the same items that Mr Mwale was distributing.

He testified that voters at different polling stations in Chibande Ward openly told him that Mr Mwale had informed them that the ballpoint pens were allegedly from the Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) and were to be used on voting day.

Mr Ngoma told the court that the voters allegedly received the items from Mr Mwale with instructions to vote for him and Tonse Alliance presidential candidate Brian Mundubile.

He added that people would disperse before meetings could commence because he did not have the items which his opponent was allegedly distributing.

“My Lord, I got deeply concerned with this situation because the people were refusing to start the meetings because I did not come with salt, soya pieces, ballpoint pens and K20, which Mr Oliver Mwale would come with,” he said.

Mr Ngoma further told the court that after casting his ballot at Kakulo Polling Station in Lukusuzi Ward on August 13, 2026, he saw Mr Mwale, in the company of Evans Manda, an NRPUP polling agent, allegedly distributing ballpoint pens and K20 notes to voters in the queue and instructing them to vote for him and Mr Mundubile.

Mr Ngoma said he felt helpless over what he described as the level of electoral malpractices, adding that there was no Police Officer at the polling station and that a village scout had instead been deployed to assist with security.

He testified that he later visited Lukusuzi Polling Station, where he allegedly found NRPUP polling agents Evans Manda and Matthews Kashimu distributing money and other materials within the polling station’s perimeter while chanting party songs and displaying NRPUP symbols.

Mr Ngoma said his efforts to seek police intervention failed because the village scout deployed to the polling station was allegedly intimidated by a large crowd supporting the opposition.

He further told the court that on voting day, he visited Kamukwezi Polling Station in Kachama Ward but was allegedly blocked by NRPUP polling agent John Lungu, whom he found allegedly distributing ballpoint pens and K20 notes to voters standing in the queue.

Mr Ngoma said he then proceeded to Mwimba Polling Station, where he found two vehicles surrounded by a large crowd about 10 metres from the polling station.

He told the court that as he approached the crowd, he allegedly saw Mr Mwale in the company of NRPUP candidate for council chairperson Dawson Tembo and other unidentified people distributing K20 notes and ballpoint pens to voters.

“I further received calls from my polling agents from Katube Polling Station, Kangobe Polling Station, Masutwe Polling Station and Ndundundu Polling Station. The situation was almost the same my lord, there was also vote buying, violence and intimidation,” he said.

The court also heard that when Mr Ngoma visited Mpingozi Polling Station in Diwa Ward, he was informed by a UPND polling agent that Mr Mwale had allegedly slaughtered a cow on August 12, 2026 and was feeding voters at a house belonging to an NRPUP polling agent near the polling station.

Mr Ngoma further alleged that Lusaka Diocese Archbishop Alick Banda distributed K50 notes, sausages and ballpoint pens to nearly 400 people at a farm in Lumezi South while allegedly instructing them to vote for Mr Mundubile and Mr Mwale.

He alleged that Archbishop Banda, in the company of Mr Mwale and his polling agent Nicholas Nkhoma, distributed the materials in Lumezi South for three consecutive days, a week before the general election.

During cross-examination by Timothy Sapato of Nkonde and Kapingula Associates, the petitioner told the court that there are no videos or pictures from Dr. Alick Banda’s farm, other than a witness who is yet to give their testimony.

Mr Ngoma’s petition comes after Oliver Mwale was declared duly elected Member of Parliament for Lumezi South after he polled 6,324 votes during the August 13, General Elections beating Mr Ngoma who got 4,946 votes.

World.title: Zambia-UAE sign MoU worth over US$2.1 billion
World.content:
Zambia and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) have signed memoranda of understanding across various sectors worth US$2.14 billion.

And President Hakainde Hichilema says Zambia looks forward to signing the Comprehensive Partnership Agreement with the UAE to increase trade between the two countries.

Witnessing the signing during the Zambia-UAE Business Forum in Abu Dhabi today, President Hichilema noted that his government will continue to prioritise increased trade and domestic reforms to attract the investment which is needed to grow the country’s economy.

The Head of State reaffirmed that Zambia remains open and ready for business and investment.

Meanwhile, President Hichilema noted that there is a lot to learn from the UAE that has harnessed its natural resources to develop its economy and raised the living standards of its people.

“As a country richly endowed with natural resources, we have much to learn from the UAE. Through the Grow Zambia Agenda, our goal is to double the size of our economy, delivering more revenue for public services, more jobs and more business for our people,” President Hichilema said.

He has since thanked the President of the United Arab Emirates, Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, for the invitation to visit his country.

World.title: First University opens in Zimba District
World.content:
Zimba District has recorded a major milestone in the education sector with the opening of its first-ever higher education institution, Africa Wesleyan University College.

‎

‎The institution, established by the Pilgrim Wesleyan Church, is expected to expand access to university education for young people in Zimba, Zambia and other parts of Africa.

‎

‎The opening of the university places Zimba on the map of higher education centres while creating an opportunity for students to pursue tertiary education closer to their communities.

‎

‎United States-based businessman and principal funder of the project, Garry Ott, who officiated at the opening ceremony, said the institution had been established to serve students beyond Zambia.

‎

‎Mr Ott said the university would provide young people from across Africa with an opportunity to access quality higher education while contributing to the development of communities.

‎

‎“This University is not only for Zimba or Zambia, but is intended to serve students from across the African continent,” Mr Ott said.

‎

He said the institution will provide an important platform for young people to acquire knowledge and skills that could contribute to the development of their respective communities and spiritual life.

‎

‎And Africa Wesleyan University College Principal, Henry Prince, said the institution was expected to enroll its first intake in January 2027.

‎

‎Dr Prince said preparations were underway to ensure that the university is ready to provide higher education opportunities to students when the first intake commences.

‎

‎And Mapatizya Member of Parliament, Emeldah Munashabantu said the establishment of the university was an investment in education and the future of young people.

‎

‎“The establishment of this university is not only an investment in education, but an investment in the future of our young people,” Ms Munashabantu said.

‎

‎She, however, appealed for the introduction of scholarships for students from disadvantaged backgrounds to ensure that financial challenges did not prevent deserving young people from accessing higher education.

‎

‎Ms Munashabantu said the coming of the university was also a fulfilment of the Pilgrim Wesleyan Church’s long-standing commitment to education in Zimba.

‎

‎Earlier, Zimba District Commissioner, Robinson Mulamfu said the university had added significant value to the face of the district.

‎

‎Mr Mulamfu said the institution would contribute to the development of the education sector and the wider community by creating opportunities for skills development and higher learning.

‎

‎Meanwhile, Wesleyan Presiding Bishop, Juden Siachitema said the establishment of the university had been made possible through endurance, hope and patience among those who had worked towards its establishment.

‎

‎Bishop Siachitema said the foundation laid for the institution carried a responsibility for the university to develop beyond being an ordinary centre of learning.

World.title: Chama district to benefit from FANSER+ Project
World.content:
Chama District Commissioner, Yobe Goma, says plans are underway to extend the Food and Nutrition Security, Enhanced Resilience Plus (FANSER+) Project to the district as the programme enters its second year of implementation.

Mr Goma says the extension of the project to the district will help reach more vulnerable rural households with interventions aimed at reducing malnutrition and strengthening household resilience.

He said this during an engagement on the implementation of the FANSER+ Project in Chama district.

Mr Goma said the project, which is implemented by the Deutsche Gesellschaft für Internationale Zusammenarbeit (GIZ) on behalf of the German Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development (BMZ), complements Government’s efforts to address malnutrition among vulnerable communities.

He said the project is being implemented in line with the First 1,000 Most Critical Days Programme under the leadership of the National Food and Nutrition Commission (NFNC).

Mr Goma said focusing on the first 1,000 days of a child’s life, from conception to the second birthday, is critical in preventing stunted growth and protecting children’s cognitive and physical development.

“By targeting the first 1,000 days of a child’s life from conception to the second birthday, we are not just tackling stunted growth, we are protecting the cognitive and physical potential of our future leaders, teachers and policymakers,” he said.

Mr Goma said malnutrition remains a quiet but devastating barrier to human capital development and requires concerted efforts from Government, cooperating partners and communities.

He said strengthening nutrition interventions at household and community level will contribute to improved health, learning outcomes and the overall wellbeing of children.

Mr Goma said the FANSER+ Project is complementing Government’s efforts to improve food and nutrition security while enhancing the resilience of vulnerable rural households.

The FANSER+ Project is being implemented in six target districts of Eastern Province, , with a focus on vulnerable rural households and the prevention of malnutrition.

Mr Goma has since called on communities to actively participate in the programme and make use of the knowledge and interventions provided to improve household nutrition.

World.title: Chisamba Magistrate Court sentences Marijuana trafficker
World.content:
A 35-year-old man has been sentenced to 28 months’ imprisonment with hard labour for trafficking in 2.1 Kilograms of marijuana by the Chisamba Magistrate Court.

Gift Phiri of Ten Miles area has been convicted and sentenced by Chisamba Magistrate, Litungi Litungi upon his own plea of guilty and admission of facts.

Phiri was facing one count of trafficking in psychotropic substances, contrary to Section 15 of the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act Number 35 of 2021 and Statutory Instrument Number 119 of 1995.

Particulars of the offence are that on September 7, 2026, Phiri trafficked in 2.1 kilograms of marijuana without lawful authority.

The court heard that, in an intelligence-led operation, Drug Enforcement Commission (DEC) officers found Phiri in possession of two pre-packed quantities of the drugs concealed in a black bucket at Ten Miles.

“On 7th September, 2026, a team of four officers from the Drug Enforcement Commission led by Isaac Nkhuwa conducted a patrol at 10 miles area after receiving intelligence information of a man dealing in Marijuana in the area,” the facts read in part.

The court further heard that samples of the drug were seized and sent to the University Teaching Hospital Food and Drug Control Laboratory in Lusaka, where analysts confirmed that the substance was cannabis sativa, with a Delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol, or THC, content of 4.7 percent, exceeding the legal limit of 0.3 percent.

Following a warn-and-caution statement conducted in Nyanja by DEC Investigation Officer Nancy Banda, Phiri confessed to the offence while in Police custody.

In mitigation, Phiri pleaded for leniency, saying he has two school-going children who look up to him and that he also takes care of his mother, who is diabetic.

In passing sentence, Magistrate Litungi stated that drug abuse has destroyed many youths and that it was the duty of the court to impose stiffer punishment on offenders to deter would-be offenders.

“The punishment for the offence which you committed is imprisonment for a term of not less than one year, but not exceeding 25-years.

“However, I have taken recognition that the convict is a first offender who has readily admitted the charge and taken into consideration his mitigating factors,” Magistrate Litungi said.

He then sentenced Phiri to 28 months’ imprisonment with hard labour, effective September 28, 2026.

The court further ordered that the drug be forfeited to the State and destroyed by burning in the presence of court officials.

World.title: Govt. disburses over K16 million to MSMES
World.content:
Government has disbursed over K16 million to 47 Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises(MSMEs) as part of efforts to strengthen local businesses and position them to tap into markets along the Lobito Corridor.

The intervention is being implemented under the Grow Zambia Agenda, with the Government providing grants and machinery to MSMEs to increase production, create jobs and take advantage of opportunities in neighbouring countries.

Acting Permanent Secretary in the Ministry of Small and Medium Enterprise Development, Lemmy Kafwamfwa said Government wants businesses in areas such as Solwezi and the Copperbelt to be ready to supply markets in Angola and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC).

Mr Kafwamfwa disclosed that the government is funding and providing machinery to MSMEs operating in Solwezi and the industrial yards in Ndola and Kitwe to increase their production capacity.

He said the support is also intended to reach women who are unbanked and young people who may not easily access financing from commercial banks.

Mr Kafwamfwa emphasised that the objective is to ensure that MSMEs operating along the Lobito Corridor can produce competitively and access markets in neighbouring countries.

World.title: Govt. extols Mbala schools on Presidential Irrigation Initiative
World.content:
Government has praised schools that benefited from the Presidential Irrigation Initiative in Mbala District in Northern Province for the way they are undertaking the programme.

Presidential Monitoring Team Leader, Kapaso Kunda, says the team is happy with the progress made so far in the implementation of the programme.

Speaking after inspecting progress at Mbala Boarding Secondary School, and St Mary’s College of Education Mr Kunda has disclosed that the team is happy with how the schools have handled the programme.

He revealed that each benefiting school had been allocated funds to undertake activities under the initiative introduced by President Hakainde Hichilema.

Mr Kunda explained that the programme has revamped production units in schools through the installation of irrigation systems and water storage tanks, enabling schools to grow maize and other crops throughout the year.

“We are happy with what we have seen, there is progress. This programme has revamped production units in schools, we have seen schools grow different crops,” he said.

“Yes this is an initiative of President Hichilema, each school was funded to undertake activities such as the installation of irrigation systems and water storage tanks, enabling schools to grow maize and other crops throughout the year,” he added.

And Mbala District Education Board Secretary, Juanitah Mulenga, said the initiative is progressing well.

Mrs Mulenga observed that the initiative will strengthen agricultural production in schools while providing learners with practical agricultural skills.

“The programme here is moving well, I would like to commend President Hakainde Hichilema for introducing the programme, it is a timely intervention that will improve school productivity and contribute to sustainable agricultural development,” she said.

And a student teacher at St Mary’s College of Education, Ignatius Musenga observed that the school will no longer need to buy maize because it would be producing its own.

Mr Musenga said the school also plans to acquire a hammer mill to process the maize that the school will be harvesting into mealie-meal.

He thanked President Hakainde Hichilema for introducing the programme, which will help the institution achieve good harvests and improve food security.

In Northern Province, the programme is supporting 35 schools, while in Mbala four schools have benefited.

The schools benefiting from the programme include St Mary’s College of Education, Kaka Day Secondary Schools, Mbala Boarding Secondary School and Lucheche Day Secondary School.
