World.title: Africa: Who Is Missing From Africa's AI Future?
World.content:
guest column

What if every baby born in Africa started life with an all-access key to the 21st century? Not a smartphone or an AI assistant, but something much more - fundamental recognition that says you are here, you are known, and you belong.

At the just-concluded UNGA81, I listened to African leaders reflect on what it will take for the continent to realize the promise of artificial intelligence. At the Unstoppable Africa session, Rwanda's Prime Minister Justin Nsengiyumva spoke about decades of government investment in digital public infrastructure, including nationwide 4G coverage and the digitization of more than 250 government services. His point was clear: "AI cannot thrive on algorithms alone." Sierra Leone's Chief Minister, David Moinina Sengeh, brought another dimension to the conversation when he reflected on Africa's history of extraction and asked whether, in the 21st century, we will allow our data to be extracted too.

These are different perspectives, but they speak to something I hear increasingly in conversations with governments across Africa - how do we make sure this next technological era strengthens our institutions, reflects our realities and creates value for our people? For those of us working in public health, answering that requires us to look much further back than the algorithm, to the foundations that determine whether people are visible to public systems in the first place.



Almost half of children under five in sub-Saharan Africa do not have their births registered. And by 2050, Africa is expected to account for one in every three births globally. This is not just a bureaucratic or administrative gap. This is a global equity gap. Whether you work in health, financial inclusion, education or agriculture; whether you are in the public or private sector, an entrepreneur, an investor or a funder, I am willing to bet that you are counting and reporting on how many people you have reached. But do you know how many people you have missed, who they are and how you can reach them? Without knowing the denominator, how can we properly evaluate our impact and hold ourselves accountable?

A government cannot fully know whether children are being vaccinated, communities are receiving health services or resources are reaching those most in need if significant parts of its population are missing from the equation. How can we close the gap if we don't know how large it is?

That is why every birth registered and every death counted matters. It gives governments a clearer picture of the population they are responsible for serving and, increasingly, creates the foundation from which people can participate in a digital society. More than 800 million people globally still lack official proof of identity, and more than half are children whose births were never registered. As governments digitize more public services, being recognized by the system will increasingly shape how easily people can access health care, education, social protection and economic opportunities.

We are already seeing African countries approach this in different ways. In Kenya, Maisha Namba is intended to provide a lifelong personal number beginning at birth. Rwanda has invested over many years in connecting civil registration, identity, and public services, while Ethiopia is expanding Fayda, its digital identification system. These examples point to a larger opportunity - to count people from birth, recognize them throughout their lives, and connect them to the services and opportunities they need. As more of those services become digital, we must also ensure that the systems intended to expand access do not inadvertently exclude people who lack the required documentation, connectivity, or digital literacy.

This becomes even more consequential as AI plays a greater role in how governments understand populations, identify risks, and allocate resources. As the Vital Strategies Foundation's and Futures analysis of AI readiness across 83 countries has shown, countries are starting from very different places, and readiness depends on much more than access to AI itself. There is enormous potential for AI to strengthen disease surveillance, help health workers make better decisions, and enable governments to respond earlier to emerging health needs. But AI learns from data, and that should force us to ask who is represented in that data and who is missing. If populations are absent or poorly represented in the systems feeding AI, technology does not suddenly make them visible. Their realities can remain absent from the insights being used to make decisions about them.

Inclusion in the AI age therefore cannot begin once an algorithm has been built. It begins with whether a child is counted at birth, whether she is recognized by the state, whether she can access health care and education, whether her experiences become part of the data used to understand her community, and whether people like her have a voice in how technologies intended to serve them are designed and governed. This is why some of the smartest investments we can make in the AI era may not look like AI investments at all. They will look like reliable birth and death registration, trusted identity systems, interoperable public infrastructure, strong data governance, skilled public-sector workforces and institutions capable of protecting people's data while using it to make better decisions.

Close 

At Unstoppable Africa, one phrase particularly resonated with me - "radical inclusion." I think that is an ambition worth carrying into Africa's approach to AI. Success should not simply mean that more AI solutions are developed or deployed across the continent. It should mean that African institutions have the capacity to shape them, African realities are reflected in the data that powers them, and the benefits reach people who have historically been easiest for public systems to miss.

That also changes the investment conversation. We should not have to build another disconnected system every time new technology or health intervention arrives. Governments, philanthropy and development partners have an opportunity to invest once, and invest well, in strong public foundations that many solutions can build upon, and that countries can own and sustain. We talk frequently about Africa's opportunity to leapfrog in the AI era, and I believe that opportunity is real. But leapfrogging still requires strong ground from which to leap.

For a continent that will soon be home to one in every three children born in the world, building that ground starts with something remarkably fundamental, making sure every child is counted, recognized and connected.

Mary-Ann Etiebet, MD, MBA, President and CEO, Vital Strategies

World.title: Nigeria: After Four-Week Working Vacation in Europe, Tinubu Departs France for Nigeria
World.content:
Abuja — President Bola Tinubu on Tuesday ended his four-week working vacation and has already departed Paris, France, for the homeward journey to Nigeria.

Presidential spokesperson, Bayo Onanuga, in a release, stated that President Tinubu's aircraft is expected to touch down at Murtala Muhammed Airport, Lagos, later on Tuesday evening.

Tinubu chose to fly to Lagos first to honour the memory of the martyr of Nigeria's democratic struggle, Chief MKO Abiola

According to the statement, on Independence Day, the President will attend the premiere of a movie honouring Abiola, the winner of the June 1993 election, at the Wole Soyinka National Theatre, Iganmu, Lagos.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

While in Lagos, Tinubu will also hold strategic meetings with political leaders and associates over several days in preparation for the 2027 elections.

The President will return to Abuja after his political engagements in Lagos.

Tinubu, who departed Abuja on August 30, 2026 for the working vacation, spent one week in London before heading for Paris.

While in Paris, he attended a private dinner with President Emmanuel Macron and also met with business leaders, including Mr Vincent Bolloré of the Bolloré Group, whose media and digital interests include Canal+, MultiChoice and Universal Music Group.

On Monday, Tinubu also met with the Chairman of First Holdings, Femi Otedola.

Last week, the President witnessed the signing of a Memorandum of Understanding between the Ogun State Government and DP World to build a Gateway deep seaport in Ogun Waterside and create a Blue Marine Economic Zone in the area.

DP World, one of the world's leading ports and logistics operators, plans to invest $7 billion for the seaport and the economic zone.

World.title: Kenya: Ruto Warns Against Attempts to Derail Dangote Refinery
World.content:
The Dangote Refinery is located in one of the Free Trade Zones in Nigeria.

Nairobi — President William Ruto has warned individuals he accused of trying to frustrate the planned Sh2 trillion Dangote refinery in Lamu, as the mega project moves closer to its groundbreaking on Wednesday.

Speaking in Kilifi on Tuesday during the issuance of title deeds, Ruto said the refinery would transform Kenya's economy and attract billions of shillings in foreign investment.

The President is scheduled to lead the groundbreaking ceremony for the East Africa Refinery in Lamu on.

The project, backed by Nigerian businessman Aliko Dangote, is expected to cost about Sh2.2 trillion and have a planned capacity of 700,000 barrels of crude oil per day.



"Kesho, kwa mapenzi ya Mungu inshallah, kesho tunaanzisha refinery ya trillion mbili pale Lamu," Ruto said.

He warned those opposing the investment against attempting to derail the project through what he described as demands for shares and other conditions.

"Hamuwezi kututapeli siku zote. Hamuwezi kutudanganya siku zote," the President said.

Ruto accused unnamed "brokers" of previously contributing to Kenya losing major investments, citing Dangote's earlier attempt to establish a cement plant in Kenya and the decision to route Uganda's crude oil pipeline through Tanzania instead.

"Mimi nawaambia, bwana, mimi niko macho mbaya sana! Hapa hamutoboi, bwana!" he said.

Ruto said the government would ensure the refinery investment was structured transparently, adding that the Kenyan government would have a stake in the project.

He further said ordinary Kenyans would get an opportunity to buy shares through the Nairobi Securities Exchange.

"Investment ya refinery is an open, transparent investment. Serikali ya Kenya itakuwa na stake katika hiyo refinery. Wakenya hawa nyinyi wote mutapata nafasi ya kununua hisa kwa hiyo refinery, transparent katika exchange yetu, Nairobi Securities Exchange," Ruto said.

His remarks come as debate grows around investment opportunities linked to Dangote's refinery projects.

The Nigerian Dangote Petroleum Refinery is currently conducting a major IPO, although Kenyan investors cannot currently subscribe to that offer directly through the NSE.

Ruto argued that Kenya needed to make it easier for investors to do business by offering incentives rather than imposing conditions that could drive investment elsewhere.

"Mwekezaji hataki kusumbuliwa, hataki masharti, anataka incentives," he said.

The refinery is expected to support petroleum processing and related industries, while Lamu Port is expected to play a major role in handling cargo and marine operations linked to the project.

Close 

A vessel carrying about 2,930 tonnes of construction equipment for the refinery arrived at Lamu Port on Saturday.

The project has, however, faced legal challenges over land. A court recently directed parties to maintain the status quo on a disputed parcel in Lamu, while declining to stop the planned groundbreaking. The case is scheduled for further hearing on October 14.

Dangote Group has also confirmed that the court ruling will not stop Wednesday's official groundbreaking ceremony, although it could affect some activities at the site.

Ruto maintained that his government would protect investments and ensure the Coast benefits from major economic projects.

"I will not allow you to undermine investments in our country. You have had enough," he said.

He also said the refinery would create jobs and investment opportunities while helping position the Coast as an important economic hub.

World.title: Madison Beer gushes over 'incredible' Justin Herbert, WAG culture is headed to college & the NASCAR swear jar
World.content:
'Nightcaps' is a daily column that catches you up on the biggest sports, news and culture stories you may have missed while pretending to do work at your desk. It runs Monday-Friday on OutKick.com.

Happy Tuesday, friends. I am thrilled to be back in the beautiful state of Tennessee.

Where have I been, you ask? Let me tell ya.

This weekend, I traveled to majestic Branson, Missouri. Or as I like to call it, Pigeon Forge Jr. (IYKYK).

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

I got the invite to check out the SMX (that's supermotocross for the uncultured) World Championship Final and the YETI Open on Table Rock Lake.

Now, if you've never been to Branson, let me paint you a picture: kitschy stores, celebrity chain restaurants and dinner theaters. Oh, and pretty much the whole town is owned by Bass Pro Shops.

But the scenery in this particular slice of the country is also stunning. Rolling hills, a big, beautiful lake, an outdoorsman's paradise. Hence, the Bass Pro Shops thing.

Anyway, on Sunday I had the honor of going fishing with none other than Bassmaster Elite Pro Cooper Gallant.

I'll admit I'm a pretty hopeless bass angler. But who better to teach me than someone who does it for a living?

So if you're into that sort of thing (that "thing" being bagging largies) stay tuned to OutKick OutDoors. Make sure you're subscribed on YouTube and following on Instagram and TikTok.

Otherwise, you might miss the absolute leviathan (not pictured) that I caught while we were out there. And that would be a real shame for you.

With that out of the way, let's get on to some Nightcaps, shall we?

College football WAGs are apparently a thing now

WAG culture has gotten completely out of control.

Look, I know — we love WAGs here at OutKick. It's become a whole genre, especially in 'Caps. But once the NFL started using the WAGs to "market to women," the whole thing just became a little too... forced?

And now, apparently, the college girls are getting in on it.

Meet Allison Kaye, a makeup artist whose entire business is traveling around the country getting athletes' wives and girlfriends glammed up for game day. She started with NFL WAGs, but this season, she's taking "Game Day Glam" to college campuses.

STAY "FEARLESS" ON THE GO! TAKE TOMI LAHREN WITH YOU. DOWNLOAD THE TLIF PODCAST NOW!

She started at Ohio State earlier this month, doing makeup for four players' girlfriends. Then she went to Penn State and did six more.

And I have to say, this woman has found herself one hell of a business model.

She doesn't just show up with a Caboodle (remember those?), either. She turns her hotel room into a whole "glam suite" with food, drinks, team decorations and free stuff from beauty brands. The girlfriends pay for the service themselves. Or with their boyfriends' NIL money.

Apparently, her weekends are now almost completely booked for the rest of football season.

There are 134 FBS football teams, approximately one bazillion players and, presumably, a whole lot of girlfriends who would rather not do their own makeup at 7 a.m. before a noon kickoff.

I don't know what Allison Kaye is charging for this, but I do know she might have stumbled upon a gold mine.

Maybe I should learn how to use a curling iron. Get a little side hustle going.

Speaking of WAGS...

Madison Beer is positively gushing over Justin Herbert

You know who could use a win right now? Justin Herbert.

The Chargers are 0-3. Their offense STINKS. And every day he has to go to work and listen to Mike McDaniel say things like "we're not standing on business" in his rolled up joggers.

But you know what Justin Herbert does have?

Madison Beer.



And Madison Beer is apparently VERY into Justin Herbert.

The singer recently hopped on Twitch and talked about their July engagement, which she described as "magical." She also said the proposal happened exactly one year after Herbert asked her to be his girlfriend and gushed about how lucky she feels to have found him.

So sure, things at work aren't going great for Herbs.

But at the end of the day, he gets to go home to Madison Beer, who is hot, wildly successful and seemingly thinks he hung the moon.

No matter what those insufferable dorks over on the "Speakeasy" podcast have to say about her.

No mailbag today (womp) because my email inbox is bone dry (minus about 100 irrelevant PR pitches). Let's remedy this for next week.

If you've ever screamed obscenities after getting cut off on the interstate or just while sitting in traffic in general, you can probably imagine the colorful language that gets thrown around during NASCAR races.

And not just during the post-race fistfights, either.

Anyway, the potty mouths are so bad that NASCAR has implemented a swear jar, and they are keeping a running tally of which expletives get used the most.

World.title: Dengue fever outbreak triggers states of emergency in 3 southern counties
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Three Florida counties have declared states of emergency amid the spread of dengue fever in the state.

As of Sept. 23, Pasco County, Hillsborough County and Pinellas County have made the declarations due to a spread of the mosquito-borne disease, according to each county’s news release.

The local emergency declarations allow county officials to expedite mosquito-control operations, make emergency purchases, coordinate response efforts and, where applicable, seek state or federal assistance or reimbursement, the releases state.

TROPICAL DISEASE SPREAD BY MOSQUITOES CLAIMS FIRST RECORDED DEATH IN SOUTHERN US STATE

Under Florida law, local emergency declarations expire after seven days unless they are renewed.

A total of 190 locally acquired dengue cases have been confirmed across six Florida counties, according to the latest Florida Department of Health surveillance report, which covered cases with onset through Sept. 19.

Of the 190 locally acquired cases, 170 were reported in Hillsborough County, seven each in Miami-Dade and Pinellas counties, three in Orange County, two in Pasco County and one in Palm Beach County.

The 190 locally acquired infections are separate from travel-associated dengue cases reported in Florida this year.

TICK-BORNE 'RABBIT FEVER' SPREADS WITH CASES REPORTED NEAR MAJOR METRO AREA

Dengue is a mosquito-borne viral illness that can cause fever, severe aches, nausea, rash and, in rare cases, life-threatening complications, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

"The Aedes mosquitoes that can transmit dengue are active during the day and thrive in warm, humid environments like those found in Florida."

Dengue is endemic in many tropical and subtropical regions, including Southeast Asia, the Western Pacific islands, Latin America and Africa. Though less common in the continental U.S., locally acquired cases have been recorded in Florida, California and Texas.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"The Aedes mosquitoes that can transmit dengue are active during the day and thrive in warm, humid environments like those found in Florida," an entomologist spokesperson at the SC Johnson Center for Insect Science and Family Health, makers of OFF!, said in a statement sent to Fox News Digital.

"As dengue cases continue to be reported in the Tampa area, taking steps to help prevent mosquito bites is especially important," the expert went on. "Staying aware of local mosquito activity and consistently protecting against bites are important steps people can take to help reduce their risk."

Stopping the spread

The Florida Mosquito Control Association (FMCA) previously said crews are increasing aerial and ground treatments in areas showing dengue virus activity, while also inspecting private properties for potential mosquito breeding sites, according to reports.

FMCA has urged residents to empty or cover standing water around their homes. The mosquito that spreads dengue is a container breeder, meaning it lays eggs in buckets, planters, plant saucers, tires, discarded toys and other objects that collect small amounts of water, experts say.

CLICK HERE TO 

The SC Johnson Center for Insect Science and Family Health entomologist shared the following recommendations to prevent the spread of mosquito-borne disease.

Use an EPA-registered insect repellent: Review, follow and apply repellent label directions to help prevent mosquito bites.

Review, follow and apply repellent label directions to help prevent mosquito bites. Eliminate sources of standing water nearby: Where there’s standing water, there can be mosquitoes. Mosquitoes need only one tablespoon of water to breed, so areas like rain gutters, birdbaths or buckets with stagnant water are all possible breeding sites.

Where there’s standing water, there can be mosquitoes. Mosquitoes need only one tablespoon of water to breed, so areas like rain gutters, birdbaths or buckets with stagnant water are all possible breeding sites. Layer repellent and sunscreen correctly: When using both sunscreen and mosquito repellent, apply sunscreen first, followed by insect repellent. Be sure to follow the label directions for both products and reapply as directed.

When using both sunscreen and mosquito repellent, apply sunscreen first, followed by insect repellent. Be sure to follow the label directions for both products and reapply as directed. Protect throughout the day: Don’t limit mosquito precautions to dawn and dusk. The Aedes mosquitoes that can spread dengue are active throughout the day, so use protection whenever mosquito exposure is possible.

The FMCA also advises people to dress in long sleeves, light colors and closed-toed shoes outdoors.

Symptoms and treatment

Many people infected with dengue have no symptoms, and most people who do become sick recover within a week or two, according to Mayo Clinic.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

In some cases, however, the illness can progress to severe dengue, a potentially life-threatening condition.

Symptoms typically begin four to 10 days after the bite of an infected mosquito.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Warning signs can develop quickly, often within a day or two after the fever subsides. Those may include severe stomach pain, repeated vomiting, unusual bleeding or bruising, difficulty breathing, extreme tiredness and irritability, or restlessness.

People experiencing warning signs of severe dengue should seek immediate medical care.

World.title: Is your personal data changing what you pay online?
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Retailers and the companies working behind the scenes can collect information about where you are, what you search for, what you buy and how you behave online. The FTC says pricing systems can use personal data to estimate how much an individual consumer may be willing to spend. That concern is now getting serious attention in Washington. On Aug. 19, 2026, the Federal Trade Commission published a proposed enforcement policy statement aimed at personalized pricing.

The FTC says it cannot ban the practice in every situation, but companies that fail to clearly tell consumers how personal data affects the prices they see could violate federal consumer protection law. So, could the information companies collect about you actually change the price, discount or product you see? Here's what the research shows and what you can do before your next online purchase.

Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways AI can help you get better healthcare.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, Get Better Healthcare With AI, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways AI can help you organize your health history, remember important appointment details, understand complicated medical information, research prescriptions and prepare smarter questions for your doctor. No technical experience is needed.

Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com

MARYLAND MOVES TO BAN SURVEILLANCE PRICING IN GROCERY STORES

Dynamic pricing and personalized pricing work differently

You've probably encountered dynamic pricing already. Dynamic pricing adjusts prices based on broader conditions such as supply, demand, available inventory, time or location. Rideshare fares may rise when lots of people need cars at once. Airline tickets and hotel rooms can also change as availability and demand shift. That does not mean every shopper will always see the exact same dynamic price. Timing, location and other market conditions can change quickly. Personalized pricing is different because information about a particular consumer helps determine the price or offer that person receives. That means two people looking for the same product could potentially receive different offers because of information connected to them.

There's also price steering. A retailer may leave the actual prices alone while changing the order of the products shown to you. FTC research found that pricing tools can use consumer data to give certain products more prominent placement, including potentially showing higher-priced products first. The FTC says consumers generally expect prices to change because of supply and demand. What can come as a surprise is a price influenced by someone's browsing habits, buying history or other personal information.

What companies can potentially learn about you

FTC research into surveillance pricing found that third-party pricing companies can use surprisingly detailed information when helping retailers tailor prices, promotions or product rankings.

That information can include:

Your approximate or precise location

Browsing patterns and history

Shopping and purchase history

Products left in an online cart

Demographic information

The time, location or channel used to make a purchase

Your behavior and preferences on a website

Even your mouse movements on a webpage

The FTC found that the pricing intermediaries it examined worked with at least 250 clients selling goods and services ranging from groceries to clothing. The FTC's research also found that companies can combine first-party information with data from outside sources. Those sources can include loyalty programs, reservation systems, ecommerce platforms and data brokers. That does not show that every one of those clients charges individualized prices. It does show that technology exists to combine detailed consumer information and use it to influence prices, discounts and which products shoppers see.

A 2026 rideshare test found big price differences

A newer investigation brings the Uber example much closer to today. In June 2026, Consumer Reports published results from a months-long study of Uber and Lyft pricing. The investigation used 174 volunteers who checked more than 40 routes across the U.S. For the 30 virtual routes in its analysis, Consumer Reports found a median gap of 42.4% between the lowest and highest price groups.

On some routes, people checking the same trip within minutes of one another received several different prices. Consumer Reports designed the study to reduce the effects of time-based pricing by having volunteers check routes at roughly the same time. However, the investigation could not control for every factor inside Uber's and Lyft's pricing systems, including driver supply, estimated arrival times, traffic, routing differences and network delays.

Uber and Lyft disputed Consumer Reports' conclusions. Both companies said they do not use personal data to personalize base fares and do not engage in behavioral or surveillance pricing. So, the study shows that riders can receive significantly different prices for similar trips checked around the same time. It does not prove those price differences were caused by personal data.

WHAT YOUR INTERNET PROVIDER, WEBSITES AND ADVERTISERS SEE

Shoppers have also seen different grocery prices online

Online groceries have produced another eye-opening example. In December 2025, Consumer Reports, Groundwork Collaborative and More Perfect Union reported that nearly three-quarters of the grocery items they tested on Instacart were offered at different prices to different shoppers. The investigation involved 437 shoppers across four U.S. cities.

Some items showed differences of as much as 23% between the lowest and highest prices. Researchers also found that totals for identical baskets varied by an average of about 7%. Using an Instacart figure for how much a household of four spends on groceries, the researchers estimated that a similar difference over a year could amount to roughly $1,200. Instacart strongly disputed that annual extrapolation and said the limited tests should not be treated as though a household would continually pay higher prices throughout an entire year. The company also said the pricing tests were randomized and did not use personal information, demographics, shopping history or individual behavior to decide who received each price.

Instacart ended the item price tests in December 2025. The company now says customers shopping for the same item at the same store location at the same time will see the same item price. So, the investigation showed that Instacart shoppers could receive different prices during those tests. It did not prove that Instacart used personal profiles to select those prices.

Online price personalization goes back years

Researchers were finding customized shopping experiences long before today's AI-powered pricing systems. In 2014, Northeastern University researchers studied 16 major retail and travel websites and found evidence of price discrimination or personalized search results on nine of them. CheapTickets and Orbitz offered reduced hotel prices to members. Expedia and Hotels.com steered some users toward more expensive hotels. Home Depot and Travelocity personalized search results for mobile users.

Priceline personalized the order of hotel search results based on a user's history of clicks and purchases. However, the researchers said those different result orders did not correlate with price, so they did not classify that Priceline example as price steering. The researchers also emphasized that most of their experiments on the 16 sites did not uncover price steering or price discrimination.

Then in 2015, ProPublica found that The Princeton Review charged different prices for an online SAT tutoring package depending on a customer's ZIP Code. Prices for its Premier package ranged from $6,600 to $8,400. ProPublica found that people living in ZIP Codes with larger Asian populations were 1.8 times as likely to be offered a higher price, regardless of income.

The Princeton Review said its pricing was based on the costs of running its business and competitive conditions in each market. It said its prices were set by geographic region rather than a customer's race. That example was geographic pricing rather than a retailer setting a unique price for each individual shopper. It still shows how data connected to where someone lives can lead different groups of consumers to receive different prices.

13 ways to reduce personalized tracking when you shop

There is no guaranteed trick for getting the lowest online price. However, you can reduce some of the information retailers, data brokers and tracking companies can connect to you while giving yourself more ways to compare offers.

1) Check the price before signing in

Look at a product while signed out before logging into a retailer or loyalty account. Then compare the price or promotion after signing in. A difference does not automatically mean personalized pricing. Membership discounts and other promotions can also explain a change. Still, comparing both views gives you more information before you buy.

2) Use guest checkout when you can

If you do not need a retailer account, consider checking out as a guest. That keeps the purchase from automatically becoming another entry in a logged-in shopping history. Guest checkout does not make you anonymous. A retailer may still receive information such as your email address, payment details, shipping address, browser data or device information.

3) Reject optional tracking cookies

When a website gives you the choice, reject optional advertising and tracking cookies. The site may still need essential cookies for things such as your shopping cart, security and payment. Rejecting optional cookies mainly reduces some tracking and advertising activity.

4) Reduce the data brokers have about you

Retailers are only one source of personal information. Data brokers and people-search companies collect information from numerous sources and combine it into profiles. FTC research found that pricing systems can incorporate third-party data, including information from data brokers. Reducing what's available through those companies may shrink one part of your broader data footprint. It does not guarantee a lower price or prevent a retailer from using information it collects directly from you. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com.

HOW SCAMMERS BUILD A PROFILE ON YOU USING DATA BROKERS

5) Compare prices in a private browsing window

A private browsing window generally creates a separate browsing session that does not use the normal session history and most existing cookies from your regular browsing window. It does not make you anonymous. Websites may still see information such as your IP address and information you provide directly. The FTC specifically points to private browsing as one step consumers might use when trying to avoid higher personalized prices.

6) Use privacy opt-outs when they are offered

Look for choices such as Do Not Sell or Share My Personal Information, Your Privacy Choices or controls for targeted advertising. The options available depend on the retailer and the privacy laws that apply where you live.

7) Limit precise location access

Review which shopping apps can access your precise location. If an app does not need your exact location, consider switching to approximate location or turning location access off. Keep in mind that websites and apps may still estimate your general location from other information, including your IP address.

8) Review app tracking permissions

Your phone may let you limit how apps track activity across other apps and websites. Turning off unnecessary tracking can reduce some third-party data collection. It will not stop a retailer from using information you provide directly through its own app, website or account. For step-by-step instructions on iPhone and Android, see our guide to improving your digital privacy.

9) Clear cookies and stored site data periodically

Cookies can help websites recognize the same browser when you return. Clearing them can remove some of those stored identifiers. However, other tracking methods may still recognize your device, and signing back into an account reconnects your activity to that account.

10) Compare the app and website

Before making an expensive purchase, check the retailer's website and app. Then compare the same product with other sellers. Any difference you find may have a simple explanation, but comparison shopping gives you a better picture of the available prices.

11) Use price-history tools

For products supported by price-history services, check whether today's deal really is lower than recent prices. A retailer's sale banner only tells you what it wants to advertise. Historical pricing can give you additional context before you buy.

12) Read the fine print on discounts

A lower price may require a loyalty membership, subscription, automatic renewal or another commitment. Make sure the offer actually saves you money after those conditions are included.

13) Consider using a VPN

A VPN can hide the public IP address assigned by your internet provider and replace it with the address of the VPN server. That can make your IP-based location appear different. The FTC specifically lists VPN use as something consumers might try when they are concerned about personalized prices. A VPN cannot erase your retailer account, purchase history, cookies or location information that an app already has permission to access. Websites may also use other signals to recognize you. For the best VPN software, see my expert review of the best VPNs for browsing the web privately on your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.

Kurt's key takeaways

What gets my attention here is how much information can now go into deciding what we see when we shop online. We do not have evidence that every retailer is quietly setting a different price for each person, and seeing two different prices does not automatically prove personal data caused the change. What we do know is that companies have technology capable of using location, browsing behavior, shopping history and other information to shape prices, discounts and product rankings. My advice is to compare prices before you buy, limit tracking you do not need and avoid assuming the first offer on your screen is the best one available. The less unnecessary information you hand over, the less there is to feed into a detailed profile about how you shop.

World.title: Stephen A Smith and ESPN should consider a full-time reunion with Skip Bayless
World.content:
Last week, Skip Bayless returned to ESPN to reunite with his former debate partner, Stephen A. Smith, on "First Take." Under a new agreement, Bayless will appear on the program on the final Friday of every month.

The history between Bayless and the show is significant.

ESPN built "First Take," its daily debate program, around Bayless in 2007. Like Smith today, Bayless initially debated a rotating cast of analysts. He pushed the network to give Smith a recurring role, but executives initially resisted after Smith's previous, unsuccessful stint at ESPN.

SKIP BAYLESS BOOSTS STEPHEN A'S SLUGGISH "FIRST TAKE" RATINGS BY 24% ON THEIR REUNION SHOW

Smith eventually joined the show on a weekly basis and became Bayless' full-time debate partner in 2012.

Together, Bayless and Smith drew an average audience that well exceeded ESPN2's typical viewership, often outperforming the main ESPN channel during the same time slot.

Bayless left ESPN for FS1 in 2016 to launch "Undisputed," a similarly formatted debate program designed to compete directly with "First Take." Bayless partnered with Shannon Sharpe at FS1, while Max Kellerman replaced him at ESPN.

Comparing the success of the two programs warrants context. ESPN reached three to five times as many morning viewers as FS1 at the time. Even so, "First Take" lost more than 20% of its audience after Bayless departed. ESPN responded by moving the program from ESPN2 to ESPN. After the move, "First Take" attracted roughly twice the audience of "Undisputed."

The gap widened after Kellerman left "First Take" and Sharpe exited "Undisputed." By 2023, "First Take" regularly drew three to four times as many viewers as its FS1 rival. Bayless ultimately left the network in 2024.

Smith and Bayless are in different positions than they were in 2012.

At the time, Bayless was one of ESPN's most viral personalities. Smith had been relegated to local radio. Today, Smith is among the most influential figures in sports media, having recently signed a five-year, $100 million contract with ESPN. Until recently, Bayless was the one without a television platform.

Bayless' transition to digital media has been rocky. His weekly show with his wife averages about 1,000 views per episode on YouTube. He has not uploaded a new episode of his eponymous podcast in nearly a year. He has, however, recently gained traction through a venture with former NFL cornerback Aqib Talib called "Gridiron."

Although Bayless accepted an invitation to become a monthly contributor to "First Take," the arrangement is undoubtedly awkward. Returning to the program you built, alongside the co-host whose career you helped build, in a limited role cannot be easy.

It is also reasonable to wonder whether Bayless believes Smith owes him the same full-time opportunity that he extended in 2012. OutKick asked Bayless about that possibility following Friday's show. He did not respond.

Honestly, Smith should consider it.

The current version of "First Take" has grown stale. The format of pairing Smith with two rotating panelists produces inconsistent results. Michael Irvin, Dan Orlovsky, Chris "Mad Dog" Russo and Marcus Spears are strong contributors. Much of the remaining rotation, however, consists of interchangeable ESPN personalities, including Chris Canty, Kimberley Martin and Domonique Foxworth.

Perhaps a more effective approach would be to reduce the size of the rotation and feature only the program's strongest personalities alongside Smith and perhaps Bayless. On Friday, Spears joined Smith and Bayless for most of the show.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

"First Take" is still one of ESPN's highest-rated programs, but its growth lags behind the network's other studio shows. ESPN's monthly press releases routinely emphasize year-over-year gains for "Get Up," "The Pat McAfee Show," "NFL Live" and other programs, but not "First Take's."

Smith himself has acknowledged the importance of evolving the program. Explaining why he wanted Kellerman removed from the program, Smith said it was necessary "to keep things fresh and make changes every three years." It has now been five years since Kellerman's departure.

Bayless also brings out a different side of Smith, one that is generally more appealing to viewers.

The formula is simple but effective: Bayless makes a provocative claim, Smith responds with theatrical indignation, Bayless defends his position and the segment often ends in good fun.

While not the most intellectually rigorous form of television, it's better than the pandering, faux sophistication that has come to define too much of sports television.

Despite his branding, Smith rarely offers a profound opinion on sports. He believes the Cowboys underachieve, Stephen Curry is the greatest shooter in NBA history and LeBron James is the second-greatest player in basketball history. Those are conventional positions.

In fact, Smith tends to expose a lack of depth when he tries to offer a unique opinion. His recent commentary on LSU, Shedeur Sanders and Deshaun Watson suggested a limited familiarity with those subjects.

Smith performs best opposite a contrarian, like Bayless. The same dynamic explains why his appearances with Will Cain and Sean Hannity on Fox News often generate more interest than his solo political monologues.

Smith, who has frequently responded to criticism from OutKick, may view that comparison as a slight. It is not. Michael Wilbon and Tony Kornheiser remain the gold standard of sports television because their partnership is stronger than either host individually. The same principle applies to Smith and Bayless.

With Pat McAfee surpassing Smith as ESPN's most relevant personality, a full-time reunion with Bayless would represent an opportunity to regain momentum. Debating Chris Canty one day and Gerald McCoy the next does not.

ESPN may be reluctant to approve a broader reunion for Bayless. Our understanding is that there was pushback about bringing him back even in a limited role.

Executive Mike Foss, who oversees the network's daily studio programming, has emphasized a shift away from "embrace debate," the slogan that once defined "First Take," in favor of authenticity and conversation. Ratings trends suggest that approach has benefited much of ESPN's daytime lineup. But not "First Take."

"First Take" is a debate show. The program has never fully recaptured the cultural relevance and virality it reached with Bayless and Smith together.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

If the plan is to keep Stephen A. in a prominent role as he approaches 60, ESPN should lean into what made him successful in sports-talk television.

It is also 2026. As Hollywood continues to demonstrate, nostalgia remains a more reliable commercial strategy than reinvention.

NYU professor Scott Galloway said Monday on "The Prof G Pod" that he sold all of his stocks in an emotional reaction to President Donald Trump’s 2016 election victory, taking a major tax hit before buying back into a more expensive market months later, a decision he estimated cost him 40% of his liquid net worth in stocks.

Galloway, a professor of marketing at NYU Stern, called the move his "biggest investment mistake" during the "Office Hours" edition of the podcast as he warned listeners about allowing emotions to drive investment decisions.

"So when he was elected in 2016, I sold all my stocks," he said. "That was stupid. The market ripped for the next year. There was so much insecurity about him actually winning that the fear had been priced in. Stocks ripped up."

THE RICH HAVE ONE FINANCIAL HABIT MOST AMERICANS IGNORE AT THEIR PERIL

Galloway said the selloff also triggered taxes on significant capital gains while he was living in New York. He said he returned to the market about six months later after stocks had risen between 10% and 20%, compounding what he described as the cost of the decision.

"So you could argue, at least notionally, that decision cost me 40% of my liquid net worth in stocks," Galloway said.

White House spokesman Davis Ingle told Fox News Digital Tuesday that Galloway’s continued criticism of Trump reflected what he characterized as an obsession with the president.

"Scott Galloway should immediately seek psychiatric help to treat his severe case of Trump Derangement Syndrome that has completely rotted his peanut-sized brain," Ingle said.

GOVERNMENTS CAN TAKE YOUR STOCKS WITHOUT YOUR PERMISSION. IT HAPPENS ALL THE TIME

Galloway criticized Trump, saying he believed the president's economic and foreign policies could ultimately damage the U.S. economy.

"I think the president is a f---ing idiot and a stain on the American experience and that the grand sum of all of these head up your a-- economic and foreign policy decisions will eventually crash this economy or result in long-term structural damage that will take decades if not generations to repair," Galloway said.

The stock market rose substantially following Trump's 2016 presidential victory. According to the federal government's 2017 Economic Report of the President, the S&P 500 climbed 3.4% in November 2016 and reached a then-record high later that month. The 2018 report said the index went on to gain 19.4% in 2017, posting increases in 11 of the year's 12 months.

DAVID MARCUS: TRUMP DERANGEMENT SYNDROME ISN'T MENTAL ILLNESS, IT'S MASS HYSTERIA

Galloway said his experience reinforced his view that investors should remain in the market rather than attempt to anticipate political or economic turning points. While discussing current elevated valuations, he recommended diversification instead of trying to predict exactly when stocks will decline.

"Trying to guess when the top happens is dangerous," Galloway said. "Probably my biggest investment mistake was the emotional reaction I had to the 2016 election of Donald Trump."

"And what the government does matter, but the majority of the economy just grinds on regardless of who is tweeting what or not tweeting what," he continued.

World.title: Sunny Hostin addresses resurfaced reports questioning her claim she was a holdout juror in 1991 murder trial

"The View" co-host Sunny Hostin addressed reporting about her identifying herself as a holdout juror in a gruesome murder case in the 1990s during the show's podcast Monday after resurfaced reports from multiple outlets said it was a man who was the holdout juror.

"Someone on the internet dug up a Daily News article from 1991 that profiled another, different person that was a holdout juror. You were quoted in this article too, but they were talking about a man that other people pointed to as saying this is the reason we couldn't come to a verdict," Brian Teta, the producer of "The View," noted during the "Behind the Table" podcast.

Hostin said she remembered him and explained that there were different counts in the case.

ATTORNEY FOR LONE HOLDOUT JUROR IN LINDSAY CLANCY MISTRIAL PUSHES BACK ON CLAIMS OF REFUSING THE LAW

"So, as I recall, and look it up for yourselves, there were three counts, I believe. One was second-degree murder, but it was intentional. Then there was the defense to that was, we could consider the insanity defense, meaning that he committed the crime, but he was not criminally responsible because of a mental disease or defect. And there was a third count, or a third issue that we dealt with, and that issue was the desecration of Monika Beerle's remains," Hostin said.

The co-host of "The View" said she felt strongly that he tried to hide the fact that he killed Beerle by dismembering her remains and that he should be found guilty of that count.

LINDSAY CLANCY HOLDOUT PRAISED AS 'AMERICAN HERO' BY LAWYER WHO SAYS HE REPRESENTS HIM

"He was insane when he killed her," Hostin said. "And he said that, he confessed that he didn't realize that she was even dead. But then he decides to dismember her. I just thought that was so clear and gruesome and despicable to do that to someone's remains. I thought that he should be found guilty of that. And everyone else did too, except for this one guy. And we were, like, kind of looking at him, like, 'That was the easy one.' It was always the easy one. But we could not reach a unanimous verdict on that count."

Teta noted that Hostin didn't mention this male juror on the show when she identified herself as the holdout juror in this trial. She clarified during the podcast that she was the holdout on a different count, the count related to the insanity defense.

During the liberal talk show earlier this month, Hostin said she was a holdout juror on a case in which a man murdered his roommate and dismembered her. Hostin felt strongly that the man, Daniel Rakowitz, also known as "Butcher of Tompkins Square Park," was insane.

The co-host shared an excerpt from a report in The New York Times about the trial, which was held in 1991. Rakowitz was acquitted by reason of insanity. Hostin, whose maiden name is Cummings and whose first name is Asunción, was quoted in a Feb. 23, 1991, New York Times report about the trial, which said, "Several jurors questioned afterward said one holdout juror was principally responsible for preventing them from returning a guilty verdict."

LINDSAY CLANCY MISTRIAL DECLARED AFTER JURY DEADLOCKS IN KILLINGS OF HER THREE CHILDREN

"The View" co-host presented the article on the show while explaining the case.

"That was me. It was because I saw clearly that he was psychotic," Hostin said during the show Sept. 22.

After revealing she was the holdout juror on the case, the New York Post reported that other contemporaneous accounts identified an unemployed man as the principal holdout. The Post wrote that "Jurors told The Post, Newsday, the Daily News and the Associated Press that the actual holdout was an unemployed man who wanted to keep the trial going so he could continue getting paid by the court for his civic duty."

"He was unemployed and liked the $15 a day and the three free meals," juror Valerie Holmes told Newsday after the verdict, according to contemporaneous coverage.

CLANCY HOLDOUT JUROR TAPS FORMER TRUMP LAWYER TO FIGHT BACK AS HE’S ‘DRAGGED THROUGH THE MUD’: ATTORNEY

The Post also cited a law enforcement source familiar with the case who said, "We were told that the juror who held out was a man. There was no other description."

Another factor, the New York Post said, was that "Hostin was quoted as a juror on the case in multiple news clips at the time, but she did not identify herself as the holdout, nor did any of the fellow jurors who talked to the press after the trial. Her statement to Newsday from the time even seemed to contradict her story."

"Unfortunately for Sunny, one cannot simply put the toothpaste back in the tube. Hopefully, she's realized what kind of internet fervor she's created with this take that goes beyond her daily hare-brained political takes," Newsbusters Managing Editor Curtis Houck told Fox News Digital in a statement regarding Hostin's latest update on the story.

"Rather, touting her juror status on such a gruesome case hopefully cuts across politics and into basic common sense. Her invocation of "shared experiences" is an utter crock. Bringing up a term from Woke 1 won't make her supposedly proud admission any less disturbing."

Teta also asked Hostin to address what he described as the "lazy take," that she "got him out of jail, and she's proud of it," referring to criticism on the internet about her revelation.

"Why would I be proud of that?" Hostin asked. "It's an experience that I had that I shared so that people would understand better. I think our lived experiences are a very good way on this show, in particular, to explain to people, current events, right?"

World.title: Supreme Court allows Trump’s ‘third country’ deportation policy
World.content:
WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court on Tuesday removed obstacles to the Trump administration deporting certain immigrants to “third countries” to which they have no previous connection.

The justices, with the court’s three liberals dissenting, granted an emergency request filed by the government seeking to block an appeals court ruling that said the current process is unlawful because the affected people are not given a proper chance to raise concerns about safety risks in violation of federal immigration law.

In the brief unsigned order, the court also said it would hear oral arguments in December and issue a definitive ruling on the legal questions raised in the litigation.

“A bad day for criminal illegals and open borders activists alike. It’s not too late to get $3,000 and a flight home,” James Percival, general counsel of the Department of Homeland Security, said in a statement Tuesday afternoon.

The Supreme Court last year allowed the policy to move forward after it was blocked by lower courts at an earlier stage of the litigation. It also later clarified its decision, at the request of the Trump administration, making it clear it applied to eight men the government wanted to send to South Sudan.

Since Trump’s second term began in January 2025, thousands of people have been sent to third countries, which include South Sudan, Eswatini and Rwanda.

Migrants deported months ago by the U.S. to El Salvador arriving at Simon Bolívar International Airport, in Maiquetia, Venezuela, last year. Ariana Cubillos / AP file

About 15,000 people were deported to third countries in 2025, according to the Migration Policy Institute, with Mexico receiving the majority.

The Supreme Court action “means that people facing removal to third countries are once again at immediate risk of being sent to places where they have no meaningful opportunity to seek protection,” said Trina Realmuto, a lawyer at the National Immigration Litigation Alliance representing plaintiffs. “That is an enormous consequence for people whose lives and safety are on the line.”

Four unnamed immigrants challenged the policy, arguing that people should have a “meaningful opportunity” to claim that they could face torture or persecution if deported to one of the third countries.

Massachusetts-based U.S. District Judge Brian Murphy agreed (It was his earlier ruling that the Supreme Court blocked last year, which led to heavy criticism from within MAGA world.)

The Boston-based 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals upheld Murphy’s most recent ruling and sided with the unnamed immigrants, citing a federal law that prevents deportations to a country where the person faces likely persecution.

Although the appeals court ruling was initially put on hold, on Sept. 23, it went into effect, prompting the Trump administration to rush to the Supreme Court.

Migrants deported from the U.S. place papers with a written message in the window of the Decapolis Hotel where they were temporarily staying in Panama City, last year. Arnulfo Franco / AFP via Getty Images file

In a court filing, Solicitor General D. John Sauer said that putting “third country” deportations on hold “created substantial logistical problems with ongoing removal operations” and has “led to added expense, potential diplomatic issues, and the inability to remove dangerous criminals.”

One scheduled flight that was to carry 70 people with criminal convictions to three different countries in the last week was immediately canceled, Sauer said.

The Trump administration has said no individualized determination is needed because the countries it has made deals with to take immigrants have said they would not mistreat them.

The government has said it would not immediately deport people if it has not received assurances from the country in question that people will not be tortured or persecuted.

Lawyers for the plaintiffs in court papers pointed out that the lower court rulings do not require anyone to be released from detention or even prevent third country removals if people are given a chance to raise objections.

The lead plaintiff, named only as D.V.D. in court records, is from Cuba and suffers from severe mental illness. He fears being sent to a country where he would not receive psychiatric treatment, the lawyers said.

People who have been deported to third countries have been mistreated, with some detained indefinitely and others subjected to physical and sexual abuse, the plaintiffs allege in court documents.

World.title: Pro-Trump TV ads paid for with Customs and Border Protection money, official says
World.content:
President Donald Trump’s administration paid for TV ads showing him in a favorable light using money intended for U.S. Customs and Border Protection, an official and a top Republican senator confirmed to NBC News.

The source of the funding for the controversial ads the White House has described as public service announcements was first reported by The Wall Street Journal.

The Department of Homeland Security, which oversees CBP, referred requests for comment to the White House, which did not immediately respond.

The unusual ads — one of which is nearly identical to a 2024 Trump campaign ad — include disclaimers stating they were paid for by the U.S. government. The administration’s apparent use of taxpayer money to produce ads that resemble campaign s has drawn bipartisan criticism.

“It’s a great message. I like the message,” Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., told reporters Monday of the most recent ad, “but it shouldn’t be paid for with taxpayer dollars.”

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., said Monday only Trump would have “the audacity to force Americans not only to watch his propaganda, but to pay for it.”

Speaking to reporters Tuesday, Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, confirmed the official’s account of the source of the funds, saying that “it was taken out of funding that was supposed to be for Customs and Border Protection” in Trump’s so-called big, beautiful bill, which Republicans passed along party lines in 2025.

Collins, who faces a difficult re-election bid this fall, said the Appropriations Committee she chairs had no role in the money that the White House used. In fact, she said appropriations bills to fund the government typically have restrictions against using one account for another purpose.

“That’s why the administration went around the appropriations process and used an account that was part of the reconciliation bill,” Collins said in the Capitol.

The first of the ads aired earlier this month and featured Trump describing how he wanted to “defeat communism,” set to the song “Love Me” by JMSN. (Lawyers for JMSN on Monday sent a cease-and-desist letter to the White House telling it to stop using his music.)

The second spot closely tracks a 2024 Trump presidential campaign ad. It shows Trump walking down a hallway as he asks people in a voiceover to join him in his “final battle” to “demolish the deep state” and “expel the warmongers from our government.”

The political ad-tracking firm AdImpact has estimated that the administration has spent more than $1.7 million to run the ads.

Earlier in Trump’s term, DHS used taxpayer money to run a series of ads featuring then-Secretary Kristi Noem encouraging immigrants living in the United States illegally to self-deport.

Sen. Jim Justice, R-W.Va., who provided a key vote to pass the megabill, cast doubt on the wisdom of Trump’s decision when asked if pulling the money from CBP was a good move.

“Well, if that’s exactly what happened, probably not,” Justice said, while adding that he’s not an expert on the legality of the move. “But at the same time, I don’t know the particulars to say, well, that those dollars can be used that way, or they can’t be used that way. I don’t know. I just don’t know.”

“I can’t imagine how smart the people in the administration are that they’ve done something that’s just going to fly right in their face,” Justice said. “I can’t imagine that they’ve done something that they know is not right, not ethical, not whatever. I just couldn’t imagine they’d do that. They’re too smart for that.”

Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., who announced his retirement last year after clashing with Trump on the megabill, tore into the president’s decision to fund those ads with taxpayer money.

“I hate it. I tell you, it feels like Viktor Orbán talking to the Hungarian people. There’s no place for that sort of thing,” Tillis said, while adding that Trump could have used political resources if he wanted to run a political ad. “If it were, you know, some clear message that was going to appeal to the broader, a real public service announcement, that’s fine. But that was not that.”

World.title: Trump’s border wall construction cut into an ancient ground carving older than Stonehenge
World.content:
An ancient ground carving that was severely damaged by the administration’s border wall construction was created before Stonehenge and Egypt’s oldest pyramid, according to recently publicized research.

The Las Playas Intaglio, a giant fish carved into the Sonoran Desert in Arizona, is now considered the oldest example in the Americas of a geoglyphic, the ancient art form that is carved into or drawn on the ground.

In April, contractors hired by the Trump administration to make way for a second wall along the Arizona-Mexico border “scraped” a 50-foot swath through the ancient carving, according to the Center for Biological Diversity, which documented the damage.

The intaglio on the ground of the ancestral homeland of the Tohono O’odham and other Indigenous tribes is estimated to be about 2,000 years older than Egypt’s first pyramid and to have been created about 1,500 years before the first construction of Stonehenge and 4,000 years before Peru’s Nazca Lines, researchers have found.

The formerly 272-foot carving had originally been thought to be about 1,000 years old. But the latest research dates the art’s creation to at least 6,500 years ago, and possibly as much as 7,500 years ago.

That age emphasizes “the significance of this site and the parallel great misfortune resulting from its damage,” the researchers said in an article published in The SAA Archaeological Record.

A comparison of images of the site of the fish-shaped intaglio (geoglyphic) before and after the border wall construction at Cabeza Prieta National Wildlife Refuge in Arizona. Courtesy Russ McSpadden / Center for Biological Diversity

“This discovery makes an already devastating loss even more profound. It’s a cultural and historical atrocity,” Russ McSpadden, Southwest conservation advocate at the Center for Biological Diversity, said in a statement.

A Customs and Border Protection spokesperson said in an email to NBC News that the contractor “inadvertently disturbed” the site and that CBP Commissioner Rodney Scott has been “engaged directly with tribal leadership to determine appropriate next steps.”

“The remaining portion of the site has been secured and will be protected in place. CBP is conducting a thorough review of construction protocols and strengthening communication procedures to ensure this does not happen again,” the spokesperson stated, adding that the agency is “committed to respecting and safeguarding cultural heritage throughout all border infrastructure projects.”

The damage to that site and construction on other parts of Tohono O’odham land and sacred Indigenous areas has strained the tenuous relationship between the tribal nation and the government. The tribe is appealing a federal judge’s decision refusing to block the administration’s border wall construction through its reservation.

While the intaglio’s site is irreparably damaged, the Tohono O’odham people are trying to stop the government from plowing through Quitobaquito Springs, a desert water source in Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument that is also considered a sacred site and holds endangered species.

In order to build the border wall and barriers, the Department of Homeland Security invoked authority granted in the Secure Fence Act of 2006 to waive numerous laws protecting the environment, water, cultural, historical and religious sites.

The Tohono O’odham Nation has long worked with CBP, which is part of the Department of Homeland Security, on border security, helping to keep drug traffickers and others from using its land for criminal activity.

The tribe’s reservation straddles the U.S.-Mexico border, and its members have permission to move between the two countries with ID checks. About 3,000 of its members are in Mexico, according to the tribal nation.

The Center for Biological Diversity stated in a news release that conservation advocates and tribal nations have long warned that border wall and secondary border barrier plans could cut through sensitive habitat and cultural sites across the region.

Wall construction in other parts of the border has sparked other lawsuits and opposition from landowners, Native American tribes, local governments, conservation groups, business owners and others.

In Texas, a tribal nonprofit for the Lipan Apache and an outdoor recreation business have opposed the border wall construction, alleging DHS is not authorized to violate the Religious Freedom Restoration Act, which they say it would do by destroying or cutting off access to sacred sites.

A federal judge ordered a temporary halt to construction in Big Bend National Park in response to the lawsuit, but construction continues on other parts of the rugged, undeveloped and remote region outside state and federal parkland.

World.title: Caleb Flynn, former ‘American Idol’ singer, found guilty of wife’s murder
World.content:
Former “American Idol” singer Caleb Flynn was found guilty of murder on Tuesday in the death of his wife, who was killed in their Ohio home in February.

A jury took little over two hours to convict Flynn on all nine counts of murder, assault and tampering with evidence.

After the verdict was read by Judge Jeannine Pratt, Flynn broke down in tears and was repeatedly seen wiping his nose and eyes. He was taken from the courtroom in handcuffs.

Flynn, a former music pastor, told a 911 dispatcher that his wife, Ashley Flynn, who worked as a school teacher and volleyball coach, had been shot multiple times in the head by an intruder. He told the dispatcher that he did not know whether the intruder was still in their Tipp City home.

In police interviews played in court, Flynn told officers that he was sleeping on the couch when he woke up to the sound of gunshots. He said that a day before the killing, a man had come to their home and handed his wife an American flag while making a “weird sales pitch for America.”

When police arrived at the home on the day of the shooting, the garage door, a side door and the center console of Flynn’s pickup truck were open. Flynn told police that he kept a gun in the console, but no weapon was found there.

Prosecutors alleged that Flynn, 40, staged the home invasion to mislead investigators and shared thoughts of killing his wife, 37, in text messages to his then-mistress. Authorities never found the gun used in the killing.

“The evidence has proven the defendant’s account to be a complete fabrication,” Matthew C. Joseph, assistant prosecuting attorney for the Miami County Prosecuting Attorney’s Office in Troy, Ohio, said in closings Tuesday.

Flynn, who had tears on his face, wiped his nose.

“While the defendant told law enforcement that he was sleeping, his electronic devices documented something different. They documented movement and activity in the hours leading up to Ashley’s murder,” Joseph said. “The defendant said he was sleeping. His devices say he was awake and moving.”

Joseph told the court that Flynn “wanted to be a victim” and wanted to “keep his mistress and have his daughters all to himself.”

“Being the victim allowed him to do that without being the husband who left his wife for a mistress,” Joseph said. “Instead, he’d be the husband whose wife was tragically murdered by an unknown intruder.”

Over eight days, the jury heard from 40 prosecution witnesses, including Alleigha Botner, who said she met Flynn when she was 20 and an intern at his church. She said they had been having an affair at the time of Ashley’s killing.

Botner, now 24, testified that Flynn had made remarks that he hated his wife and harbored thoughts of killing her. Botner sobbed on the stand as she read some of their text messages, telling the court that she regretted telling him in one message: “I want to kill her, Caleb.”

Botner said Flynn replied: “That makes two of us.”

In other text messages shown in court, Flynn discussed wanting his wife dead.

“I was up until 4 a.m. last night crying, literally trying to think of ways to kill her and not go to jail,” he allegedly wrote in an August 2025 text, about six months before the killing.

In another text, Botner said she wasn’t serious. “I’m not asking that you take her life obviously, because that’s not what you should do, and I know you actually wouldn’t,” she wrote. “But to make the divorce happen, it would change everything.”

Botner told the court that her feelings about Flynn have since changed and she hated him. When a prosecutor asked her why, she said: “Because I believe that he murdered his wife.”

The defense rested Monday without calling a single witness.

Flynn’s attorney, Patrick Mulligan, said in his closing argument that being “unfaithful doesn’t equal murder.”

“This case is wholly lacking in concrete evidence. Connecting a couple of meaningless dots doesn’t solve the case,” he said.

Flynn sang in the televised auditions in Chicago for Season 12 of “American Idol” in 2013 but did not advance to the main competition. He faces life in prison without the possibility of parole.
