Owens, author of a new book published in September, Gouged: The End of a Fair Price — And What That Means for Your Wallet, uncovers pricing schemes that corporations try to hide, and shares advice on how to protect yourself from these tactics.

Sponsor Message

"The most egregious way is personalized pricing," says Owens. Retailers "collect data on you to better ascertain how much they can charge you." That includes browsing data, demographics and purchase history. They're also using algorithms to run pricing experiments on consumers.

Still, there are ways to get a fair deal. Owens explains how to cover up your trail so it's harder for retailers to watch you — and then sell you products at personalized prices. Maybe you don't use all these techniques for smaller purchases, like a pair of shoes, but for expensive flights or other travel, it might be worth it.

Avoid shopping through retailer apps

Some retailers offer perks and discounts to customers if they shop for items using their app or website. But the incentives are not worth it, Owens says.

When you're signed in, you're giving those companies "a lot of information about yourself," she says. That includes your location and purchase history. They even "know what you click on and don't buy."

They may also run experiments on you — like figuring out "what your pain point is," Owens says. "Will she buy it at $5? $7? $12?"

You're offering a lot of data that can "potentially be turned against you in pricing decisions, whether that's fewer discounts or higher prices," she says.

toggle caption Malaka Gharib/NPR

Learn the new way to comparison shop

Comparison shopping means going to multiple retailers to check prices to find the best deal. Today, it also means ensuring that "you're not being exposed to personalized pricing," Owens says.

Sponsor Message

There are many ways you can do this. Now keep in mind this may be time consuming, but it may be worth it for big-ticket items. Check the price of a product or service across multiple devices, while logged in, while logged out, with and without incognito mode, and with and without a virtual private network (VPN), Owens says. You can also ask friends to check prices on their devices.

Let's say you're buying a sweater. You may want to look at the price at the brand's clothing store at the mall, the brand's website and ask your friend to look up the price on their phone to ensure you're getting the best price, Owens says.

Make it harder for companies to track your data

Clear your browsing data and cookies regularly. Companies collect data while you browse online. "If you can clear that data before you make a purchase, then that data isn't available to the company to use against you," Owens says.

You can go through your devices and limit the permissions that you grant to apps. Do your apps really need to know your location? Can you turn off inter-app sharing, so one app isn't sharing data with another app?

Consider using a VPN to hide your location, which may be used to charge you more. You can even run your own pricing experiments using your VPN to change your location, Owens says. "See if you can get a more competitive price coming from a different space," like the San Francisco Bay Area versus Nashville, Tenn., for example.

Shop in person, but keep in mind that personalized pricing is seeping into big retailers, too

If you can, shop for goods at local, mom-and-pop shops. If it's a service you seek, try doing it the old fashioned way. Get a cab instead of ordering a ride through an app. Call up your local restaurant, order food and pick it up instead of using a delivery app.

Sponsor Message

These small businesses may be more expensive and less convenient, but they are less likely to run "super sophisticated, algorithmic, price-fixing experiments on you," Owens says.

But a lot of these technologies are seeping into brick-and-mortar stores that are making pricing more unpredictable, she says.

Electronic shelf labels, for example, are popping up at big-box retailers and grocery stores. These labels allow retailers to change a product's price at any time, leading to "more price variation throughout the grocery store," Owens says.

Some retailers are also removing price tags altogether. "Without a posted price, it creates a lot of uncertainty for people on a budget," she says.

If you're frustrated by all these schemes, there's good news. Some states are beginning to ban personalized pricing. On October 1, a new law will go into effect in Maryland banning the use of personalized or dynamic pricing at grocery stores and third-party delivery services. And other states are considering similar bans.

More smart financial advice from Life Kit

How to eat out without spending a fortune. Personal finance and nutrition experts share simple strategies that make it possible to eat out on a budget. One tip? You might have to let go of your fast food delivery habit.

4 marketing tricks to avoid while shopping. Retailers use marketing techniques to get you to spend more, like creating a false sense of urgency or creating artificial discounts. Outsmart the gimmicks with these tips.

5 money-draining mistakes travelers make when planning a vacation. People get a lot wrong when it comes to paying for vacation, say travel experts, and that can cost serious cash. Here's how to plan a trip that's safe, adventurous and under budget.

7 surprising ways the public library can save you money. Baking pans, legal help, language classes and more — libraries can provide so much more than books. See if your local branch offers these free or discounted resources and services.

Sponsor Message

This digital story was edited by Sylvie Douglis and Lauren Gonzalez. The visual editor is CJ Riculan.

We'd love to hear from you. Email us at LifeKit@npr.org. Listen to Life Kit on Apple Podcasts and Spotify, and

World.title: Trump trade adviser says Canadian lobbyists should 'get the hell out of our country'
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

One of U.S. President Donald Trump's trade advisers is threatening repercussions for Canada if it "interferes" in the upcoming midterm elections — though it's not clear what he anticipates the country would do to impact the vote.

Peter Navarro, who has lashed out at Canada in the past, made these latest remarks during a talk at an economic conference in Washington on Tuesday.

Navarro was speaking generally about the Trump administration's trade policy when the conversation turned to the ongoing dispute with Canada. He blasted Canadians on "K Street" — an area in Washington known as a hub for lobbyists — telling them to "get the hell out of our country."

"The problem you have is you lobby this country and you've been successful in the past and you think you can keep doing that," Navarro said of Canada's approach.

"Memo to Canada: You cannot do that. That game is up and if you interfere in our elections in Maine or Michigan you will pay even more dearly."

WATCH | Maine is a critical state to determine control of U.S. Senate: Trump’s tariffs loom over pivotal Maine Senate race | Duration closed caption 2:40 The Canada-U.S. trade war is hitting Maine’s economy as voters grapple with rising costs. The fallout could shape a key midterm race that will help determine which party controls the U.S. Senate.

Navarro said he "loves" the Canadian people but has had no love for Canadian negotiators since 2016.

"You just can't trust them," he said.

During the talks that led to the Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement (CUSMA) in Trump's first term, Ottawa leaned on U.S. labour and business groups to help make its case. More recently, a number of Canadian provinces have hired their own representatives to be present for ongoing trade discussions in D.C. since Trump returned to the White House in early 2025.

Navarro didn't elaborate on what he meant by suggesting Canada could interfere in the election, but the ongoing trade war has become an election topic in the two border states he mentioned.

The Democratic nominee for Michigan's open Senate seat, Abdul El-Sayed, has sought to make trade with Canada a central ballot issue for the vote in November. Maine Sen. Susan Collins, a Republican, has opposed the trade war.

Navarro made the comments on the same day that Trump's latest trade escalation came into effect.

As of Tuesday at 12:01 a.m. ET, some Canadian alcohol products, dairy byproducts, motorcycles and molasses have been shut out of the U.S. market.

WATCH | The Canadian goods now officially banned in the U.S.: These Canadian goods are now officially banned in the U.S. | Duration 2:59 Washington��’s ban on several Canadian goods, including alcohol, molasses, motorcycles and select dairy products kick in as of Sept. 29. The list of items might come across as a head-scratcher to some but one trade lawyer suggests there’s more to this collection than meets the eye.

The White House announced the bans and some additional tariffs a few days after Canada slapped counter-tariffs on U.S. goods earlier this month. Both moves came after trade talks collapsed in August.

Speaking to reporters in the Oval Office on Monday, Trump said he expects Canada to return to the negotiating table in the coming weeks with an apology.

"I think what's going to happen is over the next three or four weeks, they're going to come to us and they're gonna say, 'We're gonna get rid of all the tariffs,"' the president said.

Trump also repeated claims that Canada has treated the U.S. "unfairly" and said it's been "one of the worst countries in the entire world" when it comes to trade.

Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc said during an unrelated news conference on Tuesday that the government has no intention of apologizing for "standing up for Canadian workers, Canadian businesses [and] defending our economy."

WATCH | LeBlanc on Trump's latest comments: Canada won't apologize to Trump for 'standing up for Canadian workers,' says LeBlanc | Duration closed caption 1:45 Asked about U.S. President Donald Trump saying he expects Canada to say 'we're sorry, sir' within a few weeks and attempt to reach a trade deal, Minister for Canada-U.S. Trade Dominic LeBlanc says Canada will return to negotiations only if the prime minister decides a deal is possible that protects Canadian sovereignty and would be in Canada's 'economic interest.'

"We are having conversations with our American counterparts. We're not negotiating detailed texts as we were five, six weeks ago. But we remain in contact with them," he said.

"If the prime minister concludes at some point that there's a deal possible, that protects the sovereignty of our country, that would be in the economic interest of the country, then we would obviously be in a position to have that conversation."

During his Tuesday remarks, Navarro suggested that Prime Minister Mark Carney and Ontario Premier Doug Ford were acting to promote their political self-interests as opposed to "what's good for the Canadian people."

"Mark Carney and Doug Ford just talk trash about Donald Trump. That's what they do and then they go up in the polls and they think that's a winning strategy," he said.

"We look at that and go, 'Oh, that's not smart. OK, do your thing. You got tariffs now.'"

Last year, Ford's government paid to run an anti-tariff ad featuring former U.S. president Ronald Reagan that sparked backlash from the White House. U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra has since likened the  to foreign meddling.

Navarro has taken heat for past comments on Canada. In 2020, he questioned Canada's role in the U.S.-led multilateral NATO mission in Afghanistan, suggesting the country's role was motivated more by a desire to curry favour with the U.S. than to support the global fight against terrorism.

Those comments spurred a former chief of the defence staff to call Navarro an "idiot."

World.title: Premier Scott Moe goes big on nuclear with plans to explore 2 large nuclear reactors in northwest Sask.
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Saskatchewan is going big on nuclear, announcing plans to explore building two large nuclear reactors in the province's northwest, with a goal of having the first online by 2042.

The Government of Saskatchewan also confirmed it has narrowed down the location of further study for its construction of small modular reactors (SMRs) to the Rafferty site near Estevan.

Premier Scott Moe said the province's new Delivering Energy Security Through Nuclear Power plan establishes an initial target of 2,600 megawatts (MW) of nuclear power generation by 2050.

"We're charting a path forward for one of the largest energy and economic development opportunities in our province's history," Moe said during a news conference at the University of Saskatchewan on Tuesday.

"Six-hundred megawatts can power the equivalent of Saskatchewan's two largest cities, Regina and Saskatoon, 2,600 megawatts could power the equivalent of 2.6 million homes."

Moe said the move will secure the electricity needed to support a growing population, large industrial projects and expanding industries.

Crown Investments Corporation Minister Jeremy Harrison said the plan focuses on four priorities for nuclear development:

Building electricity capacity for long-term growth.

Incorporating large nuclear reactors into the province's electricity supply planning.

Continuing nuclear development in Estevan.

Building on established nuclear capabilities.

“This plan gives SaskPower a clear path to meet growing demand and support the investment and industries that keep our province strong," Harrison said.

Large nuclear reactors

The 2,600 MW goal for nuclear power generation is a massive expansion of the province's nuclear plans, which had previously been restricted to SMR development and construction.

For context, SaskPower reported that the total power system demand at 10:30 a.m. CST on Tuesday was 2,829 MW. The record for most power use in the province was 3,910 MW on Dec. 30, 2021.

The SMR technology selected by Saskatchewan, the Hitachi BWRX-300, produces approximately 300 MW from a single unit.

Although SaskPower has previously said it wanted to pursue large nuclear technology, Tuesday's announcement is the first time the government has provided firm details.

The province did not confirm where the two large nuclear reactors would be constructed on Tuesday, but Moe has previously alluded to potential locations along the North Saskatchewan River.

SaskPower said it will evaluate potential locations while having "meaningful engagement with local communities and Indigenous peoples."

WATCH | Sask. government wants to build a large nuclear reactor: Sask. government wants to build a large nuclear reactor | Duration closed caption 1:11 On Jan. 28, SaskPower and the province announced their hopes to make nuclear power generation happen in Saskatchewan.

The provincial government did not explicitly say what type of nuclear reactor it would use for the large scale reactors, but Westinghouse's CEO is included in the news release and references Westinghouse and Cameco's AP1000 Gen III+ reactor.

Some of those large scale reactors are already up and running in China and the U.S., with each reactor producing approximately 1,100 MW.

SMR site selection

SaskPower also confirmed it has further narrowed down the locations for SMR deployment in southeast Saskatchewan.

The Crown corporation has previously indicated it was down to two possibilities: a site on the Boundary Dam Resevoir in the Rural Municipality of Estevan, and a location on the Rafferty Resevoir in the rural municipality of Cambria.

SaskPower confirmed Tuesday that it has selected the Rafferty site for "further study."

SaskPower says Estevan remain a key part of nuclear power plans, with the the goal of delivering at least 600 MW of nuclear power, or two Hitachi BWRX-300 units.

A final site decision is expected sometime this year, according to a SaskPower project schedule.

The first SMR is scheduled to be operational by the mid-2030s according to the same document.

World.title: N.S. senior killed ailing wife after promising to help her take her own life, court hears
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

WARNING: This story includes references to suicide and details a killing.

A 75-year-old man smothered his ailing wife in their Kingsport, N.S., home more than four years ago after she made him promise to help her take her own life, a court was told Tuesday.

Douglas Smith was sentenced in Nova Scotia Supreme Court in Kentville, N.S., to six years in prison for the death of Iris Dodd, 72, on April 30, 2022. He pleaded guilty to manslaughter in April days before he was set to stand trial for second-degree murder.

Smith and Dodd, who had serious health issues, had been married for 33 years but faced eviction and had nowhere to go, according to an agreed statement of facts.

Court documents illustrate a harrowing situation the couple, who had a "long, supportive and happy life together," found themselves in that night.

Dodd’s health had been deteriorating since she suffered a stroke in 2018 and they were going to be kicked out of their home the next day, the documents say.

She used a wheelchair, was losing her eyesight and lived with chronic pain from arthritis and fibromyalgia — a long-term condition that causes muscle pain, extreme fatigue and sleep difficulty.

She had just had a long stay in hospital due to bouts of pneumonia.

On the night she died, court documents say Dodd told her husband she didn’t want to spend her final years in a health-care or long-term care facility.

She told Smith she planned to take all of her medication at once in an attempt to overdose and Smith should leave the house so he wouldn't be culpable.

Douglas Smith and Iris Dodd lived in this home in Kingsport, N.S., for nearly eight years. They were going to be evicted the day after Smith killed Dodd. (Paul Poirier/CBC)

The only thing she needed from her husband was for him to arrange the pills because she couldn’t see them very well.

Initially, the documents say, Smith didn’t support his wife’s plan when she raised the topic abruptly.

However, “The victim was very upset and made Mr. Smith promise to help her with her plan and he promised he would,” said the agreed statement of facts.

The couple agreed they’d go ahead with the plan the following day, which helped Dodd calm down and go to sleep.

Smith couldn’t sleep, though, worrying about his wife dying alone. He became increasingly concerned her plan might fail and leave her with permanent brain damage.

“Mr. Smith resolved all these thoughts and fears in his head by getting up and holding a pillow over the victim’s face,” the agreed statement of facts said.

‘She was in distress and I eased her distress’

The day after Smith killed Dodd, he drove to the local RCMP detachment to turn himself in.

After discovering the office was closed, he called 911 from the parking lot and admitted to taking her life.

A recording of Smith's 911 call was released by the court.

The call began with a dispatcher asking Smith what emergency he was reporting. The senior replied that he wanted to report a death.

WATCH | N.S. senior killed ailing wife after promising to help her take her own life, court hears: Annapolis Valley senior sentenced to 6 years in prison | Duration closed caption 2:25 Douglas Smith killed his wife, Iris Dodd, at their home four years ago. As the CBC's Josh Hoffman explains, the couple was facing eviction, Dodd's health was failing and she had asked her husband to help her end her life. Warning: This story includes references to suicide and describes a violent killing.

The dispatcher asked if the death had been sudden or unexpected and Smith said that his wife had died and he was responsible.

Smith said he didn’t want to provide any details but the dispatcher said she required some information before an officer could be sent to meet him.

“She was in distress and I eased her distress,” Smith replied.

An officer came out of the detachment, arrested Smith and took him to a cell inside the building where Smith confirmed it was his voice on the 911 call, according to court documents.

Emotional day in court

Smith was emotional in court Tuesday, holding his head in his hands while the agreed statement of facts was read.



He wept when Crown prosecutor Daniel Rideout reached the part detailing how Smith had smothered his wife.



Smith was asked if he wanted a break but replied: "Let's get this over with."

During submissions, Rideout noted the case differed from the spate of domestic homicides in Nova Scotia in recent years.



Smith was driven by compassion when he took his wife's life, but he still broke the law and had other options available, Rideout said.

World.title: Judge tosses drug trafficking convictions for B.C. compassion club founders after constitutional challenge
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A British Columbia Supreme Court judge has ruled in favour of two harm-reduction activists convicted of drug trafficking who argued they were doing it to reduce the harms caused by toxic drugs.

Justice Catherine Murray found parts of Canada's Controlled Drugs and Substances Act unconstitutional and stayed the convictions against Jeremy Kalicum and Eris Nyx.

Murray said Kalicum and Nyx's compassion club, the Drug User Liberation Front (DULF), reduced the harms associated with the toxic drug crisis and did not negatively impact the community or public safety.

Kalicum and Nyx were found guilty last year of drug trafficking after Vancouver police raided the club in 2023.

Murray said in court on Tuesday that the pair "selflessly" put themselves to the side for the cause.

"Mr. Kalicum and Ms. Nyx have borne the burden of bringing a successful constitutional challenge, thereby doing the public interest a service at considerable personal cost," Murray said.

WATCH | Thousands have died of toxic drugs. Did politics get in the way of saving lives?:

She noted thousands of people have died due to toxic drugs since the public health emergency was declared in B.C. in 2016.

Murray put Kalicum and Nyx's convictions on hold last year to hear the constitutional challenge, where their lawyers argued that forcing drug users to rely on unregulated street drugs violates the Charter of Rights.

Murray said in her ruling then that Nyx and Kalicum's intentions were good as they tried to save lives, but that buying pure drugs on the dark web and selling them to members was not covered by an exemption that allowed for drug storage and testing.

She said the two were "agitators" who wanted to make change and were aware that they ran the risk of a trafficking prosecution.

Kalicum and Nyx's lawyers had argued that closing the club violated the rights of those who are disabled by addiction and raised their risk of death from an unregulated, illicit drug supply.

World.title: 'It's devastating': Hundreds of Stelco workers in Hamilton and Nanticoke face uncertain future due to layoffs
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Hundreds of Stelco workers in Hamilton are facing an uncertain future after the company announced Monday it will indefinitely idle its cold-rolled and coated operations at its Hamilton Works plant.

Ron Wells, the president of United Steelworkers Local 1005, says the wind-down is expected to begin Oct. 9, with about 350 workers from the Hamilton plant expected to be laid off.

He said the total layoffs could be up to 500 in total, between the Hamilton and Lake Erie Works plant in Nanticoke, Ont. Stelco has also said up to 500 workers could be affected.

"I hate using 'we're disappointed' — we're disgusted," Wells told CBC Hamilton Tuesday morning.

For families connected to the plant, the uncertainty is already taking a toll.

Jillian Watt's husband is a line worker, and has worked at Stelco in Hamilton for 21 years. She said he has not yet been told whether he will be among those laid off.

"They haven't spoken to individuals, so it's kind of still up in the air," she said Tuesday morning. Watt, who is a union representative for a Canadian Union of Public Employees heath workers local, spoke to CBC from the entrance to National Steel Car, just down the road from Stelco.

National Steel Car workers have been on strike for a 48 days and have been regularly joined on the picket line by other unionized workers.

Watt is particularly concerned about whether her husband's experience with the company is enough if layoffs are decided by seniority. She said the possibility of losing the family's main source of income is particularly stressful.

"He's a breadwinner for a family. We have four kids, you know, trying to make it by," she said. "It was a bit of a kick to the gut for both of us."

Jillian Watt says she's nervous about what will happen to her husband following the news that Stelco will be laying off about 350 workers. As of Tuesday, they have not received any notice. (Claude Beaudoin/CBC)

Watt said her husband had already been concerned about the plant in recent months, as operations were idled and orders slowed. Now, they are awaiting the verdict of what happens next. "It's very stressful," she said.

Union questions job commitments

Wells said the union was told about the layoffs during a meeting with the company Monday morning.

He said he has been talking with workers concerned about how long the layoffs could last because the company has not provided an end date.

"They're asking how long is this going to last? Should we start looking for another job?" Wells said. "People are concerned."

Ron Wells, president of USW Local 1005, says he is "disgusted" by the decision to lay off approximately 350 workers. (Meagan Fitzpatrick/CBC)

The company has said some affected workers could be offered jobs at Lake Erie Works in Nanticoke.

But Wells said the union was told there are only roughly 40 to 45 openings there — a number he says falls well short of the potential layoffs in Hamilton.

Wells is also questioning the commitments Cleveland-Cliffs made when it acquired Stelco in 2024.

He said the agreement included a commitment to maintain the number of unionized employees for five years, and he wants the federal government to enforce it.

"You have people making these decisions in Cleveland and they have no ties to our community," Well said. "If 350 Hamiltonians lose their jobs, they don't care."

Pat Persico, the senior director of corporate communications for Cleveland-Cliffs, told CBC News in an emailed statement that while Stelco is idling some of its operations in Hamilton, the company's total output of steel will not be impacted as it consolidates production at its Lake Erie Works.

"Very importantly, job opportunities at Lake Erie Works will be offered to Hamilton employees," Persico wrote in an email. "We expect that a significant number of employees affected by the indefinite idle at Hamilton should be absorbed at Lake Erie Works."

'Devastating' news for Hamilton

Hamilton Mayor Andrea Horwath said the city has been working with the federal and provincial governments in response to the announcement.

"The fight is not over," Horwath told CBC's As It Happens radio program on Monday.

LISTEN | Hamilton Mayor Andrea Horwath reacts to layoffs: As It Happens 6:54 Hamilton steelworker layoffs 'painful for our community,' says mayor As of next Friday, about 350 Hamilton, Ont., steelworkers will be out of work, according to their union. Stelco, the U.S.-owned company that operates the Hamilton plant, blames the layoffs on trade disputes between the U.S. and Canada. But Hamilton Mayor Andrea Horwath says the fight isn't over. She spoke to As It Happens host Nil Kӧksal.

She said she believes Cleveland-Cliffs is not living up to commitments made to workers and that she has asked city staff to review commitments made during the company's restructuring process.

"We're going to fight tooth and nail to have them basically live up to their commitments and protect these jobs," she said.

Karina Gould, the Liberal MP for nearby Burlington, called the decision "devastating news" for Hamilton and said the federal government is prepared to provide support to maintain operations and protect jobs.

"This is a very difficult time," Gould said.

Hamilton mayoral candidate Keanin Loomis, who is the president and CEO of the Canadian Institute of Steel Construction, also called the announcement "devastating."

"Steel jobs have supported generations of Hamilton families and remain vital to our local economy," Loomis said in a statement on social media.

The impact of tariffs has been a discussion topic on the municipal election campaign trail, with several candidates sharing proposals on how to respond to trade uncertainty.

For Watt, the announcement represents another difficult moment for a city where steel means so much.

"My grandfather, my dad, my uncles, they all worked at Stelco," she said. "My husband and my brother are there, and this is going to have a huge impact."

"It's scary times."

World.title: Hurricane Polo makes 2nd landfall on Mexico's Pacific coast
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Hurricane Polo made a second landfall on Mexico's northwestern Pacific coast on Tuesday after drenching the southern Baja California peninsula.

Landfall was near the port city of Guaymas on the Sea of Cortez in ​Sonora state. State authorities ordered emergency evacuations in southern ​municipalities including Guaymas, Empalme, Benito Juarez and Vicam. Officials said 543 people hunkered down in shelters as the storm rolled in.

Polo, a Category 1 hurricane, ​was inland at 10 a.m. local time, and the U.S. National Hurricane Center (NHC) reported ⁠maximum sustained winds of around ⁠120 km/h.

"Rapid weakening is expected as ‌the center of Polo moves farther inland," the NHC said in its bulletin.

While the hurricane was forecast to weaken over land, private forecaster AccuWeather warned its moisture-laden remnants could trigger a deluge across the U.S. Southwest and Plains.

PHOTOS | Hurricane Polo hits Mexico:

Hit Baja California as Category 2 storm

Polo earlier battered the Baja California peninsula as a more powerful Category 2 storm, turning streets into rivers and snapping trees.

However, Baja California Sur Gov. Víctor Manuel Castro said no lives were ‌lost due to the storm.

The storm was expected to dump 10 to 15 centimetres across southern and central portions of Sonora, with isolated maximum totals of 20 centimetres. Baja California Sur could face a further two to five centimetres ​of rain and the risk of life-threatening flooding and mudslides, according to the NHC.

"At my house we tied all down. ⁠We prepared very well. We expected it to be stronger, but thank God it wasn't ⁠so disastrous," Bertha Lopez, a resident of Loreto in Baja California Sur, told Reuters.

Nearly 700 people ⁠sought ⁠refuge in emergency shelters in Baja ​California Sur, and will be returning to their homes throughout the day, the head of Mexico's civil ​protection agency, Laura Velázquez, said ⁠at a news conference.

In a post on X, Mexico's Secretariat of the Navy said a ship brought 2,000 food baskets, 8,000 litres of drinking water and machinery, among other things, to the region.

World.title: LNG Canada to move forward with Phase 2 expansion project in Kitimat, B.C.
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

LNG Canada says its multibillion-dollar Phase 2 expansion in Kitimat, B.C., is going forward, in a move that could double exports of liquefied natural gas from the northern coastal facility to overseas markets.

In a statement Tuesday, LNG Canada CEO Chris Cooper said the project will create thousands of jobs and further strengthen Canada's role as a trusted energy partner.

"LNG Canada Phase 2 is another nation-building investment that demonstrates Canada can build big things when governments, First Nations partners, local communities, skilled trades, contractors and investors work together with shared purpose," Cooper said.

LNG Canada is a joint venture company made up of Shell, Petronas, PetroChina, Mitsubishi Corporation and Korea Gas Corp.

Its Kitimat plant shipped its first cargo load of LNG destined for Asian markets last year.

Speaking in Vancouver Tuesday, Prime Minister Mark Carney said the private sector investment of about $33-billion in LNG Canada's Phase 2 will make it the second-largest facility of its kind in the world.

"It will connect low-cost, low-carbon Canadian energy to global markets."

Carney said the expansion and increased LNG output will amount to billions for the national economy, and create up to 4,000 new jobs in Kitimat alone during peak construction.

But while the LNG industry has strong political support from the federal government, as well as the campaigning B.C. NDP and Conservative Party of B.C., critics worry its rapid expansion will further contribute to Canada's rising greenhouse gas emissions at a time of climate crisis.

Carney said he would announce a "historic investment" in ocean protection later Tuesday afternoon, and is set to speak at 1:30 p.m. PT.

What is LNG?

LNG is made from natural gas, a fossil fuel often extracted in northeast B.C. and Alberta through a practice called hydraulic fracturing or fracking.

It involves drilling down into the ground and injecting a mixture of water, sand and chemicals into the ground to force the release of the oil and gas.

WATCH | Some Kitimat locals concerned about LNG flaring: Locals express safety concerns over flaring gas at Kitimat’s LNG export terminal | Duration closed caption 2:19



The gas is then shipped via pipeline to terminals, which cool it to about –160 C, at which point it can be shipped overseas for use as a fuel.

The expansion project is expected to roughly double the production of liquefied natural gas from 14 million to 28 million tonnes annually, LNG Canada said.

It also said it is working with Coastal GasLink to expand the capacity of the existing 670-kilometre pipeline through the construction of five new compressor stations across northern B.C., including territory that was blocked by Wet'suwet'en hereditary chiefs and their supporters opposed to the line's construction, which led to nation-wide protests and arrests.

WATCH | RCMP make arrests over Coastal GasLink pipeline: RCMP arrests protesters at Wet'suwet'en blockade | Duration 1:44



LNG is often referred to as "clean" because burning it for fuel causes fewer emissions than coal or oil — but that claim is disputed by some analysts because of the energy and destruction it takes to produce.

One of the known impacts of fracking is an increase in earthquakes , which have been felt with increasing frequency in B.C.'s Peace River region in recent years.

Critics also point out ramping up LNG production would sharply increase the amount of emissions from natural gas production in British Columbia.

WATCH | Is LNG an example of greenwashing? Canada’s clean LNG pitch — and why not everyone is buying it | Duration closed caption 7:37



Environmentalists argue that reducing emissions carries more urgency in the wake of a federal report warning Canadians to prepare for a future that's 5 C hotter — which will lead to the disappearance of glaciers in western Canada and longer, more intense summer droughts, among other impacts.

Political priority

Still, the project has been identified as one of national importance under Carney, and has support from both the B.C. NDP and B.C. Conservative Party — who have each pledged to ramp up LNG production should they form government following the Oct. 24 election.

On the campaign trail Monday, B.C. Conservative Leader Lorne Doerkson announced his plan to make B.C. an "energy superpower," promising to cut red tape in order to triple LNG production by 2035.

WATCH | Haisla Nation Chief Councillor Maureen Nyce on LNG: What impact will LNG Canada’s Phase 2 project have on local First Nations communities? | Duration closed caption 5:37



In response, the B.C. NDP argued the plan wasn't ambitious enough, and said it already has plans to have B.C. outpace Doerkson's projections.

The B.C. Greens, meanwhile, have called for a moratorium on LNG expansion, citing environmental risks and concerns about Indigenous rights, further saying that fast-tracking projects is eroding oversight and accountability.

World.title: Police investigating after 10K litres of diesel stolen from 3 Calgary gas stations
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Sam Babcock didn’t think much of it when he got a call that his company’s fuel inventory was missing a massive amount.

Typically, the BG Fuels territory manager in southern Alberta would chalk up the dip to a simple input error. Babcock didn’t realize the loss was the first in a string of thefts equalling a loss of roughly 10,000 litres of diesel fuel, costing the company approximately $20,000.

“We’ve never seen this. Never across the country as well. At least in my time here, I’ve never experienced anything like this,” said Babcock.

BG Fuels is a Canadian wholesaler operating under the Mobil, Esso and Waypoint Convenience brands around the country. It's raising alarm after three Mobil gas stations in Calgary were hit with thefts in the last few weeks, with diesel fuel pulled directly out of underground tanks.

Most of the total was sucked up in an initial incident where the company lost about 8,000 litres of fuel, Babcock said.

Sam Babcock, BG Fuels territory manager for southern Alberta, speaks to CBC News at a Mobil gas station in Calgary. (Nate Luit/CBC)

After reviewing surveillance footage of the first theft, Babcock said it showed a truck arrive at around 4 a.m. while the station was closed and remain for roughly 25 minutes while removing diesel from the site, before driving away.

Given that a large commercial truck was used to store the fuel, Babcock pointed out anyone driving by at that hour wouldn't have thought anything suspicious was amiss.

But the thefts are creating a lot of stress for station agents, he said.

“A lot of them have come at nighttime to check in on their sites. They can’t sleep,” said Babcock, who oversees 28 gas stations in southern Alberta.

Surveillance footage shows something went wrong for the perpetrators during the second theft, resulting in only about 50 litres taken. About 2,000 litres was stolen during the final theft, Babcock said. The company said it believes the same perpetrators were involved in all three thefts, judging from the footage.

Surveillance footage shows a truck removing diesel from a Mobil gas station in Calgary early in the morning of Sept. 17, 2026. (BG Fuels)

The thefts present a large safety concern, Babcock said, as the amount of diesel stolen is a lot of flammable material that needs to be handled correctly.

Police investigating thefts

The Calgary Police Service confirmed on Tuesday that it is investigating the incidents.

Nick Wilsher, a sergeant with the service’s crime prevention team, said that while smaller thefts involving siphoning fuel are more common, thefts like what BG reported are unusual.

Wilsher compared the market for fuel to other online marketplaces where a consumer may see a cheap product, know its low price may be because it’s stolen, and “pretend ‘well, maybe it’s not.’”

“It’s not a victimless crime ... Those costs are passed on to you as the consumer," said Wilsher.

“You might think you're getting a deal, but you’re actually making it more expensive for everybody else, including yourself when you can’t buy this cheap diesel anymore. You’re going to have to get it at the pump.”

Wilsher said retailers could look to increase security, improve locks and introduce tamper-proof alarm systems and more video surveillance to protect against thefts.

He added that the surveillance footage recovered by BG is helpful to show police the kind of vehicle used in the thefts, where they came from and drove to, and to potentially give them a closer look at the people involved.

World.title: Colombia breaks diplomatic ties with Iran
World.content:
Colombia’s Foreign Ministry said Thursday that it had broken diplomatic ties with Iran and designated the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) as a terrorist organization.

The foreign ministry made the announcements in two separate statements that were published in its website.

In the first statement, the government claimed that the decision claimed to defend “national and hemispheric security, and the fight against transnational crime.”

According to the foreign ministry, the Iranian government has “alleged ties to international terrorist groups and other narco-terrorist groups that threaten [Colombia’s] security.”

Colombia also took into account the documented human rights violations committed by the Iranian government on its territory, the verified attacks against countries not involved in the Middle East conflict, the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, and the authorities’ obstruction of the International Atomic Energy Agency’s (IAEA) efforts to verify the scope of Iran’s nuclear program. Foreign Ministry

In regards to the IRGC, the foreign ministry claimed that the Iranian armed force “poses a serious threat to international peace and security” through “covert operations beyond Iran’s borders.”

“Colombia will strengthen its control and security measures to prevent individuals associated with the IRGC from entering its territory,” said the foreign ministry in a second statement.

In his 2017 book “Watch Your Backyard,” Foreign Minister Omar Bula claimed that “Iran and Islamic extremist groups such a Hezbollah and Al Qaeda have profusely penetrated Latin America.”

As part of his foreign policy, President Abelardo de la Espriella has renewed ties with the United States, Israel and the United Arab Emirates.

In a response, the Iranian government said that the accusations of the De la Espriella government go “against the principles of mutual respect” and damage both countries’ “interests and benefits.”

“It is clear that none of the arguments put forward by the Colombian government to justify this decision are valid or logical, and that this measure was adopted solely under the influence of the Zionist regime and the United States,” said Iran’s foreign ministry.

World.title: ACSN extends lockdown of Colombia’s Caribbean coast to Friday morning
World.content:
Santa Marta-based organized crime group ACSN said Wednesday that the lockdown it has imposed on parts of Colombia’s Caribbean coast will be lifted on Friday morning.

In its first formal statement, the ACSN said that “the armed strike announced for 72 hours will end at 7:00AM on Friday 25 September 2026.”

The lockdown, which was initially called for 48 hours on Monday, has devastated the legal economy in the port city, particularly after ACSN assassins uploaded videos of them opening fire at stores that ignored the order to social media.

The online videos and half a dozen burnt buses and taxis all but cleared the streets of Santa Marta, which became a ghost town on Tuesday.

“We have never seen anything like this,” one Santa Marta resident told news program El Reporte Coronell.

President Abelardo de la Espriella announced the militarization of Santa Marta, but this was barely visible in the city’s downtown area and in the majority of Santa Marta’s neighborhoods.

“There are no police or soldiers in the streets, the people feel unprotected and are in panic,” said journalist Javier Manjarres on social media platform X.

“The current situation is a consequence of the behavior of the security forces and the decisions taken by the National Government in regards to our organization,” the organized crime group said in their statement.

The ACSN admitted that the clandestine lockdown was the result of the killing of Jose Luis Perez, a.k.a. “Cholo,” one of its commanders in the region around the Sierra Nevada mountain range just outside the city.

According to the group, security forces executed Cholo in front of his wife after his arrest.

An 18-year-old farmhand with no ties to the organization was also executed by the security, his family told media.

The lockdown has been imposed throughout the Magdalena and La Guajira provinces, a region where the group dominates organized crime and controls drug trafficking route to the Caribbean.

World.title: Colombia withdraws support for ICJ genocide case against Israel
World.content:
Colombia has withdrawn its participation in South Africa’s genocide case against Israel, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) said Tuesday.

In a statement, the court in The Hague said that Colombia’s government “decided to withdraw the Declaration of intervention that it had filed… on 5 April 2024 in the case concerning Application of the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide in the Gaza Strip.”

The decision of the administration of President Abelardo De la Espriella is part of a wider attempt to restore ties with Israel and its main sponsor, the United States, and appease its Evangelical Christian support base.

In response to the ongoing genocide in Palestine, former President Gustavo Petro took a leading role in diplomatic efforts that sought to isolate Israel and seek justice for Israel’s victims through the world court.

In a response, the US Government put Petro on a blacklist and actively campaigned for the election of De la Espriella to prevent another leftist victory in elections earlier this year.

The new president, who took office in August, immediately restored diplomatic ties to Israel and lifted a ban on coal exports to the country in West Asia.

World.title: ACSN crime group shuts down parts of Colombia’s Caribbean coast
World.content:
Santa Marta-based crime group ACSN shut down parts of the city and the surrounding region after Colombia’s armed forces killed one of their commanders.

Jose Luis Perez, a.k.a. “Cholo,” and six of his comrades were killed during an offensive on Monday.

The son of Fredy Castillo, a.k.a. “Pinocho,” who is one of the alleged bosses of the crime group, was reportedly among those killed during the operation.

Shortly after, a pamphlet that was signed by the ACSN ordered an “armed strike” of 48 hours because of the “the fierce attacks that the government has been launching against our organization in the Sierra Nevada since this afternoon.”

Multiple buses were incinerated in the region around Santa Marta.

We hereby declare a 48-hour armed strike throughout the province of Magdalena, particularly along the Troncal del Caribe highway, in the city of Santa Marta, and in the banana-growing region. We do not want any businesses to remain open for a period of 48 hours. ACSN

According to President Abelardo de la Espriella, who traveled to the city, “they are trying to intimidate the public by promoting an armed strike.”

“I will not allow any criminal organization to subjugate citizens through threats and terror,” the president added.

Notwithstanding, multiple shop owners in Santa Marta and along the highway kept their shops closed on Tuesday, afraid to challenge the authority of the local crime bosses.

The district government closed public schools in neighborhoods where the ACSN is believed to have a strong presence. Public transport was suspended as videos of armed men opening fire on shops that failed to close voluntarily were posted on social media.

The ACSN control much of drug trafficking to the port of Santa Marta and to the coastline of the neighboring La Guajira province.

De la Espriella ended attempts to negotiate the group’s surrender and ordered a military approach after taking office in August.

World.title: Colombia’s war crimes tribunal warns ICC that De la Espriella supports “worst attack in history”
World.content:
Colombia’s war crimes tribunal JEP said that it would warn the United Nations and the International Criminal Court about plans of President Abelardo de la Espriella to cut its budget.

In a statement, JEP president Alejandro Ramelli raised the alarm warned about a pending proposal by far-right Senator Enrique Gomez (National Salvation) to reduce the tribunal’s budget by COP100 billion ($31.6 million), which received De la Espriella’s support.

A second proposal by another far-right party, the Democratic Center, sought to push all sentences against members of the security forces to military justice for revision.

According to Ramelli, the two bill proposals “prove the existence of a strategy to block the JEP’s functioning” and called on the international community to “put a stop to this effort to dismantle our financial system and calls for the essential resources needed for our operations to be guaranteed.”

These initiatives constitute a combined strategy of economic strangulation and the subjugation of the JEP to military criminal justice. It is the most serious attack we have ever faced against our independence and autonomy. JEP president Alejandro Ramelli

The president , who vowed to get rid of the JEP on campaign, said that the 2027 national budget “does not constitute any threat to any judge, it’s the Constitution at work.”

I do not have a policy of retaliation against the JEP. I have a duty to manage spending, demand results, and allocate the State’s limited resources to a justice system that serves everyone, not to a court that part of the country perceives—for reasons debated in Congress and in public opinion—as a system of privileges rather than an effective end to impunity. President Abelardo de la Espriella

Since March of 2018, the JEP has played a key role in clarifying crimes committed during the armed conflict that erupted in response to the insurgency of the now-defunct guerrilla group FARC.

Among other things, the JEP found that the guerrillas recruited more than 18,000 children and that the security forces assassinated more than 7,800 civilians to inflate their combat kills.

Hundreds of former guerrillas and former members of the armed forces are taking part in a transitional justice system that seeks to solve as many as possible of the hundreds of thousands of crimes committed during the decades-long armed conflict.

World.title: Colombia pulls out of international LGBT coalition
World.content:
The government of President Abelardo de la Espriella pulled Colombia out of the international Equal Rights Coalition, which promotes the rights of sexual and gender minorities around the world.

The Foreign Ministry announced its departure from the coalition in a letter addressed to the organization of which Colombia was co-president until February next year.

According to Caribe Afirmativa, a gay rights NGO that was part of the international initiative, warned that the decision was “a serious setback in foreign policy and commitments to LGBTIQ+ rights.”

We also view this action as a snub to the international community, a break from the leadership role Colombia had established, and an unequivocal political signal regarding the place the current government is willing to grant to the rights of LGBTIQ+ people. Caribe Afirmativa

De la Espriella has appointed multiple prominent far-right figures in his government and has vowed to wage a “Culture War” against what it considers “gender ideology.”

On top of this, De la Espriella and multiple of his cabinet members oppose the right of gay couples to adopt children and reportedly sacked the newly appointed planning chief because he and his gay partner had adopted a child.

World.title: Court imposes strict conditions on Colombia’s military air strikes if minors are present
World.content:
A Bogota court imposed strict conditions on Colombia’s military authorities if they want to carry out air strikes on illegal armed groups in places where victims of forced recruitment are present.

The ruling of Bogota’s 34th Family Court lifted a suspension on the strikes that had been imposed earlier this month in response to a lawsuit.

The court imposed the following conditions on air strikes to evade violating International Humanitarian Law, which prioritizes the rights of child victims of forced recruitment over the success of military operations.

Don’t assume minors are legitimate targets because they form part of an illegal armed group

Intensify the verification and cross-checking of available information on the possible presence of minors at potential targets

Explicitly include this assessment to the legal and operational assessment of the attack

Assess the foreseeable risk of an attack on the lives and integrity of the minors

Examine the existence of less harmful means, methods, timing or operational alternatives that would allow the achievement of a comparable military advantage

Rigorously apply the principles of distinction, precaution, and proportionality before authorizing and executing the operation

The court additionally ordered family welfare institute ICBF to be integrated into military operations and strengthen the pathways for disengagement, restoration of rights, comprehensive care, and reintegration of children and adolescents who are victims of recruitment, with a differentiated and territorial approach.

The court asked the Ombudsman and the Inspector General’s Office to monitor compliance of the orders issued to maximize the protection of children’s rights.

The lawsuit had been filed in a successful attempt to protect children against the violence President Abelardo de la Espriella sought to unleash on illegal armed groups that refused to demobilize.

World.title: Chile's defence minister backs trade between Punta Arenas and the Falklands
World.content:
Chile's defence minister backs trade between Punta Arenas and the Falklands

29th Tuesday, September 2026 - 09:02 UTC Full article

Asked how closer trade ties would fit with regional commitments, Barros said the “potentially most contentious” point is oil and mining exploration

Chile's Defence Minister Fernando Barros Tocornal has backed the development of commercial activity between the Magallanes region and the Falklands, saying his country's support for Argentina's sovereignty claim does not imply restrictions on trade with the archipelago. He made the remarks in an interview with Radio Polar in Punta Arenas during a visit to the region on September 24 and 25.

According to his comments, reported on Sunday by the Argentine daily La Nación, the Magallanes community has “the right to trade” and the minister sees “no impediments to those activities going ahead” within the legal framework.

Barros reiterated Chile's support for Buenos Aires, though with a nuance. “Chile has expressed its support for the Argentine claim, its sovereignty claim over the Malvinas or Falklands, but there is a fact: a friendly country has exercised sovereignty over the islands for 200 years,” he said, referring to the United Kingdom, which has administered the archipelago since 1833, with the 1982 interruption. He added that such support must be expressed in line with international law, “respecting the will and interest of the people involved and by peaceful means”. Argentina's position holds that the will of the archipelago's residents is not decisive in resolving the dispute. La Nación described the remarks as “at the very least confusing”.

The minister's words do not formally alter Chile's diplomatic position. On September 3, Presidents José Antonio Kast and Javier Milei signed a joint declaration in Santiago in which Chile reiterated its support for the sovereign rights Argentina claims over the islands, South Georgia, the South Sandwich Islands and their corresponding maritime areas.

Asked how closer trade ties would fit with regional commitments, Barros said the “potentially most contentious” point is oil and mining exploration, “which will have to be assessed in due course”, and noted that Chile's commitments in Mercosur and Unasur are “political and not legally binding”. In 2011, Mercosur members and associate states, including Chile, agreed measures concerning vessels flying the archipelago's flag.

The remarks come as a project for a sea link between Punta Arenas and Stanley advances. The Falkland Islands Development Corporation, the archipelago's economic development agency, has signed a contract with Easter Island Naviera, a Chilean company operating mainly between Valparaíso and Easter Island. According to Chilean media, the first voyage is planned for November. Some Argentine outlets present the route as an alternative to the supplies that currently reach the islands from Montevideo, some 2,000 kilometres away.

Argentina has 60 administrative proceedings open, with no penalty applied, and three criminal complaints covering ten companies and their directors over hydrocarbon exploration in waters near the archipelago. None of the allegations has been proven. In the 2013 referendum, 99.8% of voters chose, on a 92% turnout, to retain the status of a British overseas territory.

World.title: Latin American airports will need US$178 billion to nearly double their traffic
World.content:
Latin American airports will need US$178 billion to nearly double their traffic

29th Tuesday, September 2026 - 07:30 UTC Full article

The organisation also argued that airport charges, set by each country's regulators rather than by the airports themselves, account for a small share of airline costs

Airports in Latin America and the Caribbean will require investment of around US$178 billion over the next thirty years to handle demand that would rise from 809 million passengers this year to around 1.5 billion in 2045, according to projections presented in Lima at the annual assembly of Airports Council International.

The director general of the organisation's regional branch, ACI-LAC, Rafael Echevarne, estimated long-term growth of 3.1% a year and said annual infrastructure spending would need to rise from about US$3.4 billion to between US$8.6 and 8.7 billion by mid-century. In the first half of 2026, regional passenger traffic grew 1.9% and cargo 3.6%. The gathering this week brings together more than 600 executives, officials and specialists from the sector.

Globally, ACI estimates the sector will need around US$4.6 trillion in investment through 2055, after a record 9.8 billion passengers in 2025 and 4.7 billion in the first half of this year. “What really matters now is how we make sure our industry is ready for this growth,” said ACI World director general Justin Erbacci.

Echevarne warned that connectivity within the region has not recovered since the pandemic. “We have lost 20% of the city pairs we had connected,” he said, placing the loss mainly at regional airports in Peru, Ecuador and Chile. He put forward liberalisation of air transport as the main tool to reverse it: “We need to move from signing treaties of good intentions to putting that opening into practice.”

The organisation also argued that airport charges, set by each country's regulators rather than by the airports themselves, account for a small share of airline costs. According to IATA figures cited at the meeting, they represent 4.3% of operating costs globally and 5.5% in the region when air traffic control fees are included. The average charge is around US$9 per passenger.

Brazil leads regional traffic with 235 million passengers in 2025, followed by Mexico with 191 million, Colombia with 100, Argentina with 50, Peru with 43 and Chile with 36. In international trips per inhabitant, Uruguay ranks third among the Latin American countries surveyed, at 0.67, behind the Dominican Republic and Costa Rica, and nearly double Argentina's 0.34. Panama leads in total traffic per inhabitant, at 4.59.

In Argentina, the government on Monday formalised the extension to 2049 of the concession for 35 airports held by Aeropuertos Argentina, part of the Corporación América group, with an option to extend to 2056. The original concession was due to expire in 2038. The company will invest US$600 million, three quarters of it before the end of 2031, with no tariff increases and a reference internal rate of return of 14.3%, below the 17% it had sought.

World.title: Milei orders arbitration proceedings against the UK over the Sea Lion project
World.content:
Milei orders arbitration proceedings against the UK over the Sea Lion project

29th Tuesday, September 2026 - 07:30 UTC Full article

Argentina demanded that the United Kingdom take the necessary measures within that period to prevent the start or continuation of hydrocarbon exploitation and refrain from granting new permits

Argentine President Javier Milei on Monday instructed the foreign ministry and the government's legal teams to launch international arbitration proceedings against the United Kingdom over the development of the Sea Lion oil project in the basin north of the Falklands, and gave London two weeks to halt the activity before Argentina turns to the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea.

“I instructed the foreign ministry and our legal teams to begin international arbitration against the United Kingdom for the illegal plundering of our resources through the Sea Lion Project in the North Malvinas Basin. If in 2 weeks the United Kingdom does not stop the illegitimate exploitation, we will go to the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea,” the president wrote on X.

According to the statement from the Office of the President, the procedure is the one provided for in Annex VII of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, to which both countries are party. Arbitration formally begins with a written notification to the other party setting out the claim and its grounds; there is no record that such notification has been sent. Argentina demanded that the United Kingdom take the necessary measures within that period to prevent the start or continuation of hydrocarbon exploitation and refrain from granting new permits. If it does not, Argentina will ask the Hamburg-based tribunal for provisional measures, which that body can order while an arbitral tribunal is being constituted if it considers the latter would have jurisdiction on a prima facie basis.

The government bases its position on UN General Assembly resolutions 2065 and 31/49, which recognised the existence of a sovereignty dispute, urged both countries to negotiate and called on them to refrain from unilateral modifications. It argues that exploitation causes “irreversible and irreparable harm” to Argentine rights. These resolutions have the status of recommendations.

The chosen route faces a foreseeable legal obstacle. In previous cases, tribunals constituted under the Law of the Sea Convention declined to rule on disputes involving territorial sovereignty, as in the arbitration between Mauritius and the United Kingdom over the Chagos Islands in 2015 and in the dispute between Ukraine and Russia over Crimea in 2020.

The statement also includes a “categorical rejection” of the written statement the United Kingdom entered into the General Assembly record after Milei's speech, and maintains that the British overseas territory designation and the 2013 referendum have no legal validity. London holds that it has no doubt about its sovereignty, that Argentine law does not apply in the archipelago and that hydrocarbon activity is governed by local legislation in accordance with the same Convention. There was no specific British response to the announcement. The companies behind the project, Israel's Navitas and Britain's Rockhopper, have said they expect no change to their timetable, which sets first production for the first half of 2028.

The government also said it had detected operations by Thales UK Limited between the archipelago and Punta Arenas, in Chile, using a UK-registered aircraft without Argentine authorisation, and ordered sanction proceedings and criminal complaints. Argentina has 60 administrative proceedings open with no penalty applied and three criminal complaints against ten companies. None of the allegations has been proven.

World.title: Lula widens his first-round lead to five points, but the runoff remains tied
World.content:
Lula widens his first-round lead to five points, but the runoff remains tied

29th Tuesday, September 2026 - 07:21 UTC Full article

The survey, commissioned by the newspaper O Globo and TV Globo, was carried out from Thursday to Sunday with 2,400 interviews nationwide and a margin of error of two percentage points

Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has widened his lead over Senator Flávio Bolsonaro to five points in voting intentions for Sunday's first round, according to a Quaest poll released on Monday, though the two remain tied in a prospective October 25 runoff.

The survey, commissioned by the newspaper O Globo and TV Globo, was carried out from Thursday to Sunday with 2,400 interviews nationwide and a margin of error of two percentage points. Lula takes 39%, two points higher than in the previous round, and Bolsonaro, of the Liberal Party, 34%, up one. The field is completed by Augusto Cury and Ronaldo Caiado on 4% each, Renan Santos on 3% and Romeu Zema on 1%. Undecided voters account for 5%, and 10% say they will vote blank, spoil their ballot or abstain.

In a second round, the poll shows a 42% tie, with Lula up one point on the previous week and his rival unchanged. Some 49% of respondents disapprove of the government's performance and 46% approve.

A second survey, by Nexus for the bank BTG Pactual, conducted from Friday to Sunday, puts Lula on 42% and Bolsonaro on 37% when respondents are shown the list of candidates, with the president up two points and the senator unchanged. In a prospective runoff, Lula takes 46% to 44%, within the margin of error.

Both surveys confirm the trend of those published in previous weeks: neither candidate is close to the 50% plus one of valid votes needed to settle the election in the first round.

The polls were released after Lula signed Provisional Measure 1,394 on Friday, banning nationwide the operation, offering, intermediation and advertising of online sports betting and casinos, including licences granted by state governments. The measure took effect on publication, but Congress must ratify it within 120 days. It marks a reversal from the law the government itself enacted in December 2023 to regulate the sector, in which 85 companies operate legally. Lula described the phenomenon as “a public health problem”. Bolsonaro called the measure electoral, and industry associations asked the Supreme Federal Court to suspend it. According to Quaest, 62% of Brazilians support the ban.

On Sunday, October 4, Brazilian voters will elect the president, all 27 state governors, the entire Chamber of Deputies and two thirds of the Senate.

World.title: Five shipping lines warn Uruguay the port dispute is damaging its international standing
World.content:
Five shipping lines warn Uruguay the port dispute is damaging its international standing

29th Tuesday, September 2026 - 07:17 UTC Full article

The companies describe a situation of “extreme uncertainty and paralysis” at the specialised container terminal and say that so far in 2026 there have been “more than 35 days of” disruption

Five of the main shipping lines operating at the port of Montevideo have warned the Uruguayan government that the labour dispute at the Terminal Cuenca del Plata is causing “severe economic and commercial harm” and has “severely damaged Uruguay's international prestige”, in a letter addressed to six ministers.

The letter, dated September 22 and received by the ministries on September 24, is signed by Maersk Uruguay, Ocean Network Express, CMA CGM Uruguay, Cosco Shipping Lines and Hapag-Lloyd Uruguay. It was first reported by Informativo Carve. It is addressed to Economy Minister Gabriel Oddone, Labour Minister Juan Castillo, Transport and Public Works Minister Lucía Etcheverry, Industry, Energy and Mining Minister Fernanda Cardona, Livestock, Agriculture and Fisheries Minister Alfredo Fratti, and Foreign Minister Mario Lubetkin.

The companies describe a situation of “extreme uncertainty and paralysis” at the specialised container terminal and say that so far in 2026 there have been “more than 35 days of operational disruption of various kinds”. According to the letter, open-ended strikes have forced them to cancel calls and unload imports at other ports in the region, generating unforeseen costs and breaches of commitments to exporters, importers and hauliers. They argue that, because of the loss of transshipments, global operators now see the country “as an unsafe, unstable and commercially unreliable logistics enclave”, and call for “an immediate, substantive solution that restores predictability”.

The Terminal Cuenca del Plata, majority-owned by the Belgian group Katoen Natie, handles around 80% of containers at the port of Montevideo. The dispute with the port workers' union has dragged on for months, following the expiry of the previous collective agreement. The parties agree on most points of the new deal but differ over its duration: the company wants five years, while the union has said it is willing to sign for three and is seeking better terms if the period is longer.

On September 17, the executive issued a resolution declaring essential services to guarantee minimum operation of the terminal. The union rejected it as a restriction on the right to strike and went ahead with the stoppage planned for September 24 in Montevideo and Nueva Palmira. The company has said it will quantify the damage caused by the action, and exporters' and importers' chambers also report losses.

Minister Oddone has argued for reviewing “certain aspects of port regulation” to strengthen the port's competitiveness. A new tripartite meeting was held on Monday at the National Labour Directorate to examine a government proposal; no agreement was reported.

“Our economic scale is smaller than that of the region's coastal countries; therefore, we cannot afford to waste any opportunity by projecting an inappropriate image,” the shipping lines write, also warning of the risk to jobs in the industry.

World.title: Milei denies a recession and says indicators are "throwing out anything"
World.content:
Milei denies a recession and says indicators are “throwing out anything”

29th Tuesday, September 2026 - 07:09 UTC Full article

Milei linked the economic difficulties to opposition initiatives in Congress and to security concerns

Argentine President Javier Milei denied the country is in recession and questioned the reading of statistics showing rising poverty and falling economic activity. “The indicators are throwing out anything,” he said on Sunday in an interview with journalist Luis Majul on the programme La Cornisa, on the LN+ channel.

“There is no recession,” the president said, but rather “a slowdown in the pace of expansion”. He noted that a recession is technically defined as two consecutive quarters of contraction and took aim at the use of seasonally adjusted series, which he said “measure badly” amid “major structural changes” in which sectors previously protected by the state are shrinking while more productive ones expand. Economists responded that seasonal adjustment uses the historical series only to isolate effects that recur every year, such as holidays, harvests or festivities, not to measure shifts in the composition of the economy.

The president also said the country is at record levels of private consumption, exports and output, that his administration has created more than 500,000 jobs and that Argentina will string together four consecutive years of growth. He ruled out changing his economic programme.

The figures that prompted his remarks were released last week by the National Institute of Statistics and Census. Economic activity fell 2.9% in July compared with June, the largest monthly decline in six years, and 1.4% year-on-year. Poverty rose to 32.3% in the first half, 4.1 points higher than in the previous half, and unemployment reached 7.9%, the highest level under the current administration. Milei described the poverty figure as “an old snapshot” because it covers the first half, and attributed rising unemployment to “a reallocation of resources” and more people looking for work.

Markets moved the other way. Country risk, which touched a low of 402 points in July, rose above 640 basis points on Monday, its highest level of the year. JP Morgan cut its 2026 growth forecast from 2.7% to 1.5% and expects an annualised contraction of 4% in the third quarter. According to La Nación, Uruguay's country risk stands at around 65 points.

In the same interview, Milei linked the economic difficulties to opposition initiatives in Congress and to security concerns. He cited “40 attempts to bring down the fiscal balance” and “seven attempts at impeachment”, which he called “seven coup attempts”, and said the government had deported 10,000 “terrorists” in 2025 and another 20,000 so far in 2026, describing them as people who infiltrate from other countries “to try to blow up the Argentine model”. No published official statistic supports that figure. According to Security and Migration ministry data cited by La Nación, fewer than 1,700 people encountered obstacles to entering the country, a group that is not limited to terrorism-related cases.

Deputy Maximiliano Ferraro, of the Civic Coalition, filed a formal request for information asking the executive to detail how many people were expelled and how many for terrorism-related reasons. Máximo Kirchner, a deputy for Unión por la Patria, called the figure “a terrible exaggeration”.

The president also referred to the Olivos residence, which he described as “a military base” with reinforced security: “I have some heavy enemies here and around the world.”

World.title: Argentina-Based Game Studio Releases New Game Based on The Walking Dead
World.content:
Argentina-Based Game Studio Releases New Game Based on The Walking Dead

29th Tuesday, September 2026 - 00:15 UTC Full article

When The Walking Dead comic began in 2003, few could have predicted what an incredible cultural phenomenon it would become. There have been countless TV spinoffs and various games as well.

One of the latest entries to the sprawling franchise is The Walking Dead: Streets of Survival from Argentine developer Odaclick Game Studio. This new offering reimagines the All Out War arc from the main series and gives players a chance to experience it in a new way.

The Walking Dead: Streets of Survival Reimagines Negan's War

The All Out War story arc involving Negan and the Saviors was one of the most iconic parts of The Walking Dead comics and the series. For people who want to experience it again, this game offers a way to do so, but with a fresh concept. It uses retro-style graphics and side-scrolling action, making it reminiscent of classic arcade games. This new take offers something different to the television show rather than attempting to recreate it.

Even though it's a visually unique prospect, there are still plenty of familiar faces and settings for players to enjoy. The game takes place across 12 levels and involves locations like Alexandria, Hilltop, and the Sanctuary. Players have the option to control Rick Grimes, Daryl Dixon, or Michonne, and the aim of the game is to take down Negan's Saviors along with hordes of walkers.

Latest Way to Experience the Franchise from a New Perspective

One of the best things about The Walking Dead franchise is the way it constantly throws up new ways for people to experience it. When the main show was in its early seasons, Telltale Games released an official offering that complemented the series but showed events from the perspective of different characters.

There have also been iGaming offerings over the years that have given players a new way to experience the series' main characters. These include The Walking Dead and The Walking Dead 2, and there's still a variety of bingo slots online despite the main series having already ended a few years ago.

In addition to these games, the numerous spinoffs have provided viewers with different perspectives of the zombie apocalypse. Fear The Walking Dead initially gave viewers a chance to see the start of the outbreak, while titles like The Walking Dead: Dead City and The Walking Dead: Daryl Dixon showed how different locations were affected.

Plans to Extend the Franchise Further

The game from Odaclick Game Studio isn't the only way that The Walking Dead franchise is continuing to expand. According to a recent report, Scott Gimple is open to new ideas for spinoffs in the future.

While he may have confirmed that there are currently no plans beyond Daryl Dixon and Dead City, he hinted that there could be more in the future. Stating “This is still, at the latest, the middle of Walking Dead's life,” it's clear the Gimple has plenty of ideas that we are yet to see. There is almost infinite potential for the franchise, with new settings and characters to explore.

World.title: Why Ethereum’s Dollar Value Matters as Latin America Expands Digital Payments
World.content:
Why Ethereum’s Dollar Value Matters as Latin America Expands Digital Payments

29th Tuesday, September 2026 - 00:02 UTC Full article

A designer in Montevideo can finish work for a company in São Paulo after the banks have closed. The transfer may involve two currencies, several providers and a wait before the final amount becomes clear. Stablecoin services offer a different route.

Ethereum matters because many digital dollars operate across its main network and associated layer-two networks. The Ethereum to USD page from Binance put ETH at approximately $2,582.88 on 20 September 2026. Its market capitalisation stood near $315.3 billion on the same date. Both figures move continuously. For a company using Ethereum-based infrastructure, the price can influence the dollar cost of processing a transfer, even when the customer sends a stablecoin rather than ETH.

Why Is Ethereum Relevant to Latin American Payments?

Ethereum provides the base infrastructure for stablecoins, wallets and payment applications. Transactions sent directly through the network require a fee paid in ETH. The sender may never intend to keep ETH, yet its dollar value can still shape the cost.
