More companies across the Latin American economy now sell services online or work with overseas customers. Most will encounter Ethereum through a platform that manages the wallet, conversion and network connection.

Payment activity is increasingly moving beyond Ethereum's main network. Data sourced from growthepie and Etherscan show that mainnet transactions have remained near 1.1 million a day. Layer-two networks recorded a one-day high of approximately 12.5 million transactions in 2026, more than 140% above the level at the beginning of the year. That gap shows how much activity has shifted away from the main network. A payment application can use Ethereum-based infrastructure without placing every transaction directly on the main chain.

Why Are Dollar-Linked Digital Payments Growing?

Cross-border transfers can become expensive in small stages. A receiving charge may appear first, followed by a currency spread and another fee for moving the money into a local account.

The Financial Stability Board's work on cross-border payments identifies four longstanding problems: cost, speed, limited access and insufficient transparency. These affect established channels as well as newer alternatives.

Global payment behaviour is also changing. In its June 2026 market review, Binance Research reported that crypto-card spending was growing at roughly twice the pace of stablecoin supply. The finding is not specific to Latin America, but it shows digital balances moving closer to conventional checkout systems.

Return to the contractor in Uruguay. If the Brazilian client uses stablecoin settlement, the payment could arrive outside banking hours in a dollar-linked form. The contractor would then need to convert it into Uruguayan pesos or transfer it to a bank account. A network charge and conversion fee may still apply. What matters is the amount that reaches the contractor, not the speed advertised at the start. That distinction is important for small firms, which often judge a payment service by the final sum received.

How Does the ETH-Dollar Rate Change a Payment's Cost?

Ethereum charges are calculated in ETH. Their dollar value depends on how much ETH the transaction requires and what that ETH is worth at the time.

Take a hypothetical charge of 0.001 ETH. Using the 20 September price of $2,582.88, the fee would be about $2.58. It could change on another day even if the required amount of ETH stayed the same. Some providers send transactions directly through Ethereum, while others use layer-two systems that process activity separately before submitting records to the main network. Providers may combine every charge into one price or ask the customer to cover the network fee separately.

Binance's current Ethereum overview notes that the Fusaka upgrade introduced PeerDAS and capacity adjustments intended to help layer-two networks process more activity without placing the same burden on Ethereum nodes. For payment services, that work matters when it produces clearer costs and dependable processing.

What Is Happening on Ethereum's Layer-Two Networks?

Stablecoin balances are appearing on networks built around Ethereum rather than only on its main chain. Data compiled through growthepie and Etherscan put combined layer-two stablecoin supply at approximately $9.7 billion in 2026. That amount does not represent Latin American spending or show how many individual payments took place. It does indicate that layer-two networks carry enough dollar-linked value to interest wallet developers and payment companies.

The combination of a 12.5 million-transaction record and $9.7 billion in stablecoins gives this part of Ethereum a different role. Layer-two systems can handle frequent, lower-value activity while Ethereum provides the underlying settlement connection. A large network does not guarantee a smooth payment experience. Businesses still need usable records, secure access and a dependable route into local currency. Refunds may also become awkward when several providers manage separate stages.

What Will Decide Whether Regional Use Continues?

Ethereum-based payments will remain useful only when they solve an identifiable problem for the sender or recipient. A faster transfer has limited value if charges are unclear or conversion is difficult. Tracking ETH in dollars explains one part of the cost. Stronger evidence will come from payment volumes, stablecoin use and whether funds consistently reach recipients without adding another layer of confusion.

Pam Brown: Finance, loans, crypto & forex

Pam Brown is a journalist with exceptional analytical skills and a strong interest in modern financial systems. She specialises in translating complex topics like crypto, loans, and forex into clear, accessible content. Pam's precise, research-driven writing has made her a trusted voice in the financial and fintech space.

World.title: Mexican exports increased by nearly 30% through August, led by computer equipment
World.content:
Mexican exports grew at an annual rate of 40.4% in August, accumulating an increase of 29.3% through the first eight months of the year, according to the national statistics agency INEGI.

INEGI’s monthly report showed that exports reached a record US $549.4 billion during the January-August period and topped $78 billion in August.

At the same time, imports increased 34.2% in August and 26.8% through the first eight months of 2026, rising to US $77.405 billion and $539.5 billion (a new record), respectively.

As a result, Mexico recorded a surplus of $605.4 million in August, and $9.86 billion on the year through August.

The export sector was led by non-automotive manufacturing exports, up more than 63% in August, primarily due to a continuing surge in sales of computer equipment that began in 2024.

From January through August, manufacturing exports rose 30.8% annually, while non-automotive manufacturing rebounded 45%, the highest since records began in 1994.

Despite the record performance, analysts point out two concerns: the predominance of the U.S. as Mexico’s main buyer and the country’s reliance on Asia as an indispensable supplier for the fast-growing computer industry.

According to INEGI, 84.7% of Mexico’s total non-oil exports went to the U.S., while Mexico’s dependence on the U.S. in the computer sector is even more dramatic.

Mexico exported nearly $83 billion worth of servers, primarily used in data centers and artificial intelligence, and 93.9% of the servers were destined for the United States.

On the import side, processors, memory, cards and other high-value components come primarily from Taiwan, China, Malaysia, South Korea, Vietnam and Thailand with Taiwan alone supplying approximately 44% of the main inputs imported by the computer industry.

El Imparcial columnist Eduardo Ruiz Healy argued that as Mexico imports these components, assembles the equipment, and exports them (mainly to the United States), a significant portion of the value of each server is generated outside the country.

The concern here is that since the U.S. is demanding greater North American content in servers and other artificial intelligence equipment (in its bilateral trade negotiations with Mexico), the inability to produce them here could impact the export sector negatively.

Still, when paired with other data for August — oil exports down 2.8%, agricultural exports down 1.6% and automotive exports down 2.2% — it is apparent that the technological expansion cycle in the United States is supporting the Mexican economy.

With reports from El Financiero and El Economista

World.title: MND Local BCS: Hurricane Polo hits Baja California Sur, plus new regulations for swimming with whale sharks in La Paz
World.content:
On Monday, Sept. 21, Polo was designated a tropical storm off the southwestern coast of Mexico, with wind speeds of approximately 50 miles per hour (mph). Within 24 hours, winds had increased to 160 miles per hour, and Polo was suddenly one of the most terrifying types of natural disasters: a Category 5 hurricane.

The National Hurricane Center characterized the speed of Polo’s intensification as “truly remarkable,” not to mention historic. Indeed, it was one of the most rapid storm intensifications in recorded history, second only to that of Hurricane Patricia in 2015, a monster Category 5 hurricane that reached sustained winds of over 200 miles per hour.

By Tuesday afternoon, Hurricane Polo had reached sustained winds of 180 miles per hour (285 kilometers per hour), making it the third-strongest hurricane by that measure in the history of the Eastern Pacific region.

This rapid intensification was aided by climate change — sea surface temperatures in the Pacific Ocean are the highest they’ve ever been — and an exceptionally strong El Niño weather pattern, which has raised water temperatures even further. Polo’s development, per NASA, occurred over waters with surface temperatures as high as 90 degrees Fahrenheit (32 degrees Celsius).

But despite its supercharged power, Polo remained offshore as it developed, making no landfall along the southwestern coast, but causing at least four deaths in Jalisco, and inflicting property damage across parts of Colima, Guerrero, Jalisco and Michoacán.

Baja California Sur prepares for the arrival of Hurricane Polo

By Sunday, Hurricane Polo had been downgraded to Category 3, with wind speeds of “only” 125 miles per hour as it continued in an arcing, left hook-like path towards Comondú municipality in the center of Baja California Sur — but with effects expected to be felt statewide, since tropical force winds from Polo were extending up to 105 miles (165 kilometers) from the storm’s center.

Hurricane warnings were issued for both the west (between Punta Abreojos and Santa Fe) and east coasts (from Loreto to Santa Rosalía) of the state prior to the arrival of the hurricane on Monday, and the state readied its response efforts, with help from the federal government.

Classes were canceled statewide for schools on Monday, while 1,360 military personnel in engineering groups awaited deployment, in case of need from impacts such as destructive winds, flooding and storm surges. Port activities in Comondú and Los Cabos were closed over the weekend, as were 26 beaches in Los Cabos. Meanwhile, 169 shelters across all five of the state’s municipalities were readied for those potentially displaced or in vulnerable areas.

The aftermath

The most visibly affected as the storm neared was Puerto San Carlos, in the Bahía Magdalena area, where storm-driven waves flooded streets, prompting hundreds of residents to evacuate their homes and seek shelter.

But it was 84 miles farther north, near Las Barrancas, a small fishing community of a little more than 500 residents that also lies in the municipality of Comondú, that Hurricane Polo finally made landfall at 11 p.m. local time on Monday, Sept. 28. By then, it had been downgraded to a Category 2 hurricane, but still a dangerous one, with sustained wind speeds of 110 miles per hour (175 kilometers per hour).

Six hours later, at 5 a.m., Hurricane Polo reached the Gulf of California on its way to Sonora — downgraded to Category 1 — leaving behind power outages, wind damage and flash flooding, but with no reported deaths in Baja California Sur … at least pending official damage assessments.

New rules instituted for swimming with whale sharks tours in La Paz

Bucket list adventures are a big draw in Baja California Sur. There’s whale watching in Los Cabos and in Pacific Coast lagoons, and swimming with whale sharks off the coast of the state’s capital city of La Paz. (Seasonal opportunities to swim with orcas at La Ventana are currently up in the air after a pilot program for 2025-2026 expired at the end of July).

In each case, however, there are regulations in place to protect not only tourists, but also the wildlife at the center of these experiences. In Los Cabos, for example, permitted boats must remain at a minimum distance from whales (60 to 80 meters, depending on the size of the vessel).

But nowhere is the need for caution more urgent than in the state capital, La Paz, where swimming with whale sharks season (Oct. 1 to April 30) has been suspended for parts of each of the last three years (2023 to 2025) due to an insufficient population of whale sharks.

New zones unveiled for 2026

Whale sharks are listed as endangered worldwide by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN), and because La Paz is a seasonal feeding ground for juveniles, it should ideally play a key role in helping to replenish and grow the species’ population. Although whale sharks are enormous (they are the “world’s largest fish,” reaching up to 65 feet long and weighing as much as 60,000 pounds), these “gentle giants” are plankton eaters and very safe to swim with — from a human perspective.

From the wildlife perspective, very strict rules are needed to protect whale sharks from injury or undue stress due to tour activities. To this end, Mexico’s Secretariat of Environment and Natural Resources (Semarnat) has recently published new guidelines for swimming with whale shark tours in La Paz for 2026 through 2029.

The most notable change is the creation of three zones, in only one of which — Zone I, off the northern shore of the El Mogote peninsula — swimming with whale sharks is permitted. Zone II is listed as a conservation area, with Zone III restricted to transit for tour operators, and at slow speeds (7 knots or less).

Cap on boats tied to whale shark population figures

A ceiling of 56 boats per day for swimming with whale sharks is retained from previous regulations, which will be spread across four time periods for 14 boats each. Boats can bring five swimmers only, plus a guide, with encounters limited to 30 minutes. Other boats must keep at least 50 meters’ distance from those that are engaged in whale shark swims, and tourists are prohibited from touching the whale sharks (they can get no closer than two meters from the side of the fish, or three meters from its tail).

However, since the number of boats permitted for such tours (112 this year) exceeds the daily capacity allowed by half, time slots will be eagerly sought after … but closely tied to abundance. Meaning, the number of allowable boats, per the National Commission of Protected Natural Areas (Conanp), will be scaled back if the whale shark population, or lack thereof, warrants it. For instance, no boats will be allowed if there are five or fewer observable whale sharks, with a sliding scale up to the maximum of 56 boats based on closely monitored population figures.

Chris Sands is a writer and editor for Mexico News Daily, and the former Cabo San Lucas local expert for the USA Today travel website 10 Best and writer of Fodor’s Los Cabos travel guidebook. He has also contributed to numerous other websites and publications, including The San Diego Union-Tribune, Marriott Bonvoy Traveler, Forbes Travel Guide, Porthole Cruise and Travel, and Cabo Living.

World.title: Sheinbaum announces security support for Morelos after student murders
World.content:
President Claudia Sheinbaum announced a special security plan for Morelos following the murder of two teenage students who attended High School No. 2 of the Autonomous University of the State of Morelos (UAEM). The incident, which also left another young man injured, took place early on Sunday in Cuernavaca, the state’s capital.

“We are going to coordinate with the governor [Margarita González Saravia] to find out where she needs our support,” President Claudia Sheinbaum said during her Monday morning press conference. Sheinbaum also said that Interior Minister Rosa Icela Rodríguez had contacted the head of the UAEM, Viridiana Aydeé León Hernández, to learn more about the needs of the university community.

“We need to get in touch with the rector and the students to see what is happening and implement further preventive measures involving the students,” the president said.

She noted that according to data from the Public Security and Citizen Protection Ministry (SSPC), the number of intentional homicides in Morelos is declining, but crimes such as theft are on the rise.

Seven UAEM-affiliated students have been murdered in Morelos since April 2025, including Claudia Tacoronte, a Spanish student on an academic exchange program in Cuernavaca. The young woman was murdered on the night of Sept. 12 in Cuautla, after falling victim to a robbery.

Meanwhile, Cuernavaca Mayor José Luis Urióstegui Salgado acknowledged that the municipal security strategy has not succeeded.

“The patrols conducted by our police officers are becoming less visible, and criminals are taking advantage of this; that is why I called upon all of our security forces today to redouble their efforts, and I instructed the secretary and the command staff to focus more on providing support to the officers on the ground,” he noted.

Urióstegui stated that he would evaluate reinforcing police operations and warned that, if no results are seen in two weeks, changes to security leadership could occur.

“I deeply regret this situation. There should be no more homicides anywhere,” he said.

With reports from El Financiero and La Jornada

World.title: Mexico to continue tariff talks with US this week: Tuesday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Listen to this article

Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

🌀 Hurricane Polo hits Baja California Sur: Civil Protection chief Laura Velázquez said Polo made landfall as a Category 2 hurricane at midnight in Las Barrancas, Comondú, and “only” caused some flooding and toppled trees. Governor Víctor Manuel Castro Cosío reported no loss of life in the state. Velázquez said that people in temporary shelters would return home Tuesday. She added that Polo was heading for Sonora, with landfall forecast near Guaymas on Tuesday.

Civil Protection chief Laura Velázquez said Polo made landfall as a Category 2 hurricane at midnight in Las Barrancas, Comondú, and “only” caused some flooding and toppled trees. Governor Víctor Manuel Castro Cosío reported no loss of life in the state. Velázquez said that people in temporary shelters would return home Tuesday. She added that Polo was heading for Sonora, with landfall forecast near Guaymas on Tuesday. 🇲🇽🇺🇸 Ebrard heads to Washington for more trade talks: Sheinbaum said Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard was traveling to Washington, D.C., to continue talks with U.S. officials. She said Mexico is doing “well” in the trade dialogue, but acknowledged that there is no tariff agreement yet. Mexico wants the U.S. to reduce, or ideally eliminate, the tariffs imposed last year on Mexican steel, aluminum and vehicles. The talks come after the Trump administration announced in July that it wouldn’t renew the USMCA in its “current form.”

Sheinbaum said Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard was traveling to Washington, D.C., to continue talks with U.S. officials. She said Mexico is doing “well” in the trade dialogue, but acknowledged that there is no tariff agreement yet. Mexico wants the U.S. to reduce, or ideally eliminate, the tariffs imposed last year on Mexican steel, aluminum and vehicles. The talks come after the Trump administration announced in July that it wouldn’t renew the USMCA in its “current form.” 🗳️ Sheinbaum praises Morena’s candidate selection process: She said the process to pick 17 presumptive gubernatorial candidates, known for now as “state coordinators of the defense of the transformation and national sovereignty,” had “a lot of unity.” Gubernatorial elections will be held in 17 states on June 6, 2027. Asked for advice for the presumptive candidates, Sheinbaum said: “Don’t lie, don’t steal and don’t betray the people.”

Why today’s mañanera matters

The arrival of Hurricane Polo in Baja California Sur, the Mexico-U.S. trade relationship and the ruling Morena party’s selection of 17 presumptive gubernatorial candidates were among the significant topics discussed at President Claudia Sheinbaum’s Tuesday morning press conference.

Polo made landfall as a Category 2 hurricane after strengthening to Category 5 level last week. While the hurricane caused flooding and downed trees in Baja California Sur, it didn’t claim any lives in the state, according to Governor Víctor Manuel Castro Cosío.

Sheinbaum’s remarks about Morena’s selection of presumptive gubernatorial candidates came a day after the party announced who those people are in seven states.

For the time being, Morena’s presumptive gubernatorial candidates are known as “state coordinators of the defense of the transformation and national sovereignty.”

They are set to be designated as Morena’s gubernatorial candidates at a later date. Morena, Mexico’s ruling party since late 2018, supports the so-called “fourth transformation” (4T) political movement founded by former president Andrés Manuel López Obrador and now led by Sheinbaum.

Morena is currently in office in 23 of Mexico’s 32 states, while the Green Party, which is also affiliated with the 4T, is in power in San Luis Potosí. Morena will be aiming to increase the number of states it governs at the gubernatorial elections that will be held in 17 states next June.

Hurricane Polo causes flooding, topples trees in BCS

Appearing at the mañanera via video link, National Civil Protection chief Laura Velázquez reported that Hurricane Polo made landfall in Baja California Sur (BCS) as a Category 2 hurricane at midnight Tuesday. She said that the hurricane made landfall in Las Barrancas, a small town in the municipality of Comondú.

Velázquez noted that the hurricane was heading for the coast of Sonora, where it was forecast to make landfall near the port city of Guaymas on Tuesday.

She said that Hurricane Polo “only” caused some flooding in BCS and toppled some trees. Velázquez said that the municipalities of Comondú, Mulegé and Loreto had electricity and water service as of 7:30 a.m. Tuesday.

She said that people who spent Monday night in temporary shelters that were set up prior to the arrival of the hurricane would return to their homes on Tuesday.

Governor Castro said that BCS residents “behaved extraordinarily well” on Monday, following the instructions of authorities to remain indoors as Hurricane Polo approached the state and eventually made landfall. He reported that there was no loss of life associated with the hurricane in BCS.

Ebrard heads to Washington for more trade talks

Sheinbaum told reporters that Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard was traveling to Washington, D.C., on Tuesday to continue trade talks with U.S. officials.

She said that Mexico is doing “well” in its ongoing trade dialogue with the U.S., which is taking place after the Trump administration announced in July that it had declined to renew the USMCA free trade pact in its “current form.”

Mexico is pushing for a reduction, or ideally the elimination, of tariffs that the U.S. government imposed on Mexican steel, aluminum and vehicles last year.

Sheinbaum acknowledged that her government has not yet reached an agreement with the Trump administration on tariffs. Citing Mexican and U.S. sources, Reuters reported earlier this month that Mexico and the United States were “racing to reach a bilateral trade deal before the U.S. midterm elections,” which will take place on Nov. 3.

Sheinbaum praises Morena’s process to select presumptive gubernatorial candidates

A reporter asked the president about Morena’s process to select 17 “coordinators of the defense of the transformation,” men and women who will become the party’s gubernatorial candidates in elections that will take place on June 6, 2027.

“I think it was a process in which there was a lot of unity, and that was very good,” Sheinbaum said.

Morena conducted internal surveys to select its would-be candidates in states where gubernatorial elections will be held next year, among which are Nuevo León, Baja California, Guanajuato, Michoacán and Quintana Roo.

Among the designated 4T coordinators is Santiago Nieto, a former head of the federal government’s Financial Intelligence Unit, who is set to represent Morena at the 2027 gubernatorial election in Querétaro, one of just four states currently governed by the National Action Party. Another would-be Morena candidate is Clara Luz Flores, who is set to contest a second consecutive gubernatorial election in the northern border state of Nuevo León, where Citizens Movement party Governor Samuel García is currently in office.

Asked what advice she would give to 4T “coordinators,” Sheinbaum mentioned a Morena party ethos.

“Don’t lie, don’t steal and don’t betray the people,” she said.

World.title: The surprisingly long history of hot air ballooning in Mexico
World.content:
Anybody who has traveled out to Teotihuacán in the early morning will have been delighted at the sight of dozens of hot air balloons rising into the sky. Mexico’s hot air balloon tourist industry carries about 60,000 passengers annually and generates US $25 million in revenue. Business has not yet peaked, with annual growth predicted at around 7%. While the vast majority of tourists fly over the Sun and Moon pyramids, there are companies offering flights in other places, most notably San Miguel de Allende.

Indeed, the real home of Mexican ballooning might be said to be León, where the Festival Internacional del Globo is the largest balloon festival in Latin America, featuring 200 hot air balloons and attracting 400,000 spectators. It is a remarkable comeback for an activity that nearly died out at the beginning of the 20th century.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Festival Internacional Del Globo (@figleon)

The early flight of José María Alfaro Guiles

The man credited as the pioneer of ballooning in Mexico, and the first Mexican to take to the air, was José María Alfaro Guiles. His flight occurred, if it did, just six months after the Montgolfier brothers captured the world’s imagination by soaring over Paris. Guiles had no direct contact with the French pioneers and only learned of their achievement thanks to a brief report in an international newspaper.

Having some engineering skills, he decided to try ballooning for himself. Guiles started by constructing small paper balloons with little more than a nightlight to lift them. His models increased in size until on May 18, 1784, a crowd gathered in the city of Xalapa to watch him climb into the basket and successfully ascend into the sky. According to the commonly accepted account, he piloted the craft across the countryside for about 9 kilometers (5.6 miles), reaching heights of around 800 meters (2,600 feet).

This historic achievement was recorded in the Gazeta de México, then a new publication that had been founded only a few months before. The report came out June 2 and was brief: “Xalapa. There has been manufactured in this town a hot air balloon, similar to those described in the latest Gazetas from Madrid, crafted by Don Josef María Alfaro: it measures approximately 18 Castilian varas, and it is believed it will have the desired effect, given the precision and care with which it has been built, of which the public will be notified.” (A Castilian vara is a traditional Spanish unit of length equal to approximately 33 inches or 0.84 meters).

Debating the evidence behind Mexico’s first flight

However, whether José María Alfaro Guiles actually flew in his balloon is open to debate. Careful readers will note that this report is not of the flight of the balloon but of its construction, and no evidence is offered that the designer took his life in his hands and climbed into a paper balloon heated by an open fire. Pictures of the flight clearly show Guiles in a basket beneath the soaring balloon, but none of this artwork was created at the time. The first illustrations appeared many years later and were based on drawings of balloons in Europe.

The next written account of the flight was by Manuel Rivera Cambas in his “History of Xalapa,” published in 1869. Here he confirms that Guiles made a successful manned flight of nearly 9 kilometers. Rivera Cambas is said to have researched the story by accessing local municipality archives and collecting oral accounts. However, we have no details of what papers he actually read in the archives, while oral histories are notoriously unreliable, especially if collected years after the event. One major reason to argue against a successful manned flight at this early date is that there were numerous balloons built in Mexico over the next 50 years, but none were big enough to carry a passenger.

Early ballooning in Veracruz

It was Veracruz that became the first center of ballooning in Mexico. While it was noted that altitude would make ballooning more difficult in Mexico City, the emergence of Veracruz was probably a coincidence. A local merchant, Antonio María Fernández, after reading of Guiles’ design, constructed a sizable balloon and watched it ascend into the sky on Feb. 6, 1785. This captured the local imagination and led others to copy his experiment. While some of the balloons crashed and burned, a few rose and dramatically disappeared into the night sky. There was an interesting discussion about what farmers would make of a balloon if it landed close to a village. After all, peasants in France had attacked one of Montgolfier’s balloons with pitchforks.

Ballooning in Puebla

By the summer of 1785, Puebla had become another center of ballooning, and it is here that we find the first authentic attempt at a manned flight. There were two problems to overcome with a manned balloon: First, a balloon had to be a considerable size to carry a man’s weight; second, the man had to be brave enough to fly in a contraption that, based on the experience of smaller models, had a habit of bursting into flames.

The Puebla balloon was large, about 10 meters (33 feet) in height and 20 meters (66 feet) in circumference, and quite sophisticated for the time, with the skin encased in a net and a basket attached for the passenger. However, the bigger the balloon, the more difficult it was to handle on the ground, and this happened to be a windy day. The balloon might well have lifted a few meters, but it was already being thrown around by the wind. It banged against a wall, the gondola broke and the attempt was abandoned.

Foreign aeronauts introduce hydrogen technology

By this point, Mexico was being left behind by the balloon revolution. In Europe, balloonists had already progressed from heating the air with an open flame to using lighter-than-air hydrogen, a gas not readily available in Mexico. Progress in ballooning was therefore made by foreigners who brought all the necessary skills and equipment with them. General Manuel de la Barrera, a prominent businessman who owned the San Pablo Bullring, was a pioneer of ballooning in the 1830s, and he persuaded aeronaut Adolfo Theodore to bring his balloon to Mexico. Despite his reputation for having made a successful flight in Cuba, Theodore’s visit was a disaster. The paying crowd was furious when his flight in May 1833 was canceled because of the weather, while the government halted a second attempt in October over safety concerns.

Étienne-Gaspard Robert, a French aeronaut better known as Robertson, was far more successful. On Feb. 12, 1835, he lifted off in a balloon from the Plaza de Toros de San Pablo in central Mexico City and disappeared into the distance. He did not find his way back to Mexico City until Feb. 14, having traveled approximately 100 kilometers (62 miles). After this, he performed a series of exhibition flights, but he caught yellow fever in Veracruz and died in 1838.

Spectacular exhibitions and national pioneers

Ballooning was entering its golden period, and Fanny Calderón de la Barca, wife of the Spanish ambassador, left an account of an attempted flight in Mexico City in 1841. She noted the attendance of the rich and finely dressed, who were entertained by two bands. As for the balloon itself, it “swayed up and down in the midst of the plaza like a living thing.” On this occasion, the attempt to take off was abandoned after a hole was discovered in the fabric: “The people bore their disappointment very good-humouredly, although it was conjectured that the air traveller had merely proposed to himself to get their money without the slightest intention of performing.”

It was Robertson’s flights that inspired the first generation of successful Mexican balloonists, led by Benito León Acosta. Born in Guanajuato in 1819, he entered the School of Mines in Mexico City and made his first ascent on April 3, 1842. His balloon remained airborne for a little over half an hour, and in an act of showmanship, he waved the Mexican flag to the crowd below. President Antonio López de Santa Anna was among the witnesses and sponsored many of Acosta’s later flights. The hero toured Mexico, but after an accident in Morelia where he fell from the basket, he concentrated on his career as an educator.

The legacy of Joaquín de la Cantolla y Rico

Joaquín de la Cantolla y Rico was 10 years younger than Acosta, having been born in Mexico City in 1829. He entered the Military College and helped defend Chapultepec Castle during the American invasion. Starting in 1863, he built and piloted his own hot air balloons, capturing the public’s imagination with both his flying and his showmanship, often ascending while dressed in a formal frock coat and top hat. He received gifts from presidents and emperors and is featured in Diego Rivera’s murals. Even today, the small balloons flown at village festivals are known as globos de Cantoya.

For all the enthusiasm, plans to find a practical use for balloons ran up against the great stumbling block that they could not be steered. Cantolla had the idea of encasing several of them into a more streamlined shape and adding an engine — creating an airship — but lacked the resources for such an ambitious scheme. Aeronauts already suspected that winds at high altitudes always blew west to east and wondered if this might be exploited to carry goods across the Atlantic, but this idea came to nothing.

The one organization that might have made use of balloons was the army, as a tethered balloon makes a good lookout point. However, wars in Mexico were most likely to be fought in remote areas where transporting the heavy equipment required for balloons would be impractical. And so the great age of the balloon faded out with the arrival of ever more powerful and reliable airplanes.

Who could have predicted that balloons would make a US $25 million comeback flying tourists over the pyramids of Teotihuacán?

Bob Pateman lived in Mexico for six years. He is a librarian and teacher with a Master’s Degree in History.

World.title: Aeroméxico pulls its flights to Tulum with Wednesday as the last day
World.content:
Mexico’s largest international airline, Aeroméxico, has announced plans to suspend its flights to Tulum starting Thursday due to lower-than-expected demand.

Tulum opened its Felipe Carrillo Puerto International Airport in December 2023 under military control, with high hopes for its tourism industry as it aimed to reduce reliance on arrivals to Cancún airport, some 115 kilometers away.

The airport rapidly reached the 1 million passenger mark, domestic and international, under the management of Grupo Mundo Maya.

However, the elimination of airline subsidies, typical in the industry when a new airport or route begins operations, led to the cancellation of several flights in the last year.

“We are going to implement a temporary suspension,” Aeroméxico told the newspaper El Financiero. “September 30 will be the last day. The suspension is due to market conditions and to maximize our route network.”

Tulum’s tourism industry has suffered more broadly in recent months due to the huge influx of seaweed on its beaches and rising costs of accessing key destinations, such as the famous archaeological zone, which now costs 209 pesos (US $12), more than double the previous 104 pesos ($6).

Since the military took over management of the tourist area in Tulum, visitor numbers have fallen even more rapidly, El Financiero reported.

Tulum’s real estate market has also slowed, further discouraging investment in the region.

In August, Quintana Roo Tourism Minister Bernardo Cueto Riestra reported that Tulum’s hotel occupancy rate had fallen to an average of just 15%, the lowest in its history.

The Felipe Carrillo Puerto International Airport is now expected to offer seasonal flights to five destinations in Canada and the United States during the 2026-2027 winter season, but almost no flights from the U.S. in the coming months, despite the U.S. being the main market for Mexico’s Caribbean coast.

United plans to operate a biweekly direct flight between Newark, near New York, and Tulum from December 17, 2026, to January 24, 2027.

Meanwhile, together, Air Canada, Air Transat, WestJet and United Airlines will operate seven connecting services, totaling only up to 10 weekly flights. This will result in minimal use of the facility, with most airlines operating just one flight per week.

With reports from El Financiero and Reportur

World.title: Guanajuato will host a free outdoor Mexican-French circus spectacle this weekend as Cervantino Festival approaches
World.content:
Acrobats and tightrope walkers will turn Guanajuato’s historic city center into an open-air circus Saturday night, performing high above the crowd in a free opening-day show at the 54th International Cervantino Festival.

“Vértigo” — a Mexico-France collaboration adapted from the French production “Vertige” — is scheduled for 9 p.m. Saturday in Plaza Allende, the small square beside the Cervantes Theater in the historic city of Guanajuato.

The 60-minute show will combine aerial circus, dance, live music and a site-specific visual design.

The spectacle will bring together artists from Chaillot, a Paris-based national theater, and Mexican performers. Some of the acrobats and aerial balance artists (aka highliners) are affiliated with Mexico City’s Cirko de Mente.

Created by choreographer Rachid Ouramdane, musician Christophe Chassol and highliner Nathan Paulin, “Vértigo” adapts a piece first staged last year at the Grand Palais inaugural festival in Paris.

It was conceived as a mobile work, with performers suspended high above a public space and moving along tensioned lines.

The Guanajuato version was developed with Andrea Peláez, co-founder of the Mexico City contemporary-circus company Cirko de Mente, and Mexican artists.

France is the festival’s guest country this year, as part of a program marking 200 years of diplomatic relations with Mexico. The initiative recently yielded an exchange of centuries-old Aztec documents known as codices.

France’s program will include 18 presentations spanning classical and contemporary music, theater, dance, cabaret, street art, film, opera and multidisciplinary work.

The aerial circus is free, but overall, the Cervantino Festival mixes ticketed events with free events and free-access areas. It will run from Saturday, Oct. 3 through Sunday, Oct. 18.

Featuring more than 200 performances by some 2,750 artists, the event will include headliners such as Mike Patton’s Italian-song project Mondo Cane, which will open the festival at 7 p.m. Saturday.

The lineup also includes Australia’s Bangarra Dance Theatre, the German contemporary-music ensemble Ensemble Modern, Colombian salsa band Grupo Niche and Austria’s Camerata Salzburg with Spanish violinist María Dueñas.

One highlight will be an Oct. 15 tribute to the late José Alfredo Jiménez, the Guanajuato-born ranchera songwriter who wrote enduring Mexican standards including “El Rey” and “Si nos dejan.” Tenor Arturo Chacón Cruz and Mexico City-based Mariachi Gama 1000 will perform at the event at the Alhóndiga de Granaditas esplanade.

For more information, visit the festival’s official website.

With reports from Milenio, Crónica and Almomento

World.title: Peso falls to 18 to the US dollar as oil, Fed worries impact both currencies
World.content:
The Mexican peso depreciated to 18 to the US dollar on Monday, a weakening of more than 1% compared to Friday and over 6% compared to its strongest position this month.

The sharp depreciation on Monday came just weeks after the return of the “super peso” was proclaimed at a time when the peso was trading at below 17 to the greenback.

A USD:MXN exchange rate of 18, as was the going rate early Monday afternoon, represents a depreciation of 6.2% for the peso compared to its strongest closing position this month — 16.89 to the greenback on Sept. 4, according to the Bank of Mexico (Banxico).

At 3 p.m. Mexico City time, the peso was trading at 17.99 to the US dollar, according to Bloomberg.

Banxico’s closing USD:MXN rate, reported daily at 2:10 p.m., was 17.94, a depreciation of 1.3% compared to the closing rate on Friday.

The newspaper El Financiero attributed the peso’s decline on Monday to a greater aversion to risk, an increase in oil prices — which rose after U.S. President Donald Trump’s rejection of an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days — and expectations of a more restrictive U.S. Federal Reserve, which raised its benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to a target range of 3.75%-4% earlier this month.

The peso has benefited from the substantial difference between Banxico’s key interest rate (6.50%) and that of the Fed. However, that difference is now smaller than it was at the start of the month, and the gap could close further if the Fed raises its key rate again next month.

For now, the peso is back in a position it was last in almost six months ago.

In an X post on Monday afternoon, Gabriela Siller, director of economic analysis at Banco Base, wrote that the peso hadn’t traded at 18 to the dollar since March 31. In a separate post that includes a graph showing the peso trading at 18 to the dollar, she wrote: “Strong dollar or weak peso? Both.”

¿Dólar fuerte o peso débil? Ambos. pic.twitter.com/qC5YVeu0Jy — Gabriela Siller Pagaza (@GabySillerP) September 28, 2026

In another X post on Monday, Siller noted that the USD:MXN exchange rate was 18.0080 at the end of 2025.

“Everything seems to indicate that it could close around that level again [at the end of] this year,” she wrote.

With reports from El Financiero

World.title: Argentina Pensions Rise 1.66% in October: Minimum Reaches US$332 With Bonus
World.content:
Argentina · Economy

Key Facts —Increase. ANSES Resolution 284/2026 formalises a 1.66% rise for October pensions, tracking August inflation under the monthly mobility scheme. The SIPA maximum is set at ARS 2,932,174.85 (about US$1,923); the PUAM pension for over-65s rises to ARS 348,598.81, or ARS 418,598.81 (about US$275) with the bonus. —Payment calendar. October payments run from Thursday 8 October to Thursday 29 October, staggered by national ID number ending. —Contribution bases. The taxable salary floor for workers rises to ARS 146,759.98 and the ceiling to ARS 4,769,631.49 from the October period.

Argentina’s pension agency ANSES has locked in October’s numbers: a 1.66% inflation-linked rise and a confirmed ARS 70,000 bonus lift the minimum retirement income to ARS 505,748.51 — about US$332 at the official exchange rate.

The Libertador Building in Buenos Aires houses the government offices overseeing pension policy; October’s rise was formalised in the Official Gazette. (Photo: The Rio Times archive)

What ANSES Has Confirmed

Resolution 284/2026, signed by ANSES’s executive directorate and published in the Official Gazette, applies a 1.66% increase to all benefits under the SIPA pension system for the October 2026 accrual period. The adjustment follows the monthly mobility formula established by emergency decree DNU 274/2024, which ties benefits to the consumer price index measured by statistics agency INDEC — in this case August inflation.

The guaranteed minimum pension rises from ARS 428,633.20 to ARS 435,748.51 gross per month. The system’s maximum benefit is fixed at ARS 2,932,174.85 — about US$1,923 at the official rate of roughly 1,524 pesos per dollar — and does not receive extraordinary supplements. The Universal Basic Benefit (PBU), the component rewarding years of contributions, is updated to ARS 199,335.05.

The Pension Universal para el Adulto Mayor (PUAM), the benefit for over-65s without sufficient contribution history, rises to ARS 348,598.81 gross. The resolution also resets payroll contribution bases for employed workers: the taxable floor moves to ARS 146,759.98 and the ceiling to ARS 4,769,631.49 from October.

The US$46 Bonus: Who Gets It

The Executive branch ratified the continuation of the extraordinary fixed-sum pension reinforcement of ARS 70,000 — about US$46 — paid automatically alongside the regular benefit. Recipients of the minimum pension therefore take their total to ARS 505,748.51, roughly US$332. PUAM beneficiaries receive a consolidated ARS 418,598.81, and the bonus also reaches non-contributory pension beneficiaries.

Pensioners whose benefit sits above the minimum but below the absorption ceiling receive a proportional bonus topping them up to ARS 505,748.51. The bonus is non-remunerative and carries no deductions: the 3% health-insurance (PAMI) withholding — ARS 13,072.45 on the minimum — is calculated on the basic benefit only. ANSES estimates the effective take-home for a single minimum benefit at around ARS 492,676, about US$323.

October Payment Calendar

October payments to pensioners and retirees begin on Thursday 8 October and run through Thursday 29 October, staggered by the final digit of the beneficiary’s national ID number (DNI). The schedule applies to SIPA retirement and pension benefits; non-contributory pensions and family allowances follow parallel calendars published on anses.gob.ar.

Beneficiaries can audit their exact October payment before it lands: log in to anses.gob.ar or the Mi ANSES app with a CUIL number and social-security password, open “Jubilaciones y Pensiones” and select “Consultar recibo de haberes” to see the net benefit, the ARS 70,000 supplement and any statutory deductions.

Context: Pensions Against a Weak Peso

The 1.66% rise arrives as household budgets remain under pressure. As The Rio Times reported this week, Argentina’s poverty rate rose to 32.3% in the first half of 2026, and JP Morgan has cut its growth forecast for the country to 1.5%. In dollar terms the minimum pension with bonus — about US$332 — illustrates how peso weakness offsets nominal increases: the official exchange rate has slipped past 1,500 per dollar, with the informal “blue” rate near 1,565.

Monthly mobility adjustments now compound through the year rather than arriving in quarterly jumps, smoothing income for retirees but also tying purchasing power tightly to each month’s inflation reading. September’s CPI figure, due in mid-October, will determine the November adjustment.

What We Could Not Confirm

Net amounts vary by beneficiary: statutory deductions depend on individual circumstances, and the ARS 492,676 take-home estimate applies to a single minimum benefit only. The day-by-day October payment schedule by DNI ending was reported by provincial media but we could not verify every date against the full official table at publication time. Dollar conversions use the Banco Nación official selling rate of about 1,524 pesos per dollar from the last close before publication; the informal blue rate trades weaker, near 1,565. Whether the ARS 70,000 bonus continues beyond October has not been formally announced.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much is Argentina’s minimum pension in October 2026?

The guaranteed minimum pension is ARS 435,748.51 gross — about US$286 — after a 1.66% rise. With the extraordinary ARS 70,000 bonus, total income reaches ARS 505,748.51, roughly US$332 at the official exchange rate.

When does ANSES pay pensions in October 2026?

Payments run from Thursday 8 October to Thursday 29 October 2026, staggered by the final digit of the beneficiary’s DNI. Exact dates can be checked via Mi ANSES or anses.gob.ar.

How is the October 2026 pension increase calculated?

The 1.66% rise matches August inflation as measured by INDEC, under the monthly mobility formula of decree DNU 274/2024. It was formalised by ANSES Resolution 284/2026, published in the Official Gazette.

World.title: Colombia Visa Revocations Hit Two People the President Had Publicly Named
World.content:
Politics · Colombia

Key Facts — What happened The Colombia visa revocations of 28 September 2026 cover senator Martha Peralta and businessman Euclides Torres.

— Where the names came from Both had appeared on a list President Abelardo de la Espriella published in June 2026, before he took office.

— The catch Washington published no individual reason for either Colombian, and its statement does not mention the president or his list.

— Who they are Peralta sits in the Senate for the left-wing Pacto Histórico; Torres is a businessman close to former president Gustavo Petro.

— What comes next De la Espriella says more names will follow, and that United States Treasury asset sanctions could come after that.

A senator and a businessman lost their United States visas on Monday. Their names had been on a list the Colombian president published in June.

The Colombia visa revocations announced on Monday 28 September 2026 struck two people the country’s own president had named in public. Their names had been on his list since June.

The United States Department of State revoked the visas of Senator Martha Isabel Peralta Epieyú and the businessman Euclides Antonio Torres Romero. Their immediate families lost theirs as well.

Peralta sits with the left-wing opposition in the Senate. Torres is a businessman investigated over the financing of Gustavo Petro’s 2022 campaign.

The list the president read out himself

In June 2026 Abelardo de la Espriella was still a presidential candidate. In a live broadcast on Monday 8 June he read out names of Colombian politicians he accused of buying votes.

He addressed them to Christopher Landau, the deputy secretary of state and the second-ranking official at the State Department. “Le dejo aquí, subsecretario, unos nombres para que usted los tenga en el radar,” he said.

In English: I leave you some names here, deputy secretary, so you can keep them on your radar. Colombian outlets nickname Landau “el quitavisas”, the visa remover.

Infobae, a Latin American news site, listed 23 names from that broadcast the next day. Peralta and Torres were both on it.

He kept adding names through June in posts on X. La Silla Vacía, an investigative outlet in Bogotá, counts about 26 in all, every one aligned with Gustavo Petro.

La Silla Vacía also notes that he offered no evidence for the vote-buying he alleged. He won the runoff on 21 June 2026 and took office on 7 August 2026.

What Washington said, and what it left out

The Colombia visa revocations came inside a State Department statement of 28 September 2026 announcing a new regional policy. It covers people who undermine a democratically elected government through corruption or drug trafficking.

The statement describes Peralta only as a senator of the Pacto Histórico and of a smaller indigenous party. It describes Torres only as the owner of an energy, traffic-signal and public-lighting group.

It gives no individual reason for either of them. It does not mention the Colombian president, or his list, or any recommendation from Bogotá.

The statement came from Thomas Pigott, the department’s spokesman. It ties the step to a leaders’ statement of 22 September by a group called the Shield of the Americas.

That group is an American-led security pact against drug cartels, founded at a summit in Doral, Florida, on 7 March 2026. Colombia was not invited then, under Petro, and joined in August under De la Espriella.

The same statement covered 26 people in four countries under the new policy. Our report on the wider list sets out Bolivia, Ecuador and Peru.

Gustavo Petro, then president of Colombia, in a file photograph from March 2025, when the Senate rejected his labour bill.

Who the two Colombians are

Peralta is a senator for La Guajira, the desert department on Colombia’s Caribbean border with Venezuela. The Supreme Court is investigating her over contracts at the national disaster-relief agency, El Heraldo reported.

She has not been convicted of anything, and the case has stalled. Torres is investigated over the financing of Petro’s 2022 campaign, and he has not been convicted either.

El Heraldo reported that Torres has acknowledged giving logistical support to Petro’s pre-campaign. He denies financing the 2022 campaign itself.

Neither faces any charge in the United States. Visa decisions there require no court and no published proof.

“Me enteré por los medios de comunicación de que me habrían retirado la visa,” Peralta told El Heraldo. She learned of it from the press, she said, and had received no official notice.

She added that she would carry on with her work calmly, facing the country and respecting its institutions.

A president who welcomed it

De la Espriella celebrated the revocations on X on Monday evening. “La lucha apenas empieza; pronto se ampliará no solo en número, sino también en decisiones administrativas,” he wrote.

The fight is only beginning, he meant, and it will widen in numbers and in administrative measures. He then pointed at the OFAC list.

OFAC is the United States Treasury office that freezes the assets of sanctioned people and companies. Being placed on its list is far heavier than losing a visa.

Petro himself knows the instrument. Washington revoked his visa in September 2025, after he addressed a protest outside United Nations headquarters in New York.

The reaction in Bogotá

María Fernanda Cabal, a former senator, told Peralta not to expect explanations from Washington. She said the senator should instead account for public money in La Guajira.

Julián Uscátegui, a Bogotá city councillor, said he hoped more names would follow. He added that anyone who had committed crimes should answer to Colombian courts.

Iván Cepeda, the senator De la Espriella beat in the runoff, made a separate claim on Tuesday. He said on X that a plan had been revived to fabricate testimony against him in a United States case.

Cepeda gave no evidence, and Vanguardia said the closeness in time does not by itself show a link. He lost that runoff by about 252,000 votes, or 0.96 of a percentage point.

Why this matters outside Colombia

A visa is cheap for Washington to withdraw and expensive for the person who loses it. No hearing is held, no charge is filed and no evidence is published.

That makes it an attractive tool for any government that wants pressure applied to its rivals. The pressure arrives from abroad, and the domestic courts are never troubled.

Colombian institutions are not being bypassed in a formal sense, because a visa is a foreign sovereign decision. The practical effect is still that a political fight has acquired a second, foreign arena.

For foreign residents and investors, the rules of ordinary travel have not changed. The measures reach named people and their close families only.

The open question is how long the Colombian list turns out to be. De la Espriella says the number will grow; Washington has named no further Colombians so far.

More: Colombia coverage, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who lost their United States visas in Colombia?

The Colombia visa revocations of 28 September 2026 covered Senator Martha Isabel Peralta Epieyú and the businessman Euclides Antonio Torres Romero, together with their immediate families. Peralta sits for the left-wing Pacto Histórico and the Movimiento Alternativo Indígena y Social. Torres owns a group active in energy, traffic signalling and public lighting. Neither has been convicted of any offence, and neither faces charges in the United States.

Did the Colombian president ask for this?

President Abelardo de la Espriella published names in June 2026, while he was still a candidate, and addressed them to the deputy secretary of state, Christopher Landau. Infobae listed 23 names from that broadcast, including Peralta and Torres. The State Department statement of 28 September 2026 makes no mention of the president, his list or any request from Bogotá.

Does this change anything for ordinary travellers?

No. The policy applies to named individuals and their immediate family members, under Section 212(a)(3)(C) of the United States Immigration and Nationality Act. Nothing in the announcement alters visa rules for other Colombians, or for foreign residents living in Colombia. The same announcement also covered 24 people in Bolivia, Ecuador and Peru.

What is the Shield of the Americas?

It is a security grouping led by the United States and aimed at drug cartels and organised crime in the Americas. It was launched at a summit in Doral, Florida, on 7 March 2026, hosted by President Donald Trump. Colombia did not attend that summit, which fell during Gustavo Petro’s presidency. Colombia joined in August 2026, shortly after Abelardo de la Espriella took office.

World.title: Bolivia Attorney General Case Could Lead to US Extradition, Minister Says
World.content:
Politics · Bolivia

Key Facts — What happened Bolivia’s government is asking Washington, through its Foreign Ministry, for the evidence behind the corruption designation of its chief prosecutor.

— How wide it goes The United States named thirteen Bolivians, including Attorney General Roger Mariaca, and made nine more ineligible without naming them.

— The catch No Bolivian court has convicted Mariaca, and Washington has published no evidence beyond the wording of its own release.

— What could follow Defence Minister Ernesto Justiniano said the case could lead to a United States investigation and probably an extradition request.

— What comes next Mariaca refuses to step aside, and Congress meets on 5 October to consider the American list and possible inquiries.

Washington has barred Bolivia’s chief prosecutor from the United States and accused him of taking bribes to facilitate drug trafficking. His own government now wants to see the file.

The United States has barred Bolivia’s attorney general from its territory. His own government now says it wants to see the case against him.

Ministers in La Paz said on Tuesday 29 September that they were asking Washington for the evidence. They are putting the request through the Foreign Ministry.

The man at the centre is Roger Mariaca Montenegro. He is the Fiscal General del Estado, the prosecutor who heads Bolivia’s Public Prosecutor’s Office.

What Washington actually did

The US Department of State published its decision on Monday 28 September. It announced a new visa restriction policy for the Western Hemisphere.

The policy rests on Section 212(a)(3)(C) of the Immigration and Nationality Act. That clause bars foreigners whose entry could seriously damage United States foreign policy.

Under it, Washington revoked the visas of twelve named Bolivians and their families. Nine more Bolivians who hold no visa were made generally ineligible for one.

The twelve include three prosecutors, three judges and two magistrates. The rest are a former justice minister, a former head of the national customs service, a police colonel and a businessman.

Mariaca was handled by a second and different instrument. The department publicly designated him for what it called significant corruption.

That designation is made under Section 7031(c) of the State Department’s 2026 appropriations act. The law requires the secretary of state to designate foreign officials where there is credible information of significant corruption.

The department said Mariaca solicited and accepted bribes to facilitate drug trafficking. It added that he helped violent criminals evade justice.

The designation makes him and his immediate family ineligible to enter the United States. Bolivia’s attorney general has rejected the accusations in full.

The measure is about entry, not money. The State Department announced no freezing of assets, and the full list across four countries ran in our earlier report.

La Paz asks for the file

Ernesto Justiniano Urenda has been Bolivia’s defence minister since June 2026. On Monday he said the government took the American statements with complete seriousness.

The government would ask for supplementary information and supporting evidence, he said. Bolivia wants to know what the American decision rests on.

“What we are doing at this moment is making the inquiries through the Foreign Ministry,” he said. The Bolivian state news agency ABI published the remarks on Tuesday.

Fernando Aramayo, the minister of the presidency, spoke on Monday at the Casa Grande del Pueblo, the seat of government. He called the situation a test of Bolivia’s democratic institutions.

He promised cooperation with whatever investigations Bolivian bodies decide to open. He also said the executive would not comment on any specific investigation.

Plaza Murillo in La Paz, with the Legislative Palace on the square and the glass tower of the Casa Grande del Pueblo, the seat of government, behind it. File photograph. (Photo: Parallelepiped09, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0)

The word extradition enters the debate

On Tuesday the defence minister was asked how far the matter could go. He did not rule anything out.

“Yes, this could lead to an investigation, a judicial step in the United States, probably an extradition request,” he said. He added that any such decision belonged to American authorities.

He asked for caution about the others named in the American measures. He said the government had no further information about their cases.

The accusations are those of a foreign government. The Bolivian state news agency noted in its report that they do not by themselves amount to a conviction.

The Bolivian government has announced no charge against Mariaca. No Bolivian court has convicted him, and Washington has published no evidence beyond the wording of its release.

Congress takes the file

Vice-President Edmand Lara presides over the Plurinational Legislative Assembly. He has called a session for Monday 5 October to consider the American list.

His written convocation says the Assembly may form a parliamentary commission of inquiry. It also says a foreign state’s immigration measures do not by themselves establish criminal responsibility in Bolivia.

The heads of both chambers had already asked the prosecutor to step aside, as we reported on Tuesday. Lara has rejected removing him over a list issued abroad.

Mariaca refuses to go. “I will not retreat even one centimetre,” he said in a video message released by the Public Prosecutor’s Office.

He said Bolivia respects the sovereign decisions of other states and expects the same respect for its own institutions. He said his office would carry on with the cases already under way.

Bolivia’s attorney general is chosen by Congress, not by the president. The Plurinational Legislative Assembly elected Mariaca on 21 October 2024, with 115 votes of the 161 cast, for a six-year term.

That is why removing him is a parliamentary matter. Any dismissal would run through a juicio de responsabilidades, the impeachment-style process Congress uses against high officials.

What it changes for people in Bolivia

For residents, travellers and businesses, nothing changes at any border. The measures reach named individuals and their immediate families, not Bolivian citizens in general.

Bolivia takes part in the Shield of the Americas, a United States-backed regional effort against organised crime. Washington tied Monday’s announcement to a statement by that group’s leaders on 22 September.

The calmer reading is that Bolivian institutions are engaging rather than refusing. The government has asked for evidence, Congress has asked for documents, and the prosecutor has answered in public.

The unsettled part is the sequence. Bolivia has asked for the file, and no answer from Washington has been reported.

A dissenting voice from the regions

Leonardo Loza, the governor of Cochabamba, rejected the American step on Tuesday. He called it a “judicial invasion” and said Bolivia was being made to look subordinate.

“I do not defend anyone, I do not justify anyone,” he told reporters. He added that those named should be investigated, without breaking the country’s sovereignty.

The government is also answering questions about the president’s recent trip to the United States. President Rodrigo Paz has governed Bolivia since November 2025.

Nothing in the American measure obliges Bolivia to act against its own prosecutor. What follows depends on whether Washington hands over its file, and on what the Assembly then does with it.

More: Bolivia coverage, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is Roger Mariaca?

Roger Mariaca Montenegro is Bolivia’s Fiscal General del Estado, the prosecutor who heads the Public Prosecutor’s Office. The Plurinational Legislative Assembly, Bolivia’s Congress, elected him on 21 October 2024 with 115 of the 161 votes cast, for a six-year term. He was sworn in two days later. Before that he was a departmental prosecutor in Santa Cruz.

What exactly did the United States do?

Two separate things on 28 September 2026. It announced a visa restriction policy under Section 212(a)(3)(C) of the Immigration and Nationality Act, and used it to revoke the visas of twelve Bolivians and to make nine more ineligible. Separately it publicly designated Mariaca for significant corruption under Section 7031(c) of the State Department’s 2026 appropriations act. Both are entry measures; no financial sanctions were announced.

Has Bolivia’s attorney general been charged or convicted?

No Bolivian court has convicted him, and the government has announced no charge against him. Ministers say the competent Bolivian bodies will carry out whatever investigations are needed once Washington shares its material. A designation by a foreign government is an accusation, not a finding by a Bolivian judge.

Does this change anything for foreigners in Bolivia?

No. The measures apply to named individuals and their immediate families, and they concern entry to the United States. Visa rules for other Bolivians, and entry rules for foreigners going to Bolivia, are untouched by the announcement.

World.title: Bahamas Beach Access Row: Party Leader Arrested After Fence Pulled Down
World.content:
Politics · Bahamas

Key Facts — What happened Police arrested Coalition of Independents leader Lincoln Bain on Monday 28 September 2026 as he pulled down a beach fence.

— What the fight is about A US$550 million Four Seasons project has fenced part of Cabbage Beach, on the resort island across the harbour from Nassau.

— The catch Bain was released the same morning and says police laid no charge against him.

— Why a beach turned political A 60-year-old American visitor nearly drowned on Sunday after walking into the water to get around the fence.

— What comes next The environment minister says the Ministry of Works will remove the fence if the developer does not.

Police handcuffed a party leader on a Nassau resort beach and let him go the same morning. The Bahamas beach access row now has an arrest in it.

The Bahamas beach access row stopped being an argument on Monday 28 September 2026. Police handcuffed Lincoln Bain on Cabbage Beach as he and other protesters pulled a fence out of the sand.

Bain leads the Coalition of Independents, the Bahamian party known as the COI, which holds no seat in parliament. Officers in tactical gear walked him off the beach and drove him to the island police station.

He was released the same morning. Bain told The Tribune that police let him go without charge, and no charge against him has been reported since.

Why there is a fence on Cabbage Beach

Cabbage Beach runs along the resort island that faces Nassau across the harbour. The Atlantis and Riu resorts sit on it, and Bahamian vendors have worked the sand for decades.

Part of that sand is now fenced off for the Four Seasons Ocean Club Residences. The Tribune puts the project at US$550 million.

The Bahamian dollar trades at a rate of one to one with the US dollar. The Central Bank of The Bahamas says that parity has held since 1973.

The developers are Access Industries, which owns the existing Ocean Club, and the Florida firm Two Roads Development. The Four Seasons brand is the third partner, and its representatives did not answer messages from The Tribune.

The government did approve a temporary fence for erosion and beach restoration works. Zane Lightbourne, the minister of the environment and natural resources, says its conditions were not met.

“The Government of The Bahamas has an uncompromising position on Bahamians’ access to their beaches,” Lightbourne said. “The position applies to every developer operating in our country.”

His written statement said advance notice to government authorities was required before the fence went up. A public advisory process was required too, and he said neither happened.

The rescue that changed the temperature

On Sunday 27 September 2026 a 60-year-old American visitor was pulled into rough seas at Cabbage Beach. She had stepped into the water to get around the fence, on the eve of her birthday.

Lifeguards, vendors and protesters swam out and brought her ashore, and an ambulance took her to hospital. Among the rescuers was Lincoln Deal, an opposition member of parliament for the Free National Movement.

“We could’ve lost a life,” Deal told The Tribune. “That could happen to Bahamians, children, tourists.”

The Senate Building and the Queen Victoria statue on Parliament Square in Nassau, seat of the Bahamian Parliament. File photograph (Photo: Larry Syverson, CC BY-SA 2.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

Who the Coalition of Independents are

The Coalition of Independents was launched in 2021 by independents and small parties who chose Bain as leader. Its platform calls for a sovereign wealth fund, tighter immigration rules and more open government.

At the general election on Tuesday 12 May 2026 the party took 17,095 votes and won no seats. That was about 12 percent of the votes counted, according to official results reported by The Nassau Guardian.

Bain came second in his own seat, Pinewood, with 1,137 votes. He finished ahead of the Free National Movement candidate, from the party that forms the official opposition.

That is the weight behind the man the police led off the beach. He speaks for a bloc of voters with no seat in the 41-member House of Assembly.

What each side is asking for

Bain told The Nassau Guardian that the fence stood in the sea rather than on land. “This isn’t a land dispute; someone put trash in the water, and we have a right to remove it,” he said.

Lightbourne says the restoration work can go ahead once the process is put right. He says the Ministry of Works will remove the fence if the developer does not, but he could not say when.

Dis We Beach, a campaign group for beach users and vendors, wants the surveyed fence line published. It also wants that line shown against the mean high-water mark, the average line the tide reaches.

The developer’s own environmental study promises public access through the three-and-a-half-year construction period. It promises a walkway 4.6 metres (15 feet) wide afterwards, with vendor kiosks leased at a nominal US$1 a month.

Why a fence matters to the whole country

The Bahamas earns its living from visitors and from financial services sold to foreigners. A confrontation on a resort beach touches the first of those directly.

The Central Bank reported 8.5 million visitor arrivals in the seven months to the end of July 2026. That was 14.8 percent more than a year earlier.

The same bank expects 2026 growth to moderately exceed the country’s medium-term potential of 1.5 to 1.9 percent. Beaches are the product, which is why a fence on one becomes a national argument.

What is still unsettled

No count of the protesters has been published. The Royal Bahamas Police Force has posted nothing about the arrest on its own news page.

The Bahamas beach access fight has run for a month at this one stretch of sand. This is the second fence, and the first came down on Sunday 30 August 2026.

The Department of Environmental Planning and Protection stepped in that time. The government later said the department had advised that work was needed against severe beach erosion.

Bain went into a meeting with the developer within hours of walking out of the police station. Who decides where a fence may stand on a Bahamian beach is the question nobody has answered.

Frequently Asked Questions

What does COI stand for in the Bahamas?

COI stands for the Coalition of Independents. It is a Bahamian political party, not a commission or an inquiry. Independents and small parties founded it in 2021 and chose Lincoln Bain as leader. At the general election on 12 May 2026 it took 17,095 votes, about 12 percent of those counted, and won no seats in the 41-member House of Assembly.

Has Lincoln Bain been charged over the fence?

No charge has been reported. Bain told The Tribune that police released him without charge after taking him to the island police station on Monday 28 September 2026. No court appearance has been reported. The Royal Bahamas Police Force has posted nothing about the arrest on its own news page.

Can visitors still walk on Cabbage Beach?

The Bahamas beach access row is about a fence, not about whether the beach is public. Part of the sand is fenced for construction and beach restoration linked to the Four Seasons Ocean Club Residences. The environment minister has ordered that fence removed. The developer’s environmental study promises access during the three-and-a-half-year build and a walkway afterwards.

Where exactly is Cabbage Beach?

Cabbage Beach is not in Nassau itself. It lies on the resort island on the far side of Nassau Harbour, joined to the city by bridges. The Atlantis and Riu resorts front the beach, and Bahamian vendors have hired out chairs, umbrellas and water sports there for decades.

World.title: Brazil Election 2026: Lula Leads First Round, Runoff a Dead Heat in Final AtlasIntel Poll
World.content:
Brazil · Election 2026

Key Facts —First round. AtlasIntel’s final pre-election survey puts President Lula on 46.2% of valid votes against 43.1% for senator Flávio Bolsonaro, with Renan Santos third on 5.3%. Brazil votes on Sunday 4 October; if no candidate takes a majority of valid votes, a runoff follows on 25 October.

Brazil’s presidential race closed September with a split picture: President Lula has widened his first-round lead over senator Flávio Bolsonaro in the last AtlasIntel poll before Sunday’s vote, yet a head-to-head runoff remains a statistical dead heat.

Recent runoff polling between Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro has tightened into a statistical tie. (Chart: The Rio Times)
