What the Poll Shows

AtlasIntel released the survey on Tuesday 29 September, five days before the first round. In the main stimulated scenario, counted on valid votes — which exclude blank, null and undecided ballots — President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) leads with 46.2%, followed by senator Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) on 43.1%. Renan Santos (Missão) holds third place with 5.3%, ahead of writer Augusto Cury (Avante) on 2.1%, Ronaldo Caiado (PSD) on 1.8% and Romeu Zema (Novo) on 0.9%; the remaining candidates together account for 0.5%.

On the broader measure that counts all voting intentions rather than valid votes only, Lula scores 45.3% against Flávio Bolsonaro’s 42.2%, according to figures reported by the legal news portal JOTA. JOTA notes that the distance between the two front-runners grew again after two consecutive waves in which the gap had sat at the narrowest level of AtlasIntel’s 2026 series.

A Runoff Too Close to Call

The headline finding for a potential second round is a dead heat: Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro are tied at 50% each on valid votes. Counting all responses, Poder360 reports Flávio Bolsonaro at 47.7% and Lula at 47.6%, with 4.8% saying they would vote blank, null or did not know — a gap of a tenth of a point, far inside the margin of error.

AtlasIntel simulated four further runoff scenarios, all featuring Lula. The president leads Romeu Zema by 53.5% to 46.5% and Ronaldo Caiado by 51.4% to 48.6% — the latter a competitive but outside-the-margin gap on valid votes. Against Augusto Cury the advantage stretches to 56.1% to 43.9%, and against Renan Santos to 61.6% to 38.4%. No scenario tested shows any challenger defeating Lula outright, but the Flávio Bolsonaro pairing is the only one in which the challenger draws level.

How the Race Has Moved

The scale of the 2026 tightening is visible inside AtlasIntel’s own series. In late July the institute measured Lula at 44.9% of first-round intentions against 35.8% for Flávio Bolsonaro — a nine-point advantage. Through August and early September the challenger closed steadily, and the past fortnight produced the closest readings of the campaign: a week ago the institute’s runoff simulation showed Flávio Bolsonaro marginally ahead, 47.2% to 46.8%, while the first round stood at 45.8% to 43.4%.

The new wave therefore marks a double movement: Lula’s first-round cushion has re-widened from its series low, while the runoff — the scenario that decides the presidency if no one wins outright on Sunday — remains locked in a tie. Poll aggregator averages that blend AtlasIntel with Datafolha, Quaest and BTG/Nexus have consistently shown a somewhat wider Lula advantage, which points to genuine divergence between institutes rather than a settled consensus.

Five Days Out: What It Means

Brazil votes on Sunday 4 October. A candidate needs more than half of valid votes to win in the first round; failing that, the top two meet in a runoff on Sunday 25 October. On these numbers a first-round outright win is out of reach for both front-runners, making 25 October the likeliest decision date — and turning the final week of campaigning, including the last televised debate on Globo on Thursday 1 October, into a fight over the narrow band of undecided voters.

One striking divergence persists between pollsters and prediction markets: as The Rio Times reported this week, betting markets continue to price Flávio Bolsonaro as the favourite even as surveys show a tied runoff and a first-round Lula lead. Both cannot be right for long; the resolution arrives on Sunday night, when Brazil’s electronic ballot boxes deliver results within hours of polls closing.

What We Could Not Confirm

A poll is a snapshot of fieldwork conducted 23–28 September, not a forecast of Sunday’s result; late campaign events can move numbers after fieldwork closes. Institutes diverge meaningfully in 2026: Datafolha, Quaest and BTG/Nexus have at times shown wider Lula leads than AtlasIntel, and the institute’s own series has swung from a nine-point first-round gap in July to a near-tie and back within two months. Poder360’s report referenced a second runoff scenario whose full figures we could not independently verify. How the 4.8% of blank, null and undecided respondents will behave in a runoff is not measurable from this survey.

Frequently Asked Questions

What does the final AtlasIntel poll show for Brazil’s 2026 election?

Released on 29 September, the poll puts Lula on 46.2% of valid first-round votes against 43.1% for Flávio Bolsonaro, with Renan Santos third on 5.3%. A runoff between the two leaders is tied at 50% each on valid votes.

When does Brazil vote in the 2026 presidential election?

The first round is on Sunday 4 October 2026. If no candidate wins a majority of valid votes, the two front-runners contest a runoff on Sunday 25 October 2026.

How reliable is the AtlasIntel survey?

The institute interviewed 5,005 voters between 23 and 28 September 2026, with a margin of error of one percentage point and 95% confidence, under electoral-court registration BR-04391/2026. Other institutes show somewhat different gaps, so the poll is best read alongside aggregator averages.

What could not be confirmed about the poll?

Poder360 referenced a second runoff scenario whose full figures could not be independently verified. And how the 4.8% of blank, null and undecided respondents will behave in a runoff is not measurable from this survey.

World.title: Brazil Fuel Subsidy Bill Reaches US$6.2 Billion, Treasury Says Revenue Covers It
World.content:
Economy · Brazil

Key Facts — What happened Brazil’s Treasury said on 29 September 2026 that extra energy revenue outruns the cost of cheaper fuel.

— How big it is The Treasury projects R$67.5 billion (about US$12.9 billion) of extraordinary energy revenue for 2026.

— What it has cost Brazil’s fuel subsidy and tax breaks came to R$32.4 billion (about US$6.2 billion) by the end of August.

— The catch That cost figure stops at August and leaves out September’s package, priced near R$7 billion (about US$1.3 billion) a month.

— What comes next Brazil votes on Sunday 4 October 2026, and the gasoline tax cut expires five days later.

Five days before Brazilians vote, the government says the money it earns from higher energy prices more than pays for the discounts at the pump. The two figures it compared cover different periods.

Brazil’s fuel subsidy bill is smaller than the energy revenue paying for it, the National Treasury said on Tuesday. It published the figures on 29 September 2026, five days before Brazil votes.

The Treasury is the arm of the finance ministry that publishes the federal accounts. Its secretary, Daniel Leal, put the extra energy revenue for 2026 at R$67.5 billion (about US$12.9 billion).

Against that it set R$32.4 billion (about US$6.2 billion) of fuel subsidies and tax breaks, counted to the end of August. Subtract one from the other and the gap is R$35.1 billion (about US$6.7 billion).

All conversions here use a rate of 5.2204 to the US dollar. That is the Banco Central do Brasil PTAX selling rate for 29 September 2026.

The two numbers do not cover the same months

The revenue side is a projection for the whole of 2026. The cost side stops at the end of August and leaves September out.

September was the most expensive month of the year so far. Measures signed on 9 September 2026 carry a cost of about R$7 billion (about US$1.3 billion) a month.

That estimate came from Bruno Moretti, Brazil’s planning and budget minister, on the day they were signed.

Five days before the Treasury spoke, the ministry gave a fuller number. Its executive secretary, Rogério Ceron, put all of this year’s fuel measures near R$40 billion (about US$7.7 billion).

Set that against the same revenue projection and the headroom falls to R$27.5 billion (about US$5.3 billion). Both sums are the government’s own.

How Brazil is holding pump prices down

Brazil’s fuel subsidy is only one of three things working at once. None of them is a price freeze.

The first is a tax cut. Decree 13,116 of 9 September 2026 lowered federal duty on gasoline by R$0.63 a litre (about US$0.12).

The decree carries two signatures: President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and his finance minister, Dário Durigan. The duties it cut are PIS and Cofins, two federal levies charged on sales.

The same decree zeroed those levies on hydrated ethanol, worth R$0.19 a litre (about US$0.04).

Those cuts run from 10 September to 9 October 2026 and apply at the refinery and the import gate. How much reaches the pump depends on each distributor and retailer along the chain.

Brazil’s Finance Ministry in Brasília. The National Treasury, which published the figures, is part of the ministry. File photograph. (Photo: Pedro França/Agência Senado via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.)

The second is a straight payment. The state gives producers and importers R$2.12 for every litre of road diesel (about US$0.41).

The finance ministry issued that renewal as ordinance 2,946 on 25 September 2026, and it took effect on 27 September. It runs in 30-day cycles, and the ministry has set no end date.

The third is Petrobras. Brazil’s state-controlled energy company says it does not pass international swings straight through to Brazilian buyers.

On 17 September 2026 Petrobras raised diesel for distributors by R$1 a litre (about US$0.19). A federal payment of the same size cancelled the increase out.

What the tax take actually shows

The Receita Federal, Brazil’s tax agency, published its August figures on 22 September 2026. Federal revenue reached R$235.6 billion that month (about US$45.1 billion), a record for August.

That was 8.25% higher than August 2025 once inflation is stripped out. For January to August, revenue came to R$2.11 trillion (about US$404 billion), up 7.12% in real terms.

Energy did much of the lifting. Taxes on petroleum and natural gas production reached R$93.3 billion in those eight months (about US$17.9 billion).

The same taxes brought in R$16.3 billion (about US$3.1 billion) a year earlier. A temporary export duty on fuels accounted for about R$9.9 billion (about US$1.9 billion) of this year’s figure.

The Treasury expects R$21 billion (about US$4 billion) from that duty across the whole of 2026. More than half of it has yet to arrive.

The accounts are still in the red

The same release showed a primary deficit of R$13.6 billion for August (about US$2.6 billion). That was the smallest August shortfall in five years.

A primary deficit measures spending against revenue before interest on the public debt. For the year to August the central government was R$94.9 billion short (about US$18.2 billion).

Why the windfall could fade

The revenue moves with the price of a barrel and with the exchange rate. Brent traded at US$104.46 a barrel at 11 a.m. New York time on 28 September 2026.

Royalties and the export duty are calculated against dollar prices. When the real, Brazil’s currency, strengthens, the same dollars become fewer reais.

Brazil’s own 2027 budget bill assumes an average of about US$71. The Senate’s Independent Fiscal Institution, which checks the government’s numbers, assumes US$75.

About 90% of Brazil’s natural-resource revenue depends on petroleum and natural gas. That is from the institution’s report of 17 September 2026.

The same report gives the government’s own 2027 estimate for that revenue as R$176.3 billion (about US$33.8 billion).

What the critics say

Felipe Salto is chief economist at the investment house Warren. He was finance secretary of the state of São Paulo before that.

He put a blunt question to Folha de S.Paulo in April 2026, when the plan first surfaced. If a government will not reach the centre of its fiscal target in a windfall year, he asked, when will it?

Marcus Pestana is executive director of the Instituição Fiscal Independente, the Senate’s fiscal watchdog. He described the approach as a political choice in favour of fighting inflation.

The pump tells its own story. Average gasoline prices rose 3.98% between 28 February and 12 September 2026, and diesel rose 8.62%.

Those figures come from the ANP, Brazil’s federal fuel regulator. Ethanol, made inside Brazil from sugar cane, fell 12.74% over the same months.

Carlos Eduardo Oliveira Jr. leads Sindecon-SP, the economists’ union in São Paulo state. He said the payment softens part of the impact but may not cover the whole rise in costs.

What it means before Sunday

Brazilians vote in the first round on Sunday 4 October 2026. Lula is seeking a fourth term against Senator Flávio Bolsonaro.

Fuel prices feed straight into inflation and into how voters judge a government. The gasoline tax cut expires on 9 October 2026, five days after the vote.

For anyone living in Brazil, the practical point is plain. The discount at the pump is temporary, and the money behind it moves with a price set outside the country.

The government says the sums balance for 2026. Whether they balance next year depends on a number no minister sets.

More: Brazil coverage, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is the Brazil fuel subsidy a payment or a tax cut?

Both, and a third thing as well. Decree 13,116 of 9 September 2026 cut federal PIS and Cofins duty on gasoline by R$0.63 a litre (about US$0.12) and zeroed it on hydrated ethanol. Separately, the state pays producers and importers R$2.12 for every litre of road diesel (about US$0.41), renewed by ordinance 2,946 of 25 September 2026 and in force from 27 September for another 30 days. On top of that, Petrobras chooses not to pass every international swing through to Brazilian buyers.

How much has the Brazil fuel subsidy cost so far?

The National Treasury put the bill at R$32.4 billion (about US$6.2 billion) to the end of August 2026. That is R$24.4 billion (about US$4.7 billion) of direct payments plus about R$8 billion (about US$1.5 billion) of tax revenue given up. It does not include the package signed on 9 September 2026, which the planning and budget ministry costed at about R$7 billion (about US$1.3 billion) a month.

Where does the extra energy revenue come from?

Three places. Higher royalties and special participations paid by companies that produce petroleum in Brazilian waters, higher tax on the profits of those producers, and a temporary duty on fuel exports. The Treasury expects R$21 billion (about US$4 billion) from the export duty alone in 2026. The Receita Federal counted about R$9.9 billion (about US$1.9 billion) of it between January and August.

What happens to fuel prices after the election?

The gasoline and ethanol tax cuts are written to expire on 9 October 2026, five days after the first round. The diesel payment runs in 30-day cycles, and the finance ministry has said it will decide each renewal according to international prices. No end date has been announced for it.

World.title: Brazil Corporate Debt Costs Near 24% as Moody’s Warns of a 2027 Squeeze
World.content:
Business · Brazil

Key Facts — What happened Moody’s said on Tuesday 29 September 2026 that pressure on Brazilian company finances will run into 2027.

— How big The agency projects that the combined operating earnings of Brazilian companies will fall by more than 3% in 2027.

— The catch Brazil corporate debt has barely cheapened: new company loans averaged 24.19% in August 2026, against 24.93% a year earlier.

— Who feels it Moody’s names airlines, transport, chemicals and steelmakers, plus power producers and farmers exposed to El Niño.

— What could ease it Economists surveyed by Brazil’s central bank see the policy rate down at 12.00% by the end of 2027.

Brazil corporate debt still costs close to 24% a year on new bank loans, even after five cuts in the policy rate. Moody’s expects the squeeze to last into 2027.

Brazil corporate debt is not getting cheaper, even though the central bank has been cutting interest rates since March. The rating agency Moody’s says the pressure on company finances will last into 2027.

Moody’s published that assessment on Tuesday 29 September 2026. It projects that the combined operating earnings of Brazilian companies will fall by more than 3% next year.

What the agency said

Two Brazilian outlets carried the report the same day. The weekly magazine Veja summarised it, and the São Paulo financial service Finance News ran a longer Portuguese version.

Finance News ran it under the line that tighter conditions will keep pressing the credit quality of Brazilian companies. The subject is non-financial and infrastructure companies, not banks.

Moody’s points to heavy borrowing, thin liquidity and governance risk as the weights on credit quality. Slower economic growth and weaker household income make it harder to raise sales and cover the extra cost.

Companies with large debts falling due by 2028 will have to refinance, the agency says. Neither Brazilian account of the report gives a figure for how much debt that is.

The policy rate has fallen, the loan rate has not

Brazil’s benchmark interest rate is called the Selic, and a committee at the central bank sets it. It stands at 13.75% a year, in force since 17 September 2026.

A year ago it was 15.00%. Five meetings in a row have cut it by a quarter of a point each since March 2026.

Those decisions and their dates are published by the Banco Central do Brasil. The cuts add up to 1.25 points in six months.

Companies have felt almost none of that. The average rate on new bank loans to Brazilian firms was 24.19% a year in August 2026, against 24.93% in August 2025.

That is a fall of 0.74 of a point while the policy rate came down 1.25 points. Both figures are published by the central bank.

Workers at machine tools on a factory floor in Brazil. File photograph. (Photo: Marcio de Assis/Wikimedia CC)

What inflation is actually doing

Brazil’s official consumer price index is the IPCA, compiled by the statistics agency IBGE. It rose 4.22% in the twelve months to August 2026, and prices fell 0.32% during August itself.

That twelve-month rate has eased every month since May 2026, when it reached 4.72%. September’s reading has not been published yet.

The central bank aims at 3%, with a tolerance band of 1.5 points either side. Inflation is therefore inside the band and above its centre.

Which companies Moody’s singles out

Fuel and freight are the first pressure point. Airlines, transport operators and chemical makers all buy a lot of energy, and the agency expects their margins to narrow.

They can pass part of the increase on to customers. Moody’s does not expect that to cover the whole of it.

Brazilian steelmakers face a different problem: cheaper imported metal, above all from China. The agency expects that competition to press them through 2027.

For Petrobras, the state-controlled energy company, the risk runs the other way. High crude prices raise the political stakes in domestic fuel pricing, and limited price rises cap what the company keeps.

Weather is the last factor. A strong El Niño would cut the water flowing into hydroelectric reservoirs and push up the cost of generating power, Moody’s says.

Growers of soy, corn, wheat, coffee and sugarcane could lose part of a harvest, depending on the region. Smaller grain crops then raise feed costs for meat producers.

What would ease the squeeze

The rate-cutting cycle is the main relief, and it is already running. Economists surveyed for the central bank’s weekly Focus report put the Selic at 12.00% by the end of 2027.

That reading is dated 25 September 2026, and the number is the economists’ median forecast. It is not a target announced by the central bank.

Export earnings are the second cushion. Brazil sold US$250.9 billion of goods abroad in the first eight months of 2026.

That is about 10% more than in the same months of 2025. The trade surplus over the period reached US$55.3 billion, against US$43.2 billion a year earlier.

Those figures come from the trade ministry’s Comex Stat database. Export revenue is cash earned from sales, and it does not depend on Brazilian bank credit.

Slower inflation matters too, because it is what allows the central bank to keep cutting. Companies with little debt and steady cash will feel much less of this than heavy borrowers.

What it means for people with money in Brazil

For anyone holding Brazilian company bonds, the message is about margins rather than failure. Both Brazilian accounts describe pressure on earnings and on refinancing, and neither names a company at risk of default.

For savers, a high policy rate still cuts both ways. The Selic that squeezes borrowers is also what keeps Brazilian fixed-income returns comfortably above inflation.

For employees and suppliers, the sign to watch is how new spending is funded. Finance News reports the agency warning that firms financing big investments with short-term money face rising liquidity risk.

Moody’s frames all of this as a two-year stretch rather than a turning point. The policy rate is already heading down, and the cost of company credit has yet to follow.

More: Brazil coverage, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Moody’s forecast for Brazilian companies?

The rating agency said on Tuesday 29 September 2026 that credit quality at Brazilian non-financial and infrastructure companies will stay under pressure into 2027. It projects that their combined operating earnings, measured before interest, tax and depreciation, will fall by more than 3% in 2027. It points to high interest costs, heavy borrowing, slower growth, dearer fuel and freight, and the risk of a strong El Niño. Neither Brazilian account of the report gives a figure for how much company debt falls due before the end of 2028.

What is the Selic and where is it now?

The Selic is Brazil’s benchmark interest rate, set every few weeks by the monetary policy committee of the Banco Central do Brasil. It has stood at 13.75% a year since 17 September 2026. That follows five reductions of a quarter of a point each, beginning in March 2026, from a level of 15.00%. The central bank publishes each decision with its date on its own website.

Why is Brazil corporate debt still expensive if the policy rate is falling?

Banks do not pass a policy rate cut straight through to borrowers. The average interest rate on new bank loans to Brazilian companies was 24.19% a year in August 2026, against 24.93% in August 2025, according to the central bank’s credit statistics. That is a fall of 0.74 of a point, while the Selic came down 1.25 points over the same period. The series measures new loans agreed in the month, not the cost of debt already on company books.

Is Brazilian inflation rising?

Not on the latest published reading. The IPCA, Brazil’s official consumer price index, rose 4.22% in the twelve months to August 2026, the most recent month released by the statistics agency IBGE. Prices fell 0.32% during August itself. The twelve-month rate has eased in every month since May 2026, when it reached 4.72%. Brazil targets inflation of 3%, with a tolerance band of 1.5 points either side.

Sources: Veja on the Moody’s report of 29 September 2026, Finance News with a fuller Portuguese summary of the same report, Banco Central do Brasil on every Selic decision and its date, Banco Central do Brasil on average interest rates for company loans, IBGE on the IPCA consumer price index, Banco Central do Brasil on the Focus survey of economists, Brazil’s trade ministry on exports and imports

World.title: Brazil Prison Vote Lets Jailed Banker Daniel Vorcaro Cast a Ballot
World.content:
Elections · Brazil

Key Facts — What happened Jailed banker Daniel Vorcaro had his voter registration moved to the Papuda prison complex in Brasília.

— Why he still can Brazil removes political rights only after a final criminal conviction, and no court has convicted Vorcaro.

— The catch A law signed in March 2026 bans prisoner voting, but the electoral court froze it for this election.

— How rare this is Only 6,300 detainees nationwide were eligible to vote in 2024, against 12,900 at the 2022 election.

— What comes next Vorcaro can vote on 4 October 2026, and in a runoff on 25 October, from section 0420.

Brazil prison vote rules put the detained owner of the collapsed Banco Master on the electoral roll in Brasília. A new law would have stopped him, and the electoral court froze it.

The Brazil prison vote rules will put a jailed banker in front of a ballot machine this Sunday. Daniel Vorcaro, the detained owner of the collapsed Banco Master, is registered to vote on 4 October 2026.

Electoral officials moved his polling place to the Papuda penitentiary complex in Brasília. The broadcaster Jovem Pan reported on Tuesday 29 September 2026 that his section number is 0420.

Vorcaro is not held at Papuda itself. He is in a Military Police building inside the same complex, known to Brazilians as the Papudinha.

Who Daniel Vorcaro is

Vorcaro was born in Belo Horizonte in 1983. He bought the small Banco Máxima in 2021 and rebuilt it as Banco Master.

The lender grew by selling savings certificates at unusually generous rates. CNN Brasil says some promised up to 140% of Brazil’s benchmark interbank rate.

Brazil’s central bank ordered the bank into liquidation on 18 November 2025. Federal Police had arrested him the day before, and he was later released with an electronic ankle tag.

He was arrested again on 4 March 2026, on the order of Supreme Court Justice André Mendonça. Police call the inquiry Operation Compliance Zero.

Investigators suspect financial fraud and money laundering around the bank’s collapse. No court has convicted Vorcaro of anything, and he is held before trial rather than under sentence.

Mendonça moved him from the Federal Police building in Brasília to the Papudinha on 25 June 2026, according to Agência Brasil. The same order refused a defence request for house arrest.

The Papudinha is the 19th Battalion of the Federal District Military Police. CNN Brasil describes it as a building inside the Papuda complex, used for inmates who cannot be housed with the rest.

Why a prisoner can vote in Brazil

The whole Brazil prison vote arrangement rests on one line in the constitution. It takes political rights away only after a final criminal conviction.

A final conviction means a sentence with no appeals left. Vorcaro does not have one, and neither do most people inside Brazilian jails.

People held before trial therefore keep the vote. The electoral courts install ballot machines inside prisons and youth detention units so that they can use it.

That is why section 0420 exists at Papuda. Vorcaro told the Military Police he wanted to vote, Jovem Pan reported, and the message was passed to the electoral court.

The reports do not name the electoral judge who approved the change. They say only that the registration is in order for the first round and for any runoff.

A Brazilian electronic ballot machine of the kind the electoral court installs in prisons, in a file photograph. (Photo: Rio Times media library)

The right almost disappeared this year

A law signed in March 2026 would have ended it. Known as the Lei Antifacção, or anti-gang law, Law 15,358 barred anyone held in prison from registering to vote.

The Superior Electoral Court, which runs Brazil’s elections, suspended that part of the law on 23 April 2026. Its justices ruled unanimously, with Antonio Carlos Ferreira as the reporting justice.

Their reason was a constitutional rule against changing election law within a year of a vote. Brazilians call it the annuality principle, and it exists to stop governments rewriting the contest late.

The court also noted that the constitution removes the vote only after a final conviction. From 2027 the ban can take effect, unless the Supreme Court strikes the law down first.

How few detainees actually reach a ballot machine

Brazil holds about 200,000 people in pre-trial detention, according to the Senate’s news agency. Only a small share of them ever reaches the electoral roll.

A report by the federal public defender’s office counted 12,900 pre-trial detainees eligible to vote in 2022. By 2024 that number had fallen to 6,300.

The report drew on electoral court data. Its 2024 count is the most recent in that series.

In 2022 the electoral courts set up about 220 polling places inside prison units. Those sections held 14,653 registered voters, a total that also counts prison staff and poll workers.

What it means for Sunday

One ballot will not move the result. The case matters because Vorcaro’s name has run through the campaign for weeks.

President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva faces Flávio Bolsonaro in the first round on 4 October 2026. A runoff follows on 25 October if nobody wins outright.

Last week the same court suspended a Lula radio advert that tied his rival to the banker. Vorcaro is a subject of that argument, not a participant in it.

For a reader watching from abroad, the lesson is about Brazilian law rather than about one man. Detention before trial does not strip a Brazilian citizen of political rights.

That balance is narrower than it looks from outside. Congress has already passed the law that would remove it, and the electoral court has protected it for this election only.

The machine at Papuda will open on Sunday like every other one in the country. Whether Vorcaro uses it is his own decision, and the secret ballot will keep his choice private.

More: Brazil coverage, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can prisoners vote in Brazil?

Brazil prison vote rules split the jail population in two. People held before trial can vote, and people serving a final criminal sentence cannot. Brazil’s constitution suspends political rights only after a conviction that can no longer be appealed. To make the right usable, the electoral courts set up polling sections inside prisons and youth detention units. In 2022 there were about 220 such locations across the country, holding 14,653 registered voters, a total that includes prison staff and poll workers.

Where will Daniel Vorcaro vote?

At the Papuda penitentiary complex in Brasília, in section 0420, according to Jovem Pan. He is held nearby in a Military Police building inside the same complex, known as the Papudinha. The electoral court says his registration is in order for the first round on 4 October 2026 and for a runoff on 25 October. A ballot machine will be available at the complex on polling day.

What is Daniel Vorcaro accused of?

Federal Police suspect financial fraud and money laundering around the collapse of Banco Master, the lender he built out of the former Banco Máxima. The inquiry is called Operation Compliance Zero. Brazil’s central bank ordered the bank into liquidation on 18 November 2025, a day after his first arrest. He has not been convicted of anything and is held before trial, not under sentence.

Is prisoner voting about to end in Brazil?

It may. Law 15,358 of 2026, the anti-gang law signed in March 2026, bars anyone held in prison from registering to vote. The Superior Electoral Court suspended that part of the law on 23 April 2026, because Brazil’s constitution forbids changing election rules within a year of a vote. From 2027 the ban can apply, unless the Supreme Court strikes it down.

World.title: Argentina’s Nadia Podoroska’s Comeback Gains Momentum in São Paulo
World.content:
Nadia Podoroska’s return to professional tennis has moved well beyond simply testing whether her body could handle competition again. Six months after returning from a 14-month injury layoff, the 29-year-old Argentine reached the first WTA Tour final of her career at the São Paulo Open, a result that lifted her 117 places in the rankings and provided the clearest sign yet that the former Roland Garros semifinalist is again becoming a factor on the women’s tour.

Podoroska entered the WTA 250 event ranked No. 317 and unseeded, but worked her way through the draw before producing the biggest result of her week in the semifinals. She defeated former world No. 2 Paula Badosa 6-3, 6-4, ending an 0-4 career record in WTA Tour semifinals and becoming the first Argentine woman to reach a tour-level singles final since Paula Ormaechea in Bogotá in 2013.

The title ultimately went to Spain’s Kaitlin Quevedo. After Podoroska took the opening set, the 20-year-old Spaniard rallied for a 4-6, 6-4, 6-2 victory in two hours and eight minutes to claim her first WTA title. The final was played Monday, after rain prevented its completion on Sunday. For Podoroska, however, reaching the final may have carried greater significance than the result itself.

She climbed from No. 317 to No. 200 following São Paulo, continuing a remarkable ranking recovery for a player who began the season outside the Top 1,000 and returned to competition without a ranking after more than a year away. Podoroska had not played for 440 days when she returned earlier this year. Her absence began with a hip problem and was complicated by a shoulder injury, leaving her uncertain whether she would play professionally again. During her recovery, she acknowledged that she had seriously considered retirement.

Her comeback began quietly in Argentina before gathering momentum in Europe. In April, Podoroska returned to the rankings after winning an ITF W15 tournament in Madrid, where she came through qualifying and played eight matches during the week. She followed that with a W35 title in San Gregorio in June.

The results became increasingly significant as the summer progressed. At the U.S. Open, Podoroska used a protected ranking to enter the main draw and defeated Switzerland’s Simona Waltert in the first round. It was her first Grand Slam main-draw victory since the 2024 Australian Open and another important step in a comeback that initially centered more on staying healthy than chasing rankings.

São Paulo changed the scale of the conversation. Podoroska was no longer collecting matches at lower-level tournaments. She was beating established WTA players and playing for a tour-level championship.

That carries particular weight because of where she has been before. Podoroska produced one of the biggest breakthroughs in Argentine tennis in recent years when she came through qualifying to reach the 2020 Roland Garros semifinals, defeating then-world No. 5 Elina Svitolina along the way. She eventually reached a career-high ranking of No. 36 in July 2021.

Injuries repeatedly interrupted the seasons that followed, including another lengthy absence after that French Open run. Now the ranking is moving quickly in the other direction. Podoroska started 2026 around No. 1,200, climbed to No. 574 by the end of June and reached No. 317 shortly before São Paulo. Her run to the final pushed her back to No. 200.

A return to the Top 100 remains a considerable climb, but it is no longer a distant target. More importantly, Podoroska has demonstrated that she can again compete with players much higher in the rankings. After spending much of the past two years fighting simply to stay on the court, São Paulo offered something different: evidence that the Argentine’s comeback may be turning into a genuine second chapter of her career.

World.title: University of Belize and TaiwanICDF sign letter of intent to establish Taiwan-Caribbean Institute
World.content:
University of Belize and TaiwanICDF sign letter of intent to establish Taiwan-Caribbean Institute

By Zoila Palma: The University of Belize (UB) and the Taiwan International Cooperation and Development Fund (TaiwanICDF) have signed a Letter of Intent for the establishment of a Taiwan-Caribbean Institute, aimed at expanding academic cooperation and knowledge exchange between Belize, Taiwan and the wider Caribbean.

The signing took place today during a meeting between Minister of Foreign Affairs, Francis Fonseca, and Taiwan’s Minister of Foreign Affairs, Lin Chia-lung, at the Leigh Richardson Building in Belmopan.

The Foreign Ministers witnessed the signing as part of discussions focused on strengthening bilateral cooperation and reaffirming the longstanding partnership between Belize and Taiwan.

The proposed institute is expected to create new opportunities for academic collaboration, knowledge sharing and capacity building, strengthening educational ties and cooperation across the region.

The initiative forms part of ongoing efforts by Belize and Taiwan to deepen practical cooperation and advance shared development priorities, with the proposed institute expected to strengthen connections between academic institutions and promote exchanges that benefit both countries and the wider Caribbean.

World.title: Belize and Taiwan strengthen cooperation through Bilateral Agreement on Diplomatic Staff Training
World.content:
Belize and Taiwan strengthen cooperation through Bilateral Agreement on Diplomatic Staff Training

By Zoila Palma: Today, Francis Fonseca, Minister of Foreign Affairs welcomed his counterpart, Lin Chia-lung, Minister of Foreign Affairs of Taiwan to the Leigh Richardson Building, Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Belmopan.

The Foreign Ministers held bilateral talks focused on strengthening cooperation across areas of mutual interest and reaffirming the longstanding bonds of friendship and partnership between Belize and Taiwan.

Belize and Taiwan signed a Joint Communiqué on the visit, as well as a Bilateral Agreement on Diplomatic Staff Training Cooperation, aimed at strengthening the capacity and professional development of Belize’s foreign service.

The Ministers also witnessed the signing of a Letter of Intent between the University of Belize and the Taiwan International Cooperation and Development Fund (TaiwanICDF) for the establishment of a Taiwan-Caribbean Institute.

The initiative is expected to create new opportunities for academic cooperation, knowledge exchange and capacity building between Belize, Taiwan and the wider Caribbean.

The visit highlights the continued commitment of Belize and Taiwan to deepening practical cooperation and advancing shared priorities for the benefit of both peoples.

World.title: Sembrando Vida phase 2 registration continues in Corozal and Orange Walk
World.content:
Sembrando Vida phase 2 registration continues in Corozal and Orange Walk

By Zoila Palma: The Ministry of Agriculture is conducting registration activities this week for Phase 2 of the Sembrando Vida programme in the Corozal and Orange Walk Districts, targeting small producers, backyard gardeners and part-time agriculturalists.

Registration took place in Sarteneja on Monday, September 28, and continues in Patchakan today, September 29. Activities will extend to San Joaquin and the SIRDI headquarters in Buena Vista on Wednesday, September 30.

In the Orange Walk District, registration is scheduled for October 1 and 2 at the Yo Creek Agriculture Station and the Orange Walk PUP East Office.

The second phase aims to support small-scale producers and backyard farmers through the programme, which promotes agricultural production and opportunities for participating households.

World.title: Farmers in Belize District receive corn seed and fertilizer
World.content:
Farmers in Belize District receive corn seed and fertilizer

By Zoila Palma: Today, the Ministry of Agriculture shared that 25 farmers from communities within the Belize River Valley, Belize District, received agricultural inputs, including corn seed and fertilizer, to support the establishment and productivity of their crop production activities.

The beneficiaries previously participated in climate-smart agricultural training facilitated by the Caribbean Agricultural Research and Development Institute (CARDI) in August.

The training focused on strengthening farmers’ technical capacity and promoting improved production practices.

The distribution of these inputs was made possible through the Climate Resilient Agriculture Project (CRESAP), in collaboration with the Ministry of Agriculture, Food Security and New Growth Industries, as part of ongoing efforts to enhance agricultural productivity, strengthen climate resilience, and support sustainable crop production among farmers in the Belize River Valley.

World.title: Prime Minister welcomes Taiwan’s Minister of Foreign Affairs
World.content:
Prime Minister welcomes Taiwan’s Minister of Foreign Affairs

By Zoila Palma: Today, as part of the official visit of Foreign Minister of Taiwan Lin Chui-lung, he paid a courtesy call to Prime Minister John Briceno.

“Belize and Taiwan share a longstanding friendship built on mutual respect, cooperation and a commitment to advancing the interests of our people.

I warmly welcome him to Belize and look forward to our continued partnership,” the PM said.

During his visit, Minister Lin will hold bilateral talks with Francis Fonseca, Minister of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade.

The visit will conclude on Wednesday, September 30, 2026.

World.title: Governor General welcomes Taiwan’s Foreign Minister
World.content:
Governor General welcomes Taiwan’s Foreign Minister

By Zoila Palma: Today, as part of his official visit to Belize, Lin Chia-Lung, Minister of Foreign Affairs of Taiwan and his delegation paid a courtesy visit to Governor-General Dame Froyla Tzalam.

The Minister was later welcomed by Prime Minister John Briceño, joined by senior Cabinet officials and representatives from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade.

During his visit, Minister Lin will hold bilateral talks with Francis Fonseca, Minister of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade.

The visit will conclude on Wednesday, September 30, 2026.

World.title: It’s Conch time! Queen Conch season opens October 1
World.content:
It’s Conch time! Queen Conch season opens October 1

By Zoila Palma: The Belize Fisheries Department has announced that Belize’s Queen Conch fishing season will officially open on October 1, 2026, and will run through June 30, 2027, in accordance with the Fisheries Resources Act, Chapter 210 of the Laws of Belize.

The Department reminded the public that the season could close earlier if the national conch production quota is reached before June 30.

During the closed season, from July 1 to September 30, it is illegal to take, buy, sell or possess Queen Conch in Belize.

Fisheries regulations also prohibit the taking or possession of conch below the legal size and weight limits. Conch must have an overall shell length of more than 7 inches (17.8 centimetres), while minimum weight requirements apply to unprocessed, market-clean and fully processed conch meat.

The Department further reminded the public that filleted or diced conch meat other than market-clean product cannot be bought, sold or possessed without a special permit from the Fisheries Administrator. Exporters are also prohibited from exporting conch beyond the quota granted under the Fisheries Resources Act.

World.title: Azzane Domingo and Eustace Lewis walk free from ‘Tanga’ murder case
World.content:
Azzane Domingo and Eustace Lewis walk free from ‘Tanga’ murder case

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Two men accused in connection with the 2022 murder of Winston Joseph James, better known as “Tanga,” walked free from the High Court on Tuesday after prosecutors discontinued the case against them.

Azzane Domingo, 23, and Eustace Lewis, 36, had been scheduled to stand trial before Justice Candace Nanton in connection with James’ murder and the shooting of his then-partner, Marybeth Wade. However, the Crown entered a nolle prosequi after police were unable to locate a key prosecution witness, identified as Shemaud Nunez, also known as “Sabe.”

The case had already been adjourned on September 24 to give police additional time to find the witness. At that hearing, prosecutors told the court that officers, including members of GI3, were assisting with the search.

A nolle prosequi formally discontinues the prosecution but does not amount to an acquittal. The Crown may potentially bring proceedings again if sufficient evidence becomes available.

Another potential Crown witness, Wade, had previously indicated that she did not intend to testify. Wade was inside the vehicle with James when gunmen opened fire on January 21, 2022. She was shot in the arm and survived, while James was struck multiple times and killed.

James had reportedly just left his attorney’s office when he was attacked while driving a Nissan Pathfinder in the West Canal area. Following the shooting, his vehicle crashed near the canal side. Contemporary reports placed the shooting near the corner of Bishop Street and West Canal.

Domingo was charged with James’ murder in September 2024 and also faced charges arising from Wade’s shooting. Lewis was subsequently charged with abetment to murder, with prosecutors alleging that he aided Domingo.

Following a preliminary inquiry in August 2025, both men were committed to stand trial in the High Court. Public reporting at the time said the prosecution had submitted more than 25 witness statements and other documentary exhibits.

Attorney Leeroy Banner represented Domingo, while Senior Counsel Ellis Arnold represented Lewis.

Lewis, who had been on bail, left the courtroom shortly after the prosecution discontinued the case. Domingo, who had remained in custody, was released about an hour later.

Tuesday’s development comes more than four years and eight months after James was killed on January 21, 2022.

World.title: Profound sorrow
World.content:
A police vehicle seen on the campus of Wolmer’s Boys’ School on Monday after the death of a fourth-form student. Photo: Joseph wellington

DEEP sorrow and grief shrouded Wolmer’s Boys’ School on Monday after a fourth-form student collapsed in class and died.

“I don’t think we’ve ever had such a situation; meaning, it’s typical for us to have students fall ill, we take them for medical attention, and we see them back in school. It’s the first that we’re having an experience where a student has been taken for medical attention and will not be back with us,” Principal Dwight Pennycooke told journalists at the school in the Corporate Area.

The principal said he was unable to give a detailed account of the school’s initial reaction to the incident, as, after receiving the call from the school nurse informing him of the situation, he had been at Medical Associates Hospital where the student was rushed.

However, he shared that his students were compassionate and empathetic and he expected that the school would be in a period of mourning for quite some time.

“I know over the next few days it’s going to be a difficult one for his peers, his teachers, and for us the administration. We’ve never had to walk through something like this, but we will, through the grace of God, and the help of the support, walk through this and ensure that we provide the necessary support to his peers as well,” said Pennycooke.

He added that, in his absence, vice-principals had been ensuring that the school remained settled, while an early dismissal gave students and staff time to “decompress and to process” what had happened.

He further noted that he could not speak to the specifics surrounding the medical emergency, but recalled seeing the school nurse’s urgent response after receiving her call.

“I saw her running. She’s heavily pregnant, and you see her running, and so I think you would appreciate that she had the sense that this is an emergency, and so she dealt with whatever the call was… in that moment. So that is all I’m aware of,” he said.

Pennycooke reiterated that the school would continue to provide necessary support to those in mourning, noting that the Ministry of Education responded to the incident, and that counsellors were immediately deployed.

“Our young men are quite sensitive, and when it comes down to empathy and compassion, I know I’m going to have to support them quite a bit over the next couple of days… We had a counselling team here earlier. We had our women’s girls’ school counsellors come over. Now we have persons from the Ministry of Education, and no doubt we will have them again for the next couple of days,” he said.

The principal’s update followed a statement released by Wolmer’s Joint Board of Management, which detailed that the student was rushed to hospital where he was later pronounced dead after he collapsed at school.

The board expressed profound sorrow for the loss of the student and further extended its condolence to his parents, relatives, friends, classmates, teachers, and all whose lives he touched.

The board also said that affected peers and staff were being provided with emotional support and asked that the privacy of the student’s family and the school community be respected at this time.

“We also urge the public to refrain from speculation or the circulation of unverified information concerning the circumstances of his passing. The Wolmer’s family stands together in grief and will continue to support the student’s loved ones in the days ahead,” the board said.

World.title: ‘We are not breaking ranks’
World.content:
TWO defence lawyers representing murder accused Andre Ruddock appeared in court on Monday as his trial continued, despite colleagues maintaining a pledge to withdraw legal services from all criminal matters islandwide in pursuit of amendments to the Firearms Prohibition Restriction and Regulation Act 2022.

But according to attorney Anthony Williams, he and fellow counsel Venice Brown did not break ranks with their colleagues. Instead they had a duty to their client which had to be fulfilled.

“We want to make it very clear that we are not breaking ranks with our colleagues. Myself and Miss Brown are 150 per cent in support of our colleagues. However, there is a difference — the Jamaica Bar Association knows about it and they also sanctioned it. The difference is that when you are in a part-heard matter you can’t just go and strike like that. You have to seek the permission of your client in writing,” Williams told the Jamaica Observer.

“If you don’t seek the permission of your client in writing, then you can be deemed to have neglected your client and you can be sanctioned as well. Also, the court can proceed with the matter and the judge can possibly cite you for contempt of court,” Williams explained.

He added that in the absence of defence attorneys a judge may decide to proceed in a part-heard matter because lawyers are expected to be present. He said that if they don’t turn up, they do so at their own peril.

“The situation is different when you are in a part-heard matter, and the lawyer, whoever he or she is, cannot just abandon their client just like that; they have to seek the client’s permission. And in this particular case our client said, ‘Run with it.’ There are many other lawyers who are in the same position, but we have not abandoned our colleagues,” Williams stressed.

In addition to Williams and Brown, a number of attorneys showed up for their clients on Monday at the Home Circuit Court for various reasons, including that some were not in agreement with the protest action.

Essentially, the defence lawyers are arguing that the Act removes discretionary powers from judges, as it mandates a 15-year minimum sentence for an illegal gun possession conviction.

Williams’ client, Ruddock, is being tried in relation to the October 17, 2021 killing of 39-year-old Taneka Gardner in what has been described as a human sacrifice ritual at Pathways International Restoration Ministries in Albion St James. Ruddock allegedly cut Gardner’s throat on the instruction of his now deceased pastor, Kevin Smith.

Smith died in a car crash in St Catherine a few days later while being transported to Kingston to be charged with the incident.

On Monday the fourth witness in the case, a police sergeant based in St James, returned to complete his testimony which he started last week.

He described the scene at the church as “evil, fluid and chaotic”.

“People were moving from one direction to the next. One body was seen close to the pool area,” the witness recalled.

He explained that members of the Jamaica Defence Force (JDF) made their way through barbed wires to gain access to the compound of the church where three people, including Gardner and two male members of the church, lay dead.

One of the men was allegedly killed by Smith, while the police were said to have shot dead the other man who had rushed toward them with a knife. Based on the sustained gunfire and the sacrificial-type activities that were taking place at the church, the security forces had to call for adequate back-up, which included support from the military.

“The soldiers got to the barbed wire. I saw them climbing over and onto the church premises. On reaching the premises I shouted out to them. Police, accompanied by army personnel, proceeded towards a person who was kneeling behind the column at the entrance gate. I observed them accosting this person. They arrested him and carried out a search of him. The police and soldiers then forced open the big entrance gate,” the witness said.

“When they got there, the man was still in the kneeling position with white cloth over his head. He stood up and the officers searched him. When he stood up, from where I was standing [on the roof] I couldn’t see his face. I could only see the height of the person who was about 5 feet two or three inches tall. At that time there were a lot of police personnel and soldiers around this man. They took him on[to] the roadway and I couldn’t see what took place from there,” the witness said, without being able to say who the man was.

World.title: Stitchie: A legacy that connected dancehall, gospel
World.content:
Lieutenant Stitchie at the 2019 Sterling Gospel Music Awards

Lieutenant Stitchie’s voice may have fallen silent, but the influence of the veteran deejay — who commanded respect in both secular dancehall and gospel music spheres — is expected to continue reverberating across generations.

The veteran artiste, whose given name was Cleveland “Cleve” Laing, died at Kingston Public Hospital on Monday morning, one day shy of his 61st birthday.

The news comes less than 24 hours after his wife, Sophia Laing, confirmed that the entertainer had been hospitalised with a low blood count and was receiving treatment.

His passing closes a remarkable chapter in Jamaican music — one that began in dancehall and found a path to gospel.

For distinguished cultural analyst, Professor Donna Hope, Lieutenant Stitchie’s ability to remain loved across musical boundaries was rooted not only in his talent, but also in his personality that endeared him to audiences.

“Stitchie was loved because a lot of his songs were humorous. They were fun and they made people happy,” Hope said. She pointed to his enduring early hit Wear Yu Size, noting that the song was “digestible”, catchy and non-combative — qualities that helped establish his connection with listeners.

“Stitchie had an excellent career in dancehall and that followed him into gospel,” Hope continued. “I saw Mr Vegas made a post and I’m sure several others will as the news spreads because a lot of the artistes he would have came up with in that era were still close to him even though they were doing different genres.”

Entertainers and government officials took to social media to pay tribute to the deejay. Among them Prime Minister Andrew Holness, Tarrus Riley and Chevelle Franklyn (who also transitioned from dancehall to gospel).

Professor Hope shared that Stitchie’s significance extended beyond his music.

“Having a relationship with secular artistes was something Stitchie did well because he understood that it was important to minister to the sheep that ought to be brought into the fold,” she said. “This loss will be felt across genres and eras. He is a part of the industry in a way few artistes were, and so he will never be forgotten.”

Basillia Barnaby-Cuff, founder and director of Sterling Gospel Music Awards, agreed.

“I think Stitchie set a beautiful example of how you can remain an influence with people even when you’re in a different season of your life,” she said. “He was able to bridge the gap between the secular and gospel. He was still able to be on stage with secular artistes, singing gospel without compromising his walk with Christ.”

For Barnaby-Cuff, that was the essence of Stitchie’s ministry — not simply preaching to people already inside the church, but allowing his life and testimony to reach those outside it.

“It is about allowing your life to minister to those you wish will come over to Christianity,” she said.

The Sterling Gospel Music Awards family shared a particularly close connection with the artiste in his later years. A few years ago, Stitchie was honoured at the awards with the KFC Big Deal Award, an occasion Barnaby-Cuff now views with gratitude.

“I am just so happy we were able to give him his flowers while he was alive,” she said. “The gospel fraternity and we here at the Sterling Gospel Music Awards are really saddened by this news.”

Even as his health deteriorated, the organisation continued to support him, raising funds towards his care in the hope that his condition would improve.

“As the body of Christ, we are so grateful that he used the latter part of his years in ministry, and that he brought so many other persons to Christ,” she said. “He truly lived a full life and, as children of God, we don’t mourn as if we don’t have hope, and so that hope is something we hold on to and that one day we will see him again in the great resurrection.

Stitchie emerged from the competitive sound-system culture of Spanish Town in the early 1980s, working alongside artistes including Papa San and Wickerman. His breakthrough came in 1986 with the humorous Wear Yu Size, followed by songs such as Natty Dread, as his distinctive delivery and ability to connect with audiences propelled him beyond Jamaica. In 1988, he secured a recording deal with Atlantic Records, marking another significant milestone in a career that was increasingly taking him onto the international stage.

But it was his decision to walk away from secular music and embrace Christianity in 1997 that would ultimately redefine his legacy.

In 2014 he published his autobiography and among his accolades was honoured with the Order of Distinction in the rank of Officer in 2021 for his contribution to music.

World.title: Debutants Tru-Juice remaining calm despite table-topping JPL start
World.content:
Tru-Juice FC striker Daniel Roberts celebrates after scoring the winning goal in the club’s 1-0 victory over Molynes United in the Jamaica Premier League at Stadium East on Sunday. (Photo: JPL)

DESPITE Tru-Juice FC’s strong start to their debut Jamaica Premier League (JPL) season, Assistant Coach Craig Richards says it’s too early to be thinking about the play-offs.

The newly promoted club lead the JPL stadings on seven points after a 1-0 win over Molynes United at Stadium East on Sunday. Striker Daniel Roberts’s 62nd-minute strike was enough as Tru-Juice stay unbeaten after their first three games. They also join Montego Bay United and Waterhouse as the only two clubs who have yet to concede.

Richards says he was pleased with the team’s execution, after nearly a week of preparation.

“We knew that it was going to be a tough-fought game. We know how the Molynes team plays and we’ve been training all week to nullify them — and we also worked on ways to hurt them and it paid dividends,” he said.

“When we play against certain teams, we really assess them and train accordingly, so I’m very pleased. There are parts of the game that I’m disappointed with but there are aspects that I’m very pleased [about], and that’s football. I’m pleased we got three points on the board, and we look forward to the next game.”

Tru-Juice have attracted several top players to join their inaugural season, including Reggae Boyz Alex Marshall, Gadail Irving, and Tafari Chambers.

The Linstead based-club caught the eyes of many during their opening game when they thrashed reigning Caribbean Cup champions Mount Pleasant FA 4-0 and held last season’s semi-finalists, Montego Bay United, to a goalless draw.

Although starting on a positive note, Richards says they’re not placing too much pressure on themselves.

“Our objective is to play quality football and maximise on the points and [see] wherever that leads us,” he said. “Our aim is to compete. And competing can lead us to good places but as it relates to [the] objective [of] top six or whatever, if that should come then we are very welcoming for that but for now we’re taking it three games at a time.

“This is our first season. There are quite a number of teams that have been competing in this competition for some time so they have some experience. While we have experienced players, the club itself is in its first season so we continue to set different objectives at different points of the season, and we’ll see where that leads us.”

Mount Pleasant Head Coach Theodore Whitmore was pleased his team got off the mark after their 2-0 win over Dunbeholden at the Dunbeholden Sports Complex.

After losing their first two games of the season, goals from Trayvone Reid and Nicholas Nelson ensured the St Ann-based club picked up all three points.

“It doesn’t feel like three, it feels like six points,” Whitmore said. “I think we would have met our objective when we got two goals this afternoon; we didn’t concede, we kept a clean sheet, so I think it’s something that we can build on.

“When you look at the table and see Mount Peasant at the foot, nobody expects that. It wasn’t pleasing even for the fans that travel with us every Sunday, so it’s very pleasing [to beat Dunbeholden]. We look forward to the next one; and it gives us now a momentum going into the next game and into the semi-final of the Caribbean Cup.”

World.title: ALL THE KING’S MEN
World.content:
Hunain Shah (second right) of Jamaica Kingsmen celebrates with teammates (from left) Keemo Paul, Andre Russell, and Vitel Lawes after getting the wicket of Roston Chase during their Republic Bank Caribbean Premier League T20 match with St Lucia Kings in Gros Islet, St Lucia, on Friday, August 21. (PHOTO: CPLT20)

JAMAICA Kingsmen Head of Operations Atishai Mansingh says a strong collective effort will be needed to continue cricket’s revival on the island.

The Kingsmen finished runners-up of the recently concluded Republic Bank Caribbean Premier League (CPL), after losing to the Antigua and Barbuda Falcons in the final in Barbados.

It was a remarkable run for the Jamaican franchise in their first season as the Kingsmen, having been inactive for the 2024 and 2025 seasons after former owner Kris Persaud sold the franchise and moved on to the now-champions Falcons.

This season also saw the return of CPL to Sabina Park for the first time since 2019, with four games hosted in Kingston.

While pleased with the franchise’s start, Mansingh says he’s focused on helping to grow the sport locally.

“CPL coming back is not going to solve all of the issues that we have in Jamaica cricket,” he said. “It’s a spark, and what we do with that spark is what will determine whether this moment becomes a temporary celebration or the beginning of a genuine revival — and the revival is going to start from the top down.

“We want to encourage all of public and corporate Jamaica to see the highest-paying sport for what it is. The fact is, we’re not going to fill Sabina Park this year, we’re not going to fill Sabina Park next year, but we have to work towards filling Sabina Park in the years coming, because if this park is seen as a football park, as an entertainment park, for the history that it holds, every single one of us are failing. Filling Sabina Park is not about the Kingsmen putting on social media s and giving away tickets. It’s about the teamwork [and] the support which is needed to to build these cricket structures in Jamaica.”

Mansingh says cricket’s development locally cannot be driven solely by finances but must also be fuelled by passion for the sport.

“Players cannot rebuild it alone. The Government and sponsors, though we always request them, also cannot build it alone. Clubs, schools, families, businesses and supporters must all play a part,” he said.

“If we don’t put the love into the sport, who’s going to? [People] say, ‘Who’s going to fix cricket?’ ‘CPL come, they have money, they’re going to fix it’, ‘This person have money so they’re going to fix it’. Money is not going to fix this; it’s the love that we all possess for the sport that’s going to bring the happiness back to the sport.”

Mansingh says more emphasis needs to be placed on women’s cricket as well, with the debut of the Jamaica Empress team in the Women’s CPL providing a good starting point.

“Cricket is not just about a man with a ball and a man with a bat,” he said. “The women are equally important for this sport’s growth. The Kingsmen launched the first-ever Jamaica women’s CPL franchise, the Jamaica Empress. It has given an opportunity to women to see the sport as a way of employment. A sport that was always seen as a gentleman’s sport has now been seen as just simply a sport.

“That is very crucial, because when the likes of Hayley Matthews, Stafanie Taylor, Chinelle Henry are able to go to tournaments across the world and earn US$250,000 [$38 million] for a six-week tournament, that is eye-opening to state that this sport is not just going to fill the pockets of men any more but it’s going to create structures and systems for young girls to say, ‘I want to be like them when I’m older.’ ”

World.title: Wolmer’s Boys student dies after collapsing during class
World.content:
Wolmer's Boys School Gate file photo

KINGSTON, Jamaica — A fourth-form Wolmer’s Boys High School student has died following a medical emergency at the school on Monday, the school has confirmed.

In a statement, the Wolmer’s Joint Board of Management indicated that the student collapsed during class and was rushed to hospital, where he was later pronounced dead.

The board expressed profound sorrow at the passing of the young man, describing it as a deeply painful loss for his family and for the entire Wolmer’s community.

“The Joint Board extends its heartfelt condolences to his parents, relatives, friends, classmates, teachers and all whose lives he touched,” the statement read.

The school said it is providing support to affected students and members of staff and urged the public to refrain from circulating unverified information concerning the circumstances of his passing.

World.title: Lt Stitchie, dancehall icon who found new calling in gospel, dies at 60
World.content:
Lieutenant Stitchie (Photo via Instagram)

Veteran deejay Lieutenant Stitchie has died.

Observer Online understands that the entertainer, whose given name was Cleveland “Cleve” Laing, died at hospital on Monday, just one day before he would have celebrated his 61st birthday.

The tragic news comes less than 24 hours after the entertainer’s wife, Sophia Laing confirmed that he had been hospitalised with a low blood count and was receiving treatment at the Kingston Public Hospital.

READ: Lt Stitchie hospitalised with ‘low blood count’

The pioneering dancehall entertainer whose career spanned the formative years of the genre before he made a transition to gospel music, had been ailing for some time. His health issued stemmed largely from a debilitating stroke in the first week of September 2024.

Stitchie emerged from the competitive sound-system culture of Spanish Town in the early 1980s, working alongside figures including Papa San, Wickerman and Major Worries. His breakthrough came in 1986 with the humorous Wear Yuh Size, followed by Natty Dread, before his career expanded internationally with a recording deal with Atlantic Records in 1988.

But perhaps the most defining chapter of Stitchie’s life came when he left secular dancehall behind and devoted himself to ministry after becoming a born-again Christian in 1997. He subsequently built a thriving career in gospel reggae as his transition did little to diminish the respect he commanded within the wider entertainment fraternity.

His death is expected to reverberate across both communities, with artistes who shared stages, sound systems and recording studios with him likely to reflect on the contribution of a man who managed to reinvent himself without losing his place in Jamaican music history.

World.title: Bruxelles veut clarifier les responsabilités des autorités face aux catastrophes climatiques
World.content:
“Ceci étant dit, a-t-il ajouté, nous devons veiller à ce que tout soit parfaitement clair […] Qui est responsable de quoi ? Qui est chargé de la lutte contre les incendies ? Qui est responsable du financement ? Qui est chargé de la plantation d’arbres dans les villes ? Qui est responsable des mesures de santé destinées aux personnes âgées ? Et ainsi de suite.”

Pourquoi c’est important

Attribuer la responsabilité des risques peut sembler n’être qu’un détail technique. Mais lorsque ce n’est pas fait, la gestion et la prévention des catastrophes climatiques peuvent devenir confuses.

Le feu de forêt qui a causé des dégâts d’une ampleur inédite le mois dernier dans la réserve naturelle des Hautes Fagnes, en Belgique, en est un bon exemple. D’après les enquêtes menées par les médias locaux, l’incendie aurait été provoqué par des étincelles provenant de machines agricoles qui fauchait des terres complètement desséchées — et personne n’était chargé de prévenir les risques d’incendie.

Le gouvernement fédéral belge est chargé de coordonner la préparation du pays aux effets du changement climatique, mais la gestion des terres est une compétence régionale, et différentes autorités peuvent prononcer des interdictions de fauchage. Une province située près des Hautes Fagnes a imposé une telle interdiction, mais aucune autre ne l’a fait. Et un organisme régional du gouvernement wallon a chargé un prestataire de procéder au fauchage dans la réserve naturelle au plus fort de la sécheresse.

Une zone forestière calcinée à la suite d’un incendie de forêt dans la réserve naturelle des Hautes Fagnes, près de Baraque Michel, dans l’est de la Belgique, le 9 septembre 2026. | ERIC Lalmand/AFP via Getty Images

Les responsables politiques d’opposition se sont appuyés sur l’incendie des Hautes Fagnes pour réclamer de centraliser cette compétence en créant une cellule interfédérale chargée du climat. Lors d’un événement organisé en septembre, le directeur général de la DG Clima de la Commission, Kurt Vandenberghe, a estimé que la gestion de l’incendie en Belgique illustrait pourquoi l’exécutif européen cherche à clarifier les responsabilités des risques : “Cela montre clairement qu’il reste beaucoup à faire.”

Si personne ne se charge de la prévention, les gouvernements ne peuvent que réagir face à l’aggravation des catastrophes, préviennent les experts.

World.title: Tax cuts, handouts and blind hope: Europe finds few tools to fight a coming energy crisis
World.content:
"We see more EVs than ever sold in Europe now, we see electric heat pumps replacing gas boilers and oil boilers than ever before — so yes, there are actually a lot of positive things happening," EU energy chief Dan Jørgensen told reporters in a response to a question from POLITICO. "Many times, one of the best things we can do in these situations that also works in the short term is active electrification."

He added that he was "in no way implying that that is enough," and there were "many big structural things that we need to do that will not help consumers tomorrow or even this year, but there are actually also things that member states can do."

Irish Energy Minister Darragh O'Brien, whose government holds the EU's six-month rotating presidency, also described the deployment of renewables as the main way to address rising costs, emphasizing that Dublin was working to hasten the adoption of a new EU law aimed at strengthening the bloc's electricity grids.

But he said the EU's ability to address the current rise in costs was limited.

"There are flexibilities that member states have at our disposal around taxation, but I think our citizens are aware that there's no government in Europe that is going to be able to protect their citizens from every single price increase," he told reporters. "The fundamental reason for that," he said, was "our over-dependence in the European Union on imported fossil fuel."

Discussions were dominated by the question of where responsibility for addressing rising prices ought to lie. Member countries called on the Commission to institute a windfall tax on energy companies making bumper profits, while the EU executive said it was up to individual countries to decide.

World.title: Burnham tried to plot the next 7 years of UK politics in one speech
World.content:
Instead he promised a national commission on electoral reform, which would report back before the general election. “We will contest the next election with a manifesto commitment to change the electoral system,” he said — effectively putting his preferred option on the ballot paper.

It is not the only area where Britain awaits the detail. Burnham announced that he would overturn laws barring public investment in water firms, but said little about what the ownership of those firms will actually look like. POLITICO reported last month that aides were still weighing up a buffet of options and could choose multiple models at once.

Burnham touched only briefly on military spending, saying nothing of how he would reach Britain’s commitment to spend 3.5 percent of GDP on the military by 2035. Other touchstone issues for sections the British public, such as the migrants crossing the English Channel on small boats, received only brief mentions too.

It was classic Burnham. It is the way the new prime minister has worked for decades — set out the broad policy intention then work out the details later.

It was the approach he took as sport minister in the late 2000s, when he decided he wanted free swimming lessons for children and pushed for the policy without yet knowing how it could happen.

In the end, Burnham got his way on the swimming lessons. But this time he’s really in the deep end.

“We can do that to any country we want,” Guilfoyle said, according to the report, referring to political turmoil that was rocking Bucharest at the time. “We can do that here,” she added.

Papastavrou reportedly responded that the U.S. could not replace Greece’s government because it had been elected by the people. The paper noted that Guilfoyle’s lawyer disputed the description of the conversation.

“The United States values its strategic partnership with Romania, which remains strong across our shared priorities, including energy security and defense burden shifting,” a State Department spokesperson told POLITICO when asked about about Guilfoyle’s reported comments.
