World.title: Tangara carriages locked down over 'train surfing' and break-in fears
World.content:
Passengers are being barred from using the rear carriages of all Tangara trains to prevent people breaking into the crew cabs and riding on the back of them.

The policy was already in force on selected night-time and weekend services, but has now been applied to every Tangara train for the duration of the school holidays.

More than two years have passed since the government announced a $447 million program to improve security and extend the life of the aging Tangara fleet by up to 12 years.

To date, only one out of 55 Tangara trains has received the full refurbishment, including a CCTV system.

It means passengers, including those travelling on grand final weekend, will find the rear carriages of Tangaras locked and the lights turned off.

The lights will be switched off and the doors locked on the back carriages. (ABC News)

'Commuters first, dropkicks second'

Shadow NSW Transport Minister Natalie Ward said it was "embarrassing" the government had effectively surrendered to vandals and train-surfers.

"It can't be 'lights out' for commuters. You can't give up on this," she said.

"Transport policy has to be commuters first, dropkicks second."

However, state Transport Minister John Graham said misbehaviour on trains risked derailing the schedule, causing more inconvenience for commuters in the long run.

He said locking up the rear carriages was a "pragmatic step".

"It's one we don't want to take, but reliability is our number one focus."

A covering has been installed to prevent people from train surfing. (Supplied: NSW Government)

Riding a social media wave

Train-surfing or "buffer riding" has been an ongoing issue on the Tangaras, fuelled by social media videos where people post and boast about their "achievements".

The lack of CCTV on the fleet has made the trains especially susceptible to vandalism, as has the "buffer": a platform at the rear of the Tangaras from which train surfers can jump from the platform.

To eliminate the dangerous practice, Sydney Trains fitted slanted "nose cones" onto all the buffers, to deprive train surfers of a flat surface.

They have had some success.

On the T4 Eastern Suburbs and Illawarra line, there were only three incidents between July and September, whereas there were 127 cases of buffer riding in the 12 months prior.

"Those cones have made a big difference," Mr Graham said.

The nose cones have had some success in reducing incidents of train surfing. (Supplied: NSW Government)

However, Rail, Tram and Bus Union secretary Toby Warnes said the internal door to the crew cab was being repeatedly targeted.

"I've seen some of the social media videos myself," he said.

"It doesn't take much to open that. And once you have opened that, it's not then difficult to open the actual door to get out onto the [rear] platform."

He said people hoping to "big note" themselves were risking their own lives, and the safety of others.

"It puts the people who are operating the train in danger and the general public too, particularly if it's being done near stations," he said.

Internal Sydney Trains documents seen by the ABC suggest the organisation is scrambling to install new locks on crew cab doors.

Plain-clothes security officers are also patrolling some Tangara trains.

The lack of CCTV in the Tangaras makes them vulnerable to vandalism. (ABC News)

Reviving an aging fleet

The once-futuristic Tangara was introduced in 1988 and will remain in service until the mid 2030s, while a replacement is built.

The Minns government plans to build the new fleet in the Hunter, where the Tangara was manufactured, thanks to a $12 billion investment over 15 years.

Chris Minns's government is overseeing the refurbishment of the Tangara fleet. (ABC News)

However, the state opposition has criticised the speed of the Tangara refurbishment program, which includes computer, security and customer information system upgrades.

Ms Ward said the $447 million program had only refurbished a single train since it was announced in June 2024.

"It's a very long, slow process that doesn't seem to fix the problem," she said.

Mr Graham defended the speed of the program, saying the upgrade to each train would be comprehensive.

"It's so significant that [we're] testing this train as if it were a new train on the network," he said.

Sydney Trains said it hoped to have two more refurbished Tangaras in service by the end of the year.

World.title: Four years since retail laws passed, but no help for cafe owner
World.content:
It has been four years since the Tasmanian government overhauled the state's retail laws, with one of its aims to help small business owners resolve disputes without going to court.

But that has been no comfort for cafe owner Hayley Dick.

Despite the act passing parliament and receiving royal assent from the governor, only two of the 90 sections have come into effect.

It has left Ms Dick locked in a months-long dispute with her landlord over responsibility for a compliance issue: the installation of a grease trap.

It is a dispute that may end up in the courts.

Hayley Dick has written to state politicians for help. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

The Retail Leases Act 2022 reformed the Fair Trading retail laws and regulations legislated in 1998.

The laws relate to the rights and obligations of landlords and tenants of those in retail or other business premises.

The Department of Justice says when commenced, the new act will provide powers for a prescribed body to make determinations in relation to certain matters for retail tenancy disputes.

In the meantime, Ms Dick says there are limited resources to help with her dispute.

Hayley Dick says it has been a frustrating and stressful year dealing with the dispute. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

She is currently in discussion with lawyers to escalate the issue to court and estimates she may face hefty legal costs.

"I don't know where the hell to get $50,000 from," she said.

"Why is it that we don't have anywhere to go to?"

Battle of responsibility

Last year, Ms Dick took over the lease of a cafe premises in George Town, in the state's north.

A letter from TasWater to the building's owners in February, seen by the ABC, states the building will become non-compliant from August if a 1,000-kilogram grease trap is not installed.

A grease trap or arrester acts like a strainer to catch food waste in wastewater.

A grease trap keeps food scraps and other by-products out of wastewater. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

The owners passed the notice to Ms Dick, who says the alteration would cost at least $29,000

But Ms Dick's lease strictly states she is not to alter the structure of the premises.

She believes the responsibility of installing the trap sits with the building's owners.

"Because they keep saying they're not taking responsibility, we have nowhere to go but to the Supreme Court or another court to actually get a ruling on it to be able to get them to do it," Ms Dick said.

" [TasWater] can close us down at any point. "

TasWater is urging the business owners to install a "compliant liquid trade waste pre-treatment system" at the premises. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

The landlords were contacted for comment but did not respond to questioning.

Instead, they referred the ABC to other lease and business bodies such as The Real Estate Institute of Tasmania (REIT) or Tenant's Union of Tasmania.

Reform 'continuing': minister

Small Business Minister Guy Barnett responded to Ms Dick's unanswered emails after the ABC began making enquiries.

"Although other legislative priorities have affected the timing of this reform, I want to assure you that work to implement the Retail Leases Act 2022 is continuing," he wrote to Ms Dick.

"I recognise that court proceedings can be costly and time-consuming, particularly for small businesses."

Ms Dick said she had spent about $5,000 on legal fees.

Hayley Dick is not sure where to turn to resolve the dispute. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

Responding to ABC questions, Mr Barnett said the government was committed to implementing the act and its mediation arrangements.

"The bill is complex," he said.

"With feedback from a number of stakeholders identifying that further amendments were required and a commitment was made to the Legislative Council to bring the bill back to parliament before it is proclaimed [enacted]," he said.

"Retail tenancy disputes remain subject to the existing Retail Tenancies Code, and CBOS (Consumer Building and Occupational Services) can assist parties to resolve disputes, including through investigation and negotiation."

Guy Barnett says the act needs to go back to parliament for amendments. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Once commenced, the new laws would include a range of measures not currently on offer, including mandatory pre-contractual disclosures, the timing and basis for rent reviews, arrangements regarding payment of the landlord's outgoings by the tenant, security deposits and stronger compliance and enforcement powers.

Ms Dick said while CBOS could help parties negotiate, it cannot make a binding decision.

"We've already spent months trying to resolve it through lawyers without success. If CBOS-assisted negotiation also fails, the next step is still court," she said.

Launceston Chamber of Commerce's Alina Bain said it was not in the landlords' or tenants' interests to be at odds with each other.

"Any delay in business is undesirable, and courts shouldn't be used as the mechanism to resolve all disputes."

Alina Bain says it is best if businesses can avoid the courts. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

Four-year wait to enact law

Labor's spokesperson for small business Brian Mitchell raised questions in parliament in August about why the retail leases act had not been fully enacted.

The questions were taken on notice.

Ministers have 15 parliamentary sitting days to respond, which will expire in late November.

Brian Mitchell says the government has not worked fast enough to enact the law. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

"Small businesses like Hayley's are vital in Tasmania's regions and shouldn't have to break the bank to address tenancy disputes," Mr Mitchell said.

Upper House independent MLC Rosemary Armitage also noticed it was not the only act to not have come into force.

"While I've been looking into the acts that haven't been proclaimed, I have come across one from 2007, so maybe 2022 [for the retail leases act] is not as bad as I thought," she said.

"How many people would realise, though, that even when a bill has received royal assent, it hasn't been fully proclaimed?"

Among the questions put to the government in August were queries about whether the Tasmanian Civil and Administrative Tribunal was among stakeholders consulted in the review process, and what regulations remain to be drafted or finalised before the act can commence.

The path forward for Ms Dick may be clearer after the government's parliamentary response.

World.title: Manchester City found guilty in Premier League's biggest scandal
World.content:
English football giant Manchester City has been found guilty of arranging "sham" contracts as part of financial breaches that have become the biggest scandal in Premier League history.

An independent panel has found City guilty of almost all 115 unprecedented charges against it, covering a nine-year period in which the Abu Dhabi-backed team changed the landscape of the richest and most popular soccer league in the world.

City's alleged financial wrongdoing was worth more than 900 million British pounds ($1.703 billion), and Premier League chief executive Richard Masters said the ruling showed City "systematically broke Premier League rules for nearly a decade."

"This disciplinary case, and this decision, are the most significant in Premier League history," he said.

What punishment could Manchester City face?

City now faces severe sanctions, including a huge points deduction or even expulsion from the league.

The league said it would decide sanctions in a separate hearing held by the independent commission.

City has been accused of failing to provide accurate financial information, submitting inflated figures for sponsorship deals, hiding payments and breaching financial rules. (AP: Jon Super)

City has always denied wrongdoing, saying in 2023 when the charges were laid that there was a "comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence that exists in support of its position".

In a statement, the club said it was "disappointed and surprised" by the ruling, plans to appeal, and will be "relentless" in its fight to clear its name.

Any appeal by City would have to be made by Friday, local time, the league said.

The club's executives have denied any wrongdoing and plan to appeal the verdict. (AP: Jon Super)

The ruling comes after it emerged last week that the charges against City were expected to be upheld following an exhaustive process.

The Premier League initiated its case more than three years ago, but allegations first arose in 2018 from leaked club emails and documents.

What did Manchester City allegedly do wrong?

$357 million: How much Sheikh Mansour paid to buy Manchester City.

How much Sheikh Mansour paid to buy Manchester City. $7.87 billion: Manchester City's current value, the seventh-most-valuable club in world football.

Manchester City's current value, the seventh-most-valuable club in world football. $1.34 billion: The club's 2025 revenue, up from just $228 million in 2007-08.

The club's 2025 revenue, up from just $228 million in 2007-08. 8: The club's league titles after 2008, up from 2 beforehand.

The club's league titles after 2008, up from 2 beforehand. 22: The club's major trophies after 2008, up from 9 beforehand.

The club's major trophies after 2008, up from 9 beforehand. $241.8 million: The club's most expensive player transfer fee since 2008.

The club's most expensive player transfer fee since 2008. 16: The club's seasons in European top-flight tournaments since 2008, up from 1 beforehand.

City was accused of a raft of financial violations between 2009 and 2018, a period when the north-west club, long in the shadow of great rival Manchester United, was transforming itself into a record-breaking global superpower that has won multiple Premier League titles and the Champions League.

The violations included failing to provide accurate financial information and submitting inflated figures for sponsorship deals from Abu Dhabi, hiding payments, and breaching financial rules the Premier League and UEFA, European soccer's governing body, established to keep clubs financially stable by not spending beyond their means.

City also faced many other charges of failing to cooperate with the investigation between 2018 and 2023.

"An independent commission has found Manchester City guilty of all charges related to serious breaches of the Premier League's financial rules over a nine-season period," the league said.

It also found the club guilty of "the majority of charges in relation to its failure to co-operate with the league's investigation."

Regarding the sponsorship deals, the league said: "Manchester City arranged 'sham' contracts [which misrepresented the true agreement between the parties] with a number of its commercial partners, as well as relying on 'sham' agreements with others, to artificially inflate the club's revenues and reduce its costs. "The club … filed misstated accounts and concealed the true state of its finances from its auditors and football regulators."

The purpose of City's "schemes" was found to have been to "artificially inflate the club's revenues, and reduce its costs, by more than 900 million British pounds during the affected period, to appear to comply with financial rules," the league said.

The finding suggests City's rise to the top of English football, fuelled by Abu Dhabi investments that delivered expensive, star-studded squads, was achieved at least in part by evading the league's financial regulations.

What could the fallout be?

The verdict is expected to trigger a slew of lawsuits from rival clubs seeking compensation for being affected by City's actions.

Man City guilty of breaching EPL financial rules, punishment still pending Global football heavyweights Manchester City have been found guilty of 114 beaches of the English Premier League's financial regulations, after a years-long investigation.

There is also the question of whether City's top stars, like Erling Haaland and Rayan Cherki, will stay at the club and what the future holds for owner Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan.

Mr Al Nahyan, the deputy prime minister of the United Arab Emirates and a member of Abu Dhabi's royal family, bought City in 2008 and has gone on to own a group of worldwide teams — under the City Football Group banner — including New York City FC and Melbourne City.

Over the weekend, City chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak said there remained a "confidence and intent in proving the club's innocence".

The appeal could end up in the High Court in London if City feels the process in the case was unfair and/or impartial.

AP

World.title: Inside the fossil fuel industry's push into Australian classrooms
World.content:
Alison Holt had never heard of the Energy Club before she was told they would be taking over her science class.

At the time, she was teaching at Busselton Senior High School in Western Australia when she realised the series of incursions would disrupt her teaching schedule.

"I was told probably a day or two before because, you know, you've got to plan ahead very tightly being a science teacher," Ms Holt said.

"Without any consultation and any permission from the parents, we had three hours taken out of our very tight curriculum time.

"So that's nearly a week of science gone."

Former Busselton Senior High School teacher Alison Holt. (Supplied: Alison Holt)

Ms Holt recalled asking her head of department about what the program involved.

"They said, 'Oh, they just come in and, you know, talk about mining and, you know, the petrochemical industry', and immediately my hair went up on the back of my neck."

'A sustainable future' rebrand

Until 2021, the not-for-profit Energy Club WA used to be called The Petroleum Club of WA, and the initiative offered at Alison Holt's school was its Next Generation Energy Program, which has been running since 1991.

Woodside Energy and Exxon Mobil are just two of the major oil and gas companies the Energy Club lists as sponsors.

The course involves industry professionals volunteering time to deliver three lessons with a focus on "energy literacy" and career opportunities.

"We invite our valued sponsors to leverage the Next Generation Schools Program," its flyer states.

"By supporting our established initiative, you can maximise impact by pooling resources … save on development costs, and strengthen community ties through our well-connected framework."

A presentation about natural gas is part of the Next Generation Energy Program. (Supplied: Energy Club WA)

In March 2021, the non-profit decided "to rebrand and move forward as Energy Club WA so that the brand reflects the continued promise of connecting people with energy for a sustainable future".

But as the incursion got under way at the Busselton school, Ms Holt said what she observed seemed inconsistent with that message.

In one activity, the presenters used bread, chocolate spread and sprinkles to simulate how exploration drilling works.

"He'd put Nutella on one piece of bread, then he'd put sprinkles on the next piece, and he'd just make this big four- or five-layer sandwich," she explained.

Students were then invited up to "drill for oil" using plastic straws pushed down through the layers of bread.

A chemical engineer from BP delivering the Next Generation Energy Program at a school in 2023. (Facebook: Armadale Senior High School)

Ms Holt also had concerns about the way the presentations framed the role of gas.

"He spoke about … the different sectors where energy was needed, how it was provided, and then talked about how gas was the answer, you know, in the transition to renewable energy," she said.

After the first of the three sessions, Ms Holt asked whether renewable energy would also be part of the program.

"They just said, 'Oh, don't worry, in our final hour, we touch on renewables'," she said.

In a statement, Energy Club WA general manager Kate McCarthy said its educational program was reviewed by participating schools to ensure the content was appropriate.

"The classroom teacher is always present during the presentation, and the teacher and school are engaged for feedback on the program and its contents at each visit," she said.

According to the annual report, more than 1,800 students participated in the Next Generation Energy Program in 2025. (Supplied: Energy Club WA )

Mentors for the program were a mix of volunteers and those still working in the industry.

"Sponsors of the Next Generation schools program do not contribute to the committee to develop or review the contents of the program," Ms McCarthy said.

"Energy Club WA has 20 participating schools for 2026."

Design your own carbon capture solution

The Energy Club was one of at least 260 educational programs in Australia sponsored by fossil fuel companies identified in a report by climate advocacy group Comms Declare.

"Our investigation found there is an unacceptable amount of marketing to children in the very places where they should be able to trust the information they're getting," founder Belinda Noble said.

The June 2026 report highlighted a Queensland Museum program sponsored by Shell QGC that invited participants to "draw a diagram of your new carbon capture and storage solution".

Community members protesting outside Queensland Museum in May 2026. (Supplied: CommsDeclare)

Queensland Museum confirmed that some Shell QGC-branded "professional development" materials had been "retired".

Another project with broad access to Australian schools was the Teacher Earth Science Education Programme (TESEP) in Victoria, also sponsored by several coal companies.

One of its teacher resources included a unit on "greening coal", a phrase that critics argue suggests the climate impact of burning coal could be remedied.

"We would say when a company goes building trusted emotional connections with children in institutional environments, we think that can only be described as petro-grooming," Ms Noble said.

Participants in a regional basketball program supported through a Santos partnership. (Supplied: CommsDeclare/Santos)

Comms Declare's investigation found that resources giants including BHP, Chevron, Woodside, Glencore and Shell had disclosed close to $55 million in funding across just six programs and partnerships.

TESEP's website also listed renewable energy and critical minerals companies, and chair Jill Stevens rejected the suggestion the organisation was captured by industry.

"Our educational material is scientifically accurate and is not influenced by our partners," she said.

"Our industry partners are fully disclosed to all participants in our professional development."

Industry-sponsored teaching resources

Another industry-backed not-for-profit is Australian Earth Science Education (AusEarthEd), which develops science resources and programs for schools.

In its 2025 annual report it stated that 71 per cent of its funding came from the energy sector, and four of nine board members were employed by resources companies.

Fossil fuel majors are listed on the Supporters page of the AusEarthEd website. (Supplied: AusEarthEd)

One Woodside-sponsored teaching resource carries the company's logo and includes a graphic of a large shoe print over the Earth, labelled "carbon".

"While we often think that greenhouse gas emissions are only from industrial activities, we all contribute to the global carbon footprint," the material reads.

Woodside operates the North West Shelf project, a project the WA Environmental Protection Authority said if unabated would emit 385 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent.

Child and adolescent psychiatrist Cybele Dey said focusing on the carbon footprint of young people could downplay the role of governments and companies.

"Individual responsibility is not realistic," Dr Dey said.

"Also, it is a real intergenerational betrayal to be saying that a child who has much less autonomy, much less power, didn't cause the problem, somehow is responsible for this really major problem."

Woodside is also involved with in-school educational programs. (Supplied: CommsDeclare/Woodside Energy)

A Woodside spokesperson said it "encourages our employees to contribute to the community".

"We are proud that many of our people choose to volunteer their time and expertise by serving on boards of charities and not-for-profit organisations in their personal capacity and not as Woodside representatives," the spokesperson said.

"The involvement with AusEarthEd is no exception."

AusEarthEd CEO Joanne Watkins said the organisation provided "much-needed resources to schools".

"These partnerships have no influence over the materials provided to students," she said.

Training teachers for 'multiplier effect'

The Comms Declare report also noted instances whereby organisations funded by resources companies were providing accredited professional development for teachers.

For $55, one TESEP professional development course included two nights' accommodation, a field trip, a $100 fuel allowance and free teaching resources.

A 2023 article in the Australasian Institute of Mining and Metallurgy, a resource industry peak body, said the TESEP program aimed to create "well-informed, enthusiastic teachers", with a "multiplier effect" reaching tens of thousands of students.

Images of TESEP workshops and events from the program's 2025 annual report. (Supplied: TESEP)

Eve Mayes is a researcher at Deakin University, studying curriculum, teaching and corporate influence in schools. She said industry-backed education programs could shape how students learn about climate change and the energy transition.

"There have been long-standing partnerships with education communities with particular fossil fuel companies," she said.

"I think what big corporates are getting out of that is, in a sense, to purchase social licence.

"And at times that might be it, but that also might influence … how particular topic areas are taught," Dr Mayes said.

Calls for greater scrutiny

Following the release of the Comms Declare investigation, in June 2026 Greens senator Steph Hodgins-May moved a Senate motion to refer the issue to the Environment and Communications References Committee for inquiry.

The motion was unsuccessful, but Ms Noble said the debate in parliament was a first.

"While the motion did not receive enough support to establish an inquiry, the historic debate marks an important step towards greater scrutiny of fossil fuel industry involvement in childhood settings," she said in a recent statement.

The Santos Foundation supports early childhood education in Papua New Guinea. (Supplied: CommsDeclare/Santos Foundation)

For parents like Phoebe Howe, the concern is not just what the report found, but how much remains hidden from families.

"No-one can tell us as parents exactly how many millions of children are being targeted by these big coal and gas companies, where or how often," she said.

"Parents don't have the time to go out and be researching themselves exactly where and how fossil fuel companies … might be trying to influence their kids."

World.title: Coober Pedy's transition out of administration delayed indefinitely
World.content:
The government's timeline to transition the Coober Pedy council out of administration is set to be scrapped — and no new end date has been fixed.

The remote Far North council was suspended and an administrator appointed in 2019 but Coober Pedy had been due to participate in the April 2027 local government elections, which would have marked the end of the administration.

The state government this month introduced a bill to indefinitely delay that transition.

Local Government Minister Rhiannon Pearce told parliament the council was not ready to be handed back over.

"The principal administrator has advised me in the strongest possible terms of his concerns about the readiness of Coober Pedy council to return to an elected body at the next period local government elections, given the seriousness and the complexity of the issues the administrators are working to rectify," she said.

Rhiannon Pearce says the council is not ready to transition out of administration. (ABC News: Lincoln Rothall)

The council was suspended in 2019 by the former Liberal government in response to soaring debt and findings of maladministration.

Ms Pearce said those issues were exacerbated by Coober Pedy's unique position as the only council in the state responsible for delivering essential services like water and electricity.

Water delivery will be transferred to SA Water by the end of this year, while discussions are underway with the Department for Energy and Mining over electricity supply.

The move to prolong the administration comes despite "a high degree of assurance" from previous local government minister Joe Szakacs that the government "will ensure" the administration ends in 2026 — the original date for the scheduled council elections.

Hybrid model under consideration

Ms Pearce said the recent bill would allow for more flexibility around the timing of the transition, and would also facilitate a hybrid model of governance.

"Having travelled to Coober Pedy to meet with community leaders, they expressed a strong desire for a staged transition back to an elected council," she said.

Coober Pedy has been in administration since 2019. (ABC News: Haidarr Jones)

Administrator Patrick Conlon said the most significant challenges faced by the council were water delivery and debt management.

"I think that there are sufficient indications of progress on the water front and the debt front to suggest that [the end of the administration] shouldn't be too far into next year," he said.

" The issue is what structure you would make a council. It's a town of only 1,600 people. "

George Kountouris, chair of the Coober Pedy Retail, Business and Tourism Association, agreed the council was not yet ready to exit administration.

"After eight years, we've finally come to a point where things are happening," he said.

"We would be in a mess again [if the administration ended] because we owe a lot of money and that still has to be sorted.

"We don't want to get it wrong."

Caravan park owner Jason Wright felt the administration had gone on too long, and said the majority of residents were "over it".

"We have to come out of this administration because that's not doing the town any good," he said.

"But they have to put the things in place to make that transition easy for the local people."

World.title: When are the Dally M Awards? Who is the favourite?
World.content:
The NRL's and NRLW's best gather in Sydney tonight to crown rugby league's biggest stars at the Dally M Awards.

Here is what you need to know.

What time is the Dally M ceremony?

The NRL's Dally M Awards ceremony will start at 6:30pm AEST at The Cutaway in Barangaroo on Sydney Harbour.

Players are set to start arriving on the red carpet at 5:30pm.

How can I watch?

Wednesday's ceremony will be broadcast live on Fox League and Kayo Sports.

ABC Sport will be live-blogging the red carpet and the vote count.

Who are the Dally M favourites?

Brisbane Broncos fullback Tamika Upton is favoured to win her third women's award in four years, while Penrith Panthers halfback Nathan Cleary is the frontrunner for the men's award, which would be his first.

Cleary, who is in hospital after surgery on his badly broken leg, and Upton led the men's and women's counts before voting went behind closed doors earlier in the season.

Cleary led with 38 points after round 12. Warriors prop Jackson Ford was his closest competitor on 35, but suffered a pectoral injury in round 16 and missed the rest of the regular season.

Cleary's next closest competitors are a trio of fullbacks — Penrith's Dylan Edwards (32), North Queensland's Scott Drinkwater (29) and defending winner James Tedesco (27) of the Roosters.

Upton had 12 points from four NRLW games when voting became secret and faces tough competition from Roosters playmaker Tarryn Aiken (11), Raiders fullback Sheridan Gallagher (11), Brisbane halfback Jesse Southwell (10) and rugby sevens star turned Titans five-eighth Teagan Levi (9).

Players can earn a maximum of six points per game, so margins can be closed or extended quickly.

Who are the previous Dally M medallists?

Year Men Women* 2025 James Tedesco Tamika Upton 2024 Jahrome Hughes Olivia Kernick 2023 Kalyn Ponga Tamika Upton 2022 Nicho Hynes Raecene McGregor 2021 Tom Trbojevic Millie Boyle, Emma Tonegato 2020 Jack Wighton Ali Brigginshaw 2019 James Tedesco Jessica Sergis 2018 Roger Tuivasa-Sheck Brittany Breayley

*Before the start of the NRLW in 2018 the best female player was awarded the game's top international women's player.

What other awards will be handed out?

There will be NRL and NRLW Team of the Year named, highlighting the leagues' best in each position, as well as:

Rookie of the Year

Captain of the Year

Coach of the Year

Try of the Year

Tackle of the Year

The Ken Stephen Medal and Veronica White Medal will also be awarded to the men's and women's players who made the biggest contribution to their rugby league communities.

World.title: Six babies die in Qld in three years after contracting syphilis in the womb
World.content:
Six Queensland babies have died in less than three years after contracting syphilis in the womb.

New Queensland Health data shows 55 pregnant women have been diagnosed with the sexually transmitted disease so far this year and six babies have developed congenital syphilis — where the bacterial infection was passed from mother to baby.

One Queensland baby died from the preventable condition in 2026, three died in 2025, and two in 2024.

Brisbane-based infectious disease and public health physician Candice Holland said many babies born with congenital syphilis died shortly after birth. Some babies with syphilis were also stillborn.

"It is a very tragic, but a very preventable, infection in pregnant women," she said.

Public health physician Dr Candice Holland says many babies born with syphilis die shortly after birth. (ABC News: Janelle Miles)

Dr Holland said babies who survived could be left with lifelong health conditions such as blindness, deafness, developmental delays, and problems with their bones and internal organs.

"It's really important that we diagnose that syphilis infection if it occurs in pregnancy as early as possible so that we can reduce the risk of those longer-term complications in the baby," she said.

Women are recommended to be tested for syphilis three times during pregnancy.

A simple blood test can detect the disease.

Dr Holland said if women infected during pregnancy received appropriate treatment, they "have excellent outcomes for themselves and their babies".

But without testing, cases could be easily missed.

"They can have a small lesion which may go unnoticed because it usually doesn't cause any pain," she said.

"That can disappear on its own and then later, people can either have no symptoms for a long time, or they can get symptoms which can look like a lot of other infections, like influenza.

"They can have just swollen glands, rash, fevers and just feel generally unwell."

Women are recommended to be tested for syphilis three times during pregnancy. (ABC News: Janelle Miles)

Dr Holland said people could pass the infection on even when they were not experiencing any symptoms.

Australia's Chief Medical Officer Professor Michael Kidd declared syphilis a communicable disease incident of national significance in August last year amid ongoing high case numbers and concerns about congenital syphilis.

"We share a big burden of that in Queensland," Dr Holland said.

So far in 2026, 1,126 cases of infectious syphilis have been diagnosed in Queensland — about 20 per cent more than the average for the past five years at this stage of the year.

Outbreak of syphilis labelled a 'health disaster and tragedy' Forty-two babies in Australia died from congenital syphilis between 2011 and 2025, with the outbreak driving health workers into communities to raise awareness.

Since 2011, Queensland Health data shows First Nations infants make up 65 per cent of congenital syphilis numbers, accounting for 31 cases.

Robert Monaghan, who manages the First Nations Research Unit at the Kirby Institute, based at the University of NSW, said geographical isolation, shame and stigma could impede diagnoses.

"The outcomes are dire for some of our children," he said.

"In 2026, if we're looking at babies dying because of treatable diseases, it's just not acceptable in Australia.

"We need to be doing more. We need to be investing more. We need culturally appropriate services that are designed, delivered by First Nations people."

Queensland Health's Communicable Diseases Branch executive director Olivia Williams recommended that sexually active people should consider a full sexual health screen every six to 12 months, or with every new partner.

Dr Olivia Williams recommends that sexually active people should consider sexual health screens with every new partner. (ABC News: Janelle Miles)

Dr Williams said when someone was diagnosed with syphilis, it was important their sexual partners were notified so they could be tested and treated, if necessary, to prevent ongoing transmission.

"In Queensland, we have an action plan that really focuses on increasing awareness for the general public, increasing education, and training for clinicians, and improving access to testing and treatment," she said.

Syphilis is caused by the corkscrew-shaped bacterium, Treponema Pallidum.

In medieval times, it was known as "the great pox" and is referenced in the plays of William Shakespeare.

Infectious disease physician Dr Candice Holland and Queensland Health executive director communicable diseases branch, Dr Olivia Williams, with a blood testing kit for syphilis. (ABC News: Janelle Miles)

Although the infection is treatable with penicillin — or alternative antibiotics if people are allergic — case numbers have exploded across the world in the 21st century, including Australia, particularly in the past 15 years.

Without testing and treatment, the bacteria can damage major organ systems in adults, including the heart, brain, spinal cord, eyes, and bones, resulting in heart disease, mental illness, deafness and neurological problems.

World.title: Battery customers feeling 'ripped off' after solar company collapses
World.content:
Murray Wylie was fed up after shelling out a $5,000 deposit for a solar battery system in February, which Macarthur Solar had still not installed by August.

The company kept reassuring him, but Mr Wylie had doubts.

In late August he drove to Macarthur's south-west Sydney office.

But on arrival he was confronted by locked doors and a deserted office.

"I was angry because the thoughts that were building up had come true. I wasn't going to get my battery," he said.

"You feel like you're being ripped off."

When Murray Wylie questioned why the solar battery installation was taking so long Macarthur Solar told him to be patient. (ABC News: Chris Taylor)

Macarthur Solar's underlying company, Macarthur Energy, had gone bust.

Mathew Cox, a local electrician, founded it in 2015.

The ABC spoke to eight Macarthur customers who fear they lost large deposits for solar and battery installations that never arrived, ranging from $1,500 to $17,600.

Many signed up with Macarthur Solar after being attracted by a generous federal government subsidy, the Cheaper Home Batteries Program (CHBP).

The program sparked unprecedented demand, with more than 530,000 batteries installed since July 2025 at an estimated cost of more than $7.2 billion over four years.

Macarthur's customers were charged 50 per cent up-front, far above what's considered industry standard. NSW home building laws limit deposits to 10 per cent and leading solar and consumer advocates say the higher deposits may have breached those laws.

The state's Building Commission confirmed it was investigating after receiving more than 100 complaints.

Macarthur Energy owes almost $3.4 million to more than 79 unsecured creditors, including former customers and suppliers, according to a report by liquidator Daniel Soire of Jones Partners.

Sixteen former employees are also seriously out of pocket, owed more than $420,000 for superannuation, annual leave and redundancy payments.

Consumer and solar advocates say Macarthur Solar's collapse highlights glaring holes in protections.

"The current system is absolutely failing consumers," said Andy Kelly, Choice's director of consumer impact.

'Seemed fair dinkum'

Mr Wylie had rooftop panels but contacted Macarthur because he was thinking about adding a battery.

They came to his house for a consultation.

"They seemed fair dinkum," he said.

When Mr Wylie checked in at the office about when his installation would happen, he was told to be patient.

In June, the company changed the battery he would get.

Eventually, he was told it would be installed at the end of August, but that never happened.

Mark Barnes is out of pocket $6,500 after signing a contract with Macarthur Solar. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

Mark Barnes paid a $6,500 deposit that he fears he will not get back.

"We signed a contract in good faith and got nothing," he said.

Mr Barnes has now paid another installer for solar panels and a battery system, meaning he has paid twice.

The loss means the retiree, who is on a part-pension, has been left with less money to spend on his grandkids.

Mr Barnes handed his money over in December.

However, he claims the company was repeatedly "stalling".

In May, he called the battery system's supplier for help, which prompted a call from the owner, Mathew Cox, and eventually led to a commitment to install the system in July.

Despite assurances from the owner of Macarthur Solar that his system would be installed, Mark Barnes says no work has been completed at his property. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

That came and went, so he chased Mr Cox, but says he stopped responding.

Mr Barnes demanded a refund and lodged a complaint with the New South Wales Civil and Administrative Tribunal (NCAT), the state's small claims tribunal, however the company went into liquidation before his case was finalised.

The ABC has seen three NCAT and court orders secured by other customers against Macarthur Energy ordering repayment for amounts between $1,600 and $17,600.

Former staff members, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, said they were concerned sales had soared off the back of the CHBP, while installation wait times had blown out by many months.

Director of consumer impact at Choice, Andy Kelly, says consumers are being let down. (ABC News: Chris Taylor)

The warehouse was often short of stock, and customers were coming into the office to demand answers, they said.

They also claimed Mr Cox made reassurances to staff and customers which were not always kept.

Those affected by the collapse questioned how long the company had been struggling financially.

The liquidator, Mr Soire, previously met Mr Cox four times between mid-2023 and August 2026 before the company wound up.

A Fair Work Commission decision about a dispute between a former worker and Macarthur Energy, described an April 2025 meeting where Mr Cox allegedly told all employees that the company "was going into administration and that all employees had to find new jobs", although Mr Cox disputed telling staff that.

The business continued.

Mr Soire did not respond to the ABC's questions, including whether he was investigating any potential breaches of director's duties such as the possibility of insolvent trading.

Murray Wylie drove to Macarthur's office in August, only to find locked doors. (ABC News: Chris Taylor)

More regulation demanded

Some of Macarthur's customers were charged 50 per cent deposits, including Mr Barnes.

Jeff Sykes, CEO of comparison website Solar Choice, said that was highly unusual.

"50 per cent deposit is a serious red flag," he said.

"Across Australia, we see 10 per cent pretty much as the industry standard."

Solar Choice published half a dozen one-star reviews about Macarthur Energy this year, with customers venting about poor communication and complaints to regulators about unfinished installations.

Macarthur Solar’s website, which is no longer online, encouraged people to make the renewables leap. (Supplied: Wayback Machine)

The ABC requested an interview with Macarthur Solar's Mathew Cox and sent him questions but did not receive a response before publication.

Macarthur was one of thousands of solar companies impacted by changes to the CHBP, which sparked a consumer rush to get in before May 1 when subsidies reduced.

Mr Kelly said installers who over-committed faced financial shortfalls if they did not complete their work before May 1, because the rebate was paid only after the job and they would not receive the higher rebates they expected.

He said Macarthur Solar's collapse showed the need for strong penalties.

He also wants a mandatory code of conduct for companies accessing subsidies under the CHBP and an expansion of ombudsman schemes, as well as other action recommended by the consumer watchdog, the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC).

Macarthur's customers and consumer advocates have questioned whether state and federal regulators were too slow to intervene, given the huge number of complaints.

"That's very concerning from my perspective and sounds like the exact harm that a lot of these consumer protection rules are designed to prevent," Mr Sykes said.

A spokesperson for the Building Commission NSW said it was investigating, "allegations of requests for deposits which exceed the legal limit as well as a lack of Home Building Compensation Fund (HBCF) coverage by the business."

The commission can suspend or cancel a licence and issue financial penalties.

Do you know more about this story? Email michaelatkin@protonmail.com or contact him via the Signal secure messaging app +61 447 279 901.

Macarthur Energy has previously been fined $4,000 for taking an excessive deposit, lacking Home Building Compensation Fund coverage, and not performing work after taking money.

In a rare step, the ACCC confirmed it "has several investigations currently underway in relation to the sales practices of solar and battery installers."

The Clean Energy Regulator said in a statement it had passed information to the ACCC and state consumer protection agencies and was considering whether compliance action was warranted.

However, the regulator insisted most solar companies were doing the right thing under the CHBP.

Energy Minister Chris Bowen said the rebate could not be claimed until a battery was installed and the government had zero tolerance for poor behaviour.

World.title: Trump rejects AI laws after tech titans agree to ‘self-police’ AI development
World.content:
BusinessMarketsAI Trump rejects AI laws after tech titans agree to ‘self-police’ AI development Maggie Eastland and Skylar Woodhouse September 30, 2026 — 6:39am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

President Donald Trump shot down the idea of new regulations on artificial intelligence after meeting at the White House with top industry executives and signing with them an agreement for industry self-regulation amid growing global concerns over threats posed by the technology. Speaking on Tuesday after a luncheon with nearly two dozen Silicon Valley leaders, including Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei and Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang, Trump said existing laws would be enough to safeguard Americans from AI’s potential risks. “I think I’m seeing tremendous self-policing. And they understand that they have to self-police,” Trump told reporters outside the West Wing. President Donald Trump flanked by many of America’s top tech company executives at the White House, including (from left, in first row) Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang and SpaceX’s Elon Musk. Bloomberg Trump said the tech executives signed an agreement that is “morally binding,” without providing details, and floated the idea of a “committee” of roughly 10 people that would help “watch over the whole enterprise.”



“There’s a belief that there should be tremendous self-regulation, and we automatically have regulation with the Department of Justice, the FBI, all of that, but the self-regulation is very important,” the president told reporters in a brief appearance with his guests. The agreement sets what House Speaker Mike Johnson described as a “voluntary” set of “commitments” by the industry to implement “robust internal controls and layers of internal and external review.” Johnson, who attended the meeting, said the text would be released later. ‘I think I’m seeing tremendous self-policing. And they understand that they have to self-police.’ US President Donald Trump The luncheon at the White House was joined by other technology industry attendees including Meta boss Mark Zuckerberg, Palantir Technologies CEO Alex Karp and OpenAI President Greg Brockman. The decision to even engage on AI safety had appeared to mark a shift for Trump, who only last week rejected fears of catastrophic risk as “a hoax.” Other industry attendees were expected to include Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk and Advanced Micro Devices’ Lisa Su, according to a list released by the White House. Vice President JD Vance, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and White House Science and Technology Policy Advisor Michael Kratsios also planned to join.



Pressure to take action has increased following high-profile security breaches by rogue AI models that fuelled calls by Silicon Valley AI developers and world leaders for new standards on the technology. Related Article AI Anthropic warns investors its AI could pose ‘existential risks to humanity’ Yet Trump’s remarks splashed cold water on the notion that his administration might move away from its hardened opposition to new government AI safeguards and become more open to new rules. During remarks on Tuesday, Trump signalled his continued distaste for regulations. “We have a very big lead, and we’re going to keep our lead, and it’s a very positive thing,” the president said, referring to his desire to maintain the US’s edge in the global AI competition.



“I will never stifle the growth of a technology that will be bigger than the industrial revolution,” Trump said earlier in the day at the unveiling of an AI chatbot, America.gov, intended to help Americans navigate government services. “We can’t stifle it, and we’re leading by a lot.” The debate has posed a political conundrum for Trump, who has cast himself as one of the nation’s loudest champions of AI, arguing that its unfettered development is key to beating China and sustaining the US economy. But polls show Americans have rapidly become more wary of the technology’s risks, including job loss, higher electricity costs and major cyberattacks, threatening to put Trump on the wrong side of the issue ahead of the November midterm elections. Trump has recently become preoccupied with AI’s name, suggesting he sees the controversy surrounding the technology as a branding problem more than an issue with its potential dangers. The president said on Tuesday he would sign an executive order later in the day renaming it “super intelligence.” Shortly before the meeting began, Trump posted on his Truth Social network a guest seating chart that put Huang and Musk at either side of the president. His desire to maintain close ties with the industry was also on full display. When reporters entered the room, the executives were lined up behind the president as if they were posing for a group photo and Trump gushed about their contributions to the US.



“The one thing that we all have in common is we love our country and we love the world, and we want to make sure it’s a safe place,” he said. The president did appear to acknowledge growing public discontent with the AI rollout. He indicated that the companies in attendance would work more closely with local communities to ease concerns over the impact of new data centre construction. “They’re going to do things for the community that will be really financially beneficial and otherwise beneficial,” Trump said, without providing specifics. The lunch took place after Trump met with Amodei on Sunday, bringing together two men at opposite ends of the AI safety debate. The late-night dinner marked their first private sit-down after months of rocky relations between the Anthropic chief and the administration over safety-related issues involving the company’s AI tools. Amodei has long warned about AI’s existential risks, and he propelled the safety debate into the mainstream with a September 12 essay, promising to slow development of the most advanced models and urging more regulation. His pledge to pace development was embraced by his rivals, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Musk. Loading



Highlighting those concerns, OpenAI said on Monday it would hold back a version of its Astra model while it establishes stronger safeguards. Saachi Jain, OpenAI’s head of safety systems, said the in-development GPT-6.1 Astra model wasn’t as good as the company wanted when it came to “staying within scope and authorisation, and how it communicates back to the user about the type of work it’s done.” Related Article Updated

AI OpenAI halts powerful new AI model over fears it could go rogue Earlier this month, Johnson responded to dire warnings coming from within the AI industry by saying that Congress “potentially” will need to impose guardrails, though he cautioned it would likely take “some time” to fashion legislation with broad enough support to pass. Ahead of the lunch, Johnson said he’d “been urging this meeting for a long time” and added he hoped it would lead to voluntary steps to mitigate AI risk, such as audits or other transparency measures.



“The leading minds need to get together at the White House and have this discussion,” Johnson said Tuesday on CNBC. The AI companies “have fiduciary obligations to their own corporations, of course, but we have a broader obligation to the people and to safety and to ensuring that this is done right and well.” In the near term, US Congress is unlikely to act on any AI legislation. House lawmakers have already left town for recess and won’t return until after the midterms, and the Senate is preparing to begin its own preelection recess later this week. Bloomberg, with Reuters and AP The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. Sign up to get it every weekday morning.

World.title: Lindsay Clancy’s lawyer now questions whether she killed her three children
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaCourts Lindsay Clancy’s lawyer now questions whether she killed her three children Michael Casey and Jennifer Peltz Updated September 30, 2026 — 6:30am ,first published 2:50am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Lindsay Clancy’s lawyer has argued that there wasn’t enough evidence to prove she killed her three children, a striking turn after a lengthy trial that focused more on her mental state than on whether she took their lives. “This entire case is based on speculation,” attorney Kevin Reddington said on Tuesday (US time) during the first hearing since Clancy’s initial trial ended on September 4 with a deadlocked jury. They were split 11 to 1 in her favour. Lindsay Clancy in Plymouth Superior Court on Tuesday at a hearing focused on the next steps in her case. Greg Derr/Pool The Patriot Ledger via AP During the trial, Reddington didn’t dispute that Clancy killed the children at the family’s home in 2023. Instead, the defence sought to persuade the jury that the 36-year-old former labour and delivery nurse was not criminally responsible because of mental disease, a rare condition called postpartum psychosis. But at Tuesday’s hearing, Reddington sought to persuade Judge William Sullivan – the same judge who presided over the first trial – to acquit her.



There is, Reddington contended, not enough evidence “that this woman killed those children”. He pointed to matters ranging from her condition when she was found, badly injured and bleeding, in the yard outside her home to her lack of memory of what happened when she woke up in a hospital. At the first trial, her now ex-husband and first responders testified that she tried to kill herself immediately after killing the children. “Where is the admission? Where does she say that she did this?” Reddington asked, going on to recap his arguments that she also was psychotic and delusional at the time of the children’s deaths. Related Article Courts Lindsay Clancy’s ex-husband breaks silence after controversial mistrial Prosecutor Shanan Buckingham called his argument “laughable”, pointing to witness testimony that Clancy said she heard voices instructing her to kill her children. Clancy was the only one home at the time with the children and her DNA was found on exercise bands used to strangle them, she added. “For the first time, the defendant is arguing that there is no evidence she did this,” Buckingham said. “I’d suggest to you the entire record is voluminous as to information supporting the fact that she did this.”



During the trial, Paul Zeizel, a clinical and forensic psychologist and defence witness, testified that he overheard her saying a disembodied male voice told her she had no choice but to kill the children and then herself. Before trial Reddington filed a motion in which he said Clancy would be willing to stipulate in writing “to her involvement in the underlying conduct resulting in the death of the three young children”. The judge didn’t immediately rule on the motion, and no trial date was set. Clancy’s attorney, Kevin Reddington, argued there was not enough evidence to prove she had killed her three children. Greg Derr/Pool The Patriot Ledger via AP The prosecution maintains that Clancy knew her actions were wrong when she used exercise bands to strangle five-year-old Cora, three-year-old Dawson and eight-month-old Callan Clancy. They said she contrived to get her husband out of the house that evening by sending him to pick up medicine for one of their children and dinner for the family.



Prosecutors have yet to decide whether to retry Clancy, Plymouth County District Attorney Timothy Cruz said after the hearing. They could choose to retry her on first-degree murder charges or seek to try her only on lesser charges, including second-degree murder or manslaughter, or drop the case entirely. Related Article Updated

Courts Judge declares mistrial in Lindsay Clancy murder case that gripped America “We are going to do what we can for the children,” Cruz told reporters outside the court. “That is what this case is about.” Sullivan said he wanted to set a new trial date, but both sides pushed back – arguing that the judge should rule on several motions in front of him first. Initially, the defence urged the court to set a new trial date soon. But on Tuesday, Reddington told Sullivan he couldn’t see having a new trial before June due to his schedule.



Clancy’s attorneys have asked the judge to dismiss the criminal case, a motion that will be heard November 2. Among other things they have argued that the judge should have ousted the one juror who favoured a murder conviction after the jury foreperson complained he was refusing to listen to the law on reasonable doubt. The juror, Michael Desronvil, has said through his lawyer that he had no doubts about his stance. Desronvil told Fox News’ Hannity in a brief video statement on Monday that “the whole focus has been on me, but we want to reel everything back and put the focus on the three angels”, meaning the children. Among other motions pushed back was a Commonwealth request for a gag order that would bar attorneys and their supporters “from making extrajudicial statements to the media that would have a substantial likelihood of materially prejudicing the criminal proceeding”. Reddington has given a series of interviews since the mistrial and held walking news conferences almost every day during the proceedings. Prosecutors, in contrast, never talked to reporters.



The livestreamed trial generated intense public interest and drew attention to maternal mental health after childbirth. About a dozen Clancy supporters, most dressed in pink, stood outside court on Tuesday waiting for her to arrive. Related Article Analysis

Courts Clancy faces years of confinement, no matter what comes next Clancy remains charged with murder and is expected to stay at a psychiatric hospital until her case is resolved. Clancy could have been sentenced to life in prison if convicted of murder. If acquitted, the judge could have ordered her confined to a mental health facility. AP

World.title: Can Burnham save Britain? Finally, he reveals his plans – with one glaring omission
World.content:
Analysis WorldEuropeUK politics Can Burnham save Britain? Finally, he reveals his plans – with one glaring omission David Crowe September 30, 2026 — 6:28am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: Andy Burnham just did something daringly different at an annual speech that is often heavy on theatre and light on ideas. The British prime minister outlined at least six major reforms in his address to the annual Labour Party conference after candidly admitting to the failures of the last decade. UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham speaks at the Labour Party annual conference in Liverpool on Tuesday. Bloomberg He also made an emotional plea for the United Kingdom to stick together at a time when many of its own people – not only those in Scotland and Wales – seem convinced it is broken beyond repair. He was blunt about the referendum 10 years ago to leave the European Union. “Brexit has done more harm than good,” he said. This cleared the way for a debate on how to restore ties with the EU at a summit to be held later this year.



The instant analysis in the British media was that Burnham had fired the starting gun on the next election – due in 2029 – with an agenda to renew Labour after its drift under former leader Keir Starmer. This was true, albeit banal. The key question was not whether Burnham could save Labour, but whether he might save Britain. Burnham embraces his mother, Eileen, and brother, John, after delivering his speech. Getty Images “I won’t pretend some of this won’t be difficult,” he said at one point. “I accept I may pay a political price. But someone has to go through the pain barrier and rip the plaster off.” Australians might want to watch Burnham closely because some of his challenges have parallels in Canberra, even though times are tougher in Britain on every front.



His first major pledge was to restore the stock of public housing to ease a serious crisis with rising rents. He promised to give councils greater power to get new construction underway. Related Article Analysis

UK politics Farage says Britain is broken and only Reform can fix it. Now the pressure is on to deliver If absentee landlords left rental properties in disrepair, he said, councils would force them to renovate. Legislation would be passed if necessary to make this happen. His second plan was to reverse the privatisation of water utilities under Conservative leader Margaret Thatcher three decades ago. This touches a nerve with British households dealing with poor water and sewerage services due to low investment by private operators. In one glaring example, Thames Water is close to financial collapse after big investors, including Macquarie Bank, loaded it with debt and took out generous dividends. Burnham wants to restore public ownership if a private operator is no good.



The third pledge was ambitious, although uncertain. He said he would set up a new public operator of the national electricity grid to compete with private energy companies. He made cost, not climate change, the key message on energy. He said he would be “pragmatic” about oil and gas from the North Sea – a hint that he would back new projects to boost supply. The fourth agenda item was all about social care for the aged and vulnerable. He promised to deliver more care for the elderly in their own home – a policy choice already underway in Australia – and said there would be a new National Care Service to offer free support. UK Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch. Getty Images “There is only one real answer: a person-centred, high-quality care service that starts in the home,” he said. “A system in the best traditions of this party, where everyone contributes and everyone is covered, free at the point of use, and no care charges paid out of your basic state pension.” This sounded too good to be true. It could be incredibly expensive and far more generous than the means-tested system in Australia, where pensions help fund private aged care. The details are still to come.



Where will the money come from? This was Burnham’s fifth big idea – and his bravest moment. He swept away Britain’s iconic and bipartisan policy on pensions: the “triple lock” decided in 2010 to ensure pensions rise at the rate of inflation, average wage growth or 2.5 per cent each year, whichever is higher. Related Article Analysis

UK politics Britain’s budget blues will end Burnham’s honeymoon The state pension now costs £154 billion ($292 billion) per year, more than twice the defence budget, according to the Institute for Fiscal Studies. Thanks to the triple lock, it has risen from 4.3 to 4.9 per cent of national income since 2010. This is higher than in Australia; one reason is that Britain lacks Australia’s superannuation system. Burnham promised to replace this with a double-lock: increasing the pension by inflation or 2.5 per cent, whichever is higher. This abandons a Labour pledge from the last election, but the new leader said the change would take effect in 2030, after the next election. This political manoeuvre borrowed from Anthony Albanese, who dumped an old promise on the “stage three” tax cuts as prime minister in January 2024, but made sure the changes would not take effect until after the 2025 election.



This involves serious risk for Burnham, given that the Conservatives can appeal to older voters who stand to lose, but the plan could help fund at least some of the new social care services those same voters may support. The sixth big idea from Burnham was about the voting system that delivers victory to the candidate who is “first past the post” in every electorate. In most races, Britain only counts the primary vote on the ballot paper, a fundamentally different approach to Australia’s preferential system. Reform UK Leader Nigel Farage. Getty Images Burnham did not name his favoured reform but clearly wants to drop the “first past the post” method. He promised to set up a National Commission for Electoral Reform to recommend a new system, which he would take to voters as a policy pledge at the next election. This suggests the 2029 election would be fought on the current system, not the new one. Over time, however, Burnham seemed intent on bringing Britain closer to the Australian system.



Labour could, of course, benefit from preferential voting because it could gain the second preferences of Greens voters. But it could also work for Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch, because her party might benefit from preferences from small right-wing parties. Related Article Opinion

UK As three countries move to quit UK, a Brexit reversal might be its only hope George Brandis Former high commissioner to the UK and federal attorney-general It might even help Reform UK, led by Nigel Farage, if he keeps the party’s core support ahead of the Conservatives. Whether this backfires on Burnham is impossible to predict when the next election is not due until 2029 and the subsequent one in 2034. The overall impact might strengthen the major two parties after the shift to smaller parties under the current system. The Burnham agenda had some gutsy commitments. At the heart of it, however, was a vacuum. The Labour leader offered nothing on economic reform and fiscal repair. He mentioned growth, but he did not have a specific plan to give it a boost.



He spoke about giving hope to about 1 million young people who are not in education, employment or training – the so-called NEETs – but warned against “crude” cuts to welfare. He said what the Labour faithful wanted to hear, not what they needed to be told. Without cuts, the incentives may never change and the national budget may never be repaired. The British economy grew just 0.4 per cent in the last quarter, just as mediocre as the Australian economy. In Britain, however, public sector net debt is now 95 per cent of economic output (GDP). In Australia, federal net debt is 19 per cent. Even allowing for state debt in Australia, the contrast is stark. Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey reacts as Burnham speaks. Getty Images Burnham cannot spend his way out of Britain’s doom spiral. The Chancellor of the Exchequer, John Healey, will reveal the budget on October 28. With debt already high, any false move can spook the bond market, which means the fiscal plan should be about saving money. Burnham rose to the leadership on high hopes 10 weeks ago. Now he has bold plans to give his government purpose and direction. But none of his ideas will be enough if he cannot fund them with a stronger budget and match them with a serious growth agenda. World.title: Anthropic warns investors its AI could pose ‘existential risks to humanity’
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesAI Anthropic warns investors its AI could pose ‘existential risks to humanity’ Tom Saunders September 30, 2026 — 5:40am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Anthropic has warned investors that its technology could pose “existential risks to humanity” as it prepares to list on the sharemarket. The AI company warned in the prospectus for its planned initial public offering (IPO) filing that its models could exhibit unpredictable behaviours including attempts to “resist shutdown”, to “conceal or manipulate information” and behaviour “resembling blackmail”. Anthropic is expected to launch the most highly valued IPO of all time soon, worth up to $US2 trillion ($2.85 trillion). But investors beware. AP “Our development of highly advanced models, platforms, and applications and expansion of use cases could further increase the risk that our models cause harm,” Anthropic said in the filing, according to Reuters, which first reported the news. The tech company dedicated almost a third of the IPO document, which was circulated within a small group of partners, to “risk factors”.



Anthropic is expected to launch the most highly valued IPO of all time soon, worth up to $US2 trillion ($2.85 trillion). However, the risk disclosures make it harder to value the creator of the Claude AI assistant app. Anthropic devoted roughly 80 pages in its prospectus to laying out risk factors, nearly twice the 48 pages it used to describe its business. Its warning about the risk to humanity is the latest in a slew of recent alerts about the dangers of artificial intelligence. Pope Leo XIV recently rebuked Jensen Huang, the Nvidia chief executive, for downplaying the dangers posed by AI. Pope Leo said that while he had read that Nvidia was launching new safety tools for AI, he questioned Huang’s overall commitment to AI safety.



The pontiff said on Monday: “He’s the same one, however, that says there should be no limits placed and no government regulation.” Related Article Updated

AI OpenAI halts powerful new AI model over fears it could go rogue He added: “I do think that the concerns raised by many of the experts, specialists in AI, should be taken seriously.” Anthropic and OpenAI have faced scrutiny over a recent spate of hacking incidents by advanced AI agents. Evan Hubinger, a senior safety researcher at Anthropic, recently estimated a greater than 10 per cent chance that AI could kill humans within the next decade.



His comments were in response to another post on X, from Jacob Coxon, an AI researcher who had just quit Anthropic and previously worked at OpenAI. Coxon said that neither company was acting responsibly and that they were “gambling with our lives”. Jensen Huang has repeatedly downplayed the risk of AI slipping out of human control. Bloomberg Dario Amodei, the founder of Anthropic, told the UN Security Council last week that AI could threaten humankind and was “the most important global security issue facing the world today”. He also led public calls for slowing down the pace of development with a focus on enhancing safety measures. His calls were backed by Sam Altman, the leader of OpenAI, and Elon Musk, which owns xAI.



Anthropic devoted roughly 80 pages in its prospectus to laying out risk factors, nearly twice the 48 pages it used to describe its business. Related Article Exclusive

AI Anthropic boss to skip Senate grilling into rogue AI agents The company also warned that models were increasingly recognising when they were being watched, adjusting their behaviour to make them harder to monitor. The share sale prospectus warned Anthropic could face legal claims from customers and users over the actions of rogue artificial intelligence agents, though the legal framework is uncertain, Reuters reported. However, Anthropic did not disclose how much it was investing in safety. Earlier this month, the startup said that in a single week in July about 6 per cent of the computing power it was using for AI research went into work on safety.



Anthropic reported a net loss of $US42 billion in 2025. It plans to spend $US518 billion on cloud, computing and infrastructure obligations in the coming year, according to the prospectus. Sales grew 12-fold in 2025 to nearly $US4.6 billion, though the company lost more than $US8 billion on an operating basis. Anthropic was contacted for comment.
