World.title: A gorgeous, tranquil Scandinavian hotel is, surprisingly, in Bali
World.content:
★★★★½ Reviews & adviceHotel reviews A gorgeous, tranquil Scandinavian hotel is, surprisingly, in Bali John Borthwick September 30, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The hotel Hygge Hotel and Villas Seminyak Hygge Hotel and Villas Seminyak opened in 2025. Check-in Step under the archway portal of this boutique property in Kerobokan district, and a cone of silence seems to descend. The bray of street traffic drops away, the check-in routine is completed swiftly, and soon you’re led down a lush garden path towards your suite. Alongside you, the pool already beckons.



The look 



A spirit house altar stands at one corner, and the rest is a riot of blooms and foliage that this island of green-thumbed gods specialise in. Plonk a deckchair anywhere on the garden lawn and read, scroll or snooze. Or wander to the pool, the very well-equipped gym or large yoga studio. The room The bedroom in a Family Villa. The Hygge’s 29 rooms and 12 luxury villas range from single rooms and mezzanine studios to walled, two- and four-bedroom pool villas. I’m in a 70-square-metre Mezzanine Garden View Studio, with the bedroom and bathroom above an open-plan ground floor that contains a full kitchen and casual lounge room. The suite’s virtues include fine linen, overhead fans, a coffee maker, Wi-Fi, water purifier and sofas that convert to extra beds. The air-conditioning needs to be on in the upstairs bedroom when the afternoon sunlight hits its broad windows. All areas of this family-friendly retreat are smoke-free. There are a kitchen and lounge area in the Mezzanine Garden View Studio.



The food The resort is an offspring of Jakarta’s stylish Hygge Coffee and Roastery. Breakfast at its cafe-restaurant is a beautiful thing and accompanied by water sounds from the nearby vertical garden. The menu section headed “Whispers in a Cup” might not feature smorrebrod, but its Danish wholegrain breads, boost juices and truffle eggs Benedict, plus serious coffee, are a formidable heart-starter. Later in the day, the menu heading switches to “Stories on a Plate”. The tale I select is a simple cosmopolitan lunch of calamari fritti, caesar salad and irresistible waffles and ice-cream. Imported wine, cocktails and beer are available. The Residence is a spacious retreat complete with living areas and a private outdoor hot tub. Out + about Kerobokan’s busy nearby streets, such as Jalan Cendrawasih and Jalan Kerobokan, offer a good range of day spas, international eateries, cafes and fashion boutiques. The closest surf beach, Batu Belig, is a five-minute drive away and has a row of casual warung restaurants where the beer is cold and the view infinite, especially at matahari terbenam, or sunset hour. Nearby, Desa Potato Head beach club packs them in, while a shoreline walk further south brings you to 15th-century Petitenget Temple, one of the few local sites of Balinese culture.



The verdict Hygge Hotel and Villas is a sanctuary, with honeymoon-level privacy in the pool villas and exceptional staff service. Tranquility base Bali. Related Article Bali Bali needs more places like this outstanding dining spot Essentials The resort is 13 kilometres north of Denpasar’s I Gusti Ngurah Rai International Airport. Transfer via Bluebird metered taxi or Grab ride, with travel time up to one hour. Rooms from $120 a night and two-bedroom pool villas from $280. Hygge Hotel and Villas Seminyak, Jalan Petitenget, Gang Cendrawasih 9, Seminyak.

Phone +62 811 870 309. See hyggeseminyak.com



Our score out of five

★★★★½ Highlight Intelligent design, gorgeous decor, sumptuous garden and a cafe that is excellent value for money. In fact, cosy and convivial. Lowlight



Some teething issues with the over-complex television system. The writer stayed as a guest of Hygge Hotel & Villas Seminyak.

World.title: The ‘utterly delicious’ one-pan chicken dish Julia Busuttil Nishimura cooks every week
World.content:
The Melbourne food writer shares three chicken recipes from her new cookbook, including a Thai-inspired dish, a spiced pomegranate overnight marinade and a salad with ranch dressing and croutons.

A lemony tomato and bean broth. Spaghetti served with broad bean and basil pesto. A seasonal salad with fig, sugar snap peas and halloumi. For Julia Busuttil Nishimura, everyday cooking goes beyond tangible elements such as simplicity and deliciousness.

It’s also about the ebb and flow of seasons, sitting together around the table after the meal has finished or foraging through the pantry for favourite ingredients. It can even be about things as ordinary as messy benchtops, too many dishes and another trip to the shops.

“It is beautiful and life-enhancing and needn’t be complicated,” she writes in the introduction of her latest cookbook.

The collection, Simple Pleasures, is dedicated to the joy of cooking that punctuates our day-to-day life, and is filled with the types of pared-back recipes for which Busuttil Nishimura has become known.

It includes a chapter dedicated to pasta, as well as sections about soups, vegetables and salads, plus lots of homemade bakes, both sweet and savoury. Chicken dinners (many one-pan or equally easy and simple to make) are a perennial favourite, and feature heavily throughout.

World.title: A field guide to the dissolution of Parliament
World.content:
The Herald at Arms Extraordinary to the King delivers the 2023 dissolution proclamation on the steps of Parliament. Dissolutions are always public. So you know what to expect on Thursday morning, below is a photo rundown from 2023's dissolution of the 53rd parliament.

To dissolve a Parliament, you need a proclamation - a statement about six lines long, but those six lines hold immense constitutional power.

The proclamation will send the Parliament to its final resting place (probably a page on Wikipedia).

Office of the Clerk/Louis Collins

The proclamation powerful enough to dissolve the 53rd Parliament sits atop a table next to an offering of chocolates and lollies.

Office of the Clerk/Louis Collins

The Clerk of the House of Representatives, David Wilson, gives the proclamation a final once-over before heading out onto the steps. Despite their fleeting nature, dissolutions involve key players suiting up in their full ceremonial glad rags. For the Clerk and his assistants that means itchy wigs, black gowns, and stiff, pointy popped collars.

Office of the Clerk/Louis Collins

Herald of Arms Extraordinary to the King, Phillip O'Shea, poses in his ceremonial uniform while holding a black rod (but not THE black rod used at Parliament's opening).

Unless you're a diehard royalist or are particularly well-versed in His Majesty's Officers of Arms, the name Phillip O'Shea may mean little. You could easily pass him in the cereal aisle at the local supermarket without realizing you'd just walked past a member of the King's official household.

Office of the Clerk/Louis Collins

O'Shea shows off his royal cufflinks, of which very few were ever made.

O'Shea's role is, in part, a modern-day link between New Zealand and the College of Arms in London (the royal authority responsible for matters of heraldry). It's not hard to imagine a medieval equivalent standing in the village square shouting, "Make way for the King!"

Today, however, O'Shea's duties include advice on things like medals, and participating in the formal dissolution and opening of Parliament. He has witnessed his fair share of triennial ceremonies since being appointed to the role in 1978. He remains the only person to have ever held the position of New Zealand Herald at Arms Extraordinary to the King.

Office of the Clerk/Louis Collins

Chamber Officers line the steps to form a guard of honour for the officials.

Office of the Clerk/Louis Collins

Adorned in a tailcoat, medals, and his bespoke royal cufflinks, O'Shea is a key protagonist. Following a karanga, he, the Clerks, and Parliament's Tumu Whakarae (Principal Cultural Advisor, Kura Moeahu) are led out onto the steps by the Serjeant-at-Arms.

Office of the Clerk/Louis Collins

Above them, the NZDF Brass Quintet, positioned up on the balcony, jolts onlookers with a fanfare of trumpets and horns that would make the likes of Fat Freddy's Drop jealous.

Office of the Clerk/Louis Collins

The Herald of Arms Extraordinary to the King reads out the proclamation from the Governor-General.

Like most examples of state pageantry in New Zealand, the proclamation tradition originates in the UK, where historically proclamations were read at public posts in London and Edinburgh whenever a new sovereign was crowned or a Parliament dissolved. In recent years, the ceremony has become distinctly Aotearoa, integrating te ao Māori into proceedings.

Office of the Clerk/Louis Collins

The Clerk David Wilson signs to confirm his role as an official witness. For the proclamation to be official, it must be read publicly and witnessed by the Clerk of the House and two other official witnesses, typically the Deputy and Assistant Clerks.

And just like that, the 53rd Parliament is no more. Like a packet of Raro, New Zealand's legislature dissolves in minutes.

Office of the Clerk/Louis Collins

Kura Moeahu offers a whaikōrero that transcends the parliamentary context:

"Let us put to sleep the challenging times, let us dissolve and rest. Let us put to sleep the 53rd Parliament of New Zealand… so that there is calm in the universe, calm on land, calm on the ocean, and calmness amongst the nation. May there be calmness in everyone's journey."

Office of the Clerk/Louis Collins

Following Moeahu's remarks, the Ngāti Pōneke kapa haka group breaks into God Defend New Zealand with vocal gusto, backed by the NZDF brass quintet. The group also performed the waiata He Hōnore while the three witnesses complete the signing.

Office of the Clerk/Louis Collins

The Kapa Haka group poses for a photo following the conclusion of the ceremony.

Office of the Clerk/Louis Collins

After the national anthem, Moeahu sounds the pūtātara to officially bring the ceremony to a close.

Office of the Clerk/Louis Collins

This signals the Serjeant-at-Arms Steve Streefkerk to lead the officials back up the red carpet and inside Parliament House for a well-earned cup of tea (or maybe Raro).

With a Parliament put to sleep, the official election machinery can officially awaken from its three-year slumber. The official election writ will be issued on Writ Day, a few days after dissolution.

The writ acts as the Governor General's formal instruction to the Electoral Commission to organise the general election (as if they need the reminder), detailing key cut-off dates for candidate nominations and for the official return of the writ.

While the red carpet is rolled up and stowed away after the dissolution, it won't gather dust. It will be back out on the steps, alongside many of the same familiar faces, for the opening of the next Parliament once the votes are counted and someone secures the keys to the Beehive.

You can watch Thursday's dissolution of Parliament at 11am on Thursday 1 October on Parliament's forecourt, or on Parliament TV (streamed here). You can read more about the dissolution on the Parliament Website here.

World.title: Woman found dead at Christchurch home, police launch homicide probe
World.content:
A homicide investigation has been launched after a woman was found dead at a home in Edgeware's Christchurch.

Detective Senior Sergeant Colin Baillie said police were called to Purchas St just before 6am on Wednesday.

A woman was found dead, he said, and a second person at the house was speaking with police.

"Police are not seeking anybody else in relation to this incident, and there is not believed to be any risk to public safety."

A scene guard was in place and residents could expect to see an increased police presence in the area on Wednesday.

World.title: 'A sad indictment': Flour replaces nearly 40kg of cocaine exhibit in Fiji court
World.content:
Fiji police have confirmed that nearly 40 kilograms of cocaine stored in a High Court exhibit room were found to have been replaced with flour.

The 39 cocaine bars were stored in the Suva High Court exhibit room. According to local media reports, the street value of the missing cocaine was valued at about FJ$30 million (US$14m).

Earlier this month, Fiji Police launched an investigation after seven out of the 39 cocaine bars had went missing.

In a statement on Tuesday, Fiji Police confirmed that "forensic tests" on the remaining drug exhibits had all returned negative.

"The exhibits were all tampered with and the investigation is focused on those directly charged with the management of the exhibits at the High Court Registry," the statement said.

Police also confirmed that one person of interest allegedly involved in the incident is currently out of the country and will be questioned.

Fiji's Justice Minister Siromi Turaga described the disappearance of the drugs as "shocking".

"No stone will be left unturned. Anyone found guilty will be held accountable," he told parliament on Tuesday afternoon.

Turaga asked the public to "trust the process" and allow the police to lead the investigation.

Opposition MP Jone Usamate said "the replacement of the cocaine with flour" was a "sad indictment".

"How do we know now that what is in all those exhibits [held at the Suva High Court] is actually there?"

Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka, less than a week ago, told local reporters that the security of the exhibits at the Suva High Court needed to be more secure.

World.title: NZ accused of breaking climate change promise with EU, but Todd McClay rejects claim
World.content:
A Dutch environmental group claims New Zealand has broken its climate change promises in the free trade agreement with the EU and is lodging the first complaint of its kind through the European Commission.

The group, Both ENDS, is using the complaints mechanism known as Single Entry Point and said this first climate test could be precedent setting.

The most extreme consequences could be losing access to the lucrative European market, but the group is seeking compliance rather than the suspension of trade benefits.

It claims New Zealand failed to uphold its legal commitments in the EU-NZ FTA not to weaken environmental protections in order to "encourage trade or investment," and to effectively implement the Paris Agreement.

But the Trade Minister is firing back, saying its "not for overseas countries, organisations or lobby groups to tell New Zealand how to meet its obligations".

The group said lodging the complaint was going to be "huge" in the EU because there's such significant public scrutiny about "how our policies are in line with our Paris commitments."

BothENDS said the Single Entry Point exists so that "European civil society can ask the Commission to enforce the sustainability commitments in EU trade agreements."

New Zealand organisations cannot themselves file a complaint, but a number of groups and individuals have added their support as co-sponsors, including Greenpeace, Ngāti Pukenga, Ora Taiao, Environmental Law Initiative, Mike Smith and Professor Jane Kelsey.

The legal commitment from New Zealand comes in the form of a 'non-regression' clause in its trade deal, prohibiting it from reducing environmental protections and a section on trade and climate change stating the Parties recognise the importance of "taking urgent action to combat climate change and its impacts."

Concerns were raised early in the political term that the coalition risked breaching its trade agreements due to various policies.

Most recently, the Greens wrote to the European Commissioner responsible for trade and economic security, asking the EU to assess whether New Zealand was failing its obligations.

Now, Both ENDS has filed a complaint, seeking compliance rather than the suspension of trade benefits - which the trade agreement allows for at the end of a long process. The group makes it clear a government can stop that outcome by complying.

Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen at EU headquarters in Brussels in 2022. AFP

The group noted the relevant clauses in the EU-NZ FTA, which came into force on 1 May 2024, specifically Article 19.2(4), Article 19.6(2), Article 19.6(3), and Article 19.7(3). Specifically 19.2(4) which states a "Party shall not weaken or reduce the levels of protection afforded in its environmental or labour law in order to encourage trade or investment." Also those committing the parties to "effectively implement the Paris Agreement."

At the time the deal was struck in 2022, then Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern described it as containing "ground-breaking commitments on environment, labour rights and gender equality as foundational parts of a trade and sustainable development chapter".

The European Commission also celebrated it as a landmark agreement that included "unprecedented sustainability commitments, including respect of the Paris Climate Agreement and core labour rights."

The complaint's concern was "a pattern, not a single decision, and one that has escalated."

BothENDS said the New Zealand government had taken a "series of connected decisions" since the deal came into force that weakened domestic climate safeguards, naming a range of them as part of the complaint.

The complaint argued the government had no credible plan to meet its climate commitments, with an estimated 84 million-tonne emissions shortfall and a potential $4.4-5 billion cost for offshore mitigation. It noted comments by Prime Minister Christopher Luxon in June that "we ain't sending billions of dollars offshore."

It also highlighted a weakened methane target, removal of agriculture from carbon pricing, reversal of the offshore oil and gas exploration ban, a $200 million Gas Security Fund and planned LNG import facility, and legislation preventing climate-related claims against major emitters.

Regarding oil and gas exploration, it noted the reversal was presented as a way to "reinvigorate investment in petroleum exploration" and in announcing its move to prevent companies from being sued over damage caused by greenhouse gas emissions, the government noted it was committed to "attracting overseas investment."

Why the complaint is significant

Fernando Hernandez Espino, the head of trade and investment policy at Both ENDS, told RNZ the group had been following trade policy of the EU for years, and the climate promises in the EU-NZ FTA were already of interest.

The group monitors all trade agreements signed with the EU.

"What makes this case very significant is that this is the so-called gold standard," he said.

"There is no other trade agreement with the EU where regressing or rolling back on climate policies has consequences like this one, and in this particular case, it's about losing the access to the European market."

"So this is unique."

Hernandez Espino said the Single Entry Point had only been used a handful of times in the context of labour rights violations, "no case has ever reached a panel yet," he said describing the next step in the process, but noted this case wasn't about violation of labour rights or access to markets..

"This is the very first complaint on environmental and climate grounds," he added, saying it was going to be "huge" in the EU because there's such significant public scrutiny about "how our policies are in line with our Paris commitments."

The process was lengthy he said, describing how the EU Commission would first assess the case against the text published. If the group's claims are seen as valid, the Commission would begin talks with the New Zealand government, which would have to respond.

"If that doesn't happen, then a independent panel will be set up, and eventually, if the violations persist, then basically the access to the market will be lost."

But he said he just wanted New Zealand to go back to what it promised.

"What we are observing is not in line with our expectations: the regression of the policy, the denying of access to justice in the context of emitters, the lowering of the standards just to attract trade and investment - it is not what we agreed upon."

Hernandez Espino said they were asking two governments to "keep their word: New Zealand to keep its promises it signed, and Europe to enforce what has been signed."

Government response

McClay told RNZ New Zealand took its international obligations seriously and "always meets them."

"We are compliant with the EU free trade agreement."

He said it was "deeply disappointing" to see New Zealand organisations joining with "foreign actors to attack New Zealand."

"This harms our exporters and the jobs they provide."

McClay referenced the complaint made by the Greens to the European Commission "which was rejected."

"We have always been clear that we are committed to meeting our environment and climate obligations. However, it is for the New Zealand Parliament and our government to decide how we do this.

World.title: Fee questions for Fisher Funds KiwiSaver members
World.content:
Audio player for " Why do I pay tax on my KiwiSaver? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/business/1654521%2Ffee-questions-for-fisher-funds-kiwisaver-members

Fisher Funds is in the process of merging its KiwiSaver funds, and says a small number of its investors will end up paying higher fees.

It is transferring members of its Fisher Funds KiwiSaver Scheme into its Fisher Funds KiwiSaver Plan.

It said it wanted to reduce the number of schemes it offered and remove complexity.

A website article about the proposal said: "Your fees will remain the same or lower."

But that is not the case for every member.

Fisher Funds moved Fisher Funds Two members into the equivalent Fisher Funds KiwiSaver Plan in June.

The second transfer is of Fisher Funds KiwiSaver members to the Fisher Funds KiwiSaver Plan.

The FMA has recently approved that transfer and it is expected to be completed by 6 October.

Jody Kaye, chief product and strategy officer, said Fisher Funds Two growth fund fees had increased from 1.06 percent to 1.14 percent in June last year when private equity was added as an asset class, and the fees in the Fisher Funds KiwiSaver Plan were 1.13 percent at the date of the transfer.

The other group that could be paying higher fees than they were in the past is investors in a GlidePath product.

Fisher Funds chief product and strategy officer Jody Kaye. Supplied / Fisher Funds

"For the vast majority of clients, fees will be the same or slightly lower. The only exception is for GlidePath clients, and this is slightly complicated," Kaye said.

"The Fisher Funds KiwiSaver Plan GlidePath feature incorporates more funds, and it offers a more complete solution than was possible with the Fisher Funds KiwiSaver Scheme. As a result of the additional funds, the fees for Fisher Funds KiwiSaver Plan Glide Path for clients under the age of 46 will pay slightly higher fees."

A 30-year-old would see their fee increase from 1.13 percent to 1.21 percent.

Financial Markets Authority executive director of licensing and conduct supervision, Clare Bolingford, said it would consent to such a transfer if it was satisfied that the terms and conditions of the new scheme were no less favourable to members than those of the existing scheme, and that the transfer is otherwise reasonable.

Clare Bolingford. Supplied

"In reaching our decision, we considered a range of factors, including the overall impact on members, the reasons for the transfer, expected benefits and costs, service impacts, fee changes, and any submissions received from affected members.

"Fees are not considered in isolation and are assessed alongside other relevant factors, including investment strategy, asset allocation, and expected member outcomes.

"Members have been provided with detailed information about the transfer, including detailed disclosure of changes to GlidePath settings, asset allocation, and fees."

World.title: Former Speaker and MP for Te Tai Hauāuru Adrian Rurawhe dies
World.content:
Audio player for " Chloe Swarbrick discusses rise in polls " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/politics/1654486%2Fformer-speaker-and-mp-for-te-tai-hauauru-adrian-rurawhe-dies

Chloe Swarbrick discusses rise in polls Morning Report Download MP3 8m

The former speaker and MP for Te Tai Hauāuru Adrian Rurawhe has died.

A statement from his family noted "with deep sadness" he passed after a "recent illness."

"The whanau are slowly coming to terms with such a great loss. Not only to our whanau, but to his church Te Haahi Ratana, his Iwi of Ngāti Apa and Whanganui, and his former colleagues in the House of Representatives where he served as a Member of Parliament from 2014 to January 2026."

Adrian Rurawhe was first elected to Parliament in 2014 as the Labour MP for Te Tai Hauāuru and went on to serve four consecutive terms.

Over the course of his parliamentary career, he held several senior roles including Speaker of the House of Representatives from August 2022 to December 2023.

Audio player for " Family pays tribute to Adrian Paki Rurawhe " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/politics/1654486%2Fformer-speaker-and-mp-for-te-tai-hauauru-adrian-rurawhe-dies

Family pays tribute to Adrian Paki Rurawhe Morning Report Download MP3 6m

Rurawhe announced early this year he would retire from politics on Waitangi Day.

He said he'd spent the summer thinking about whānau and church, and retiring would allow him to be more involved.

Rurawhe was the grandson of two former MPs, Matiu and Iriaka Rātana, and the great-grandson of TW Rātana, the founder of the Rātana church.

Whānau member Piriwiritua Rurawhe told Morning Report Rurawhe had left politics this year to take time for himself.

"We knew he had some ailments but Adrian was a very private man even to his closest, and kept things close to his chest."

Adrian Rurawhe as Speaker of House in 2023. (File photo) Louis Collins

The decision was primarily made to take a break from the public arena and spend time with his whānau, he said.

"There was nothing more important to Adrian than his siblings, nephews and nieces and mokopuna."

Piriwiritua Rurawhe said Rurawhe was a very courteous and very kind man who he said would be remembered both for his kindness and his considered approach to everything he did.

In a statement from Labour, leader Chris Hipkins called Rurawhe "one of the finest people ever to sit in the New Zealand Parliament."

"He carried the mana of his people and of the Speaker's Chair with dignity and respect. He was firm without ever needing to raise his voice, and he was universally respected across every party in the House.

"Members of every party sought his counsel because they knew it would be honest, considered, and given in confidence.

Rurawhe's first day as speaker. (File photo) VNP / Phil Smith

"Aotearoa is poorer for his passing, and Parliament will miss him deeply," Hipkins said.

Green Party co-leader and former colleague Chlöe Swarbrick told Morning Report on Wednesday Rurawhe was a "beautiful, beautiful man" who brought calm to the House of Parliament - a place that wasn't often calm.

Swarbrick said he had a kindness and a "generosity of spirit" - however he was also robust with a "spine of steel" behind the scenes.

"That's a huge loss to our country," she said.

MP Adrian Rurawhe gives his valedictory speech to MPs in Parliament in January 2026. VNP / Phil Smith

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon said Rurawhe was an MP who carried real mana and was respected on all sides of the House.

"As Speaker he was fair and calm, as a Member of Parliament he was steadfast and committed to his people, and as a man he was warm and humble.

"He will be missed and he will be remembered. Rest in Peace."

In Rurawhe's valedictory speech in January this year he said one of his biggest honours was to serve as Speaker - though admitted it was not a position he had ever imagined he would hold.

Rurawhe said he was originally offered the Assistant Speaker role in 2017, but opted for the Junior Whip position instead as he "wasn't too keen".

He then took up the role a few days later after Hipkins, then Leader of the House, rang him to say Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern was asking him to reconsider.

"I'm thinking, pull that Jacinda card eh?"

Three years later, Ardern asked him to be Deputy Speaker, which after admitting his initial disappointment he did not have a ministerial role, was assured there was a pathway to that or to become Speaker.

"I pinch myself almost every day, wonder how this guy from Rātana Pā gets to be the Speaker of this House."

World.title: Will rosier government books catch the eye of global ratings agencies?
World.content:
Audio player for " Jo Moir and Corin Dann discuss pre-election fiscal update " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/business/1654059%2Fwill-rosier-government-books-catch-the-eye-of-global-ratings-agencies

Jo Moir and Corin Dann discuss pre-election fiscal update Morning Report Download MP3 7m

Global credit ratings agencies concerned about the New Zealand economy should find some encouragement in Treasury's opening of the books, according to economists.

However, they say longer-term challenges remain, and it's not likely to be until next year that there is any clarity on whether New Zealand might be subject to a future downgrade.

Treasury is now forecasting a $4 billion surplus for the 2028/29 financial year - significantly higher than the $2.5 billion expected in May, when the books were last opened.

Over the four-year forecast period, $15 billion less would need to be borrowed.

Both Moody's and Fitch Ratings, while retaining their triple-A credit ratings, downgraded their outlook for the New Zealand economy to negative earlier this year.

A major factor in the outlook downgrades appeared to be concern that higher debt-servicing costs would add pressure to New Zealand's fiscal outlook.

A downgrade to a negative outlook can be seen as a warning that, without changes, a full ratings downgrade could be on the cards.

Any future downgrade of New Zealand's credit rating could be damaging, as it may prompt investors to demand higher interest rates on New Zealand bonds.

Infometrics principal economist Brad Olsen. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Infometrics principal economist Brad Olsen said the ratings agencies would be pleased by the stronger return to surplus.

"So, I think the ratings agencies will be encouraged by that earlier return to surplus because part of that is also a stronger actual tax take that we've already seen. That's not just forecast; it has come through."

The need for less borrowing was also seen as a positive.

"And so the fact that the government is able to borrow $4 billion less in the current financial year is a great starting point from a ratings agency point of view, because it says that you're already on that pathway forward. It's not just anticipated in a couple of years' time; it is happening."

Bagrie Economics economist Cameron Bagrie was more circumspect about how markets and ratings agencies would view the government's finances, particularly over the longer term.

"New Zealand's had a track record. They've been pretty good at fiscal consolidation. We've done it numerous times, so they're (rating agencies) believing, I think, more in the track record, the discipline that we saw previously."

Bagrie said New Zealand now faced an ageing population and pressure on healthcare and defence spending, and meeting those challenges would require some significant trade-offs.

Bagrie Economics economist Cameron Bagrie. RNZ / Alexander Robertson

He said that while spending in those areas could increase in coming years to meet those challenges, the rest of the government budget would need to shrink by 2.9 percent of gross domestic product.

"You don't shrink government expenditure by 2.9 percent of GDP without dishing out some cuts to core government services. The issue is: where are those cuts going to be?"

Treasury Secretary Iain Rennie acknowledged the longer-term challenges facing New Zealand when presenting Treasury's forecasts, warning that rising costs from superannuation, debt financing and defence would increasingly consume a larger share of government spending.

Olsen agreed that more attention needed to be paid to the long-term challenges.

"Like I say, my bigger worry is that, sure, the next couple of years look a lot better in terms of the fiscal position. In the long term, though, those superannuation costs, the fact there's a lot of defence investment that still needs to go on, and the value of land transport funding being effectively flat, if not down, into the future - all of that says that we are more capacity-constrained heading forward."

ANZ's economics team said the PREFU was not the snooze-fest they had anticipated, and the more optimistic and updated forecasts have resulted in a meaningful downgrade in New Zealand's borrowing programme.

However, when it comes to the rating agencies, they said we would have to wait until next year to get clarity on whether a downgrade was likely.

World.title: What the government's $4b surplus means for the election
World.content:
Audio player for " Parties under pressure to show how election promises add up " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/politics_election-2026/1654041%2Fwhat-the-government-s-4b-surplus-means-for-the-election

Parties under pressure to show how election promises add up Morning Report Download MP3 3m

Analysis - A rosier than expected opening of the government books would have lifted the Finance Minister's spirits after another bad poll that could see Nicola Willis not even return to Parliament.

The list MP and deputy leader of the National Party will be spending the next five weeks screaming from the rafters about the work she has done to increase the forecast surplus and hold the line in such economically fragile times.

The party's whole mantra is that it's better at the economy than the alternative government and Tuesday's pre-election fiscal update (Prefu) gave it some hard evidence to use in that fight.

The surplus, which is forecast to land a year earlier than expected, will likely reach $4 billion - up from the $2.5b laid out in May's Budget.

That's thanks to the economy picking up enough to have businesses invest and grow more - and "higher and more persistent inflation" - ultimately gifting Treasury's accounts more tax revenue than expected.

Audio player for " Nicola Willis discusses Pre-election Economic and Fiscal Update " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/politics_election-2026/1654041%2Fwhat-the-government-s-4b-surplus-means-for-the-election

Nicola Willis discusses Pre-election Economic and Fiscal Update Morning Report Download MP3 6m

The irony being the surplus looks better because working Kiwis are paying more tax to grow the pie.

The improved forecasts meant the government intended to borrow $15b less over the next four years.

But while Willis was positively beaming as she entered Treasury to deliver the news on Tuesday, it also followed fast with a warning.

This was not the time to spend up big or "give a green light to open the cheque book" with an election on the horizon.

Being fiscally responsible and careful with every dollar of taxpayers' money is the reputation Willis has been trying to build for herself her entire time in office.

It's led to tiny operating allowances, some sizeable cuts that have brought with them a lot of protest and at times hurt, and an insistence from Willis that it was all for the greater good.

That promise of future greatness is what Willis will be hoping people read Tuesday's Prefu as delivering.

With both National and Labour wallowing on 28 percentage points in Monday night's 1News Verian poll it suggests voters might be looking elsewhere for hope and optimism.

The cost of living crisis rolls on with fuel prices back up at almost the same dizzying heights they were at the peak of the Middle East crisis and no end in sight.

Even Treasury Secretary Iain Rennie used a large chunk of his address at Prefu to warn the continued unknown factors in the conflict and global volatility made medium- to long-term forecasts very difficult to gauge.

Treasury Secretary Iain Rennie. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

In one respect Willis put the cost of living ahead of all else when she waved goodbye to reaching surplus a year earlier - next year - to prioritise a continued freeze on the fuel excise tax in January.

Labour has gone further, promising to freeze it for the next three years, but having not released their fiscal plan yet it's unclear what that might cost and how taxpayers could end up footing the bill on it down the track.

National and Labour are expected to deliver fiscal plans that align with Prefu and run the risk of being subjected to a narrative of "fiscal holes" if there's even a hint the numbers don't add up.

Some of the minor parties have spent election after election getting away with making grand promises with half-baked costings - the logic being it's National and Labour that lead the negotiations and it's on those parties to ultimately make the maths add up.

But that model may be coming to an end with the 1News-Verian poll giving ACT and New Zealand First 20 percentage points to National's 28.

There's so little in it, it's hard to know who would be leading what in any post-election chats.

The Green Party is already eyeing up the baubles of office with co-leader Chloe Swarbrick suggesting in any negotiations with Labour it would need to take seriously the idea of giving portfolios like finance, climate change, and energy to the lefter-leaning party.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins rubbished the idea saying Barbara Edmonds would be finance minister in any government he led, and slapped Swarbrick down for getting ahead of herself when the campaign has only just started and voting hasn't even opened.

Opportunity on Tuesday was busy laying out bottom lines for any talks - this from a party that hasn't even made it into Parliament at this point.

World.title: Crossland to miss NRL grand final with four-game ban for Cleary tackle
World.content:
Newcastle Knights hooker Phoenix Crossland has been suspended for four games by the NRL judiciary for the tackle that left Penrith's Nathan Cleary with a broken leg.

Crossland pleaded guilty to the dangerous contact charge on Tuesday before fronting the judiciary to learn his fate.

He will now miss this Sunday's NRL grand final.

The ban would also rule him out of New Zealand's three World Cup pool games.

Crossland was sent off for a hip drop tackle on Cleary in the 36th minute of Newcastle's preliminary final win over the Panthers.

Cleary suffered a compound fracture and a dislocated ankle.

Crossland was represented by barrister James McLeod, who made the case for his client to receive a two or three-week ban.

Crossland cited his career record, telling the judiciary he had never before been sent off. He admitted he got the execution of the tackle wrong but insisted "wasn't trying to hurt anyone".

Phoenix Crossland said he made a remorseful call to Nathan Cleary after the incident. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

Arguing for a four-game suspension, the NRL said Crossland's tackle failed to exercise a proper duty of care and, while accidental, did not show enough caution towards Cleary.

Crossland told the judiciary was deeply remorseful for Cleary's injury and had reached out to the Panthers star.

"I called him yesterday. It was obviously a tough phone call," Crossland said.

"I reached out to his dad [Panthers coach Ivan Cleary] as well.

"Nathan was great, he said not to worry about and he understood it was an accident.

"He was such a gentlemen, he told me to stop saying sorry.

"He's my favourite player in the game by a mile. He's the best player in the game and I look up to him."

Phoenix Crossland was sent off in the 36th minute of the preliminary final for the tackle. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Crossland described the incident and fallout as a low point in his life. In his submissions, McLeod produced abusive Instagram messages that had been directed towards Crossland in the past 48 hours.

"It's killing me, it's been the worst couple of days of my life," Crossland said.

"It's meant to be the best week of my life and it's been far from it."

The verdict sets up a scenario where 19-year-old Knight Diesel Hagan could make his NRL debut in a grand final.

It would be the first time such a debut has taken place in 90 years. Eddie Lockhart was the last to do it in 1936, for Balmain.

Harrison Graham will almost certainly shift to a starting role for Newcastle in the grand final, while other options for the Knights include Thomas Cant and Jermaine McEwen.

World.title: Brazil beat Socceroos in fractious, entertaining clash
World.content:
The Socceroos have fallen to a 4-2 defeat against Brazil in front of 52,423 fans at Lang Park in Brisbane.

Fresh from a superb performance in Townsville on Friday night, the Socceroos will once again take plenty from a contest that ebbed and flowed throughout 90 thoroughly engaging minutes.

With Tony Popovic naming an unchanged team for just the second time in his tenure, it seems likely that this XI is the one that will start the Asian Cup in January.

On the basis of what they showed against the number five team in the world, they should serve Australia very well indeed.

Australia fell behind early to a Brazil team that came out the blocks firing, scoring through a superb Vanderson strike in the opening three minutes.

They could have fallen even further behind when Pat Beach pulled off two sensational saves to twice deny Raphinha just a couple of minutes later.

The Socceroos had barely had control of the ball at that stage, the promised response from a badly burned Brazil team in full evidence.

However, the hosts showed superb composure and self-confidence to hit back, gradually regaining control in the midfield and scoring two goals in the space of four minutes to take the lead mid way through the first half.

Alessandro Circati turned home a corner at the back post, a goal initially ruled out for offside before VAR intervened.

Connor Metcalfe's stunner gave the Socceroos the lead. (Getty Images: Albert Perez)

Then, Connor Metcalf prompted an explosion of joy from the home fans in the stands by drilling home a magnificent strike just minutes later, taking a touch and hammering a left-footed shot into the top corner from the edge of the area.

The pressure was clearly getting to Brazil, with the normally Imperturbable Carlo Ancelotti screaming into the face of the assistant referee after Tete Yengi was fouled.

The visitors drew level on the stroke of half time, first of two penalties awarded to the visitors converted by skipper Raphinha after another lengthy VAR review when the referee inexplicably failed to give a penalty after Harry Souttar made a rough challenge.

Tempers threatened to boil over in the second half when Endrick and Souttar clashed, Aziz Behich coming in a sparking a small melee in front of the Socceroos bench.

That finally sparked Brazil, who turned the style back on as Bruno Guimarães finished a sumptuous move from the left to give the visitors the lead.

Vinícius Júnior was then fouled in the penalty area and converted to seal the victory in front of the biggest football crowd ever at Lang Park.

"Honestly, they [the Socceroos] press really well," Ancelotti said.

"They are really well organised, they surprised us in this sense.

"They put much more pressure in the front and we had difficulty to build from the back.

"They are a very good team, in my opinion."

Follow all the action from Lang Park in our live blog.

World.title: Silver lining for Freo captain after grand final injury nightmare
World.content:
Fremantle have had some badly needed good news in the wake of its AFL grand final disaster, confirming captain Alex Pearce will not need surgery.

The Dockers are confident the key defender will return to training in the pre-season.

As the post-mortem continues following Saturday's devastating loss to Brisbane, Fremantle said Pearce suffered a partially ruptured Achilles tendon, as well as a calf strain.

Pearce was giving chase early in the third quarter of the grand final when he suddenly fell to the ground.

Two trainers helped him from the field, with one of the most shattering images of the loss being Pearce hobbling past the premiership cup on crutches at the post-game presentations.

Brisbane coach Chris Fagan and several of his players offered their best wishes to Pearce soon after the final siren.

Alex Pearce went down with his injury during the third quarter of the grand final. (ABC News: Lucy Murray)

Coach Justin Longmuir said losing the Dockers' defensive general cost them, especially during Brisbane's last-gasp comeback.

"Thankfully Alex has not had a complete rupture of his Achilles tendon and he will not require surgery," Fremantle football boss Joe Brierty said on Tuesday in a club statement.

"Scans have revealed a partial tear of his Achilles tendon and also a significant calf strain.

"As it stands, we expect Alex to return to training in pre-season."

Also on Tuesday, chief executive Simon Garlick was the latest key Docker to defend Wharfie Time and dismiss its activation as a factor in their heartbreaking loss.

Lions coach Chris Fagan and several of his players have said since that they had a plan if Wharfie Time was sounded, vowing they would try to use it to their own advantage.

But Garlick followed Longmuir and Brierty in denying Wharfie Time had torpedoed the Dockers.

"We know teams, including ours, have scenario plans for being a few goals down or up with a few minutes to go," Garlick told SEN.

"Brisbane executed that plan exceptionally well on Saturday, clearly. It's clearly a plan they would've had regardless of Wharfie Time."

It remains unclear whether Wharfie Time is now sunk.

"Our fans love Wharfie Time. We've just lost a grand final in the most heartbreaking way," Garlick said.

"We're not about to throw out things that make us who we are.

"We'll work through that."

World.title: Dockers captain to avoid surgery after grand final injury
World.content:
Fremantle Dockers captain Alex Pearce will avoid surgery and is expected to return to training in the pre-season, after scans confirmed he suffered only a partial tear of his Achilles tendon in Saturday's dramatic AFL grand final loss to Brisbane.

Pearce was forced off in the third-quarter after going down while chasing the ball in the Dockers' seven-point defeat.

Fremantle football manager Joe Brierty said Pearce's prognosis was promising.

"Thankfully Alex has not had a complete rupture of his Achilles tendon and he will not require surgery," Brierty said.

Scans confirmed Pearce suffered a partial tear of his Achilles tendon. (ABC News: Lucy Murray)

"Scans have revealed a partial tear of his Achilles tendon and also a significant calf strain."

He said Pearce was expected to return to pre-season training.

Injury prompted career concerns

There had been fears for Pearce's future had scans shown the worst, with a complete tear and an extended time on the sidelines likely raising questions about the 31-year-old's career.

Freo faithful left to wait for slice of history The Fremantle Dockers return to Western Australia to cheers and love from a small group of fans, as supporters ponder the grand final loss.

The positive news for Fremantle comes after a heartbreaking week, in which the club fell devastatingly short of its first premiership, giving up a 17-point lead in the final four minutes as the Lions claimed three straight flags for the second time in club history.

It also comes as the Dockers confirmed they would not be holding any public events to thank the fans for their support, with Brierty defending the decision on 102.5 ABC Perth.

"From our perspective we'll still celebrate the year and I'm sure all our members and fans will," Brierty said.

"But right here and now our focus is on making sure that we exit the right way and prepare ourselves to have a really strong pre-season, and that starts with making sure we've set the players up for the off-season."

'Wonderful season'

Fans took to 102.5 ABC Perth to voice their disappointment about the loss, while also praising the team for its stellar season.

"We've got to thank them for the wonderful season they've had," one supporter said.

Another supporter fondly recalled greeting the players in 2013 at the Subiaco Oval after their grand final loss that season, saying "it was really joyous."

Four-time grand finalist and ABC football expert Sharrod Wellingham said greeting the fans after Saturday's loss would have been a nice gesture.

"It's a little thing, but it would've meant a lot to so many, don't you think?" Wellingham said.

World.title: Cat at centre of concussion waiver saga forced into medical retirement
World.content:
Geelong premiership defender Jake Kolodjashnij has been medically retired due to concussion.

Kolodjashnij was the player who signed a secret waiver in his Geelong contract in 2024, requiring him to take all legal responsibility for future brain trauma so he could keep playing at the club.

The Cats were fined $140,000 last month for failing to officially notify the AFL about the concussion waiver in Kolodjashnij's contract.

The fine comprised $100,000, plus a suspended sanction of $40,000 from last October, stemming from a league investigation into the club's third-party agreements.

After news broke in early August that the Cats had struck a secret deal with a player with a history of concussion, Kolodjashnij identified himself as the player involved.

AFL in bind over concussion insurance The Geelong concussion waiver raises serious concerns about how the AFL will insure players who suffer traumatic brain injuries.

Kolodjashnij, 31, played AFL and VFL for the Cats earlier in the year but did not feature at any level after the concussion scandal emerged.

The versatile defender played 11 AFL games this season, taking his career tally to 209, including the 2022 premiership.

"I am so grateful for the many fond relationships and memories the Geelong Football Club has provided me," Kolodjashnij said in a statement.

"Football has been such a significant part of my life.

"I feel lucky to have shared it with some of my closest friends, and to have had the on-field success that we had during my time at the club."

Kolodjashnij's twin brother Kade, who played for Gold Coast and Melbourne, also retired due to concussion.

Geelong football boss Andrew Mackie paid tribute to the popular defender, who was a mainstay in the Cats' backline between 2015 and 2024.

"Jake's contribution to our football club extends far beyond his impact on the field," Mackie said in a statement.

"He earned enormous respect through the way he approached his football, the care he showed for his teammates and his unwavering team-first attitude.

"Jake built a reputation as one of the competition's most reliable defenders. His coaches and teammates had complete confidence he would take on whatever role was required and get the job done.

"His career has been defined by consistency, resilience and selflessness. The determination and professionalism he displayed throughout his journey are qualities that made him such a valued teammate and person within our football club."

World.title: One last 'last' for Broncos legend Ali Brigginshaw in NRLW grand final
World.content:
Retiring Brisbane legend Ali Brigginshaw has one more NRLW match to play, but her competitive drive is just as strong as the day she took up playing rugby league at the age of 10.

The 38-year-old five-eighth will play against old foes the Sydney Roosters in the grand final with a team-first mentality, but also with the determination to get one over opposite number Jocelyn Kelleher the same way she did in the 20-8 preliminary final victory against Gold Coast.

Rugby sevens superstar Teagan Levi was wearing the number six and Brigginshaw had her measure.

"All the talk has been about her and I took it really personal[ly," she said.

"I said to the girls, 'I will do whatever I can to make sure I can shut her down.'

"I am just really proud. We trained extremely hard to get to this moment, but I am also proud of myself … 38 years old and I put myself in this position to be the best teammate and work my bum off whenever I play."

Teagan Levi and the Titans threatened the Broncos' premiership defence. (Getty Images: Mackenzie Sweetnam)

When Brigginshaw won her fourth NRLW title last year, there were a couple of conversations about retiring with a premiership.

"People were saying it was a good ending, but I had all the belief in this team that we were going to get [to another grand final]," she said

"The hardest thing is getting there. You get there and you put yourself in the best position to compete and win it.

"It is a huge week and I am just excited to do it again because you never know when it is going to be your last … and this will be my last."

Brigginshaw calls herself, winger Julia Robinson and prop Chelsea Lenarduzzi "the OGs", being the three original Broncos from 2018 who are aiming for a fifth premiership with the club, while fullback Tamika Upton hopes to add a third Broncos crown to two won with Newcastle in 2022 and 2023.

Broncos into fifth NRLW grand final Brisbane will get the chance to send retiring club legend Ali Brigginshaw out a winner in the grand final after it overpowered Gold Coast 20-8 at Robina.

Only Michael Hancock and Kevin Walters have achieved the feat in Broncos history.

"We are the OGs. We are also good mates and they are part of the reason I love the Broncos," Brigginshaw said.

"Duzzi is passionate about everything she does and Robbo is the heart. The love they both have for the team and the jersey is what I love.

"We all just bleed for this jersey, and the best thing is that I see other people who want to do it and love the place as much as I do."

The Broncos lost eight players from last year's grand final side, but the new-look outfit, featuring superstar halfback Jesse Southwell, has bought in to the club's systems and culture.

"It is kind of frustrating how people forget how many we lost," Brigginshaw said.

"To win a premiership with them, then rebuild and get back here again … proves we have the right people here to give ourselves the best opportunity."

As a result of Brigginshaw's impending departure, everything at Red Hill has a "last" associated with it this year, whether it be her last game at home in a club match or her last preliminary final.

"It is just a bit of a joke around 'the last last'," she said.

"I have got there now, so let's have a crack."
